# Skyhook and Aster: A Learning Guide

This guide teaches the science, mathematics and engineering behind two codebases. **Skyhook** is a design study for a spinning tether in orbit. **Aster** is an asteroid mission planner. It has 25 chapters in three parts: **Part A** (A1 to A12) on Skyhook, **Part B** (B1 to B12) on Aster, and **Part C** (C1) on how the two fit together.

## Who this is for and what it assumes

The guide is written for the owner who directs both projects. Aster names Hudson as its final authority (aster: AGENTS.md §7), and Skyhook's register of known deviations leaves each open decision to him (skyhook: docs/DEVIATIONS.md). The guide fills in the technical depth beneath his decisions.

It assumes what a first-year engineering student brings:

- high-school physics and chemistry;
- basic calculus (what a derivative and an integral mean);
- the ability to read a short piece of simple code.

Everything else is built from the ground up: units and scientific notation (A1), vectors (A2, B2), exponentials and logarithms (A4), probability (A8), JSON (A11), hashes and git (A12, B12), and how computers store numbers (A12, B8). If a section feels too basic, skim it; project material follows.

## The two projects and how they relate

**Skyhook (Part A).** Skyhook is a rotating momentum-exchange tether, or "rotovator", planned for a 610 km orbit. It would catch payloads from suborbital trajectories at the bottom of its swing and throw them from the top. The Rev A reference design throws to GTO and high-elliptical orbits at a 2.5 km/s tip speed. Cislunar throws at 2.8 km/s are a revenue-gated option, and Mars-class escape at 3.5 km/s is a Phase 3 growth option. Each throw takes momentum from the tether and lowers its orbit. The main plan to put it back is electrodynamic reboost: thrust without propellant, from solar-powered electric current (Chapter A5). The investment thesis is "high-energy delta-v substitution", not cheaper trips to low orbit (skyhook: README.md).

The project is in Phase 0. The README says everything before the Phase 1 demonstrator "is paper study and materials qualification" (skyhook: README.md, "Heritage") [Certain that the README says so]. The code is Python physics and finance models, Excel workbooks, a pytest suite, browser simulators and a digital twin. All of it is meant to take its numbers from one canonical file, `params/rev_a.json` (skyhook: README.md, Rule 1). Chapter A11 shows where tools still drift from it.

**Aster (Part B).** In its own words, Aster "plans asteroid missions in the browser and answers mission-analysis questions over MCP — and every number it produces carries its source, its confidence class, and the commit it was computed from" (aster: README.md). The website shows a catalog of 41,906 near-Earth objects: 41,698 asteroids and 208 comets (Section B1.3). It also has a porkchop planner for launch energy (C3), Δv, departure declination (DLA) and delivered mass. The MCP server, published on npm as aster-mission-mcp@0.1.0, gives AI agents seven tools.

Both front ends are built from the same TypeScript core, `src/v2` (aster: README.md, "One core, two interfaces"). The published package and the live site were built at different commits, though (Section B1.2). Each MCP answer comes in an evidence envelope that carries provenance and a confidence class. When a tool cannot answer, it returns a structured refusal instead.

The repository also holds a pre-registered study of whether AI agents pass that evidence on faithfully (Slice 16, Chapter B11). Its main contrast analysis has not been computed yet; the README schedules it for Slice 21 (aster: README.md). Aster plans only the outbound leg (aster: src/v2/SLICE_20_FOUNDING.md §1, a draft).

**How they connect (Part C).** The two projects meet at one number, **C3**, the departure energy per kilogram. Aster works out where a probe must go, when, with how much C3 and in which direction. Skyhook offers that energy as a tether throw instead of a rocket burn. The handoff works only if the departure direction, the arrival burn and the evidence behind each number travel with C3 (Chapter C1, "Main idea").

The one joint study is PM-001, on an unmerged Skyhook branch. It pulled real Aster porkchop cells through the MCP tools and ran them through Skyhook physics. Its screening result is that one 2.8 km/s catch delivers more probe mass than a whole Falcon 9 launch on all 11 targets that had usable cells [Likely; a screening result]. Its demand result is that historical probe mass, about 0.2 t/yr, is far below Skyhook's 152 to 242 t/yr minimum viable market. So probes are a niche, not the volume business (skyhook, unmerged: docs/research/pm001_probe_missions.md §4 and "Bottom line" item 5; Section C1.7).

The two keep their numbers honest in different ways: Skyhook with a canon file, confidence labels and test gates; Aster with envelopes, invariants and oracles (Section C1.8).

## How to use this guide

Each part climbs from basics to the hardest project material, so read in order if you can. Part B does not need Part A. It rebuilds what it uses, such as gravity (Section B3.2) and orbital energy (Section B6.1).

| Goal | Read | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| Fast overview | A1, B1, C1, then each other chapter's "Main idea", "Limits and known problems" and "Key takeaways" | Each chapter's verdict |
| Skyhook physics first | A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, A7 | Motion, orbits, rockets, the throw, tether mass, simulation |
| Business first | A1, A4, A9, A10, then Section C1.10 | What a throw replaces, the business case, markets, risk, law (A9 uses results from A6 and A8) |
| Uncertainty and statistics | A8, B11 | Monte Carlo for Skyhook; confidence intervals for the agent study |
| Software first | A11, A12, B8, B9, B10, B12 | Data, tests, numerics, the web app, the MCP server, process |
| Evidence and honesty | A1, A11, B1, B10, B11, then Section C1.8 | How each project labels, checks and refuses |
| Mission design | A3, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7 | Orbits, frames, Lambert's problem, porkchops, launch |
| Aster only | B1 to B12 in order | Self-contained |
| Integration | A3, A4, B6, B7, then C1 | Section C1.2 maps each mission question to its chapter |

## Conventions

**Confidence labels.** Important claims carry one of three labels:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| [Certain] | A textbook fact, or a fact checked in the repository for this guide |
| [Likely] | Supported by evidence, but not proven |
| [Speculative] | An informed guess |

Skyhook's own files use the same three words (skyhook: CLAUDE.md, "Confidence labels"). A label quoted from a file is that file's, not the guide's. Some labels are qualified. "[Certain as arithmetic]" means the calculation is right, even if its inputs are less sure. "[Certain that STATUS says so]" means the document says it, not that it is true.

Aster has a separate system. Its confidence classes `measured`, `derived` and `assumed` say how Aster obtained a number (Section B1.1). Do not mix the two systems.

**"(from memory, verify)"** marks a fact the writer recalled rather than read in a repository file. Treat it as something to check, not as evidence.

**"Recomputed for this guide"**, "re-run for this guide" and "(guide-computed)" mean the writers worked the number out again while writing, from repository inputs, the repositories' own code run read-only, or live calls to the published Aster tools. A "fact-check" is a second, independent pass that did the same. The check scripts and saved tool replies were working files. They are not in either repository, so the guide does not cite them by name.

**File paths.**

- Part A paths are relative to the Skyhook repository root, for example `params/rev_a.json`. Once a chapter has given the full path, it may shorten it to the file name (`rev_a.json`).
- Part B paths are relative to the Aster repository root, for example `src/v2/porkchop/delta-v.ts`. `README.md:3-5` means lines 3 to 5 of that file.
- Part C, this front matter and the back matter prefix each path with its repository: `skyhook: physics/skyhook_physics.py`, `aster: mcp/README.md`. "skyhook (unmerged):" marks a file that exists only on an unmerged branch.

Paths are relative to a repository root, never to the folder this file sits in.

**Chapter and section labels.** Chapters are A1 to A12, B1 to B12 and C1. Section A5.6 means section 6 of Chapter A5. Every guide section reference carries its part letter. Worked examples keep their chapter's own numbering, without a letter: Worked Example 5.3 is the third example in the fifth chapter of the part you are reading. A reference to a worked example in another chapter names that chapter, as in "Chapter A1 (Worked Example 1.10)".

**The § sign.** In running text, a bare § number usually points to a section of a repository document, not of this guide. "AGENTS.md §9" is section 9 of Aster's AGENTS.md, and "PM-001 §4" is section 4 of that study. A § followed by a part letter, as in §C1.9, is a section of this guide.

## Where this file lives

The same file sits in both repositories:

- **Skyhook:** `docs/LEARNING_GUIDE.md`, beside the glossary and the verification memo.
- **Aster:** `LEARNING_GUIDE.md` at the repository root.

Aster's copy sits at the root because Aster's `docs/` is not a documents folder. It is the Vite build output that GitHub Pages serves. The build settings say `outDir: 'docs'` and `emptyOutDir: true`, so every build wipes and regenerates that folder (aster: vite.config.ts; aster: AGENTS.md §9). A guide stored there would be deleted by the next build. The root already holds Aster's other top-level documents, such as README.md and STATUS.md.

## How each chapter is built

Every chapter follows the same pattern:

1. It opens with a bold **Main idea**: the whole chapter in one or two sentences.
2. It builds from first principles. Each term is defined when it first appears and then applied to the project's real numbers.
3. Its **worked examples** show every step, with numbers read from the repositories or re-run from them.
4. It ends with **"Limits and known problems"**, **"Key takeaways"** and **"Where this lives in the repo"**. The first covers what the models leave out, what is unverified and where code and documents disagree; those notes often mark a decision the project still has to make. The last is a table mapping each concept to its files and functions.

Formulas appear in fenced code blocks in plain-text notation, with their units. After Part C, back matter collects project status items, review questions and a glossary.

# Part A: Skyhook

## Chapter A1: Orientation: what Skyhook is and how to read its numbers

**Main idea:** Skyhook is a plan for a very long spinning cable in orbit that catches slow payloads at the bottom of its swing and throws them fast at the top, and the project states its claims as numbers that should each carry a unit, a source and a confidence label, so reading those numbers well (and noticing when one is missing) is the first skill you need.

This chapter does two jobs.

The first half (sections A1.1 to A1.6) tells the story. It covers what the machine is, why anyone would pay for it, the three design options, the phased plan, the folders in the repository and the rules the project works by.

The second half (sections A1.7 to A1.15) is a toolkit. It covers units, prefixes, scientific notation, rounding, unit conversion, ratios, the "g" unit and how to read the canonical JSON file. Every later chapter uses these tools. Each tool is taught on real Skyhook numbers.

Two conventions run through the whole guide:

- **Confidence labels.** **[Certain]** means a textbook fact, or something re-checked in this repository. **[Likely]** means supported but not proven. **[Speculative]** means an informed guess.
- **Sources.** Every project-specific number names the file it came from. Facts recalled from memory rather than read in the repo are marked "(from memory, verify)".

The repository read for this chapter is the `main` branch at commit 34935cb. (A **commit** is one saved snapshot in the project's history; section A1.5 explains.)

---

### A1.1 What a skyhook is

#### Starting from nothing

Begin with four plain ideas.

An **orbit** is the path of an object that is falling freely around Earth. It moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing the ground as it falls. Chapter A3 explains why.

The **centre of mass (CoM)** is the balance point of an object. If you could put a finger under it, the object would balance there.

A **tether** is a cable that carries load only in **tension** (pulling). It cannot carry **compression** (pushing). A rope can pull a cart. It cannot push one.

**Rotation** means spinning about a point. Here the point is the CoM.

#### The definition the project uses

The founding document defines a skyhook as a **rotating momentum-exchange tether**: "a very long, very strong cable in orbit around Earth, spinning end-over-end around its own center of mass while that center of mass orbits the planet" (`docs/project_instructions.md`, Part I). [Certain that this is the project's definition.]

The **payload** is the thing being delivered, for example a satellite. The **tip** is each end of the cable.

**Momentum** is mass times velocity; Chapter A2 builds it up. **Momentum exchange** means the tether hands some of its own momentum to the payload. The tether slows down a little and the payload speeds up (Chapter A5).

The program uses three names for the same machine: **rotovator**, **skyhook** and rotating momentum-exchange tether. The glossary says "skyhook" is preferred in external communications (`docs/glossary.md`, entry "Rotovator").

#### The picture: a wheel that does not quite touch the road

Think of a bicycle wheel rolling along a road.

- The hub moves forward at the bike's speed.
- The top of the wheel moves forward at twice the bike's speed.
- The bottom of the wheel, where it touches the road, is momentarily at rest.

Now imagine the wheel lifted just off the road, still carried forward at the bike's speed, but spinning a little too slowly to roll. Its rim now moves more slowly around the hub than the hub moves forward. Its bottom point is not at rest, but it is slower than the hub. Its top point is faster than the hub.

A skyhook is that slow-spinning, lifted wheel. The hub is the CoM, moving at orbital speed. The spokes are the two tether arms. The bottom tip is slow. The top tip is fast.

A vehicle launched from Earth only has to reach the slow bottom tip. The tip grabs it, carries it half a turn and lets go at the top, where it is moving fastest.

#### Three kinds of speed

Speeds only mean something relative to something else. Three reference points appear in the repo.

| Term | Measured relative to | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Tip speed** (`v_tip`) | the tether's own CoM | 2.5 km/s |
| **Inertial speed** | a frame centred on Earth's centre that does not rotate (it stays fixed against the distant stars) | lower tip ≈ 5.06 km/s |
| **Ground-relative speed** | Earth's spinning surface | lower tip ≈ 4.59 km/s |

The ground-relative speed is lower than the inertial speed because Earth's surface is itself moving east. A vehicle launched eastward from the equator gets that speed for free.

#### The overview formulas

These are stated here and derived later (Chapters A2 and A3).

```
v_tip            = ω × L                   (tip speed relative to the CoM)
v_lower_inertial = v_orb − v_tip
v_lower_ground   = v_orb − v_tip − v_earth  (EQ-3, prograde equatorial orbit)
v_upper_release  = v_orb + v_tip            (EQ-3)
boost per pass   = v_upper − v_lower = 2 × v_tip
```

- **ω** (the Greek letter omega) is the spin rate, in radians per second. A **radian** is the angle at which the arc length equals the radius. A full circle is 2π radians, about 6.283.
- **L** is the half-length, from the CoM to one tip.
- **v_orb** is the orbital speed of the CoM.
- **v_earth** is the speed of Earth's surface at the equator.
- **Prograde** means orbiting in the same direction Earth spins.

`CLAUDE.md` lists the ground-relative and release lines as EQ-3. The first line (v_tip = ω × L) is from `docs/project_instructions.md` §2.2, and the last line is simple subtraction. `physics/skyhook_physics.py` implements EQ-3 in `v_lower_tip_groundrel_kms()` and `v_upper_release_kms()`. [Certain as first-order kinematics. The code itself labels the ground-relative version [Likely], because it "ignores atmospheric effects and tip oscillation", and labels the release version [Certain] but "first-order".]

#### The Rev A numbers

**Rev A** is the name of the project's current frozen design (section A1.3). All values below are read from `params/rev_a.json`.

| Quantity | JSON key | Value |
|---|---|---|
| CoM altitude | `orbital.com_altitude_km` | 610 km |
| Half-length L | `geometry.tether_half_length_km` | 320 km (so 640 km tip to tip) |
| Tip speed | `kinematics.v_tip_kms` | 2.5 km/s |
| CoM orbital speed | `orbital.v_orb_kms` | 7.55 km/s |
| Lower-tip altitude | `geometry.tip_altitude_lower_km` | 290 km |
| Lower tip, ground-relative | `kinematics.v_lower_tip_groundrel_kms` | 4.59 km/s |
| Upper-tip release speed | `kinematics.v_upper_release_kms` | 10.06 km/s |
| Rotation period | `geometry.rotation_period_min` | 13.4 min |
| Tip acceleration | `kinematics.tip_acceleration_g` | 1.99 g |

#### Worked Example 1.1: the speeds at the two tips

Inputs:

- v_orb = 7.5563 km/s, computed by `v_orbital_kms(610)` in `physics/skyhook_physics.py`. (The JSON stores 7.55; section A1.11 explains the gap.)
- v_tip = 2.5 km/s (`params/rev_a.json`, `kinematics.v_tip_kms`).
- v_earth = 0.465 km/s, written directly inside `v_lower_tip_groundrel_kms()` in `physics/skyhook_physics.py`.

Steps:

```
1. Lower tip, inertial:   7.5563 − 2.5           = 5.0563 km/s  → "~5.06" (materials/core.md)
2. Lower tip, ground:     5.0563 − 0.465         = 4.5913 km/s  → 4.59   (rev_a.json)
3. Upper tip, release:    7.5563 + 2.5           = 10.0563 km/s → 10.06  (rev_a.json)
4. Boost per pass:        10.0563 − 5.0563       = 5.0000 km/s  = 2 × 2.5
```

Where does 0.465 km/s come from? Earth's equator goes once around per sidereal day (one turn relative to the stars). Using an equatorial radius of 6,378.137 km and a sidereal day of 86,164 s (both from memory, verify):

```
circumference = 2 × π × 6,378.137 km = 40,075 km
speed         = 40,075 km ÷ 86,164 s  = 0.4651 km/s
```

This uses Earth's **equatorial radius**, the distance from Earth's centre to the equator. Earth is slightly flattened, so this is a little larger than its **mean radius** (average radius, 6,371 km in the code). Using the equatorial radius is right for the speed of the equator. Worked Example 1.10 (section A1.11) shows that the canonical file mixes these two radii elsewhere.

Result: the payload enters at about 5.06 km/s inertial and leaves at about 10.06 km/s. The tether has added 5.0 km/s. [Certain, as arithmetic on the repo's inputs.]

#### Worked Example 1.2: how long one swing takes

Inputs: v_tip = 2.5 km/s and L = 320 km (`params/rev_a.json`). μ = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² (`orbital.mu_earth_m3s2`). Mean Earth radius 6,371 km (`R_EARTH_KM` in `physics/skyhook_physics.py`).

Spin period:

```
ω = v_tip ÷ L = 2.5 km/s ÷ 320 km       = 0.0078125 rad/s
T = 2π ÷ ω   = 6.28319 ÷ 0.0078125       = 804.25 s
804.25 s ÷ 60 s/min                       = 13.40 min   (rev_a.json: 13.4)
```

Orbit period, for contrast. The repo does not store this, so it is computed here with T = 2π√(r³/μ) from Chapter A3:

```
r        = 6,371 + 610 = 6,981 km = 6.981 × 10⁶ m
r³       = (6.981 × 10⁶)³              = 3.4021 × 10²⁰ m³
r³ ÷ μ   = 3.4021 × 10²⁰ ÷ (3.986 × 10¹⁴) = 8.5352 × 10⁵ s²
√(r³ ÷ μ) = 923.86 s
T_orbit  = 2π × 923.86 s               = 5,804.8 s = 96.75 min
spins per orbit = 96.75 ÷ 13.40        = 7.2
```

Result: the tether turns about seven times per orbit. A payload rides half a turn, 13.40 ÷ 2 = 6.70 minutes, from catch to release.

This exposes a slip in the founding document. Part I says "Half an orbit and half a rotation later, the payload is released". Half an orbit is 96.75 ÷ 2 = 48.4 minutes, which is 48.4 ÷ 13.40 = 3.61 rotations. After 3.61 rotations the payload would not be at the top of the swing. So the sentence cannot be right as written for Rev A. The release comes half a rotation after the catch. `materials/core.md` gets it right: "released half a turn later". [Certain]

#### What a skyhook is not

**It is not a space elevator.** A space elevator is a static cable anchored at the equator and reaching past geostationary altitude (35,786 km). It needs materials that do not exist at scale. A skyhook flies freely, is "hundreds to a few thousand kilometers long", and uses fibres that can be bought today (`docs/project_instructions.md`, Part I; `docs/objections_faq.md`, Q1). [Certain that these are the repo's claims; the distinction itself is standard.]

**It is not free energy.** Every throw takes momentum out of the tether, so its orbit sinks a little. The project plans to pay it back with **electrodynamic (ED) reboost**: pushing a current through the tether against Earth's magnetic field, powered by sunlight. Catching payloads that are coming down also refills it. The glossary calls this accounting the **momentum bank**, also called the **momentum ledger** (`docs/glossary.md`, entry "Momentum bank / Momentum ledger"). Chapter A5 covers it. [Certain that momentum must be repaid; the method is Chapter A5's subject.]

**It does not, the README says, need new physics.** The README calls the program "a scaling and operations challenge, not a new-physics challenge". It cites this flight heritage (`README.md`, Heritage table):

| Mission | Year | What the repo says it proved |
|---|---|---|
| SEDS-1/2 | 1993–94 | 20 km tether deployment |
| TSS-1R | 1996 | 19.7 km; >3,500 V and >1 A of ED power |
| YES2 | 2007 | 31.7 km; payload delivery by tether swing |
| TEPCE | 2019 | propellantless electrodynamic thrust |

Read the fine print. **VM-001** is the project's first verification memo (`docs/verification_memo.md`, dated 2026-06-12): a red-team check of key numbers against outside sources. It says TEPCE's "current levels were too low for large maneuvers — it validated the system chain, not high-authority reboost". The README itself says the scaling step, "a *rotating* tether making a *catch*", is still ahead: it is the Phase 1 demonstrator "D2" (section A1.4). The founding document describes D2 as "the first ever orbital momentum-exchange **catch and throw**" (Part VI). None of the four listed missions did that. [Certain that the listed heritage is small-scale and that the repo treats a rotating catch as not yet flown; the claim that scaling needs no new physics is [Likely].]

### A1.2 Delta-v and the investment thesis

#### Delta-v, the currency of spaceflight

**Delta-v** (written **Δv**, "change in velocity") is the total speed change a vehicle must make to get from one path to another. Its unit is km/s.

Δv is the currency of spaceflight. Rockets pay for it with **propellant** (fuel plus the oxidiser it burns with). The cost grows exponentially with the Δv needed. Chapter A4 shows why.

A few destinations appear everywhere in the repo:

- **LEO** (low Earth orbit): orbits a few hundred kilometres up. (Formally LEO reaches up to about 2,000 km; from memory, verify.)
- **GEO** (geostationary orbit): a circular orbit 35,786 km up, where a satellite circles once per day and seems to hang still over one spot.
- **GTO** (geostationary transfer orbit): a long ellipse whose high point reaches up toward GEO altitude.
- **TLI** (trans-lunar injection): the push that sends a payload toward the Moon (`docs/glossary.md`).

**Upmass** means mass lifted to orbit.

#### The thesis in one sentence

The README states the investment thesis: "high-energy delta-v substitution ... not LEO upmass displacement, which is structurally vulnerable to reusable launch cost compression" (`README.md`). `CLAUDE.md` repeats it.

In plain words:

- The program does **not** try to be the cheapest ride to LEO. Reusable rockets keep pushing that price down. A business built on undercutting them could be crushed.
- It sells the **extra** Δv beyond LEO, toward GTO and higher. Customers pay a large premium for that today.

An analogy: do not open a cheaper bus line on a route that a giant is about to make nearly free. Run the steep mountain pass the giant still charges a lot for.

#### Two velocity numbers that must not be confused

`materials/core.md` keeps two numbers apart and calls mixing them "a known diligence trap":

| Number | Value | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Δv the tether **gives** the payload | 5.0 km/s per pass | 2 × v_tip, from catch to release (Worked Example 1.1) |
| Δv the launch vehicle **saves** on ascent | about 2.5 to 3.0 km/s | the rocket stops 2.5 km/s short of orbital speed; the 3.0 version also books Earth's rotation and ascent losses |

Both are real. They answer different questions. Chapter A4 derives the second one. [Certain that `materials/core.md` defines them this way.]

#### Worked Example 1.3: the "price umbrella"

The repo argues that the premium for reaching GTO is the space the business lives in. It calls this the price umbrella.

Inputs (`finance/DEMAND_SENSITIVITY_FINDINGS.md`, verification table, all marked CONFIRMED there): Falcon 9 price $74M; 22,800 kg to LEO (maximum performance); 8,300 kg to GTO (maximum performance); 5,500 kg to GTO on the standard bookable plan. Skyhook's conservative price is $500/kg (`materials/core.md`).

Steps:

```
1. $/kg to LEO        = 74,000,000 ÷ 22,800 = $3,245.61/kg
2. $/kg to GTO (max)  = 74,000,000 ÷ 8,300  = $8,915.66/kg
3. GTO premium (max)  = 8,915.66 − 3,245.61 = $5,670.05/kg   (core.md: "≈ $5,670/kg")
4. $/kg to GTO (book) = 74,000,000 ÷ 5,500  = $13,454.55/kg
5. GTO premium (book) = 13,454.55 − 3,245.61 = $10,208.94/kg (core.md: "≈ $10,209/kg")
   (at full precision, 13,454.545 − 3,245.614 = 10,208.93; the last cent
    differs only because steps 1 and 4 were rounded first, see section 1.11)
6. Skyhook price vs smaller premium: 500 ÷ 5,670 = 0.088, i.e. 8.8%
```

Result: the conservative price is about one eleventh of the smaller premium (5,670 ÷ 500 = 11.3). That is what `materials/core.md` means by "an order of magnitude under that premium". [Certain as arithmetic; the $500/kg price itself has no named customer, see Section A1.6.]

Step 1 nearly reproduces `rev_a.json`'s anchor `economics.launch_price_anchor_dedicated_kgs = 3245`; `DEMAND_SENSITIVITY_FINDINGS.md` says the confirmed figure "essentially matches" the "existing" anchor. Note that $3,245.61 rounds to $3,246, which is what that file writes. The JSON's 3245 is what you get by dropping the fraction instead of rounding it. The repo does not say how 3245 was first derived; its note says only "Falcon 9 dedicated; Feb 2026 price increase". The $1 difference is trivial, but it shows how two files can carry slightly different versions of "the same" number.

The same file records a trap worth remembering. An earlier research note used 22,000 kg as the divisor and got $3,364/kg. The file says that was "a wrong payload figure, not a real price drift". [Certain]

#### A tension with the founding mission

The founding mission statement aims to reduce "the marginal cost of delivering payloads from Earth's surface to orbit and beyond by at least an order of magnitude" (`docs/project_instructions.md`, Part I). **Marginal cost** is what one more kilogram costs the operator to deliver, as opposed to the price charged (Chapter A9). Phase 3 has an "Earth-surface-to-orbit marginal cost target" of "< $300/kg falling toward < $100/kg" (Part VI).

That reads like LEO upmass displacement, which the README thesis rules out. Other passages were updated to Rev A (`docs/DEVIATIONS.md` item 5 says §2.2 and §2.3 "were corrected in 2c27b05", and §2.2 now quotes 2.5 km/s), and §7.8 already says "never frame the skyhook as rocketry's replacement". [Likely] the mission statement and the Phase 3 cost target predate the thesis and were not re-aligned. A reader should treat the README thesis as current.

### A1.3 Rev A and its three tiers

#### Words first

A **design revision** is a frozen, named version of the design. "Rev A" is the current one in the repo. A "Rev B" document (RB-001) exists only outside the repo (`handoff.md`, open item 4). `docs/program_manifest.md` records that the Rev B work "wrongly promoted 3.5 to reference" and was corrected on 25 Aug 2026: "the repo stays canon".

**Canon** means the official values. `CLAUDE.md` says `params/rev_a.json` "is the canonical single source of truth".

A **tier** is a tip-speed option aimed at a class of destination.

Rev A is a three-tier ladder. `handoff.md` insists on this and warns: "Never quote these from memory ... read the JSON."

#### The tiers at a glance

All values from `params/rev_a.json` (`kinematics` and `mass_ratio` blocks).

| Tier (JSON location) | v_tip | Destination | C3 (km²/s²) | Apogee altitude | Mass ratio (30% derate) | Fibre at 5 t payload | Tip load | Status in the file |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| reference (`kinematics`) | 2.5 km/s | GTO / high-elliptical | −8.06 | 85,222 km | 121.83× | 609.1 t | 1.99 g | Rev A reference |
| `cislunar_revenue_gated_option` | 2.8 km/s | TLI / lunar apogee | −1.94 | 397,819 km | 295.27× | 1,476.3 t | 2.5 g | "[Likely]"; "Requires a named cislunar anchor customer" |
| `phase3_growth_option` | 3.5 km/s | Mars-class escape | +13.05 | none (escapes) | 3,085.95× | 15,429.8 t | 3.9 g | "[Likely]"; "Phase 3 growth option only, NOT the near-term Rev A reference" |

How to read the columns, briefly (each gets a full chapter later):

- **C3** (characteristic energy) is a measure of orbital energy. Negative means the payload stays bound to Earth. Positive means it escapes. Chapter A3.
- **Apogee** is the highest point of an orbit.
- **Mass ratio** here is tether mass divided by payload mass. "121.83×" means the tether has 121.83 times the mass of one payload. Chapter A6.
- **Derate** is a planned cut in usable fibre strength to allow for joints, seams and ageing. 30% derate means the design assumes only 70% of the datasheet strength. Chapter A6.
- The **safety factor (SF)** is how many times stronger than the expected load a part is designed to be. Rev A uses SF 2.5 (`materials.safety_factor`). It is applied on top of the derate. Chapter A6.

The file also fixes destination thresholds, as tip speeds needed (`market_thresholds`): GTO about 2.1 km/s, TLI about 2.8, escape (C3 = 0) about 2.9, Mars-class 3.3 to 3.5. Its note says: "Do not move these thresholds to match the chosen reference." [Certain]

#### Worked Example 1.4: small steps in speed, giant steps in mass

Inputs: the tip speeds and fibre masses in the table above (`params/rev_a.json`).

```
Tip speed ratio, cislunar vs reference:  2.8 ÷ 2.5          = 1.12   (+12%)
Fibre ratio,     cislunar vs reference:  1,476.3 ÷ 609.1    = 2.42   (+142%)

Tip speed ratio, Phase 3 vs reference:   3.5 ÷ 2.5          = 1.40   (+40%)
Fibre ratio,     Phase 3 vs reference:   15,429.8 ÷ 609.1   = 25.3   (+2,430%)
```

Result: 12% more tip speed needs 142% more fibre. 40% more tip speed needs about 25 times the fibre. The mass formula contains an exponential of the square of tip speed, so mass explodes as speed rises (Chapter A6). [Certain]

This is why the program lowered its reference "3.5 → 2.8 → 2.5 km/s" (`docs/DECISION_LOG.md`, §5).

#### Two errors the project made and fixed

`handoff.md` records two errors, "both from quoting canon by memory":

1. 3.5 km/s was once treated as the reference. It was corrected to 2.5.
2. Later documents mixed the cislunar tier up with the 3.5 tier, and costed 3.5 km/s at "~440× when canon is ~3086× (7× too light)". The resulting claim that "the 3.5 growth option carries the business at 67–73%" is marked "RETRACTED".

`docs/DECISION_LOG.md` §1 traces the 440× figure. The correct formula at 3.5 km/s and 0% derate gives 440.40×, a match to four significant figures. So 440× was most likely that value, later mislabelled as the conservative case. Its lesson: "an unsourced correct number is still a liability." [Likely, which is how the log itself labels this addendum: "numerical coincidence plus plausibility, provenance chain unrecoverable".] (**Provenance** is the record of where a number came from.)

#### Common misreadings

- **"The tiers are the conservatism ladder."** No. The ladder (section A1.6) varies how cautious the assumptions are at a fixed 2.5 km/s. The tiers change the destination. `DECISION_LOG.md` §6 records that the workbook once mixed these up, with tip speeds 2.0/2.8/3.5 across its three columns. It was fixed so all three columns run at 2.5 km/s.
- **"The reference is the business."** `handoff.md` says: "Reference (2.5) is thin — a stepping stone. The near-term business is the 2.8 cislunar tier". It is gated on two things. The first is a **construction launch** price, the $/kg paid to launch the tether's own material while building it, below about $686/kg. The second is a named **anchor customer**, a first committed customer big enough to justify the build (`rev_a.json` `cislunar_revenue_gated_option.note`; `README.md` open item 3). [Likely; this is a program judgment, recorded in `handoff.md` and `docs/program_manifest.md`.]

### A1.4 The phased roadmap (Phase 0 to Phase 4)

#### The bootstrap idea

The founding document calls its roadmap **bootstrap-shaped**: "each phase is small enough to finance, produces revenue or decisive risk-retirement on its own, and physically becomes part of the next phase" (`docs/project_instructions.md`, Part VI). Its image: "The skyhook grows like a city, not like a cathedral."

A **budget class** is a planning range, not a quote. "Years" count from program start, not calendar years. (The Phase 0 plan's **Gantt chart**, a bar chart of tasks against time, says "Month 1 = program kickoff".)

#### The five phases

All rows from `docs/project_instructions.md`, Part VI.

| Phase | Years from start | Budget class | What it contains | Exit test |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 Foundations | 0–2 | $10–30M | digital twin, fibre and joint qualification, grapple prototype on the ground, regulatory groundwork | sim validated against flight data; joint statistics; capture demo video |
| 1 Orbital Demonstrators | 2–5 | $60–150M | D1 "Spinner" (2–10 km rotating tether); D2 "Catch" (20–50 km, first orbital catch and throw of a tens-of-kg test mass) | repeated catch/throw with the momentum ledger closed by ED reboost |
| 2 "Lariat" | 5–10 | $1–3B | 200–400 km class tether, 100–300 t hub, tip speed "initially 1.5–2.0 km/s", growing toward 2.5–3 | positive operating cash flow; >100 commercial exchanges; an insurance record |
| 3 "Mainline" | 10–18 | $5–15B | "HASTOL-class geometry": ~600–700 km total length, tip speed 3.5+ km/s, lower tip at ~100–150 km | none stated; marginal-cost target < $300/kg falling toward < $100/kg |
| 4 Network | 18+ | not stated | second Earth skyhook; a lunar skyhook | none stated |

A **digital twin** is a computer model detailed enough to stand in for the real machine in tests (Chapter A7). A **grapple** is the catching mechanism at the tip. **HASTOL** (Hypersonic Airplane Space Tether Orbital Launch) is a Boeing / Tethers Unlimited tether-launch study from about 1999–2001. The glossary calls it the "Closest literature ancestor of our Phase 2 design" (`docs/glossary.md`, entry "HASTOL").

A standing financing rule sits under all of this: "no phase may be initiated whose failure would be existential to the company" (`docs/project_instructions.md`, §7.6).

#### Where the program actually is

`README.md` gives the status: "Phase 0 — Pre-Phase 0 Study / Infrastructure". The repo contains a Phase 0 plan, early software (the dynamics model `physics/tether_dynamics.py` and the browser twin in `tools/twin/`), a kitchen-scale splice-test protocol (`docs/st001_splice_test.md`) and vendor outreach (`docs/outreach_log.md`). It shows no evidence of Phase 0 funding, or of the planned hardware workstreams (the joint campaign and the capture demonstration) having started. [Certain that the repo shows none; what exists outside the repo is unknown.]

#### Worked Example 1.5: adding up the Phase 0 budget

The Phase 0 plan is in `tools/financial/skyhook_phase0_plan.xlsx`, sheet "Spend Curve". Its quarterly totals are in **$k**, meaning thousands of dollars.

Inputs (eight quarters, $k): 1,950; 2,450; 2,700; 2,700; 2,600; 2,250; 1,850; 1,500.

Steps (a running total, which is what the sheet's "Cumulative" row shows):

```
1,950
1,950 + 2,450 =  4,400
4,400 + 2,700 =  7,100
7,100 + 2,700 =  9,800
9,800 + 2,600 = 12,400
12,400 + 2,250 = 14,650
14,650 + 1,850 = 16,500
16,500 + 1,500 = 18,000 $k
```

Convert: 18,000 × $1,000 = $18,000,000 = $18M.

By workstream, the same sheet sums to $4,000k (digital twin), $5,000k (joint and materials handbook), $6,000k (capture demonstration) and $3,000k (regulatory and partners). The Gantt sheet's headers carry the same $4M, $5M, $6M and $3M. 4 + 5 + 6 + 3 = 18.

Result: $18M. It matches `params/rev_a.json` `economics.phase0_capex_M = 18` and sits inside the founding document's $10–30M class. [Certain]

#### Which phase is Rev A?

This is unclear, and the documents disagree.

- `docs/project_instructions.md` §2.2 calls the 610 km / 320 km / 2.5 km/s design "our Phase 2 reference design".
- Part VI says Phase 2 is a 200–400 km class tether at 1.5–2.0 km/s initially. Rev A is 640 km long, which is Phase 3 scale.
- Phase 3 in Part VI runs at 3.5+ km/s. Rev A runs at 2.5 km/s.

There is a second mismatch at the bottom of the swing. `rev_a.json` puts the lower tip at 290 km. The founding document's preferred vehicle (§4.4) reaches "~100–150 km altitude and ~4 km/s". Rev A needs 4.59 km/s ground-relative at 290 km. The §2.2 text even contains a leftover drafting line, "...wait — for an atmosphere-grazing design we want the tip much lower", and then quotes "80–150 km" for a HASTOL-class design.

[Certain that the files disagree.] The practical effect: the founding document's launch vehicle (~4 km/s at ~100–150 km) is not the vehicle Rev A needs (4.59 km/s ground-relative at 290 km). Later files work from the Rev A figure (`docs/providers/README.md` asks for providers in "the ~4–5 km/s class"; `finance/LEG_COST_FINDINGS.md` uses a computed 4.591 km/s). No document found in this reading reconciles the two. [Likely]

### A1.5 A map of the repository

A **repository** (repo) is a folder of files whose full history is tracked by **git**, a version-control tool. Each saved snapshot is a commit, named by a short code such as 34935cb. A **branch** is a separate line of history. `main` is the official one. An **unmerged branch** holds work that has not yet been accepted into `main`, so it is not official.

The README has a folder map, but it is out of date (see "Limits" below). This is the real layout on `main`, from a directory listing.

| Folder or file | What it holds | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| `params/rev_a.json` | the canonical numbers (Rule 1) | this one |
| `params/service_mxer_draft.json` | a draft, marked "DRAFT — non-canonical; do not cite as design" | 10 |
| `physics/skyhook_physics.py` | EQ-1 to EQ-7; loads `rev_a.json` at import | 2–6 |
| `physics/tether_dynamics.py` | a 17-node planar tether model, the seed of the digital twin (`MORNING_REPORT.md`) | 7 |
| `tests/` | six test files: physics, dynamics, finance, finance tiers, export grid, analysis layer | 12 |
| `finance/` | the Python financial model, analysis scripts, `*_FINDINGS.md` reports, `decision_grid.json` | 9–10 |
| `tools/financial/` | Excel workbooks: financial model, Phase 0 plan, risk register; a cash-flow chart | 9 |
| `tools/sims/` | interactive JSX and HTML simulators, the program website, the orbit theater, the BF-001 break-even frontier, the ST-001 splice-test field kit, a superseded calculator | 12 |
| `tools/twin/` | the JavaScript digital twin; `verify.mjs` checks it against `golden.json` | 7, 12 |
| `scripts/` | `generate_golden.py` (makes the twin's reference run), `init_repo.sh` | 12 |
| `materials/` | `core.md`, the approved investor copy, plus HTML and PDF teasers | 9 |
| `docs/` | founding document, glossary, verification memo, decision log, deviations register, FAQ, outreach log, manifest, the archived original README, the ST-001 splice-test protocol | 11 |
| `docs/research/`, `docs/regulatory/`, `docs/providers/` | literature reviews and market pricing; the conjunction whitepaper; a mandate for rocket-leg pricing | 10–11 |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | automatic tests on pushes to `main` or `dev` and on pull requests to `main` (see below) | 12 |
| `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md` | front door and working rules | this one |
| `handoff.md`, `MORNING_REPORT.md` | session notes from 31 Aug 2026 and an overnight run on 2026-07-02 | 11 |

A few file types in that table need a word. **JSX** is JavaScript with HTML-like tags mixed in, used by the React web library. **Node.js** is a program that runs JavaScript outside a web browser. **pytest** is a Python tool that runs test functions and reports which pass. **openpyxl** is a Python library that reads Excel files.

**CI** (continuous integration) is a service that runs checks automatically whenever code changes. Here it runs on pushes to the `main` and `dev` branches and on pull requests to `main`. It installs Python 3.11, pytest and openpyxl, runs `pytest tests/ -v --tb=short`, then runs `python3 physics/skyhook_physics.py` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`). A comment inside `load_ladder_from_workbook()` in `finance/skyhook_finance.py` still says "CI installs pytest only"; the workflow file now installs openpyxl too, so the comment is stale. Chapter A12 covers CI.

An analogy: `params/` is the recipe card. `physics/` and `finance/` are the kitchen. `tests/` is the taste test before anything is served. `docs/` is the cookbook plus the diary of past mistakes.

`handoff.md` tells the next working session to read itself, `params/rev_a.json` and `docs/program_manifest.md` "before doing anything". A suggested first reading order for the owner, from this guide: `README.md`, then `params/rev_a.json`, then `materials/core.md`, then `handoff.md`, then `docs/DECISION_LOG.md`.

### A1.6 The execution rules and the confidence labels

#### The nine rules

`README.md` lists "Nine execution rules (from founding document)":

| # | Rule | In plain words |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Single source of truth | numbers come from `params/rev_a.json`; any deviation is stated |
| 2 | Show the physics | every claim traces to an equation, a cited study or a labelled assumption; "No magic numbers" |
| 3 | Engineering-economics coupling | every design change is costed: tether mass, capex, cadence or $/kg |
| 4 | Conservatism ladder | quote Conservative / Baseline / Optimistic; the financial base case uses Conservative only |
| 5 | Bootstrap discipline | start small, earn revenue, grow |
| 6 | Honesty about hard parts | name the hard problems in every document |
| 7 | Glossary maintenance | keep `docs/glossary.md` current |
| 8 | Confidence tagging | label claims [Certain] / [Likely] / [Speculative] |
| 9 | Tests before refactors | `pytest tests/` must pass before any merge to `main` |

A **magic number** is a value in a calculation with no stated source. **Capex** (capital expenditure) is money spent to build things. **Cadence** is how often catches happen, in catches per day.

The five hard parts named under Rule 6 are tether joints at scale, hypersonic rendezvous precision, fibre survivability, conjunction management and Phase 2 financing (`README.md`). Three words need defining. A **rendezvous** is a meeting of two vehicles at matched position and speed. **Hypersonic** means faster than about five times the speed of sound (from memory, verify). **Conjunction management** means avoiding collisions with other objects in orbit.

`docs/DECISION_LOG.md` §10 (dated 2026-09-02) later added a sixth: **creep** in the HMPE fibre, meaning slow permanent stretching under a steady load. Creep is carried as a named hard part, status "OPEN".

Two fibres appear in that story. **HMPE** (high-modulus polyethylene, the fibre family sold as Dyneema and Spectra, also called UHMWPE; from memory, verify) is the bulk fibre in Rev A's construction baseline, "Spectra/UHMWPE core + Zylon outer arm" (`rev_a.json`, `materials.construction_baseline`). **Zylon** (PBO) is a commercially available high-strength polymer fibre and Rev A's `primary_fiber`. The founding document lists both among materials that "exist today" (Part I).

Note one oddity. Every mass ratio stored in the same file is computed from Zylon's strength and density alone (5.8 GPa, 1,560 kg/m³, through V_c = 2.73 km/s), not from a core-plus-arm mix. Chapter A6 returns to this. [Certain that `rev_a.json` states both.]

#### The rule count does not match between files

- The README says nine rules come "from founding document". The founding document's Part IX lists only seven, the same as README rules 1 to 7 (`docs/project_instructions.md`, Part IX).
- `CLAUDE.md` has its own five "non-negotiable" rules: run pytest first, never hardcode a physics parameter, label every claim, conservatism ladder, no magic numbers.

README rules 8 and 9 exist in substance only as `CLAUDE.md` rules 3 and 1. `docs/program_manifest.md` repeats the error: it describes the founding document as having "nine execution rules". [Certain] Nothing breaks because of this, but "nine rules from the founding document" is not literally true.

#### The three confidence labels

From `README.md` and `CLAUDE.md`:

- **[Certain]**: supported by strong evidence, or derivable from first principles or strong flight data.
- **[Likely]**: supported by evidence, with minor modelling assumptions.
- **[Speculative]**: an educated estimate, never used in the financial base case.

The labels appear inside code **docstrings** (the explanatory text at the top of a Python function, as in `physics/skyhook_physics.py`) and inside JSON strings (for example `"confidence": "[Likely]"` on both tier blocks in `rev_a.json`).

An analogy: a weather forecast that says "90% chance of rain" versus one that says "maybe". The label tells you how hard to lean on the number.

#### Ask "Certain about what?"

[Certain] often means "the arithmetic is reproduced, given the model's inputs". It does not mean "this will happen".

An example. `MORNING_REPORT.md` labels the conservative "NPV@10% of −$3,883M" as "[Certain within model assumptions]". **NPV** (net present value) is all future cash flows converted to today's money at a stated yearly **discount rate**, here 10%; Chapter A9 builds it up. The arithmetic is right. But one of its inputs, the $500/kg customer price, has "no named customer" (`docs/DECISION_LOG.md`, §8).

Another. `materials/core.md` labels the 121.83× mass ratio "[Certain — EQ-6]". The equation is certain. But `rev_a.json` labels the 30% derate that produces 121.83× as "[Likely]".

So read a label as a statement about the evidence for one step, not about the whole chain.

#### Other label systems you will meet

| System | Where | Labels |
|---|---|---|
| Confidence | everywhere | [Certain] / [Likely] / [Speculative] |
| Trust legend | `docs/program_manifest.md` | [Verified] / [Anchored] / [Planning] / [Demo] |
| Verdicts | `docs/verification_memo.md` (VM-001) | ✅ CONFIRMED / 🔶 CORRECTED / ⚠️ NUANCE |

They answer different questions. Do not translate one into another without checking.

#### The conservatism ladder in numbers

The ladder is three columns of assumptions in `tools/financial/skyhook_financial_model.xlsx`, sheet "Assumptions". `finance/skyhook_finance.py` reads it with `load_ladder_from_workbook()`. Selected rows:

| Input | Conservative | Baseline | Optimistic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Strength retention (1 − derate) | 0.70 | 0.85 | 1.00 |
| Mass ratio at 2.5 km/s (`rev_a.json`) | 121.83× | 64.30× | 40.32× |
| Construction launch | $2,500/kg | $1,500/kg | $800/kg |
| Cadence | 1 catch/day | 2 | 3 |
| Customer price | $500/kg | $500/kg | $500/kg |
| Payload per catch | 5,000 kg | 5,000 kg | 5,000 kg |
| Tip speed | 2.5 km/s | 2.5 km/s | 2.5 km/s |

Rule 4 says the financial base case uses only the Conservative column. Chapter A9 works through what that column produces.

### A1.7 Quantities and SI units

A **physical quantity** is a number times a **unit**. "2.5 km/s" is a quantity. "2.5" on its own means nothing: it could be metres, kilometres or dollars.

**SI** (Système International) is the world's standard set of units. It has seven **base units**, defined on their own (from memory, verify): the metre (m, length), kilogram (kg, mass), second (s, time), ampere (A, electric current), kelvin (K, temperature), mole (mol, amount of substance) and candela (cd, light intensity).

**Derived units** are built from base units. The four this guide needs most:

```
newton  N  = kg·m/s²    force    = mass × acceleration
joule   J  = N·m        energy   = force × distance      = kg·m²/s²
pascal  Pa = N/m²       stress   = force ÷ area
watt    W  = J/s        power    = energy ÷ time
```

An analogy: base units are letters; derived units are words spelled with them.

A small illustration. Lifting 1 kg by 1 m against gravity of 9.81 m/s² takes 1 × 9.81 × 1 = 9.81 J.

Where these show up in the repo (`params/rev_a.json`, `materials` and `orbital` blocks). The `materials` block describes Zylon, the primary fibre (section A1.6).

| Key | Value | Kind of quantity |
|---|---|---|
| `tensile_strength_GPa` | 5.8 | **stress**: force per area the fibre can carry before breaking |
| `density_kgm3` | 1560 | **density**: mass per volume |
| `specific_strength_MJkg` | 3.72 | **specific strength**: strength ÷ density, an energy per mass |
| `mu_earth_m3s2` | 3.986 × 10¹⁴ | **gravitational parameter** μ: Earth's mass times the gravitational constant (Chapter A3) |

The repo also uses several non-SI units: km/s, minutes, **tonnes** (t, 1,000 kg), kWh, "g" and dollars. Each needs converting before it goes into an SI formula.

Two common slips:

- The kilogram is a base unit even though it carries the prefix "kilo".
- Stress is force per area, not force. A thicker rope of the same fibre carries more force at the same stress.

---

### A1.8 Metric prefixes, and money shorthand

A **prefix** multiplies a unit by a power of ten.

| Prefix | Symbol | Factor | Repo example |
|---|---|---|---|
| nano | n | 10⁻⁹ | — |
| micro | µ | 10⁻⁶ | — |
| milli | m | 10⁻³ | — |
| kilo | k | 10³ | km, kg, kWh |
| mega | M | 10⁶ | MJ/kg; Mg (megagram) |
| giga | G | 10⁹ | GPa |
| tera | T | 10¹² | — |

Case matters. "m" is milli and "M" is mega, a factor of 10⁹ apart. A milligram (mg) and a megagram (Mg) differ by 10⁹.

A **megagram** is 10⁶ g = 1,000 kg = 1 tonne. `docs/DECISION_LOG.md` §3 gives the HASTOL study's (section A1.4) tether-control-station mass as "150 Mg for a 15 Mg payload". So its mass ratio is 150 ÷ 15 = 10×, which is what `rev_a.json` stores as `heritage.HASTOL_mass_ratio_at_SF3 = 10`. The "at SF3" in the key name means "at safety factor 3".

Money uses its own shorthand. It looks like the metric prefixes but follows finance custom:

| Written | Means | Repo example |
|---|---|---|
| $k | thousands of dollars | Phase 0 spend curve in $k (Worked Example 1.5) |
| $M | millions of dollars | `phase0_capex_M = 18` → $18 million |
| $B | billions of dollars | Phase 2 budget class "$1–3B" |
| "$8,741M" | $8,741 million = $8.741 billion | conservative total capex (`MORNING_REPORT.md`) |

---

### A1.9 Scientific notation

**Scientific notation** writes a number as m × 10ⁿ, with m between 1 and 10. Computers write the same thing as **E-notation**: `3.986e14` means 3.986 × 10¹⁴.

Rules for combining them:

```
(a × 10^p) × (b × 10^q) = (a × b) × 10^(p+q)
(a × 10^p) ÷ (b × 10^q) = (a ÷ b) × 10^(p−q)
```

A small illustration: (2 × 10³) × (3 × 10⁴) = 6 × 10⁷.

A negative exponent means small, not negative. The digital twin matches the Python model to a maximum position error of "1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰" (`materials/core.md`). `tools/twin/verify.mjs` reports this as a relative error, so it is a pure fraction: 0.00000000016.

The "e" in `3.986e14` is not Euler's number e (section A1.12). It is just shorthand for "× 10 to the".

#### Worked Example 1.6: reading μ and changing it to kilometres

Input: `rev_a.json` stores `"mu_earth_m3s2": 398600000000000.0`.

Step 1, count the places. After the leading 3 there are 14 digits, so:

```
398,600,000,000,000 = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²
```

Step 2, convert to km³/s². A cubed unit takes its conversion factor cubed:

```
1 km   = 10³ m
1 km³  = (10³ m)³ = 10⁹ m³
μ      = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² ÷ 10⁹ m³/km³ = 3.986 × 10⁵ km³/s² = 398,600 km³/s²
```

This is exactly the line `MU_EARTH / 1e9` in `apogee_from_release()` in `physics/skyhook_physics.py`. The workbook stores the same value as 398,600 (`tools/financial/skyhook_financial_model.xlsx`, Assumptions). [Certain]

Result: 398,600 km³/s². Converting km to m does not convert km³ to m³ by the same factor. You must cube the factor.

---

### A1.10 Unit conversion and dimensional analysis

To convert units, multiply by a fraction equal to one, such as (1,000 m ÷ 1 km). Unwanted units cancel like common factors. It works like a currency exchange: you multiply by the rate and the old label drops out.

**Dimensional analysis** means checking that the units on both sides of an equation match. If they do not, the equation is wrong.

The conversions this repo uses most:

| From | To | Factor | Where the code does it |
|---|---|---|---|
| km/s | m/s | × 1,000 | `v_tip_kms * 1e3` in `tip_acceleration_g()` |
| km | m | × 1,000 | `(altitude_km + R_EARTH_KM) * 1e3` in `v_orbital_kms()` |
| GPa | Pa | × 10⁹ | `characteristic_velocity_kms()` |
| s | min | ÷ 60 | `rotation_period_min()` divides seconds by 60 |
| kg | t | ÷ 1,000 | `annual_upmass_t()` in `finance/skyhook_finance.py` |
| MJ | kWh | ÷ 3.6 | `marginal_cost_per_kg()` in `finance/skyhook_finance.py` |
| g/cm³ | kg/m³ | × 1,000 | VM-001 lists Zylon at "1.54–1.56 g/cm³"; the JSON uses 1,560 kg/m³ |

Why is 1 kWh exactly 3.6 MJ? A **kilowatt-hour** is one kilowatt of power for one hour:

```
1 kWh = 1,000 W × 3,600 s = 3,600,000 J = 3.6 MJ        [Certain]
```

Remember that kWh is energy, while kW is power. MJ/kg is energy per kilogram, not energy.

#### Worked Example 1.7: why strength ÷ density is a speed squared

Inputs: σ = 5.8 GPa and ρ = 1,560 kg/m³ (`params/rev_a.json`, `materials`). The Greek letters **σ** (sigma) and **ρ** (rho) are the usual symbols for stress and density.

Step 1, the units:

```
σ/ρ has units  (N/m²) × (m³/kg) = N·m/kg = J/kg
and            J/kg = (kg·m²/s²)/kg = m²/s²
```

So strength divided by density is an energy per kilogram, which is also a speed squared.

Step 2, the numbers:

```
σ = 5.8 GPa = 5.8 × 10⁹ Pa
σ/ρ = 5.8 × 10⁹ ÷ 1,560 = 3.718 × 10⁶ J/kg = 3.72 MJ/kg   (rev_a.json specific_strength_MJkg: 3.72)
```

Step 3, take the speed:

```
V_c = √(2σ/ρ) = √(2 × 3.718 × 10⁶) = √(7.436 × 10⁶ m²/s²) = 2,726.9 m/s = 2.73 km/s
```

Result: **characteristic velocity** V_c ≈ 2.73 km/s (`rev_a.json` `V_c_kms`). It is the fibre's built-in speed scale, defined as EQ-4 in `CLAUDE.md` and computed by `characteristic_velocity_kms()`. The glossary puts it this way: a tether with no taper "can sustain a tip speed of V_c at safety factor 1"; going faster needs a cable that thickens toward the centre. Chapter A6 explains what it means physically. [Certain]

A handy fact falls out: 1 km²/s² = 10⁶ m²/s² = 10⁶ J/kg = 1 MJ/kg. So a number in km²/s² can be read straight off as MJ/kg.

#### Worked Example 1.8: from energy per kilogram to dollars per kilogram

`marginal_cost_per_kg()` in `finance/skyhook_finance.py` turns the energy needed to restore the tether's orbit into an electricity bill.

Inputs:

- v_orb = 7.5563 km/s from `v_orbital_kms(610)`; v_tip = 2.5 km/s.
- Conservative column of the workbook (read by `load_ladder_from_workbook()`): power-chain efficiency 0.15, electricity $0.08/kWh, ops and wear $12/kg.

Steps:

```
1. Energy per kg the code books:  2 × 7.5563 × 2.5     = 37.78 km²/s² = 37.78 MJ/kg
2. Electricity in, at 15%:        37.78 ÷ 0.15         = 251.9 MJ/kg
3. In kWh:                        251.9 ÷ 3.6          = 69.97 kWh/kg
4. Cost of that electricity:      69.97 × $0.08        = $5.60/kg
5. Add ops and wear:              5.60 + 12.00         = $17.60/kg
```

The function returns 17.597, which rounds to $17.60/kg. [Certain as a reproduction of the code.]

A **power-chain efficiency** of 0.15 means only 15% of the electricity bought ends up as useful orbital energy.

A warning. The repo holds three different energy-per-kilogram figures for this one job: "~30 MJ/kg" (`docs/project_instructions.md` §7.1), 37.78 MJ/kg (this code) and "44.8 MJ/kg = 12.4 kWh/kg" (`docs/research/mp001_market_pricing.md` §3a). MP-001 does not show how 44.8 was derived, and this guide could not reproduce it from repo inputs. Two natural candidates computed here with the code's v_orb and μ = 398,600 km³/s² are 43.03 MJ/kg (the change in total orbital energy, kinetic plus gravitational, from the lower tip at r = 6,661 km to release at r = 7,301 km) and 45.27 MJ/kg (the same, but starting from the 4.59 km/s ground-relative speed). The unit conversions in each file are correct (44.8 ÷ 3.6 = 12.4); the definitions differ. Chapter A5 reconciles them. [Certain that the three figures disagree; which definition is right is Chapter A5's subject.]

#### Worked Example 1.9: from catches per day to dollars per year

Inputs (Conservative column, workbook Assumptions): 1 catch/day, 5,000 kg per catch, $500/kg.

Steps, following `annual_upmass_t()` and `annual_revenue_M()` in `finance/skyhook_finance.py`:

```
1. Catches per year:   1 /day × 365 days/yr        = 365 /yr
2. Mass per year:      365 × 5,000 kg              = 1,825,000 kg/yr
3. In tonnes:          1,825,000 ÷ 1,000           = 1,825 t/yr
4. Revenue per year:   1,825,000 kg × $500/kg      = $912,500,000/yr
5. In $M:              912,500,000 ÷ 1,000,000     = $912.5M/yr
```

Result: 1,825 t/yr and $912.5M/yr at full capacity. `handoff.md` quotes the same figure when it reports that "no realistic customer shortlist amortizes a 1,825 t/yr capacity-sized cost base". [Certain as arithmetic; whether anyone will buy 1,825 t/yr is [Speculative] and is Chapter A10's subject.]

The founding document §7.3, describing a mature Phase 3 system, calls 2 catches/day "conservative utilization" and gets "~3,650 t/yr". In the workbook, 2/day is the Baseline column, not Conservative. The prose and the model disagree about what "conservative" means. [Certain]

### A1.11 Significant figures, rounding, precision and tolerance

#### The words

- **Significant figures** are the digits that carry information. 7.55 has three. 0.0078 has two (leading zeros do not count).
- **Rounding** cuts a number to fewer digits. "Round half up": 4.585 becomes 4.59.
- **Precision** is how finely a number is stated.
- **Accuracy** is how close it is to the truth.
- **Relative error** compares a value to an expected one: |actual − expected| ÷ |expected|.
- **Tolerance** is the error a check is willing to accept.

An analogy: a bathroom scale that reads 70.000 kg every time is precise. If you really weigh 72 kg, it is not accurate.

```
relative_error = |actual − expected| / |expected|
```

The test file sets its tolerance with a comment worth remembering: `TOL = 0.02  # 2% relative tolerance; anything tighter is false precision` (`tests/test_rev_a_physics.py`).

#### Worked Example 1.10: two Earth radii hidden in the canonical file

Inputs:

- `orbital.com_altitude_km = 610` and `orbital.com_radius_km = 6988` (`params/rev_a.json`).
- `R_EARTH_KM = 6371.0`, the mean radius (`physics/skyhook_physics.py`).
- μ = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² (`rev_a.json`).

Step 1, spot the two bases:

```
JSON:  6,988 − 610 = 6,378 km   → the equatorial radius (6,378.137 km, from memory, verify)
Code:  6,371 + 610 = 6,981 km   → the mean radius
```

Step 2, compute orbital speed on each basis with EQ-2, v = √(μ/r):

```
r = 6.981 × 10⁶ m:  μ/r = (3.986 × 10¹⁴) ÷ (6.981 × 10⁶) = 5.7098 × 10⁷ m²/s²;  √ = 7,556.3 m/s = 7.5563 km/s
r = 6.988 × 10⁶ m:  μ/r = (3.986 × 10¹⁴) ÷ (6.988 × 10⁶) = 5.7041 × 10⁷ m²/s²;  √ = 7,552.5 m/s = 7.5525 km/s
```

Step 3, see which stored numbers follow which basis:

| Stored in `rev_a.json` | Value | Matches |
|---|---|---|
| `v_orb_kms` | 7.55 | 7.5525 rounds to 7.55 (6,988 basis); 7.5563 would round to 7.56 |
| `v_upper_release_kms` | 10.06 | 7.5563 + 2.5 = 10.0563 → 10.06 (6,981 basis); 6,988 would give 10.05 |
| cislunar `v_upper_release_kms` | 10.36 | 7.5563 + 2.8 = 10.3563 → 10.36 (6,981 basis); 6,988 would give 10.35 |
| phase-3 `v_upper_release_kms` | 11.05 | 7.5525 + 3.5 = 11.0525 → 11.05 (6,988 basis); 6,981 would give 11.06 |
| `c3_kms2` | −8.06 | `apogee_from_release(2.5)` gives −8.061 with r_tip = 6,371 + 930 = 7,301 km (6,981 basis). On the 6,988 basis, r_tip = 7,308 km and C3 = 10.0525² − 2 × 398,600 ÷ 7,308 = 101.053 − 109.086 = −8.03 |

The 6,988 km figure has a visible origin: the founding document's §2.2 worked example says "Center of mass altitude: 610 km (orbital radius ≈ 6,988 km), v_orb ≈ 7.55 km/s". [Likely] `v_orb_kms` and the Phase 3 release speed were carried over from that example, while the other fields were recomputed later with `R_EARTH_KM`.

Step 4, apply the test tolerance:

```
|7.5563 − 7.55| ÷ 7.55 = 0.0063 ÷ 7.55 = 0.00083 = 0.083%   < 2%  → passes
```

Result: the canonical file disagrees with itself by about 0.05% in orbital speed. The 2% test tolerance cannot detect it, by design. The founding document §2.2 shows the same seam when it writes "~7.55 + 2.5 ≈ 10.06"; in fact 7.55 + 2.5 = 10.05.

The gap is physically tiny. It matters as a lesson: "canonical" does not mean "internally consistent". This split is recorded on two unmerged branches: `claude/skyhook-fixes-2026-10-22` adds it as item #10 of `docs/DEVIATIONS.md`, and `claude/creative-canon-claim-audit` analyses it field by field in `docs/research/ca001_canon_claim_audit.md` (which also makes the "carried over" inference above). It is not in `docs/DEVIATIONS.md` on `main`, whose register stops at item 9. [Certain]

#### Worked Example 1.11: how many digits does 121.83× deserve?

Inputs: σ = 5.8 GPa (two significant figures) and ρ = 1,560 kg/m³ (`rev_a.json`). VM-001 gives a density range of 1.54–1.56 g/cm³ (`docs/verification_memo.md`). The mass ratio is computed by `integrated_mass_ratio()` in `physics/skyhook_physics.py` at 2.5 km/s, SF 2.5 and 30% derate.

Step 1. "5.8 GPa" at two significant figures could mean anything from 5.75 to 5.85.

Step 2. Recompute at the corners (each run used `characteristic_velocity_kms()` then `integrated_mass_ratio()`):

| σ (GPa) | ρ (kg/m³) | V_c (km/s) | Mass ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5.85 | 1,540 | 2.7563 | 112.95× |
| 5.80 | 1,560 | 2.7269 | 121.83× (canon) |
| 5.75 | 1,560 | 2.7151 | 125.64× |

```
low corner:  (112.95 − 121.83) ÷ 121.83 = −7.3%
high corner: (125.64 − 121.83) ÷ 121.83 = +3.1%
```

Step 3. Rounding an input also moves the answer. Using the stored V_c of 2.73 instead of 2.7269 (a 0.11% change) gives 120.84× instead of 121.83×, a 0.81% change. The formula multiplies small input errors about sevenfold here.

Step 4. Rounding order matters too:

```
rounded first:  121.83 × 5,000 kg = 609,150 kg = 609.15 t → could round to 609.2 t
full precision: 121.8261 × 5,000 kg = 609,130 kg = 609.13 t → 609.1 t (rev_a.json)
```

Result: an honest statement is "about 120×, somewhere between roughly −7% and +3% from rounding of the fibre data alone". That is before any doubt about the 30% derate itself. The two decimals in "121.83×" are a reproducibility tag, so that anyone re-running the code gets the same digits. They are not a claim of accuracy to 0.01%. Keep full precision through a calculation and round once at the end. [Certain as arithmetic; the input ranges used are illustrative.]

---

### A1.12 Ratios, percentages, percentage points and "×"

#### The words

- A **ratio** is a ÷ b. If a and b share units, the ratio has none.
- A **percentage** is a ratio times 100.
- A **fraction** here is a ratio between 0 and 1. `derate_fraction = 0.3` means 30%.
- A **percentage point** (pt) is the plain difference between two percentages.
- A **relative change** is (new − old) ÷ old.
- **"N×"** means "N times as much".

```
percent          = (part ÷ whole) × 100
relative change  = (new − old) ÷ old
retention        = 1 − derate
```

Prefer "121.83 times the payload's mass" to "121.83 times heavier". "Heavier" invites an off-by-one reading (is it 121.83 times, or 122.83 times?).

A relative change needs its base. A $50 price that rises 10% to $55 and then falls 10% ends at $49.50, not $50.

#### Worked Example 1.12: points versus percent

Input: `finance/SENSITIVITY_FINDINGS.md` and `MORNING_REPORT.md` say the conservative case closes if derate falls to "≤ 21.2%", a move of "−8.8 pts".

```
1. In points:              30% − 21.2%       = 8.8 percentage points
2. As a relative drop:     8.8 ÷ 30          = 0.293 = 29.3%
3. In retention terms:     0.70 → 0.788;  (0.788 − 0.70) ÷ 0.70 = +12.6%
```

Result: one fact, three numbers: −8.8 points, −29.3% relative, +12.6% retention. Always ask which one a document means. The finance code stores `strength_retention = 0.7`; `rev_a.json` stores `derate_fraction = 0.3`. They are the same fact written two ways. [Certain]

A second example from the same table: cadence must reach "≥ 1.10 catches/day (+10.4%)". Since 1 × 1.104 = 1.104, the true threshold is about 1.104, displayed as 1.10.

#### Worked Example 1.13: how wrong was "440×"?

Inputs: the correct Phase 3 ratio, 3,085.95× (`rev_a.json`), and the old figure, 440× (`handoff.md`). At 0% derate, `integrated_mass_ratio(3.5, …)` gives 440.40× (`docs/DECISION_LOG.md` §1 addendum).

```
1. As a factor:            3,085.95 ÷ 440.40          = 7.0    → "7× too light"
2. As a shortfall:         1 − 440.40 ÷ 3,085.95      = 1 − 0.143 = 0.857 → 85.7% too low
3. Tip-speed change, 3.5 → 2.5:  (2.5 − 3.5) ÷ 3.5    = −28.6%
4. Mass-ratio change:      (121.83 − 3,085.95) ÷ 3,085.95 = −96.1%  (a factor of 25.3)
```

Result: the old figure was 85.7% too low. Cutting tip speed by 28.6% cut tether mass by a factor of about 25. [Certain]

#### e and ln, just enough to read the repo

**e** ≈ 2.71828 is a mathematical constant (from memory, verify). **exp(x)** means eˣ. The **natural logarithm**, **ln**, undoes it: ln(eˣ) = x.

They matter because the rocket equation, EQ-1 in `CLAUDE.md`, is

```
Δv = v_e × ln(m0 ÷ mf)
```

where **v_e** is the rocket's exhaust speed, **m0** is its starting mass and **mf** its final mass. Chapter A4 derives it.

`materials/core.md` uses the inverse: removing 5.0 km/s from a stage with a 3.5 km/s exhaust speed is a mass ratio of

```
e^(5.0 ÷ 3.5) = e^1.4286 = 4.17
propellant share = 1 − 1 ÷ 4.17 = 0.760 → "~76% propellant"
```

Notice that this illustration uses the 5.0 km/s figure (what the tether gives the payload), not the 2.5–3.0 km/s ascent saving from section A1.2. It answers the question "how much rocket would the payload need to get the same boost itself?".

Do not confuse the two mass ratios. The rocket's m0 ÷ mf (`mass_ratio_required()` in `physics/skyhook_physics.py`) is a different quantity from the tether-to-payload ratio M ÷ m (EQ-6). Same words, different things.

---

### A1.13 g as a unit of acceleration

**Acceleration** is how fast velocity changes, in m/s² (metres per second, per second).

**Standard gravity**, written **g** or g₀, is a fixed reference acceleration of 9.80665 m/s². It is exact by definition (from memory, verify). The code sets `G_STD = 9.80665` in `physics/skyhook_physics.py`.

An acceleration "in g" is simply the acceleration divided by 9.80665. A 2 g load feels like weighing twice your normal weight.

Three things "g" does **not** mean here:

- It is not grams. The key `tip_acceleration_g` is a g-load.
- It is not the strength of gravity at 610 km. It is a fixed unit.
- The tip load is not weight. It comes from spinning, as a **centripetal acceleration**: the inward pull needed to keep something moving in a circle (Chapter A2).

#### Worked Example 1.14: the load on a payload at the tip

Inputs: v_tip and L for each tier (`params/rev_a.json`); `G_STD` = 9.80665 (`physics/skyhook_physics.py`). The formula is a = v²/L (Chapter A2), implemented in `tip_acceleration_g()`.

```
2.5 km/s:  v = 2.5 × 1,000 = 2,500 m/s;  L = 320 × 1,000 = 320,000 m
           a = 2,500² ÷ 320,000 = 6,250,000 ÷ 320,000 = 19.53 m/s²
           19.53 ÷ 9.80665 = 1.99 g                          (rev_a.json: 1.99)

2.8 km/s:  a = 2,800² ÷ 320,000 = 7,840,000 ÷ 320,000 = 24.50 m/s²
           24.50 ÷ 9.80665 = 2.50 g                          (rev_a.json: 2.5)

3.5 km/s:  a = 3,500² ÷ 320,000 = 12,250,000 ÷ 320,000 = 38.28 m/s²
           38.28 ÷ 9.80665 = 3.90 g                          (rev_a.json: 3.9)
```

Result: 1.99 g, 2.50 g and 3.90 g. All match the file. The test `TestTipKinematics::test_payload_qualification_load` in `tests/test_rev_a_physics.py` fails if the reference ever reaches 6 g, its "payload qualification warning threshold". [Certain]

The workbook divides by 9.81 instead of 9.80665 (inside a Design Calcs formula in `tools/financial/skyhook_financial_model.xlsx`). That gives 1.9910 instead of 1.9916 g. Both round to 1.99, but it is another duplicated constant that could drift.

---

### A1.14 Signs and shorthand that carry meaning

Some numbers carry meaning in their sign. The clearest is **C3**.

- `c3_kms2 = −8.06` for the reference. Negative means the payload's energy is below what escape needs. It stays bound to Earth, on an ellipse reaching 85,222 km.
- `c3_kms2 = +13.05` for the Phase 3 tier. Positive means it escapes Earth.

The suffix `_kms2` means km²/s², an energy per kilogram (and so also MJ/kg, by section A1.10). It is not km/s², an acceleration. Chapter A3 derives C3 in full.

Other shorthand in the repo:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ≈ or ~ | approximately |
| ≥ / ≤ | at least / at most |
| ± | plus or minus; e.g. tip speed modulated "~±3%" (`docs/glossary.md`) |
| Y15, Y17 | year 15 or 17 of the program's cash flow, not 2015 or 2017 |
| NPV@10% | net present value at a 10% discount rate: future money converted to today's value (section A1.6; Chapter A9) |
| **payback** | the year cumulative cash first turns positive (Chapter A9) |
| SF | safety factor (section A1.3); Rev A uses 2.5 (`rev_a.json`) |
| **Mach** | speed ÷ local speed of sound |

#### Worked Example 1.15: checking a loose number, "Mach 13.6"

Input: the founding document says the lower tip's 4.59 km/s ground-relative speed is "≈ Mach 13.6 at altitude" (`docs/project_instructions.md` §2.2).

```
Mach = speed ÷ speed of sound,  so  speed of sound = speed ÷ Mach
4,590 m/s ÷ 13.6 = 337.5 m/s
```

Result: 337.5 m/s is close to the speed of sound near sea level, about 340 m/s (from memory, verify). It is not a value for high altitude. At 290 km there is almost no air, so a Mach number has little meaning there. Read "Mach 13.6" as "very fast", not as a design number. [Likely]

---

### A1.15 How to read a JSON file

#### The format

**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is a plain-text format for structured data. Any text editor can open it. It has only a few building blocks:

| Building block | Looks like | Example from `rev_a.json` |
|---|---|---|
| **Object**: a set of key–value pairs | `{ "key": value, ... }` | the whole file; each block such as `"orbital": { ... }` |
| **Key**: a name, always in double quotes | `"v_tip_kms"` | |
| **Number** | `2.5`, `610`, `398600000000000.0` | `"v_tip_kms": 2.5` |
| **String**: text in double quotes | `"Zylon PBO"` | `"primary_fiber": "Zylon PBO"` |
| **Array**: an ordered list | `[a, b]` | `"mars_class_C3_8_to_13_tip_speed_kms": [3.3, 3.5]` |
| **null**: "no value" | `null` | `"fiber_cost_per_kg": null` |
| true / false | `true` | (not used in this file) |

Commas separate items. The order of keys inside an object carries no meaning. JSON allows **no comments**.

An analogy: nested folders. `kinematics` is a folder. `cislunar_revenue_gated_option` is a subfolder in it. `v_tip_kms` is a file in that subfolder, holding the value 2.8.

#### The shape of `rev_a.json`

The file has ten top-level blocks: `_meta`, `orbital`, `geometry`, `kinematics`, `materials`, `mass_ratio`, `reboost`, `market_thresholds`, `economics` and `heritage`. A trimmed excerpt, copied from the file:

```json
{
  "_meta": {
    "revision": "Rev A",
    "last_verified": "2026-07-02",
    "verification_memo": "VM-001"
  },
  "orbital": {
    "com_altitude_km": 610,
    "mu_earth_m3s2": 398600000000000.0,
    "v_orb_kms": 7.55,
    "_v_orb_note": "sqrt(mu/R_orbit); Certain"
  },
  "kinematics": {
    "v_tip_kms": 2.5,
    "cislunar_revenue_gated_option": {
      "confidence": "[Likely]",
      "v_tip_kms": 2.8
    }
  },
  "economics": {
    "fiber_cost_per_kg": null,
    "_fiber_cost_note": "WEAKEST INPUT — no vendor quote; obtain from Toyobo/Avient/Toray"
  }
}
```

#### This file's conventions

**Notes stand in for comments.** Since JSON has no comments, keys that start with `_` hold human notes. Example: `"_tip_accel_note": "v_tip^2 / L = (2500)^2 / 320000 = 19.53 m/s^2 = 1.99 g; Certain"`. Many notes carry a confidence label.

**null means unknown, not zero.** `fiber_cost_per_kg` is null because there is no vendor quote. `docs/DECISION_LOG.md` §8 adds that the model therefore "prices fiber *launch*, not fiber *purchase*". A zero would claim fibre is free. A null says nobody knows.

**Units live only in the key names.** The numbers carry none. Learn the suffixes:

| Suffix | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `_km` | kilometres | `com_altitude_km` 610 |
| `_kms` | km/s | `v_tip_kms` 2.5 |
| `_kms2` | km²/s² (energy per kg), not km/s² | `c3_kms2` −8.06 |
| `_m3s2` | m³/s² | `mu_earth_m3s2` |
| `_min` | minutes | `rotation_period_min` 13.4 |
| `_g` | multiples of standard gravity | `tip_acceleration_g` 1.99 |
| `_GPa`, `_kgm3`, `_MJkg` | GPa, kg/m³, MJ/kg | Zylon entries |
| `_t` | tonnes | `fiber_mass_t_at_5000kg_payload` 1476.3 |
| `_M` | millions of US dollars | `phase0_capex_M` 18 |
| `_kgs` | US dollars **per kg** (misleading: it reads like "kg per second") | `launch_price_anchor_dedicated_kgs` 3245 |
| `_fraction`, `_ratio` | no unit | `derate_fraction` 0.3, `tip_speed_to_Vc_ratio` 0.92 |

A related trap sits in the finance code. The field `ascent_losses_ms` in `finance/skyhook_finance.py` holds 1800.0 in the Conservative column, and it means 1,800 m/s (the workbook row is labelled "Ascent losses (m/s)"). In SI, "ms" means millisecond.

#### Reading it in code

A Python **module** is a `.py` file whose functions and values other code can import. `physics/skyhook_physics.py` loads the JSON file once, when the module is imported. The real code is:

```python
def load_params() -> dict:
    """Return the Rev A canonical parameter dict."""
    with open(_PARAMS_PATH) as f:
        return json.load(f)        # JSON object -> Python dict

PARAMS = load_params()
```

Reading values from it then looks like this (results shown as comments):

```python
PARAMS["orbital"]["com_altitude_km"]                                 # 610
PARAMS["kinematics"]["cislunar_revenue_gated_option"]["v_tip_kms"]   # 2.8
PARAMS["market_thresholds"]["mars_class_C3_8_to_13_tip_speed_kms"][1]  # 3.5 (arrays count from 0)
PARAMS["economics"]["fiber_cost_per_kg"]                             # None (Python's null)
```

Documents often write the same path with dots: `kinematics.cislunar_revenue_gated_option.v_tip_kms`.

#### Worked Example 1.16: what happens when a key does not exist

This is a real case on `main`.

`tools/sims/skyhook_no_leo_stress_test.jsx` is the simulator `CLAUDE.md` calls canonical. Line 48 reads:

```js
massRatioArmRange: revA.mass_ratio.tether_to_payload_single_arm_range,
```

Step 1. List the keys that actually exist under `mass_ratio` in `rev_a.json`:

```
integrated_tether_to_payload_both_arms,  tip_speed_to_Vc_ratio,  _ratio_note
```

There is no `tether_to_payload_single_arm_range`.

Step 2. In JavaScript, reading a missing key gives `undefined`, silently.

Step 3. Line 79, `const twoArmMassRatio = REVA.massRatioArmRange[1] * 2;`, sits at the top level of the file, so it runs as soon as the file loads. Indexing `undefined` throws an error. A Node.js check of the same pattern printed `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading '1')`.

Step 4. Python would have failed one step earlier, and more clearly: `PARAMS["mass_ratio"]["tether_to_payload_single_arm_range"]` raises `KeyError`.

Result: the declared canonical simulator would crash on load. `tools/sims/skyhook-sim.jsx` is a four-line re-export of it, so it inherits the crash. Yet `CLAUDE.md` lists both simulator flags ("Launch-price default drift" and "Strategy simulator overlap") as "[Certain] ... resolved", with no mention of this. [Certain from reading the code and a Node semantics check; the simulator was not run in a browser.]

By contrast, `tools/twin/params-loader.js` shows the safe pattern. Its `validateShape()` checks a list of `REQUIRED_PATHS` (plus one mass-ratio key) and throws a clear "FATAL" error if any is missing, instead of falling back to defaults.

Two more cautions:

- Editing a JSON value changes nothing unless some code reads that key. A search of the Python, JavaScript and HTML files on `main` finds no code that reads `com_radius_km`. The unmerged branch `claude/skyhook-fixes-2026-10-22` (`docs/DEVIATIONS.md` item #10) reaches the same finding: "The field is read by no code".
- A stored value can disagree with its own note or with a neighbour. Worked Example 1.10 showed `v_orb_kms` following one Earth radius while the tip-radius notes use another.

### Key takeaways

- A skyhook is a spinning tether in orbit. Its lower tip moves slower than orbital speed, its upper tip faster. At Rev A the tip speed is 2.5 km/s, so a payload gains 5.0 km/s per pass.
- The thesis is to sell high-energy Δv (to GTO and beyond), not to compete on cheap LEO launch.
- Rev A has three tiers: 2.5 km/s reference (121.83×, 609.1 t), 2.8 km/s cislunar option (295.27×, 1,476.3 t) and 3.5 km/s Phase 3 option (3,085.95×, 15,429.8 t). Small speed gains cost huge mass.
- The program is at "Pre-Phase 0". It has an $18M Phase 0 plan and no evidence in the repo of funding or hardware.
- `params/rev_a.json` is the source of truth. Units live in key suffixes. Notes live in `_` keys. `null` means unknown.
- Always carry units, convert before computing, keep full precision and round once at the end.
- A confidence label applies to one step of evidence. Ask "Certain about what?"
- Several documents disagree with each other and with the code. When they do, trust the JSON and the tested code, and say which you used. Even these are not perfect: the JSON mixes two Earth radii (Worked Example 1.10), and the simulator declared canonical crashes on load (Worked Example 1.16).
