## Chapter A2: Motion, force and rotation

**Main idea:** Every Skyhook tip speed is two motions added together as arrows, the hub's orbital motion plus the tip's spin around the hub, and holding a payload on that spin takes a steady inward pull from the tether that the payload feels as about 2 g.

This chapter gives you the mechanics needed to read four numbers in `params/rev_a.json`. You will be able to rebuild each of them by hand. As in Chapter A1, "canon" means the official values stored in that file.

| Quantity | Canon value | Field in `params/rev_a.json` | Function in `physics/skyhook_physics.py` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rotation period | 13.4 min | `geometry.rotation_period_min` | `rotation_period_min()` |
| Tip acceleration | 1.99 g | `kinematics.tip_acceleration_g` | `tip_acceleration_g()` |
| Upper-tip release speed | 10.06 km/s | `kinematics.v_upper_release_kms` | `v_upper_release_kms()` |
| Lower-tip ground-relative speed | 4.59 km/s | `kinematics.v_lower_tip_groundrel_kms` | `v_lower_tip_groundrel_kms()` |

One input is taken on trust here: the hub circles Earth at about 7.55 km/s. Chapter A3 explains why. In this chapter, "the hub moves at v_orb" is simply given.

We start with units and arrows, then Newton's laws, then circles, then viewpoints ("frames"). At the end we assemble the Rev A tether and check every number against the code.

### A2.1 Quantities and units

A **physical quantity** is a number times a **unit**, for example "320 km". A number without a unit means nothing. "2.5" could be 2.5 m/s, a gentle jog, or 2.5 km/s, a thousand times faster.

The **SI** (Système International) is the standard set of units. Three **base units** matter here:

| Base unit | Symbol | Measures |
|---|---|---|
| metre | m | length |
| kilogram | kg | mass |
| second | s | time |

**Derived units** are built from the base units:

```
speed          m/s
acceleration   m/s²     (metres per second, per second)
force          N        1 newton = 1 kg·m/s²
```

A **newton** (N) is the force that speeds up 1 kg by 1 m/s every second. A **kilonewton** (kN) is 1,000 N.

**The repo habit.** `params/rev_a.json` stores lengths in km and speeds in km/s. The field names end in `_km` or `_kms` so you can tell. The functions convert to metres inside the formula. For example, `tip_acceleration_g()` (`physics/skyhook_physics.py` lines 122–131) computes:

```python
a_ms2 = (v_tip_kms * 1e3) ** 2 / (L_km * 1e3)
```

The `* 1e3` turns km into m. [Certain]

**Why this matters.** Watch what happens to v²/L at Rev A if you mix units:

```
wrong (km/s squared, divided by metres):   2.5² / 320,000  = 0.0000195    meaningless
consistent km units:                        2.5² / 320      = 0.01953 km/s²
convert km/s² to m/s²:                      0.01953 × 1000  = 19.53 m/s²
```

A missed km-to-m conversion is a factor-of-1,000 error. The Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 partly because one team used pound-force seconds and another used newton-seconds (from memory, verify). Units are not bookkeeping. They are part of the physics.

### A2.2 Scalars and vectors

A **scalar** is a quantity with size only. Mass (5,000 kg), time (13.4 min) and temperature are scalars.

A **vector** is a quantity with size and direction. Displacement, velocity, acceleration and force are vectors. Draw a vector as an arrow. The arrow's length is its **magnitude**. The way it points is its **direction**.

**Analogy.** Directions to a café: "300 m east, then 400 m north." The café is 500 m away "as the crow flies". The two legs are the vector's parts. The 500 m is its magnitude.

Those parts are called **components**. Pick two perpendicular axes, x and y. Any flat (two-dimensional) vector is "so much along x plus so much along y". Pythagoras gives the magnitude:

```
v   = (v_x, v_y)                components, m/s
|v| = sqrt(v_x² + v_y²)         magnitude, m/s
```

Tiny example: v = (3, 4) m/s, so |v| = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 m/s.

A **unit vector** is an arrow of length exactly 1. It carries direction only. Multiply it by a number to get an arrow of that length in that direction. The **orbit theater** (`tools/sims/skyhook_orbit_theater.html`), a 3D browser animation of the tether, uses unit vectors called `radial()` and `tangent()` (lines 110–111): one points straight up away from Earth, one points along the direction of travel.

**Speed versus velocity.** **Speed** is a scalar: the magnitude of the velocity. **Velocity** is the vector. A tether tip moving round a circle at a steady 2.5 km/s has constant speed but a velocity that changes every instant, because its direction keeps turning. This one distinction drives most of this chapter.

**Project tie-in.** `params/rev_a.json` stores magnitudes only: `"v_tip_kms": 2.5`. Directions are implied by words such as "at the bottom of the swing". The simulators store full vectors as components. The **digital twin** (`tools/twin/`) is a browser simulation that models the tether as a chain of 17 point masses, called **nodes**, joined by stretchy segments. It keeps a flat list of `[x, y, vx, vy]` for every node (`tools/twin/physics.js` lines 88–91, "Earth-centered inertial frame"). Its `tipSpeedRelCom()` (lines 344–347) turns a velocity vector back into a speed with `Math.hypot(vx, vy)`, which is exactly sqrt(vx² + vy²). The Python model `physics/tether_dynamics.py` uses the same layout. [Certain]

### A2.3 Position, displacement, velocity and acceleration

Four linked ideas describe motion.

- **Position** (r): where something is, measured from a chosen origin. It is a vector.
- **Displacement** (Δr): the change in position between two moments. The Greek letter Δ ("delta") means "change in".
- **Velocity** (v): how fast position changes, and in which direction.
- **Acceleration** (a): how fast velocity changes, in size or in direction.

In calculus language, velocity is the **derivative** of position with respect to time, and acceleration is the derivative of velocity. A derivative is just "the rate of change at an instant". Over a finite time you use averages:

```
Δr = r(t₂) − r(t₁)                     displacement, m
v  = dr/dt     average: Δr / Δt        velocity, m/s
a  = dv/dt     average: Δv / Δt        acceleration, m/s²
```

If acceleration is constant and you start at rest:

```
v = a·t              speed after time t
x = ½·a·t²           distance after time t
```

Tiny example: a car goes from 0 to 100 km/h in 10 s. First convert: 100 km/h = 100,000 m ÷ 3,600 s = 27.8 m/s. Then a = 27.8 ÷ 10 = 2.78 m/s².

**Acceleration does not mean "speeding up".** Any change of velocity counts, including a change of direction alone. A tip on a circle at constant speed is accelerating all the time (Section A2.8).

**Project tie-in: why acceleration makes the catch hard.** The founding document asks the catch vehicle to match the tip "within meters" of position and "within ~1 m/s" of velocity, over a window of "3–10 seconds" (`docs/project_instructions.md` §4.3). Acceleration decides how long a match lasts. If the tip accelerates at a rate a (in m/s²) relative to a coasting vehicle, a perfect velocity match grows into a 1 m/s mismatch after t = 1/a seconds.

The catch-window study on an unmerged branch (claude/creative-catch-window-lab, `docs/research/cw001_catch_window.md`, Bottom line item 2) uses a relative acceleration of 20.34 m/s² (Section A2.10 explains where that number comes from):

```
velocity gate ±1 m/s:   t = 1 / 20.34              = 0.049 s  = 49 ms
position gate ±10 m:    t = sqrt(2 × 10 / 20.34)   = sqrt(0.983) = 0.99 s
```

So the velocity match survives for about 49 ms either side of the best moment, not seconds. That study labels this arithmetic [Certain], and it is a screening study on a branch that is not merged. The guide returns to it under "Limits and known problems".

### A2.4 Relative velocity and vector addition

Every velocity is measured relative to something. "60 km/h" on a car means relative to the road. **Relative velocity** is the velocity of one object as seen from another.

The rule for chaining viewpoints is vector addition:

```
v(A relative to ground) = v(A relative to B) + v(B relative to ground)
```

**Analogy.** An airport moving walkway runs at 1.0 m/s. Walk forward on it at 1.5 m/s and you pass the floor at 1.0 + 1.5 = 2.5 m/s. Turn round and walk back at 1.5 m/s and you pass the floor at 1.0 − 1.5 = −0.5 m/s, which means 0.5 m/s backwards.

**The key rule.** You may add or subtract plain speeds only when the arrows are parallel or opposite. Otherwise you must add the components.

Tiny example: a boat heads straight across a river at 3 m/s. The current runs downstream at 4 m/s. The two arrows are perpendicular. The boat's speed past the bank is sqrt(3² + 4²) = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 m/s, not 3 + 4 = 7 m/s.

**Project tie-in.** **EQ-3**, the repo's tip-speed equation in `physics/skyhook_physics.py` (Section A2.13 writes it out), is the walkway problem.

- The hub is the walkway. It moves along its orbit at v_orb.
- The tip is the walker. It moves at v_tip relative to the hub.
- At the very top and bottom of the swing, the tip's arrow is parallel or opposite to the hub's arrow. So EQ-3 can use plain addition and subtraction.
- At any other angle you need components. The orbit theater does this with `THREE.Vector3` arrows in `tipVel()` (`tools/sims/skyhook_orbit_theater.html` lines 117–122).

[Certain] Section A2.13 works this out with real numbers.

### A2.5 Newton's three laws

Isaac Newton's three laws of motion (published 1687, from memory, verify) are the foundation of everything in the physics module.

**First law (inertia).** An object keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed unless a **net force** acts on it. The net force is the sum of all forces, added as vectors. **Inertia** is the tendency to keep doing what you are doing.

A consequence follows at once. Anything moving in a circle is not moving in a straight line. So something must be pushing or pulling it toward the centre.

**Second law.** The net force equals mass times acceleration:

```
F_net = m · a        F in newtons (N), m in kg, a in m/s²
p     = m · v        momentum, kg·m/s
F_net = dp/dt        general form: force is the rate of change of momentum
```

**Momentum** (p) is mass times velocity. It is a vector. Chapter A5 is built on it.

Tiny example: a 1,000 kg car accelerating at 2.78 m/s² needs F = 1,000 × 2.78 = 2,780 N of net push from the road.

**Third law.** Forces come in equal and opposite pairs. If the tether pulls the payload inward, the payload pulls the tether outward with the same force.

**How the code uses each law.**

| Law | Where it shows up | What the code does |
|---|---|---|
| First | `tools/sims/skyhook_orbit_theater.html` `loop()`, lines 152–159 | After release, only gravity acts on the payload. It coasts. |
| Second | `tools/twin/physics.js` `_deriv()`, line 236 and line 260 | Gravity gives `gf = -mu/r³` times position; each segment force is divided by node mass: `ax[j] += fx / this.m[j]` |
| Third | `tools/twin/physics.js` `_deriv()`, lines 258–263 | A segment adds `+fx` to node j and subtracts the same `fx` from node j+1 |

The third-law lines are worth reading once, because they are so plain:

```javascript
ax[j]     += fx / this.m[j];       // segment pulls node j one way
ay[j]     += fy / this.m[j];
ax[j + 1] -= fx / this.m[j + 1];   // and node j+1 the opposite way
ay[j + 1] -= fy / this.m[j + 1];
```

The Python reference model, which the JavaScript twin is a port of, has the same structure (`physics/tether_dynamics.py` lines 222–225). [Certain]

**Two consequences for Skyhook.**

- *Release is the first law in action.* Releasing the payload means removing the tether's force. The payload then moves off along the direction it was travelling at that instant: the **tangent** to the circle. It is not "flung outward".
- *Catching and throwing is the third law in action.* When the tether speeds the payload up, the payload slows the tether down, and the tether's orbit sinks. The founding document calls this trading momentum (`docs/project_instructions.md` §2.4). Chapter A5 covers the bookkeeping.

**Common mistakes.**

| Mistake | Correction |
|---|---|
| "A force is needed to keep moving." | A force is needed to *change* motion. |
| "At release, the payload is flung outward." | It leaves along the tangent, at the velocity it had. |
| "Centripetal force is a special kind of force." | It is a job that a real force does: tension for the tether, gravity for an orbit, tyre friction for a car. |

### A2.6 Mass, weight, standard gravity and g-load

**Mass** (kg) is how much matter an object has. Equivalently, it is how hard the object is to accelerate. A 5,000 kg payload has the same mass on the launch pad, in orbit and on the tether tip.

**Weight** (N) is the force of gravity on that mass:

```
W = m · g        W in N, m in kg, g = local gravitational acceleration in m/s²
```

So "kg" is not a weight. Bathroom scales quietly divide by g to show you kilograms.

**Standard gravity** g₀ is a fixed reference number:

```
g₀ = 9.80665 m/s²   (exact, by definition)
```

It was adopted as a convention in 1901 (from memory, verify). It is not the gravity at any particular place. Real surface gravity runs from about 9.78 m/s² at the equator to about 9.83 m/s² at the poles (from memory, verify).

A **g-load** expresses an acceleration as a multiple of g₀:

```
n = a / g₀       dimensionless, read as "n g"
```

#### Proper acceleration: what you actually feel

An **accelerometer** is a small mass on a spring. It cannot sense gravity, because gravity pulls the mass and its case equally. It senses only the *other* forces: a floor pushing up, a cable pulling, a rocket engine thrusting. What it reads is called **proper acceleration**: those non-gravitational forces divided by mass.

| Situation | What an accelerometer reads |
|---|---|
| Standing on the ground | 1 g, upward (the floor pushes you up) |
| In **free fall**, which includes being in orbit | 0 g |
| Payload hanging on the Skyhook tip | about 2 g, pointing toward the hub (Sections A2.9 and A2.10) |

**Analogy.** In a lift (elevator) that starts upward, you feel heavier. If the cable snapped, you and the car would fall together and you would float inside it. Nothing about gravity changed. Only the floor stopped pushing.

**Orbit is not "no gravity".** Gravity weakens with distance from Earth's centre as μ/r², where μ is Earth's gravitational parameter (Chapter A3 explains it). Using μ = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² (`params/rev_a.json` `orbital.mu_earth_m3s2`) and the code's radii (`R_EARTH_KM = 6371.0`, `physics/skyhook_physics.py` line 40):

```
at the surface   r = 6,371 km:   g = 3.986e14 / (6.371e6)²  = 3.986e14 / 4.059e13 = 9.82 m/s²
at the hub       r = 6,981 km:   g = 3.986e14 / (6.981e6)²  = 3.986e14 / 4.873e13 = 8.18 m/s²
ratio                             8.18 / 9.82                = 0.83
```

Gravity at 610 km is still 83% of surface gravity. Astronauts float because they and their station fall together, not because gravity has gone. [Certain]

The 9.82 m/s² surface figure is slightly above g₀. This simple formula ignores Earth's spin and its flattened shape, which both lower the gravity you measure at the surface (from memory, verify).

**Project tie-in.** `G_STD = 9.80665` (`physics/skyhook_physics.py` line 41) converts m/s² into g in `tip_acceleration_g()`. The same value appears in `tools/twin/physics.js` line 23, in `finance/leg_cost.py` line 46 (`g0_ms2`, where it turns rocket **specific impulse**, an engine-efficiency rating measured in seconds, into exhaust speed; Chapter A4 explains it), and as a duplicate local constant in `tests/test_tether_dynamics.py` line 39.

Two tools use a different "g". `tools/sims/skyhook_program_site.html` (lines 1172, 1177, 1191, 1209) and `tools/sims/skyhook_calculator.jsx` (lines 252, 268) divide by 9.81. At Rev A that gives 19.53125 / 9.81 = 1.99095 g against 19.53125 / 9.80665 = 1.99163 g. The difference is 0.03% and harmless. It does mean the repo has two definitions of "g". [Certain]

#### Worked example 2.1: mass versus weight for the design payload

Input: payload mass m = 5,000 kg (`params/rev_a.json` `mass_ratio.integrated_tether_to_payload_both_arms.payload_mass_kg_for_tonnage`, line 82). Standard gravity g₀ = 9.80665 m/s² (`physics/skyhook_physics.py` line 41). Hub-altitude gravity 8.179 m/s² (computed above).

```
weight on the pad:            W = 5,000 × 9.80665  = 49,033 N  ≈ 49.0 kN
gravity force at 610 km:      F = 5,000 × 8.179    = 40,895 N  ≈ 40.9 kN
what it feels while coasting at 610 km:              0 g (free fall)
```

Gravity still pulls on the payload with about 41 kN in orbit. The payload feels nothing, because nothing else pushes on it. Keep this in mind: on the tether tip, the payload will feel the tether, not gravity. [Certain]

### A2.7 Angles, radians and angular velocity

Degrees are a human convention: 360 to a circle. Physics prefers the **radian** (rad). One radian is the angle at which the arc you travel along the circle equals the radius. A full circle is 2π radians:

```
2π rad = 360°            1 rad ≈ 57.3°
s = r · θ                arc length (m) = radius (m) × angle (rad)
```

**Angular velocity** ω (the Greek letter omega) is how fast an angle changes, in rad/s. On a rigid spinning object, a point at distance r from the centre moves at:

```
ω = dθ / dt              rad/s
v = ω · r                m/s
```

**Intuition.** On a merry-go-round, every point turns through the same angle in the same time. So all points share one ω. Points further out travel bigger circles in that time, so they move faster.

Tiny example: a merry-go-round turns once every 6 s. ω = 2π / 6 = 1.047 rad/s. A child sitting 3 m out moves at v = 1.047 × 3 = 3.14 m/s.

**Units that look alike.** rad/s, **revolutions per minute (rpm)** and revolutions per second (**hertz, Hz**) are different. Convert with 1 revolution = 2π rad.

**Project tie-in.** The tether spins at ω = v_tip / L. The code sets it directly:

```python
self.omega = cfg.v_tip_kms * 1e3 / L      # physics/tether_dynamics.py line 96
```

and `this.omega = (cfg.vTipKms * 1e3) / L` in `tools/twin/physics.js` line 103. The legend of the program site (`tools/sims/skyhook_program_site.html`, the project's explainer web page) quotes "v_tip/L ≈ 0.0078 rad/s" (line 241). Worked example 2.2 computes it exactly. A point halfway out along the arm, 160 km from the hub, moves at 0.0078125 × 160 = 1.25 km/s relative to the hub. [Certain]

### A2.8 Uniform circular motion: period and centripetal acceleration

**Uniform circular motion** means going round a circle at constant speed. Three formulas describe it:

```
T   = 2π·r / v  = 2π / ω         period: time for one full lap, s
f   = 1 / T                      frequency: laps per second, Hz
a_c = v² / r   = ω²·r  = ω·v     centripetal acceleration, m/s², pointing to the centre
```

**Period** (T) is circumference divided by speed. That one is easy. **Frequency** (f) is its inverse: laps per second.

**Centripetal acceleration** (from Latin for "centre-seeking") needs a picture. Here is a calculus-light derivation.

1. In a short time Δt, the object moves round by an angle Δθ = ω·Δt.
2. Its velocity arrow keeps the same length v but turns through that same angle Δθ.
3. The change in the arrow is a short arrow of length about v·Δθ. It points toward the centre of the circle.
4. Divide the change by the time: a = v·Δθ / Δt = v·ω.
5. Substitute ω = v / r: a = v² / r.

So a body on a circle accelerates toward the centre even though its speed never changes. [Certain]

**How it scales.**

| Change | Effect on a_c = v²/r |
|---|---|
| Double the speed, same radius | 4 times larger |
| Double the radius, same speed | half as large |
| Double the radius, same ω | twice as large (a_c = ω²r) |

Tiny example: a car takes a bend of radius 50 m at 20 m/s. a = 20² / 50 = 400 / 50 = 8 m/s², which is 8 / 9.80665 = 0.82 g. Tyre friction supplies the force.

#### Worked example 2.2: Rev A spin rate, period and tip acceleration

Inputs:

| Input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Tip speed relative to the hub, v_tip | 2.5 km/s = 2,500 m/s | `params/rev_a.json` `kinematics.v_tip_kms` (line 23) |
| Half-length, L | 320 km = 320,000 m | `params/rev_a.json` `geometry.tether_half_length_km` (line 16) |
| Standard gravity, g₀ | 9.80665 m/s² | `physics/skyhook_physics.py` `G_STD` (line 41) |

Step 1, spin rate:

```
ω = v_tip / L = 2.5 km/s / 320 km = 0.0078125 rad/s
in degrees:     0.0078125 × 57.2958 = 0.4476 °/s
in rpm:         0.0078125 × 60 / (2π) = 0.0746 rpm
```

Step 2, period:

```
circumference = 2π × L = 2 × 3.14159 × 320   = 2,010.62 km
T             = 2,010.62 km / 2.5 km/s       = 804.25 s
in minutes    = 804.25 / 60                  = 13.404 min      (canon: 13.4)
```

Step 3, centripetal acceleration at the tip:

```
a = v_tip² / L = 2,500² / 320,000 = 6,250,000 / 320,000 = 19.53125 m/s²
check with ω:  a = ω² × L = 0.0078125² × 320,000 = 0.000061035 × 320,000 = 19.53125 m/s²
```

Step 4, convert to g:

```
n = 19.53125 / 9.80665 = 1.99163 g      (canon: 1.99)
```

The repo agrees. Calling the functions directly gives `rotation_period_min(2.5, 320)` = 13.40412865531645 and `tip_acceleration_g(2.5, 320)` = 1.9916332284725162. [Certain]

The tether turns once every 13.4 minutes, and a payload on the tip is pulled toward the hub at almost exactly twice the standard Earth gravity.

#### Worked example 2.3: the same tip speed on shorter or longer tethers

Why is the tether so long? At a fixed tip speed, a = v²/L. A shorter tether means a tighter circle and a harder pull. Inputs: v_tip = 2.5 km/s (`params/rev_a.json`), g₀ = 9.80665 m/s². The 6 g threshold comes from `tests/test_rev_a_physics.py` line 113.

| Half-length L | a = 2,500² / L | g-load | Period 2πL/v |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 km | 6,250,000 / 50,000 = 125.0 m/s² | 12.75 g | 2.09 min |
| 100 km | 6,250,000 / 100,000 = 62.5 m/s² | 6.37 g | 4.19 min |
| 150 km | 6,250,000 / 150,000 = 41.7 m/s² | 4.25 g | 6.28 min |
| **320 km (Rev A)** | 6,250,000 / 320,000 = 19.5 m/s² | **1.99 g** | **13.40 min** |
| 600 km | 6,250,000 / 600,000 = 10.4 m/s² | 1.06 g | 25.13 min |

Two inverse questions:

```
L that gives 6 g at 2.5 km/s:     L = v² / (6 × g₀) = 6,250,000 / 58.84 = 106,220 m ≈ 106 km
v_tip that gives 6 g at L = 320 km: v = sqrt(6 × 9.80665 × 320,000) = sqrt(18,828,768) = 4,339 m/s
```

At 320 km, the tip could spin up to about 4.34 km/s before hitting the test's 6 g line. So at Rev A's length, tip speed is limited by tether mass, not by g-load: `params/rev_a.json` puts the conservative tether-to-payload mass ratio at 121.83x for 2.5 km/s and 3,085.95x for 3.5 km/s (Chapter A6). [Certain as arithmetic]

On short tethers the g-load does bite. The in-space fork study in `finance/inspace_fork.py`, a draft that its own header calls non-canonical, sweeps half-lengths of only 50–150 km (`L_HALF_GRID_KM`, line 43). It accepts only geometries with `tip_g <= 2.0` (`select_reference()`, line 166), so g-load is an active design filter there. [Certain]

#### The three speed tiers

`params/rev_a.json` defines a reference tier and two options. The v² scaling shows clearly:

| Tier | v_tip | ω = v_tip/L | Period | a = v²/L | g-load (canon) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rev A reference | 2.5 km/s | 0.0078125 rad/s | 13.40 min | 19.53 m/s² | 1.99 g (1.99) |
| Cislunar option, revenue-gated | 2.8 km/s | 0.00875 rad/s | 11.97 min | 24.50 m/s² | 2.50 g (2.5) |
| Phase 3 growth option | 3.5 km/s | 0.0109375 rad/s | 9.57 min | 38.28 m/s² | 3.90 g (3.9) |

Canon values are from `kinematics.cislunar_revenue_gated_option` and `kinematics.phase3_growth_option`. Canon stores no periods for the two options; the period column is computed with `rotation_period_min()`. Going from 2.5 to 3.5 km/s is a 40% speed increase but a 96% load increase, because 1.4² = 1.96. [Certain]

The tier names are destinations. Per `params/rev_a.json`, the 2.5 km/s reference throws to GTO/high-elliptical orbits (long ellipses reaching geostationary height and beyond), the 2.8 km/s option reaches cislunar (Moon-distance) energy, and the 3.5 km/s option reaches Mars-class escape. Chapter A3 explains these orbits.

### A2.9 Tension: the force that supplies the inward pull

**Tension** is the pulling force carried along a rope or cable. A cable can pull. It cannot push. If you try to push on a rope, it goes slack.

Both dynamics models code this rule literally. In `tools/twin/physics.js`, a segment shorter than its rest length gets no force (line 249, `if (ext <= 0.0) continue; // slack cable`), and a damped tension is clamped at zero (line 256, `// a cable cannot push`). `physics/tether_dynamics.py` has the same lines (210 and 219). [Certain]

**Tension supplies the centripetal force.** The first law says a payload on the tip would fly off in a straight line. The second law says the inward force needed is mass times centripetal acceleration. The tether supplies it:

```
T_tip = m_payload · v_tip² / L = m_payload · ω² · L        N
```

Tiny example: a 0.5 kg ball on a 1 m string turns twice per second. ω = 2 × 2π = 12.57 rad/s. T = 0.5 × 12.57² × 1 = 0.5 × 158 = 79 N.

#### Worked example 2.4: the pull on a 5-tonne payload

Inputs: m = 5,000 kg (`params/rev_a.json` line 82); a = 19.53125 m/s² (Worked example 2.2); g₀ = 9.80665 m/s².

```
tension at the tip:        T = 5,000 × 19.53125     = 97,656 N ≈ 97.7 kN
weight on the ground:      W = 5,000 × 9.80665      = 49,033 N
ratio:                     T / W = 97,656 / 49,033  = 1.99
crane-load equivalent:     97,656 / 9.80665         = 9,958 kg
```

The tip holds a 5 t payload as hard as a crane on Earth holds about 10 t. That is just under twice the payload's ground weight. [Certain]

**Tension grows toward the hub.** Tension at any point along the arm must hold everything outboard of it: the payload plus all the tether beyond that point. Each bit of tether at distance s from the hub needs its own inward pull, m·ω²·s. Adding these from the tip inward gives the tension at each point.

The twin does exactly this sum in `_discreteStaticTensions()` (`tools/twin/physics.js` lines 192–207):

```javascript
acc += this.m[j] * this.omega ** 2 * Math.abs(this.s[j]);   // add m·ω²·|s| of each outboard node
t[j] = acc;                                                  // tension carried by segment j
```

The Python version is `_discrete_static_tensions()` (`physics/tether_dynamics.py` lines 160–174). This growth of tension toward the hub is why the tether must get thicker toward the middle. Chapter A6 calls that taper and turns it into tether mass. [Certain]

#### Centrifugal force: a viewpoint effect

Ride along on the spinning tether and the payload seems to be pushed outward. That apparent push is called **centrifugal force** ("centre-fleeing"). It is a **fictitious force**: it appears only because your viewpoint is rotating (Section A2.11).

Now take a non-rotating viewpoint that rides with the free-falling hub. Gravity still acts on the payload, but it pulls the hub almost equally, so in this falling viewpoint it nearly cancels (the small leftover is the gravity gradient of Section A2.10). That leaves one force that matters: the inward tension. The payload accelerates inward, as Section A2.8 says. Both descriptions predict the same tension, 97.7 kN. They are two ways of doing the same sum. [Certain]

A common mistake is to say "centrifugal force throws the payload out at release". It does not. Release removes the tension, and the payload carries on along the tangent.

### A2.10 What the payload feels: g-loads on the ride

From catch to release, the payload hangs on the tip. Its accelerometer reads about 2 g, pointing along the tether toward the hub. For the payload, "down" points away from the hub.

That "down" turns with the tether. At the bottom of the swing, the payload's "down" points toward Earth. Half a turn later, at the top, it points away from Earth. It is like a slow Ferris wheel whose seat is bolted to the spoke.

**How long the ride lasts.** A payload caught at the bottom and thrown at the top rides about half a turn. Half the 13.40 min inertial period is 6.7 min. Measured from "straight down" to "straight up" along the turning local vertical, it is about 15.56 / 2 = 7.8 min (Worked example 2.6 explains the 15.56). [Likely; derived here. The actual release phase is chosen per mission, `docs/project_instructions.md` §5.1.] So this is a load held for minutes, not a brief jolt.

**Load thresholds in the repo.**

| Where | Rule | Source given? |
|---|---|---|
| `tests/test_rev_a_physics.py` `test_payload_qualification_load` (lines 108–113) | asserts tip g < 6.0, "payload qualification warning threshold" | No |
| `tools/sims/skyhook_calculator.jsx` line 153 | warns when `atip > 60` m/s² (about 6.1 g) | No |
| `tools/sims/skyhook_program_site.html` lines 1177, 1209 | warns above 6 g ("re-rate payload adapters and grapple") | No |
| `finance/inspace_fork.py` `select_reference()` line 166 | accepts only `tip_g <= 2.0` | No |
| `docs/objections_faq.md` #10 | 1.99 / 2.50 / 3.9 g are "within standard satellite qualification levels, comparable to launch loads", labelled [Certain] | Points only to "Site calculator; legend", not to any qualification standard |

For comparison, the Space Shuttle throttled its ascent to stay near 3 g (from memory, verify). Satellite launch design loads are typically a few g along the rocket's axis (from memory, verify). None of these comparisons is in the repo.

The founding document is careful: payloads and capture gear "must be rated for this, plus dynamic transients" (`docs/project_instructions.md` §2.2). The next worked example shows that even the steady part is a little larger than 1.99 g.

#### Worked example 2.5: the load the payload actually feels at the catch

The 1.99 g figure is the centripetal term only. It treats the tether as if it spun in empty space. In orbit, one more effect enters: the **gravity gradient**, meaning that gravity is slightly different at the two ends of a long object.

Think it through in steps.

1. The hub is in free fall. It accelerates toward Earth at g_hub, the gravity at its own radius.
2. The lower tip goes round the hub. So its total acceleration is g_hub (down) plus the centripetal part v²/L (up, toward the hub).
3. Gravity at the lower tip is stronger than at the hub, because the tip is 320 km closer to Earth.
4. Gravity alone would pull the tip down harder than the hub. So the tether must pull up a little more than v²/L to keep the tip on its circle. The extra is g_tip − g_hub.

Inputs: μ = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² (`params/rev_a.json`); hub radius R0 = 6,981 km (6,371 + 610, `physics/skyhook_physics.py` line 40 and `rev_a.json` `orbital.com_altitude_km`); L = 320 km; v²/L = 19.53125 m/s² (Worked example 2.2).

```
lower-tip radius          R0 − L = 6,981 − 320                 = 6,661 km
gravity at lower tip      3.986e14 / (6.661e6)²                = 8.98377 m/s²
gravity at hub            3.986e14 / (6.981e6)²                = 8.17903 m/s²
gravity gradient          8.98377 − 8.17903                    = 0.80473 m/s²
felt acceleration         19.53125 + 0.80473                   = 20.33598 m/s²
in g                      20.33598 / 9.80665                   = 2.074 g
```

At the upper tip the same logic gives 8.17903 − 7.47778 = 0.70126 m/s² extra, so 20.2325 m/s² = 2.063 g.

An accelerometer on the payload reads about 2.07 g at the catch, not 1.99 g. That is 4% more. Call this the **felt load at the catch**. The unmerged catch-window study reaches the same answer (branch claude/creative-catch-window-lab, `docs/research/cw001_catch_window.md`, Bottom line item 6: "the payload sees 2.07 g at the catch, not canon's 1.99 g", gradient 0.805 m/s²). That study is careful to say canon "is not wrong, it is a different quantity". The 20.34 m/s² used in Section A2.3 is this felt acceleration. [Certain as arithmetic; the canon number is not wrong but answers a different question]

**Transients come on top.** A real catch jerks the tether. The repo's **dynamic load factor**, the ratio of peak to steady tension during a catch, is estimated at about 1.30 to 1.47 and labelled [Speculative] (`docs/glossary.md`, "Dynamic load factor"). Chapter A7 covers it.

### A2.11 Reference frames

A **reference frame** is a viewpoint: an origin, a set of axes and a clock. You measure positions and velocities against it. The same object can have very different speeds in different frames. None of them is "the true one". But every stated number belongs to a stated frame, and mixing frames causes real errors.

Two kinds matter.

- An **inertial frame** does not accelerate and does not rotate. In practice that means its axes are fixed relative to the distant stars. Newton's laws work in it exactly as written. (An Earth-centred frame is not perfectly inertial, because Earth itself circles the Sun. For motion near Earth the error is negligible, which is why everyone uses it.)
- A **rotating frame**, or more generally a **non-inertial frame**, turns or accelerates. In it, extra fictitious forces appear: centrifugal force, pushing outward, and **Coriolis force**, pushing sideways on anything that moves within the frame.

**The frames Skyhook numbers live in.**

| Frame | Who "sits" in it | Rotates? | Skyhook numbers that live here |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Earth-centred inertial (ECI)** | an observer fixed to the stars, at Earth's centre | no | hub 7.55 km/s; upper-tip release 10.06 km/s; lower tip 5.06 km/s (`materials/core.md`; `docs/program_manifest.md` line 6 "catch 5.05 km/s ECI") |
| Hub frame, non-rotating | a rider on the hub who does not spin | no | v_tip = 2.5 km/s "relative to center of mass" (`docs/project_instructions.md` §2.2) |
| Tether-fixed frame | a rider on the tether | yes, at ω | the payload is at rest and "feels" about 2 g outward |
| **Local vertical** frame (often called LVLH, local-vertical local-horizontal) | axes pointing "down to Earth" and "along track" | yes, once per orbit | defines the "bottom" and "top" of the swing |
| Earth-fixed (ground) | the launch pad | yes, once per day | lower tip about 4.59 km/s "ground-relative" (strictly 4.57 km/s in this frame at the tip's 290 km height; see Limits, item 5) |

**Converting between frames.**

```
sliding frames:       v(object, seen in A) = v(object, seen in B) + v(frame B, seen in A)
rotating frame:       v_inertial = v_origin + ω_frame × r_rel + v_rel
     v_origin   velocity of the frame's origin, m/s
     ω_frame    the frame's own rotation rate, rad/s
     r_rel      position measured from that origin, m
     v_rel      velocity seen inside the rotating frame, m/s
```

The symbol × here is a **cross product**: for motion in a plane, ω × r is an arrow of length ω·|r| at right angles to r. The middle term, ω_frame × r_rel, is the one people forget. Section "Limits and known problems" shows a project tool that forgets it.

**What the repo uses.** Both dynamics models work in ECI. `tools/twin/physics.js` says so in its class comment (line 90) and gives each node the initial velocity `vOrb + this.omega * this.s[i]` (line 160). Here ω is the inertial spin rate. Earth is drawn fixed in the twin because "the ECI frame is non-rotating" (`tools/twin/twin.js` lines 478–480). `physics/tether_dynamics.py` does the same (line 139). [Certain]

#### Worked example 2.6: one spin every 13.4 minutes, but a bottom pass every 15.6

The 13.4 min period from Worked example 2.2 is the time for one turn **relative to the stars**. "Bottom of the swing" is defined relative to the local vertical: the arm pointing straight down, toward Earth's centre. The "straight down" direction itself turns once per orbit, at the hub's **orbital angular rate** n, in the same direction as the spin. So the arm has to turn a little more than one full circle to point straight down again. The time it takes is the **bottom-to-bottom interval**.

Inputs: ω = 0.0078125 rad/s (Worked example 2.2); v_orb = 7.55631 km/s from `v_orbital_kms(610)` (`physics/skyhook_physics.py` lines 79–91); r = 6,981 km.

```
orbital angular rate        n = v_orb / r = 7.55631 / 6,981           = 0.0010824 rad/s
orbit period                2π / n = 6.28319 / 0.0010824              = 5,804.8 s = 96.75 min
spin relative to vertical   ω − n = 0.0078125 − 0.0010824             = 0.0067301 rad/s
bottom-to-bottom time       2π / 0.0067301                            = 933.6 s  = 15.56 min
cross-check                 1 / (1/13.404 − 1/96.747) = 1 / 0.064268  = 15.56 min
per orbit                   96.747 / 13.404 = 7.22 spins, but 7.22 − 1 = 6.22 bottom passes
```

So the lower tip reaches the bottom of its swing about every 15.56 minutes, not every 13.4. [Certain as arithmetic for a rigid tether]

The twin agrees. Its physics port (`tools/twin/physics.js`, gravity on, Rev A parameters) was run for one orbit for this guide. Starting from straight down at t = 0, the lower tip pointed straight down again at 952.2 s, 1,904.4 s, 2,856.6 s and so on: every 15.87 min. That is slightly longer than 15.56 min because, in orbit, the average tip speed sags to about 2,458 m/s (Limits, item 1). Put that sagged speed into the same formula and it gives 2π / (2,458 / 320,000 − 0.0010824) = 952.2 s, exactly what the twin measured. [Certain; run on commit 34935cb]

The repo never states this interval. The founding document says launch windows "recur every tether rotation that passes over the site" (`docs/project_instructions.md` §5.1), without giving a value. Anyone using 13.4 min as the interval between bottom passes overstates their frequency by about 16–18% (15.56 / 13.404 = 1.16; 15.87 / 13.404 = 1.18).

**A bottom pass is not automatically a catch opportunity at your launch site.** The bottom passes happen at different places along the orbit. Here is the size of the effect for an equatorial, prograde orbit. Inputs: n and the 933.6 s interval from above; Earth's spin rate ω_E = 7.292 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s (computed in Worked example 2.7 below from the sidereal day, which is from memory, verify).

```
hub's rate over the ground          n − ω_E = 0.0010824 − 0.0000729            = 0.0010095 rad/s
time between passes over one site   2π / 0.0010095                            = 6,224 s = 103.7 min
ground track between bottom passes  933.6 s × 0.0010095 rad/s = 0.9425 rad    = 54.0° of longitude
bottom passes per site pass         6,224 / 933.6                             = 6.67
```

Consecutive bottom passes are about 54° of longitude (about 6,000 km along the equator) apart. The hub passes over a given site about every 104 minutes, and only some of those passes line up with a bottom pass. The suborbital vehicle can fly some distance downrange to meet the tip, so the match does not have to be exact. This is the "rotation/orbit phase" timing that §5.1 says launches are planned around. [Likely; derived here, not in the repo]

### A2.12 Earth's rotation and the equatorial prograde credit

Earth spins once a day, west to east. A launch pad on the equator is carried eastward even while the rocket sits on it.

- **Prograde** means moving in the same direction Earth turns (eastward for an equatorial orbit).
- **Retrograde** means moving the opposite way.
- A **sidereal day** is one rotation measured against the stars, about 86,164 s. It is about 4 minutes shorter than the 86,400 s solar day, because Earth also moves along its path round the Sun (from memory, verify).

Earth's surface speed at latitude φ (the Greek letter phi) is:

```
ω_E = 2π / T_sidereal                     Earth's spin rate, rad/s
v_surface(φ) = ω_E · R_eq · cos φ         m/s
     R_eq   Earth's equatorial radius
     φ      latitude: 0° at the equator, 90° at the poles
```

#### Worked example 2.7: where the 0.465 km/s comes from

Inputs: sidereal day 86,164.0905 s and equatorial radius 6,378.137 km (both from memory, verify); code value 0.465 km/s (`physics/skyhook_physics.py` line 109).

```
ω_E = 2π / 86,164.0905           = 6.283185 / 86,164.0905   = 7.292116e-5 rad/s
v at the equator = ω_E × R_eq    = 7.292116e-5 × 6,378.137  = 0.46510 km/s
with the 6,371 km mean radius    = 7.292116e-5 × 6,371      = 0.46458 km/s
with a 24 h solar day            = 2π / 86,400 × 6,378.137  = 0.46383 km/s
```

The code's 0.465 km/s matches the sidereal, equatorial value. The code itself does not compute it; it is typed in as a number. [Certain]

**Why it is a "credit".** The repo's **Earth-rotation credit** is this 0.465 km/s. A rocket standing on the equator already moves eastward at 0.465 km/s in the inertial frame. The lower tip moves eastward at 5.056 km/s in that frame (Section A2.13). So the rocket only has to add 5.056 − 0.465 = 4.591 km/s. That 4.591 km/s is what the repo calls the lower tip's **ground-relative speed**. A retrograde design would cost 0.465 km/s extra instead, a swing of 2 × 0.465 = 0.93 km/s between the two.

The gap between the hub's orbital speed (7.556) and the catch speed (4.591) is 2.965 km/s. The tether supplies 2.5 km/s of it. Earth's rotation supplies the other 0.465 km/s, which is 0.465 / 2.965 = 15.7%.

Be clear about what that credit is. It is not a benefit of the tether. Any rocket launched due east from the equator gets the same 0.465 km/s. But it does shrink the vehicle that must reach the tip, so the site choice matters to the catch-vehicle design (Chapter A4). [Certain as arithmetic]

**Latitude shrinks it.**

| Launch latitude | Surface speed 0.465 × cos φ |
|---|---|
| 0° (equator) | 0.465 km/s |
| 28.5° (Cape Canaveral, from memory, verify) | 0.465 × 0.879 = 0.409 km/s |
| 45° | 0.465 × 0.707 = 0.329 km/s |
| 60° | 0.465 × 0.5 = 0.233 km/s |

[Certain: the cos φ rule is textbook geometry.] And the full credit only applies to an orbit that travels due east. An orbit tilted to the equator gets only part of it. Why an equatorial orbit needs an equatorial site is a Chapter A3 topic.

**How the code handles it.** `v_lower_tip_groundrel_kms()` has a yes/no switch:

```python
v_earth_rot = 0.465 if equatorial_prograde else 0.0  # km/s at equator [Certain]
```

(`physics/skyhook_physics.py` line 109; the switch defaults to `True` at line 98.) There is no latitude, no orbit tilt (inclination) and no retrograde case. No inclination or launch-site field exists anywhere in `params/rev_a.json`. A search of every file on main (commit 34935cb) for "inclin" or "latitud" finds nothing at all. The same 465 m/s is duplicated as `V_EQ = 465` in `tools/sims/skyhook_calculator.jsx` line 6. The finance model `finance/leg_cost.py` calls the function with `equatorial_prograde=True` (line 81), so the whole cost chain silently assumes an equatorial site. [Certain]

### A2.13 Putting it together: the Rev A tether and EQ-3

#### The parts

A **rotovator** is a long tether in orbit that spins end over end, so its tips sweep down toward Earth and up away from it. (The repo glossary calls it "Hans Moravec's 1977 term" (`docs/glossary.md` line 45). `docs/verification_memo.md` says the word was popularized and trademarked by Robert Forward and that the glossary was updated, but the glossary still credits Moravec. Chapter A1 also flags this.)

- The **hub** is the central station. It carries power, control and ballast (`docs/project_instructions.md` §4.2). The founding document says "its mass dominates the system". The repo's own numbers do not bear that out yet: the [Speculative] 200 t hub default in `physics/tether_dynamics.py` (line 77) is about a third of the 609.1 t of conservative fiber in `params/rev_a.json`. [Certain as a comparison of the two stored numbers]
- The **centre of mass** (CoM) is the mass-weighted average position of the whole system. With balanced arms it sits at the hub. The code uses "hub" and "CoM" almost interchangeably.
- The two **tips** carry the capture hardware at each end. The founding document calls the catching mechanism a **grapple** (`docs/project_instructions.md` §4.3).
- The **half-length** L is the distance from hub to each tip.

**Rev A geometry** (all from `params/rev_a.json`):

| Item | Value | Field or arithmetic |
|---|---|---|
| Hub (CoM) altitude | 610 km | `orbital.com_altitude_km` (line 9) |
| Half-length L | 320 km; full tether 640 km | `geometry.tether_half_length_km` (line 16) |
| Lower-tip altitude at bottom of swing | 610 − 320 = 290 km | `geometry.tip_altitude_lower_km` (line 17), labelled Likely |
| Upper-tip altitude at top of swing | 610 + 320 = 930 km | radius 7,301 km in `kinematics._upper_release_note` (line 27) |
| Tip speed relative to hub | 2.5 km/s | `kinematics.v_tip_kms` (line 23) |

The tether is treated as a **rigid body**: an object whose points keep fixed distances from each other. Any rigid motion is "the motion of one reference point plus a rotation about it". For Skyhook the reference point is the hub:

```
v_point = v_hub + ω × r(point relative to hub)       vector form
|ω × r| = ω · d, at right angles to the arm           d = distance from the hub
```

The tether spins **prograde**, in the same sense as the orbit. That makes the lower tip slower than the hub and the upper tip faster. The twin's initial state confirms it: the lower tip sits at s = −L and gets velocity `vOrb + omega * s`, which is less than v_orb (`tools/twin/physics.js` line 160). [Certain]

#### EQ-3

Set axes with x pointing along the hub's direction of travel and y pointing straight up, away from Earth.

```
EQ-3b  upper tip (arm points +y):    v = v_orb + v_tip                 inertial, along x
EQ-3a  lower tip (arm points −y):    v = v_orb − v_tip                 inertial, along x (first step)
       lower tip, "ground-relative": v = v_orb − v_tip − v_earth       then subtract the pad's 0.465
EQ-3c  tip acceleration:             a = v_tip² / L                   (Section A2.8)

not part of EQ-3, derived here:
       arm horizontal:               |v| = sqrt(v_orb² + v_tip²)       arrows at right angles
```

`v_upper_release_kms()` returns `v_orbital_kms(alt) + v_tip_kms` (`physics/skyhook_physics.py` lines 113–119). Its **docstring** (the explanatory text at the top of a Python function) labels this [Certain] and says it is "first-order; ignores orbital radius difference upper/lower tip". `v_lower_tip_groundrel_kms()` (lines 95–110) subtracts v_tip and 0.465. Its docstring labels it [Likely], because it "ignores atmospheric effects and tip oscillation".

#### Worked example 2.8: EQ-3 for all three tiers

Inputs: μ = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² (`params/rev_a.json` `orbital.mu_earth_m3s2`); hub altitude 610 km (`orbital.com_altitude_km`); `R_EARTH_KM = 6371` (`physics/skyhook_physics.py` line 40); Earth credit 0.465 km/s (line 109); tip speeds 2.5, 2.8 and 3.5 km/s (`rev_a.json` `kinematics`).

Step 1, hub speed (Chapter A3 explains the formula; here we only evaluate it):

```
r     = 6,371 + 610 = 6,981 km = 6.981e6 m
v_orb = sqrt(3.986e14 / 6.981e6) = sqrt(5.7098e7) = 7,556.3 m/s = 7.55631 km/s     (canon: 7.55)
```

Step 2, the reference tier, v_tip = 2.5 km/s:

```
lower tip, inertial:          7.55631 − 2.5          = 5.05631 km/s
lower tip, ground-relative:   5.05631 − 0.465        = 4.59131 km/s     (canon: 4.59)
upper tip, inertial:          7.55631 + 2.5          = 10.05631 km/s    (canon: 10.06)
```

Step 3, the options:

| v_tip | Lower tip, ground-relative | Upper tip | Canon |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.8 km/s | 7.55631 − 2.8 − 0.465 = 4.29131 | 7.55631 + 2.8 = 10.35631 | upper 10.36; no lower value stored |
| 3.5 km/s | 7.55631 − 3.5 − 0.465 = 3.59131 | 7.55631 + 3.5 = 11.05631 | 3.59 and 11.05 |

One small oddity: 11.05631 rounds to 11.06, but canon stores 11.05 for the 3.5 km/s option (`kinematics.phase3_growth_option.v_upper_release_kms`). It looks like truncation. The 0.05% difference is harmless. [Certain]

Step 4, what it means: 4.59131 / 7.55631 = 0.608. The catch vehicle must reach about 61% of the hub's orbital speed, before gravity and drag losses (Chapter A4). Across the swing, the payload goes from 5.06 to 10.06 km/s inertial, a gain of 5.0 km/s = 2 × v_tip (`materials/core.md`, "The boost, plainly"). Chapter A5 explains where that speed comes from.

The repo's self-check agrees: `verify_rev_a()` reports v_orb 7.5563 against 7.55 and v_upper 10.0563 against 10.06, both inside 2%, "ALL PASS". The downstream finance model reads EQ-3a live: `finance/leg_cost.py` `canonical_inputs()` stores `v_catch_ground_rel_kms` from this function, and `finance/LEG_COST_FINDINGS.md` line 19 prints 4.591 km/s. [Certain]

#### Worked example 2.9: why plain addition holds only at the top and bottom

EQ-3 adds plain speeds. Section A2.4 said that only works for parallel arrows. Check the in-between angles.

Inputs: v_orb = 7.55631 km/s (Worked example 2.8); v_tip = 2.5 km/s (`params/rev_a.json`).

Put the upper arm at angle θ from straight up. Its velocity relative to the hub is at right angles to the arm. It has an along-track part 2.5 × cos θ and a radial part −2.5 × sin θ (negative means downward). Add the hub's 7.55631 to the along-track part, then use Pythagoras.

| θ from top | Along-track | Radial | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0° (top) | 7.55631 + 2.5 × 1 = 10.0563 | 0 | 10.0563 km/s |
| 30° | 7.55631 + 2.5 × 0.8660 = 9.7214 | −2.5 × 0.5 = −1.25 | sqrt(94.505 + 1.5625) = 9.8014 km/s |
| 90° (horizontal) | 7.55631 + 0 = 7.5563 | −2.5 | sqrt(57.098 + 6.25) = 7.9591 km/s |
| 180° (bottom) | 7.55631 − 2.5 = 5.0563 | 0 | 5.0563 km/s |

The plain sum is exact only at the top and bottom. Release a little early or late and the payload leaves slower, and tilted up or down. That is why release timing matters. The site's mission planner does this same component split (`tools/sims/skyhook_program_site.html`, `mpCalc`, line 1285: `vt=vorb+vtip*Math.cos(rad), vr=vtip*Math.sin(rad)`). It measures the angle the other way, so its radial part has the opposite sign; the speeds are the same. [Certain]

**Rolling-wheel analogy.** Chapter A1 used this picture; here is the arithmetic. A car wheel rolling without slipping has its bottom point momentarily at rest on the road and its top point moving at twice the car's speed. A Skyhook is a wheel that rolls too slowly to stop its bottom point. For the lower tip to stand still over the pad, first-order EQ-3a would need v_tip = 7.55631 − 0.465 = 7.091 km/s. Rev A's 2.5 km/s is 35% of that.

Materials set the ceiling. A fiber's **characteristic velocity** V_c is a figure of merit for how fast a tether made of it can spin; for Zylon at Rev A specs it is about 2.73 km/s (`docs/glossary.md`; Chapter A6). [Certain as arithmetic]

#### Worked example 2.10: what a release-timing error costs

The founding document requires release timing "< 10 ms" and warns that a 1 s error at 3.5 km/s "misplaces the velocity vector substantially" (`docs/project_instructions.md` §4.3). Here is the size of "substantially".

In a time error Δt, the arm turns by Δθ = ω·Δt. The tip's velocity arrow (length v_tip) turns by the same angle. The tip of that arrow moves about v_tip × Δθ. So:

```
velocity error  |Δv| ≈ v_tip · ω · Δt = (v_tip² / L) · Δt = a_tip · Δt
```

Centripetal acceleration *is* the rate at which the tip's velocity direction turns. Inputs: v_tip and L from `params/rev_a.json`; ω from Worked example 2.2.

| Tier | Δt | Arm turns | Velocity error ≈ a_tip × Δt |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.5 km/s | 1 s | 0.0078125 rad = 0.448° | 19.53125 × 1 = 19.5 m/s |
| 2.5 km/s | 10 ms | 0.0000781 rad = 0.0045° | 19.53125 × 0.010 = 0.20 m/s |
| 3.5 km/s | 1 s | 0.0109375 rad = 0.627° | 38.28 × 1 = 38.3 m/s |
| 3.5 km/s | 10 ms | 0.000109 rad = 0.0063° | 38.28 × 0.010 = 0.38 m/s |

The 10 ms rule keeps the release error near 0.2 m/s at the reference tier. A 1 s slip would misdirect the throw by about 20 m/s. [Certain]

Near the top, that error is almost all direction, not speed. Release 1 s late at the 2.5 km/s tier:

```
arm angle past the top     Δθ = 0.0078125 rad
along-track part           7.55631 + 2.5 × cos(0.0078125) = 7.55631 + 2.49992 = 10.05623 km/s
radial part                −2.5 × sin(0.0078125)          = −0.01953 km/s = −19.5 m/s
speed                      sqrt(10.05623² + 0.01953²)     = 10.05625 km/s
```

The speed drops by only about 0.06 m/s. But the velocity now has a 19.5 m/s downward part, so it points about 0.11° below horizontal. Chapter A3 shows how that tilt changes the orbit. [Certain as arithmetic]

#### The hub moves when a payload is caught

The hub is the centre of mass only when the arms balance. Catch 5 t at one tip and the centre of mass shifts toward it. Using the [Speculative] 200 t hub default (`physics/tether_dynamics.py` `TetherConfig.hub_mass_kg`, lines 75–77) and 609.1 t of fiber (`params/rev_a.json` `conservative_30pct_fiber_mass_t`; the "30% derate" is a planned 30% cut in usable fiber strength for seams and ageing, Chapter A6):

```
shift = m_payload × L / M_total = 5 × 320 / (200 + 609.1 + 5) = 1,600 / 814.1 = 1.97 km
as a share of L:                  1.97 / 320 = 0.61%
```

That matches the "CoM shift (~0.6%)" quoted in the docstring of `catch_and_measure()` (`physics/tether_dynamics.py` line 354). Chapter A5 follows the consequences. [Certain as arithmetic; the hub mass is Speculative]

#### How the repo checks these numbers

Two tools appear here. **pytest** is the standard Python test runner: it runs every function whose name starts with `test_` and reports pass or fail. **CI** (continuous integration) means GitHub re-runs those tests automatically on every push.

| Check | What it tests | Result on commit 34935cb |
|---|---|---|
| `tests/test_rev_a_physics.py` `TestTipKinematics` (lines 63–121) | upper release and tip g within 2% (`TOL = 0.02`, line 33); g < 6; 0 < lower tip < v_orb | 27 of 27 tests in the file pass (about 0.2 s) |
| `tests/test_tether_dynamics.py` `TestV1RigidRotorLimit` (lines 44–73) | with gravity off, the 17-node model reproduces v_tip and v²/L within 1% over one turn ("~804 s") | 2 passed, with one pytest deprecation warning |
| `verify_rev_a()` (`physics/skyhook_physics.py` lines 260–301) | V_c, v_orb, v_upper, tip g, mass ratio within 2% | ALL PASS |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | installs `pytest openpyxl`, then runs `pytest tests/ -v --tb=short` and `python3 physics/skyhook_physics.py` on pushes to main or dev and on PRs to main | configured; no JavaScript is run |

[Certain; the first three were run for this guide] One environment note: `test_fiber_cost_flag` in the same file reads the Excel workbook and needs the `openpyxl` package. With a pytest that lacks it, that one test fails with `ModuleNotFoundError` and the count becomes 26 of 27. CI installs `openpyxl`, so CI is not affected.

### Limits and known problems

Each item says what the problem is, the evidence, and why it matters.

1. **EQ-3 is first-order: the real tip speed wobbles.** EQ-3 assumes a rigid tether on a perfect circle in empty space. In orbit, the gravity gradient trades spin back and forth with the orbit. The glossary puts the wobble at about ±3% and the sag in the average at 1.5–2% ("Gravity-gradient tip-speed modulation", [Likely]). `physics/tether_dynamics.py` `run_measuring()` (lines 254–275) explains it. The repo's own labels and sizes differ slightly: that docstring calls the effect [Certain] and "~3%", and the `catch_and_measure()` docstring says "~4%".

   A one-orbit run of `tools/twin/physics.js` for this guide gave a mean tip speed of 2,458.0 m/s (−1.68%). The instantaneous value ranged from 2,401.3 to 2,515.8 m/s (±2.3% about the mean), and the mean centripetal load was 1.926 g. [Certain for the run; Likely for the physics claim] *Why it matters:* the tip speed behind the 4.59 and 10.06 km/s figures carries a physics spread that canon does not show. In this run the instantaneous tip speed sat between 99 m/s below and 16 m/s above the canon 2,500 m/s, depending on spin phase. The glossary notes that the nominal spin must be set slightly above target.

2. **Canon's 1.99 g is not what the payload feels.** It is the centripetal term alone. The felt steady load at the catch is about 2.07 g (Worked example 2.5), and catch transients may multiply peak tension by about 1.30–1.47 ([Speculative], `docs/glossary.md`). [Certain as arithmetic] *Why it matters:* payload adapters and grapples should be rated on the larger, felt numbers, as the unmerged CW-001 study also recommends.

3. **"Rotation period" is the inertial period, not the catch interval.** Bottom-of-swing passes come about every 15.56 min (analytic) or 15.87 min (twin), not every 13.4 min (Worked example 2.6). The repo states neither figure. Over a fixed equatorial site the hub passes only about every 104 min, and only some passes line up with a bottom pass. [Certain as arithmetic; the scheduling consequence is Likely] *Why it matters:* cadence claims such as "multiple opportunities per day" (`docs/project_instructions.md` §5.1) and any catch scheduling need frame-correct numbers. Using 13.4 min overstates bottom passes by 16–18%, and the per-site cadence is lower still.

4. **The Earth-rotation credit is an all-or-nothing switch with no site behind it.** The 0.465 km/s literal (`physics/skyhook_physics.py` line 109) applies only if `equatorial_prograde=True`, and `finance/leg_cost.py` line 81 always passes `True`. No inclination or launch-site parameter exists. The literal sits awkwardly with CLAUDE.md Rule 2 ("Never hardcode a physics parameter"). The header of `tools/twin/physics.js` (lines 13–17) argues that universal constants are exempt, but it names only `R_EARTH_KM` and `G_STD`. The labels also clash: a [Certain] literal sits inside a [Likely] function whose docstring says "~0.46 km/s". [Certain] *Why it matters:* the credit is 15.7% of the 2.965 km/s gap between orbital speed and catch speed, so it sizes the catch vehicle. From a 28.5° site it falls to 0.409 km/s, and for a tilted orbit it falls further.

5. **"Ground-relative" is not "air-relative", and the Mach numbers mix frames.** A **Mach number** is a speed divided by the local speed of sound. Assume the thin upper air turns with Earth, a standard approximation that ignores winds. Then the air at 290 km moves eastward at ω_E × 6,661 km = 7.2921 × 10⁻⁵ × 6,661 = 0.4857 km/s, faster than the surface. Relative to that air, the lower tip moves at 5.0563 − 0.4857 = 4.571 km/s, not 4.591. [Certain as arithmetic] The Mach figures disagree with each other:
   - `docs/project_instructions.md` §2.2: 4.59 km/s "≈ Mach 13.6", implying a sound speed of 337.5 m/s.
   - `tools/sims/skyhook_program_site.html` line 346: "≈ Mach 15" applied to the inertial 5.1 km/s.
   - `finance/LEG_COST_FINDINGS.md` line 11: "~4.6 km/s / ~Mach 15", implying 307 m/s.

   337 m/s is close to sea-level sound speed (about 340 m/s, from memory, verify). At 290 km the air is so thin that a Mach number means little. *Why it matters:* **aerothermal** loads (the heating and pressure from moving through air) depend on the air-relative frame, and investors may read "Mach 15" as a measured requirement.

6. **The 6 g payload threshold has no source.** It appears in `tests/test_rev_a_physics.py` (lines 108–113), the calculator and the site, all without a citation. `docs/objections_faq.md` #10 labels "within standard satellite qualification levels" as [Certain], but points only to the site calculator and legend, not to any qualification standard. The tip load is held for minutes, unlike short launch transients. [Certain that no source is given] *Why it matters:* readers may mistake a project heuristic for a sourced qualification limit, and the duration of a load matters as well as its peak.

7. **The orbit theater shows the wrong tier on main and mixes frames on every branch.**
   - On main, `tools/sims/skyhook_orbit_theater.html` hardcodes `VTIP=3.5` (line 39) and says "Phase-3 reference design" (line 201). `docs/DEVIATIONS.md` (the repo's register of known departures from canon) row 4 says "Leave", because the deviation labels itself. But the word "reference" contradicts canon's 2.5 km/s reference. DEVIATIONS itself suggests renaming the message for this reason.
   - `docs/program_manifest.md` line 6 says the theater "gained a Rev A/Growth toggle" on 25 Aug 2026. The theater on main has no toggle. The claim may refer to site files delivered outside this repo.
   - Unmerged branch claude/skyhook-fixes-2026-10-22 (commit 1bb064c) adds a 2.5 / 2.8 / 3.5 tier switcher that defaults to 2.5. Its copy of `docs/DEVIATIONS.md` marks row 4 "OVERRIDDEN 2026-10-22". The five other unmerged branches carry the identical theater file.
   - Neither version fixes a frame mix-up. The theater measures the spin angle from the rotating local vertical (`tetherDir()`, line 112 on main; `spinA += OM*sdt`, line 151), so the drawn arm turns at OM + ORB_OM in inertial terms. But `tipVel()` (lines 117–122) adds only L × OM.

     The theater's geometry was re-run for this guide, in Node and again in Python. At the top of the swing, the drawn tip moves 0.346 km/s faster than the velocity it hands to a released payload: 11.403 against 11.056 km/s on main (3.5 km/s tier), and 10.403 against 10.056 km/s in the fix branch's 2.5 km/s tier. The gap is exactly L × ORB_OM = 320 × 0.0010824 = 0.346 km/s. The displayed spin period, 2π/OM (9.6 min on main, 13.4 min in the fix branch's 2.5 tier), is really the bottom-to-bottom time. The drawing's true inertial period is 2π / (OM + ORB_OM): 8.71 min on main and 11.77 min in the 2.5 tier. [Likely; this guide's reproduction, not covered by any repo test]

   *Why it matters:* this is the most visual tool in the repo. Viewers see a tip that does not move at the speed it throws.

8. **Thin test coverage for this chapter's numbers.** `rotation_period_min()` is defined but never called anywhere, so the stored 13.4 is not machine-checked. `tether_dynamics.py` prints the period from its own `2*math.pi/sim.omega` (line 376). The 4.59 km/s value is only checked to lie between 0 and v_orb (`test_lower_tip_groundrel_is_suborbital`). `tip_altitude_lower_km` is not checked at all. `verify_rev_a()` skips all three.

   The 2% tolerance (`TOL = 0.02`) is far looser than real basis differences, such as 0.05% between the two radius choices in item 9. Separately, the test named `test_reference_upper_release_is_cislunar_not_escape` has a docstring that says "below cislunar and escape", the opposite of its name. [Certain] *Why it matters:* canon and code could drift apart without CI noticing.

9. **Two radius bases.** `params/rev_a.json` stores `com_radius_km: 6988`, which is 6,378 + 610 (equatorial radius). The code uses 6,371 + 610 = 6,981 km (mean radius). That gives v_orb = 7.55253 against 7.55631 km/s. Both round to canon's 7.55. Chapter A3 owns this issue.

   The issue is recorded as DEVIATIONS #10 only on the unmerged fix branch. [Certain]

10. **The founding document contradicts itself about the catch point.** [Certain]
    - §2.2 gives the 290 km lower tip, then writes "wait —" and switches to an "80–150 km" **HASTOL**-class tip while keeping the 610 / 320 / 2.5 numbers. HASTOL is the "Hypersonic Airplane Space Tether Orbital Launch" study by Boeing and Tethers Unlimited, in which a hypersonic aircraft meets the tip (§2.2). 610 − 320 cannot be 80–150.
    - §4.4 sizes the launcher for "~100–150 km altitude and ~4 km/s" and says it "needs only ~40–45% of orbital velocity". But 4 / 7.55 = 53%, and Rev A's catch is at 290 km and 4.59 km/s, which is 61%.
    - `docs/program_manifest.md` line 6 still lists the §2.2 worked example as open.

    *Why it matters:* the vehicle in §4.4 does not reach the Rev A tip. Chapter A4 picks this up.

11. **The catch window is milliseconds, not seconds, unless something actively tracks the tip.** Section A2.3 showed that a velocity match lasts about ±49 ms. The unmerged CW-001 study puts the passive window at about 98 ms, against the "3–10 seconds" in §4.3 and the "few seconds to tens of seconds" in the glossary's "Catch window" entry. CW-001 also sizes the fix: a multi-second window needs about 2.07 g of sustained tracking by the vehicle or a tip-side line. [Certain as arithmetic, per CW-001 on an unmerged branch] *Why it matters:* the founding document's rendezvous requirement, and the claim that the rendezvous is "not a physics problem" (§5.2), rest on a window that passive physics does not provide. Chapter A7 covers catch dynamics.

12. **Hub mass and spin-up are unbudgeted.** The 200 t hub is a [Speculative] midpoint (`physics/tether_dynamics.py` lines 75–77). **Spin-up**, getting the tether turning in the first place, is described only in words: "over weeks" by "electrodynamic torque and/or tip thrusters" (`docs/project_instructions.md` §4.5). No angular-momentum or energy budget for it exists on main. [Certain] *Why it matters:* the CoM shift per catch and the spin-up cost both scale with masses that nobody has fixed yet.

### Key takeaways

- A vector has size and direction. Speeds add as plain numbers only when the arrows are parallel or opposite.
- Constant speed on a circle still means acceleration: a = v²/r, toward the centre. At Rev A, 2,500² / 320,000 = 19.53 m/s² = 1.99 g.
- The tether's tension supplies that inward force: about 97.7 kN on a 5 t payload, roughly twice its ground weight. Release removes the tension, and the payload leaves along the tangent.
- Orbit is free fall, not zero gravity. On the tip, the payload feels the tether: about 2.07 g at the catch once the gravity gradient is included.
- EQ-3 is "hub velocity plus spin velocity": 7.556 + 2.5 = 10.056 km/s at the top, 7.556 − 2.5 = 5.056 km/s at the bottom (inertial), and 5.056 − 0.465 = 4.591 km/s after the equatorial launch-pad credit.
- Every number belongs to a frame. The 13.4 min period is relative to the stars. The bottom of the swing recurs about every 15.6 min somewhere along the orbit, and much less often over any one launch site.
- The tip is not in free fall, so a perfect velocity match with a coasting vehicle lasts only about ±49 ms (unmerged CW-001 study), not the seconds the founding document assumes.
- The 0.465 km/s credit exists only for an equatorial, prograde design. The repo has no parameter for site latitude or orbit inclination.
- The physics module, tests and twin agree with canon. Gaps remain: an unsourced 6 g limit, unpinned period and lower-tip values, and a frame mismatch in the orbit theater.

## Chapter A3: Gravity and orbits

**Main idea:** Where a thrown payload ends up is set by one number, its orbital energy at the instant the upper tip lets go, and that number comes from Newton's gravity, the speed at release, and the exact distance from Earth's centre at which the release happens.

Chapter A2 gave you speed, force and rotation. This chapter adds gravity. By the end you should be able to take the inputs in `params/rev_a.json` and reproduce, by hand, five numbers: the 7.55 km/s orbit speed, the 13.4-minute spin, the release energy C3 = −8.06 km²/s², the 85,222 km apogee, and the market thresholds of 2.1 / 2.8 / 2.9 / 3.3–3.5 km/s. You will also meet several bookkeeping problems the repo has not yet fixed.

Some topics belong to later chapters. Rockets and **Δv** ("delta-v", the change in velocity that a burn or a throw gives a payload) budgets are in Chapter A4. Where the throw's energy comes from, and why the tether's own orbit drops, is in Chapter A5. Why faster spin costs so much tether mass is in Chapter A6. Simulation is in Chapter A7.

### Symbols used in this chapter

| G | Universal gravitational constant | m³/(kg·s²) |
| M | Mass of Earth | kg |
| m | Mass of the small body (payload, tether node) | kg |
| μ ("mu") | Gravitational parameter, μ = G·M | m³/s² or km³/s² |
| r | Distance from Earth's **centre** | km |
| h | Altitude above the surface | km |
| R_E | Earth's radius | km |
| v | Speed measured in a non-rotating frame centred on Earth | km/s |
| ε ("epsilon") | Specific orbital energy (energy per kg) | km²/s² = MJ/kg |
| a | Semi-major axis of an orbit | km |
| e | Eccentricity of an orbit | no unit |
| r_p, r_a | Perigee radius, apogee radius | km |
| T | Orbital period | s or min |
| C3 | Characteristic energy | km²/s² |
| v∞ | Hyperbolic excess speed | km/s |

---

### A3.1 Gravity: Newton's law of universal gravitation

Every lump of matter pulls on every other lump. The pull grows with the masses. It shrinks with the square of the distance between their centres. That is the whole law. The rest of this chapter is consequences.

Three words first.

- **Mass** is how much matter an object has. It is also how hard the object is to speed up or slow down. Unit: kilogram (kg).
- **Force** is a push or a pull. Unit: newton (N), where 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². Chapter A2 covered F = m·a.
- **Weight** is the force gravity puts on a mass. A 1 kg bag of sugar weighs about 9.8 N on the ground. It still has 1 kg of mass anywhere in the universe.

**Newton's law of universal gravitation** says:

```
F = G * M * m / r^2

F  = gravitational force between the two bodies        [N]
G  = universal gravitational constant ~ 6.674e-11      [m^3/(kg s^2)]  (from memory, verify)
M  = mass of the big body (Earth ~ 5.972e24 kg)        [kg]            (from memory, verify)
m  = mass of the small body                            [kg]
r  = distance between the two CENTRES                  [m]
```

The square on r is the **inverse-square law**. Double the distance and the force drops to one quarter. Triple it and the force drops to one ninth.

**Analogy.** Think of a can of spray paint aimed at a wall. Hold it twice as far away and the same paint covers four times the area, so each patch gets a quarter as much. Gravity "spreads out" over area in the same way.

One fact makes orbital arithmetic possible. A round planet pulls on outside objects as if all its mass sat at its centre. Newton proved this in the *Principia* of 1687 (from memory, verify). So **r is measured from Earth's centre, not from the ground.** Mixing up the two is the most common error in orbital arithmetic, and this repo has a version of it (section A3.3). [Certain]

#### The acceleration form

Divide both sides by m. Since a = F/m (Chapter A2):

```
g(r) = G * M / r^2        [m/s^2]

g(r) = acceleration of anything at distance r from Earth's centre
```

The small body's mass m has cancelled. A 5 t payload and a 1 g bolt fall the same way, if there is no air. [Certain]

Be careful with two similar letters. Capital **G**, the **universal gravitational constant**, is the same everywhere and never changes. Small **g** is the local acceleration, and it changes with r. The repo also defines `G_STD = 9.80665` m/s² in `physics/skyhook_physics.py` (line 41). That is **standard gravity**, a fixed convention used only to turn accelerations into "g's". For example, `tip_acceleration_g()` divides by it to report the tip load of 1.99 g. It is not the real gravity at any Skyhook altitude.

#### The vector form used in the code

Gravity has a direction: toward Earth's centre. Code that moves things in two or three dimensions writes it as a **vector**, an arrow with a length and a direction:

```
a_vec = - mu * r_vec / |r_vec|^3

r_vec   = position arrow from Earth's centre to the object   [m]
|r_vec| = length of that arrow, i.e. the distance r          [m]
minus   = "pointing back toward the centre"
```

Dividing by |r|³ instead of |r|² is a small trick. One factor of |r| turns `r_vec` into a direction of length 1. The other two give the inverse square.

`physics/tether_dynamics.py` uses exactly this. Its docstring (line 11) says: "Per-node point-mass gravity a = -mu*r/|r|^3 (NOT the uniform-gradient approximation)." Inside `_deriv()` the line is `gf = -mu / (r2 * math.sqrt(r2))`, where `r2` is r². Each of the simulation's lumped masses feels its own gravity at its own distance. That matters because the two ends of a 640 km tether feel noticeably different pulls (section A3.4 and Chapter A7). [Certain, read in repo]

**Common misconceptions.**

- "Heavier things fall faster." No. Mass cancels, ignoring air.
- "r is altitude." No. r is distance from Earth's centre.
- "G and g are the same." No. G is universal; g depends on where you are.

---

### A3.2 The gravitational parameter μ

Orbits never need G and M separately. They only need the product. Engineers fold it into one number, the **gravitational parameter**:

```
mu = G * M_Earth  ~ 3.986e14   [m^3/s^2]
```

Why fold them? Tracking satellites measures μ very precisely. G on its own is one of the least precisely known constants in physics (from memory, verify). So using μ directly is both simpler and more accurate. [Certain]

**Units check.** μ/r has units of m³/s² ÷ m = m²/s². That is a speed squared. This is why √(μ/r) will come out as a speed in section A3.5.

**The project's value.** `params/rev_a.json` stores `orbital.mu_earth_m3s2 = 398600000000000.0`, which is 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s². `physics/skyhook_physics.py` loads it on line 39 as `MU_EARTH`. The founding document quotes the same value (`docs/project_instructions.md` §2.2). [Certain]

**Check it against G·M.** With G = 6.6743 × 10⁻¹¹ and M = 5.9722 × 10²⁴ kg (both from memory, verify):

```
G * M = 6.6743e-11 * 5.9722e24 = 3.98603e14 m^3/s^2
```

That is within 0.0006% of the repo's value. A more precise published μ is 3.986004418 × 10¹⁴ (from memory, verify). The repo's four-figure value differs from it by about one part in a million. That is negligible here. It means μ alone limits results to about six significant figures. Section A3.17 shows a bigger error source, the choice of Earth radius, which limits them to about four.

#### The unit trap: m³ to km³

Most orbital work uses kilometres. Converting μ is a common trap.

```
1 km   = 1,000 m
1 km^3 = 1,000 * 1,000 * 1,000 m^3 = 1e9 m^3

mu = 3.986e14 m^3/s^2  /  1e9  =  398,600 km^3/s^2
```

You divide by 10⁹, not 10³. `apogee_from_release()` does exactly this: `mu_km3s2 = MU_EARTH / 1e9`. If you divided by 1,000 instead, μ would be a million times too big, and every speed (which goes as √μ) would come out 1,000 times too big. [Certain]

From here on, this chapter uses **μ = 398,600 km³/s²** with distances in km and speeds in km/s.

---

### A3.3 Radius versus altitude, and which Earth radius

Gravity cares about distance from the centre, the **orbital radius** r. People quote height above the ground, the **altitude** h. The link is:

```
r = R_E + h

r   = orbital radius, from Earth's centre   [km]
R_E = Earth's radius                        [km]
h   = altitude above the surface            [km]
```

**Which Earth radius?** Earth is slightly squashed by its spin. Its **equatorial radius** is about 6,378.137 km. Its **polar radius** is about 6,356.752 km. Its **mean radius**, an average over the whole surface, is about 6,371.0 km (all three from memory, verify).

The physics module uses the mean radius. Line 40 of `physics/skyhook_physics.py` reads `R_EARTH_KM = 6371.0  # mean radius [Certain]`. Note that this constant is typed into the code, not loaded from `rev_a.json`. The JavaScript twin mirrors it (`tools/twin/physics.js`, `export const R_EARTH_KM = 6371.0`), with a comment explaining that universal constants are not design parameters. The tests use the literal 6371 too (`tests/test_rev_a_physics.py` line 79). [Certain]

**The three radii Skyhook uses.** All are on the code's mean-radius basis.

| Point on the tether | Altitude (source) | Radius r |
|---|---|---|
| Lower tip (catch) | 290 km (`rev_a.json` `geometry.tip_altitude_lower_km`) | 6,371 + 290 = **6,661 km** |
| Centre of mass (CoM) | 610 km (`rev_a.json` `orbital.com_altitude_km`) | 6,371 + 610 = **6,981 km** |
| Upper tip (release) | 610 + 320 = 930 km (half-length 320 km, `geometry.tether_half_length_km`) | 6,371 + 610 + 320 = **7,301 km** |

The **centre of mass (CoM)** is the balance point of the whole tether (Chapter A2). It is the point that follows a clean orbit. The tips swing around it.

The 7,301 km figure is written into `rev_a.json` itself, in `kinematics._upper_release_note`, `kinematics._c3_note` and `market_thresholds._note`. It is also computed on line 156 of `skyhook_physics.py`: `r_tip_km = R_EARTH_KM + com_altitude_km + tether_half_length_km`. [Certain]

#### A known inconsistency: 6,988 km versus 6,981 km

`params/rev_a.json` also stores `orbital.com_radius_km: 6988` (line 10). But 6,371 + 610 = 6,981, not 6,988. The number 6,988 is 610 + **6,378**. It uses the *equatorial* radius. Every calculation in the code uses the *mean* radius. [Certain]

Call the Earth radius that a number was computed with its **radius basis**. Here there are two: the code's mean basis (CoM at 6,981 km) and the stored equatorial basis (CoM at 6,988 km). A **canon** value, meaning a value stored in `params/rev_a.json`, should state or at least follow one basis.

Some facts about this field:

- A search of `*.py`, `*.js`, `*.jsx`, `*.html` and `*.json` files on main finds `com_radius` only in `rev_a.json` itself. No code reads it. [Certain]
- The founding document repeats it: "Center of mass altitude: 610 km (orbital radius ≈ 6,988 km), v_orb ≈ 7.55 km/s" (`docs/project_instructions.md` §2.2). So does the program site's symbol table (`tools/sims/skyhook_program_site.html` line 239). Yet that site's own JavaScript uses `RE=6371` (lines 794, 975 and 1268) and `RE=6371e3`, the same radius in metres (line 1133).
- Main's `docs/DEVIATIONS.md` does not list it. Its closing "Not deviations (checked and cleared tonight)" line even names `params/rev_a.json`, but that check was about the 2.5 km/s reference, not the radius. It is logged as row #10 only on an unmerged branch (unmerged branch `claude/skyhook-fixes-2026-10-22`, `docs/DEVIATIONS.md` row 10). That row says the difference "is small … but it is internal canon disagreement" and leaves the fix as a "Hudson decision: correct it to 6981 … or annotate it as equatorial-radius basis."

The effect on the numbers is worked out in section A3.17. In short: it is small, but a few stored values follow one basis and the rest follow the other.
