## Chapter A7: Dynamics and simulation

**Main idea:** The repo predicts how the tether moves by cutting it into 17 beads joined by springs and stepping Newton's laws forward in tiny time slices with a method called RK4; four gates (V1–V4) and a cross-language check show that the code solves its own equations extremely well, but the model is planar, undamped and idealised, so its headline catch number (a dynamic load factor of 1.467) is a first estimate, not a design value.

Chapters A2 to A6 dealt mostly with steady states: a tether spinning at a constant rate, on a circular orbit, carrying a constant load. Real operations are not steady. A payload is caught, the cable jerks, waves run up and down, and gravity tugs the spin faster and slower on every turn. Describing change over time is called **dynamics**. Describing balanced, unchanging loads is called **statics**.

This chapter builds the tools for dynamics from scratch:

- what a differential equation is, and what "state" means (Sections A7.2–A7.3);
- how a computer steps time forward, and why the simplest method fails (Sections A7.4–A7.7);
- how conservation of energy and angular momentum become tests (Section A7.8);
- how a continuous cable becomes beads and springs (Sections A7.9–A7.11);
- what gravity does to a long spinning cable (Section A7.12);
- how fast the model vibrates and how that sets the time step (Section A7.13);
- the four verification gates and the catch transient (Sections A7.14–A7.15);
- the browser "digital twin" and how it is checked against Python (Sections A7.16–A7.18).

Other chapters hold the background. Newton's laws, radians and circular motion are in Chapter A2. Gravity, orbits and the 6,981 km versus 6,988 km radius question are in Chapter A3. Momentum, energy and the catch as a collision are in Chapter A5. Stress, strain, the taper and the error function are in Chapter A6. Uncertainty methods are in Chapter A8. Testing and **continuous integration (CI)**, the automatic test run on every push to the shared repository, are covered in general in Chapter A12.

A note on numbers. Values read from a file are cited by path. Values marked **(guide-computed)** were produced for this guide by running the repo's own code read-only on commit 34935cb, without changing any file.

---

### A7.1 Why simulate at all

The closed-form equations in `physics/skyhook_physics.py` answer questions like "what is the tip speed?" with one line of algebra. EQ-3, for example, adds the orbital speed and the tip speed. These formulas assume a perfectly rigid, perfectly steady tether.

Some questions have no such formula:

- What happens to the cable tension in the seconds after a 5 t payload is caught?
- Does the spin stay steady while the tether orbits through Earth's uneven gravity?
- How long do vibrations last, and how big do they get?

For these, we build a **model**: a set of equations that stand in for the real object. Then we run a **simulation**: we let a computer work out, step by step, what the equations predict over time. A **digital twin** is a simulation detailed and trusted enough to stand in for the real machine when planning operations (Chapter A1).

`docs/project_instructions.md` §4.5 makes this a requirement. It asks for "a full multibody flexible-dynamics simulation (validated against YES2 and SEDS flight data)" as a Phase 0 deliverable. **Multibody** means many connected parts. **Flexible** means the parts can stretch and bend. **Validated** means checked against real measurements.

The repo's answer so far is `physics/tether_dynamics.py`. Its docstring calls it the "Seed of the Phase 0 digital twin" (line 4). `MORNING_REPORT.md` rates it "Trust with caveats … Good seed for the digital twin; not a design tool yet" (line 62). [Certain]

---

### A7.2 A differential equation is a rule for change

A **derivative** is a rate of change. If position x changes by 0.5 m in 0.1 s, its rate of change is about 5 m/s. Written dx/dt, the derivative of position with respect to time is velocity. The derivative of velocity is acceleration. (Chapter A2, section A2.3.)

A **differential equation** is an equation that contains a derivative. It does not hand you the answer directly. It gives you a rule: "given where things are now, this is how fast they are changing."

**Analogy.** A sat-nav says "in 200 m, turn left". It never shows you the whole route at once. Follow its rule repeatedly and you trace out the route.

For a point mass, Newton's second law (Chapter A2) gives two such rules:

```
dx/dt = v                 position changes at the rate "velocity"
dv/dt = a = F(x, v) / m   velocity changes at the rate "acceleration"

x = position (m)    v = velocity (m/s)    t = time (s)
F = net force (N = kg·m/s²)    m = mass (kg)
```

**Tiny example.** Throw a ball straight up at 10 m/s. The rule is dv/dt = −9.81 m/s². After 1 s the velocity is 10 − 9.81 = 0.19 m/s. After 2 s it is 10 − 19.62 = −9.62 m/s, falling. [Certain]

Two kinds of differential equation matter here:

- An **ordinary differential equation (ODE)** has derivatives with respect to one variable only, here time.
- A **partial differential equation (PDE)** has derivatives with respect to more than one variable.

A real cable obeys a PDE, because its motion depends on time and on position along the cable. Computers handle ODEs more easily. The bead-and-spring model in section A7.9 turns the cable's one PDE into many ODEs, one pair per bead. [Certain]

**In the repo.** `TetherSim._deriv(st)` (`physics/tether_dynamics.py` lines 185–229) is the rule. Give it the current state and it returns the rate of change of every number in it: velocities for the position slots, accelerations for the velocity slots. Everything else in the simulator either sets up that rule or steps it forward.

Two common misunderstandings:

- "We solve the equation once and get a formula." For a 17-bead tether in Earth's gravity no formula exists. We must step through time.
- "The simulation is the physics." Not quite. The differential equation is the physics model. The stepping method is an approximation to that model. Both can be wrong in different ways.

---

### A7.3 State: the numbers that fix the future

The **state** of a system is the smallest list of numbers that, together with the rule, fixes its whole future. For point masses, the state is every position and every velocity. You do not need the history, only the present. [Certain]

**Analogy.** A chess position. The board and whose turn it is decide every legal continuation. How the pieces got there does not matter.

`TetherSim` stores the state as one flat list (docstring, lines 84–86; built at lines 134–139):

```
state = [x0, y0, vx0, vy0,  x1, y1, vx1, vy1,  ...,  x16, y16, vx16, vy16]
```

That is 4 numbers for each of 17 nodes, so 68 numbers. Each checkpoint in `tools/twin/golden.json` stores exactly these 68 values. [Certain]

The numbers are measured in an **Earth-centred inertial (ECI) frame**. Its origin is Earth's centre and its axes do not rotate with the Earth or the tether. In an **inertial frame** Newton's laws hold as written, with no extra "fictitious" forces such as centrifugal force (Chapter A2, section A2.11). The model is **planar**: everything happens in one plane, the orbital plane, so there is no z coordinate. [Certain]

Masses are not part of the state. They are **parameters**: fixed inputs that the rule uses. There is one exception. A catch adds 5,000 kg to node 0 partway through a run. Both `catch_and_measure()` (line 357, `self.m[0] += payload_kg`) and the browser twin (`tools/twin/twin.js` line 319) change the mass list directly. That is a sudden jump in a parameter, and section A7.16 shows it matters for the energy check.

Acceleration is not part of the state either. `_deriv()` recomputes it from positions on every call.

---

### A7.4 Time stepping and the time step dt

A computer cannot follow time continuously. It jumps forward in slices of fixed length **dt**, the **time step**. After n steps the time is t = n·dt. A method that turns "rate of change now" into "state one step later" is called an **integrator**, because it does numerically what integration does in calculus. [Certain]

**Analogy.** A flipbook. Each page is one time step. If the pages are far apart, a fast-moving figure jumps about and the motion looks wrong.

The rule of thumb: dt must be small compared with the fastest motion in the system. A useful count is steps per period of the fastest oscillation:

```
steps per period = T_fast / dt        (tens to hundreds is comfortable)
```

The repo uses three time steps:

| Where | dt | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Gates V1, V3, V4 | 0.05 s | `tests/test_tether_dynamics.py` lines 64, 104, 116, 121 |
| Gate V2 | 0.1 s | same file, line 85 |
| Golden run and browser twin | 1/60 s | `scripts/generate_golden.py` line 27; `tools/twin/twin.js` line 429 |

The slow motions in the model are long:

| Motion | Period | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Spin (relative to the stars) | 804.25 s = 13.40 min | guide-computed; `rev_a.json` `geometry.rotation_period_min` = 13.4 |
| Orbit | 5,804.8 s = 96.75 min | guide-computed from `TetherSim.orbit_period_s()` (line 180) |
| Fastest stretching vibration | 8.69 s | guide-computed, section A7.13 |

So the fastest motion sets dt, not the spin or the orbit. Gate V2 at dt = 0.1 s runs one orbit in 58,048 steps (guide-computed: 5,804.8 / 0.1, rounded by `run()` at line 250).

Smaller is not always better. Each step costs computer time, and tiny rounding errors add up over more steps. And the step the physics uses need not match the screen's frame rate. The twin deliberately keeps them separate (section A7.16).

---

### A7.5 Explicit Euler, and why it drifts

The simplest integrator is **explicit Euler** (named after Leonhard Euler). It uses only the slope at the start of the step:

```
x_new = x_old + dt · v_old
v_new = v_old + dt · a(x_old)
```

**Analogy.** Driving with your eyes shut between glances, holding the heading you had at the last glance. On a bend you always drift to the outside. For an orbit or a spinning tether, "outside" means more energy.

The repo does not use Euler. It is taught here because it shows clearly why the choice of integrator matters.

#### Worked example 7.1: Euler on the tether's own tip spring

The lightest node in the model is the lower tip, node 0. It hangs on the softest spring, segment 0. Treat that pair alone as a **simple harmonic oscillator**: one mass on one spring, with the other end held fixed. It is the textbook vibrating system. [Certain]

Inputs (both guide-computed from `TetherSim(TetherConfig())`, section A7.9 and A7.10): tip node mass m = 2,266.93 kg; tip spring k = 703.43 N/m. Time step dt = 0.1 s, the V2 value. Start stretched by x = 1 m, at rest (v = 0).

```
1. Natural rate     ω0 = √(k/m) = √(703.43 / 2,266.93) = √0.310300 = 0.55705 rad/s
2. Period           T  = 2π / ω0 = 6.28319 / 0.55705 = 11.28 s
3. Acceleration     a  = −(k/m)·x = −0.310300 × 1 = −0.310300 m/s²
4. Euler step 1     x1 = 1 + 0.1 × 0 = 1.000000 m
                    v1 = 0 + 0.1 × (−0.310300) = −0.031030 m/s
5. Energy           E = ½mv² + ½kx², so E/E0 = x² + v²/(k/m)
                    E0/E0 = 1
                    E1/E0 = 1.000000² + 0.031030²/0.310300 = 1 + 0.003103 = 1.003103
```

One step adds 0.31% energy. The same algebra in general gives an exact factor per step:

```
E_new = E_old · (1 + (ω0·dt)²)          explicit Euler, undamped spring
      = E_old · (1 + 0.055705²) = E_old · 1.003103
after 1,000 steps:  1.003103^1000 = 22.2
```

After 1,000 steps (100 s, about nine swings) the energy is 22 times too large. Because the factor is always bigger than 1, explicit Euler gains energy on an undamped oscillator at any time step. [Certain]

**Damping** means any effect, like friction, that drains energy out of a vibration. "Undamped" means there is none, so the true energy of this spring would stay exactly constant. Every gain in the table above is therefore pure integrator error.

#### What Euler does to the real model

For this guide, four small integrators were written that all call the repo's own `TetherSim._deriv()`. Each ran the default model (gravity on) for one spin, 804.25 s. The table gives the energy change as a fraction of |E0|, the size of the starting total energy (guide-computed).

| Method | dt | Energy change, (E_end − E0)/\|E0\| | Tip speed at end |
|---|---|---|---|
| Explicit Euler | 1.0 s | +1.4 × 10¹²⁶ (blew up) | 3 × 10⁶⁷ m/s |
| Explicit Euler | 0.1 s | +7.3 × 10⁻³ | 2,825 m/s |
| RK4 (repo's own `_rk4_step`) | 0.1 s | +3.4 × 10⁻¹⁶ | 2,440 m/s |

At the V2 time step, Euler adds 0.73% of the total energy in one spin. That is more than seven times gate V2's 0.1% limit, reached within a single spin, which is only about a seventh of an orbit. The added energy is 57% of the tether's spin kinetic energy (guide-computed, using the spin energy from section A7.8). The tip ends the spin 385 m/s faster than in the accurate RK4 run: 2,825 against 2,440 m/s. (The RK4 value is below 2,500 m/s because of the real gravity-gradient dip described in section A7.12.)

**Sign trap.** The total energy is negative, about −2.28 × 10¹³ J, because the tether is bound in orbit (Chapter A3, section A3.7). A positive change means the energy went up, toward zero. Dividing by E0 instead of |E0| would flip the sign of every entry in the table.

---

### A7.6 RK4: the integrator the repo actually uses

Both the Python model and its JavaScript copy use the **classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta method**, **RK4** (named after Carl Runge and Martin Kutta). The Python docstring says "Fixed-step RK4 integration" (`physics/tether_dynamics.py` line 13). The code is `_rk4_step()` (lines 231–239) and its JS twin `_rk4Step()` (`tools/twin/physics.js` lines 272–292). **Fixed-step** means dt never changes during a run. [Certain]

```
k1 = f(y_n)
k2 = f(y_n + (dt/2)·k1)
k3 = f(y_n + (dt/2)·k2)
k4 = f(y_n + dt·k3)
y_{n+1} = y_n + (dt/6)·(k1 + 2·k2 + 2·k3 + k4)

y = the whole 68-number state;   f = _deriv;   k1..k4 = four slope estimates
```

The idea: sample the slope four times across the step, once at the start, twice at the midpoint and once at the end. Then step with a weighted average, weights 1, 2, 2, 1 out of 6.

**Analogy.** Before driving a stretch of road, look at it at the start, twice in the middle and at the end, then steer by the average.

**What the code does not use.** Spring-and-orbit simulators often use "velocity Verlet" or another "symplectic" method. This code uses neither. It uses RK4 in both languages. Section A7.7 explains what that difference means. [Certain]

#### Worked example 7.2: one RK4 step by hand

Take the simplest rule, dy/dt = −y, starting at y = 1, with step h = 0.1. The exact answer is known: y(0.1) = e^(−0.1).

```
k1 = −(1)                           = −1
k2 = −(1 + 0.05 × (−1))             = −(0.95)     = −0.95
k3 = −(1 + 0.05 × (−0.95))          = −(0.9525)   = −0.9525
k4 = −(1 + 0.1 × (−0.9525))         = −(0.90475)  = −0.90475
sum = k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4 = −1 − 1.9 − 1.905 − 0.90475 = −5.70975
y1 = 1 + (0.1/6) × (−5.70975) = 1 − 0.0951625 = 0.9048375

exact  e^(−0.1)   = 0.9048374
Euler  1 − 0.1    = 0.9000000      (error 4.8 × 10⁻³)
RK4                 0.9048375      (error 8.2 × 10⁻⁸)
```

RK4 is 60,000 times more accurate here for four times the work. [Certain]

**Order.** RK4 is "fourth order". Halving dt cuts the error over a fixed time span by about 2⁴ = 16. Euler is first order: halving dt only halves the error. [Certain]

#### RK4 is excellent, but not perfect, on oscillations

For the same spring as Worked example 7.1, the energy factor per RK4 step can be worked out exactly. With h = ω0·dt:

```
energy factor per step = 1 − h⁶/72 + h⁸/576
at dt = 0.1 s:  h = 0.055705,  h⁶ = 2.988 × 10⁻⁸,  factor = 0.999999999585
after 1,000 steps:  0.99999959
at dt = 1.0 s:  h = 0.55705,  factor = 0.999601,  after 1,000 steps: 0.671
```

So RK4 slowly loses energy on an undamped spring. At the repo's small time steps the loss is far below anything measurable. At a large step it would visibly damp the motion. [Certain, guide-computed]

RK4 also has a **stability limit**. For an undamped oscillation it stays bounded only if ω·dt is below about 2√2 ≈ 2.83 (from memory, verify). Beyond that it blows up. Section A7.13 shows the repo is far inside this limit.

Two cautions:

- "Fourth order" does not mean energy is conserved forever. The error is tiny but has a steady direction (section A7.7).
- RK4 assumes the forces change smoothly. A slack cable breaks that assumption: tension drops suddenly to zero when a segment stops being stretched (`_deriv()` lines 209–211). Accuracy falls at such switches [Likely]. No gate run ever goes slack (section A7.15), so this has not been tested.

---

### A7.7 Symplectic integrators: the road not taken

A **symplectic integrator** is a stepping method that respects the geometry of Newtonian motion. Technically it preserves **phase-space area**: the area a small patch of possible states occupies in a plot of position against velocity. The practical result is what matters: it exactly conserves a slightly altered energy, called the **shadow energy**. The true energy then wobbles inside a narrow band but never drifts away, even over millions of steps. [Certain, textbook]

Two common ones are **semi-implicit (symplectic) Euler**, which updates velocity first and then uses the new velocity to move the position, and **velocity Verlet**, which moves the position using the current acceleration and then updates velocity with the average of the old and new accelerations:

```
Semi-implicit (symplectic) Euler:
    v_new = v_old + dt · a(x_old)
    x_new = x_old + dt · v_new                 <- uses the NEW velocity

Velocity Verlet:
    x_new = x_old + dt·v_old + ½·dt²·a_old
    v_new = v_old + ½·dt·(a_old + a_new)       a_new = a(x_new)
```

The only difference between explicit and semi-implicit Euler is the order of the two lines. That small change turns runaway growth into a bounded wobble.

**Same spring, semi-implicit Euler, dt = 0.1 s** (inputs from Worked example 7.1):

```
v1 = 0 + 0.1 × (−0.310300 × 1)        = −0.031030 m/s
x1 = 1 + 0.1 × (−0.031030)            =  0.996897 m
E1/E0 = 0.996897² + 0.031030²/0.310300 = 0.993804 + 0.003103 = 0.996907
```

The energy dips by 0.31% instead of rising. It does not run away, because the method keeps a slightly different quantity exactly constant. That quantity is the "shadow energy" for this spring (textbook result, checked here):

```
Q = (k/m)·x² + v² − dt·(k/m)·x·v
Q0 = 0.310300 × 1² + 0² − 0                                    = 0.310300
Q1 = 0.310300 × 0.996897² + 0.031030² − 0.1 × 0.310300 × 0.996897 × (−0.031030)
   = 0.308377 + 0.000963 + 0.000960                            = 0.310300
```

Q never changes, so the true energy can only wobble in a narrow band around it. [Certain, guide-computed]

#### Comparison on the real model

The same guide-written steppers, all calling the repo's `_deriv()`, ran one spin (804.25 s) of the default model (guide-computed):

| Method | dt | Energy change / \|E0\| | Angular-momentum change / H0 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Explicit Euler | 0.1 s | +7.3 × 10⁻³ | +1.0 × 10⁻⁴ |
| Semi-implicit Euler | 0.1 s | −2.4 × 10⁻⁷ | +5.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ |
| Velocity Verlet | 0.1 s | +1.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ | +1.9 × 10⁻¹⁵ |
| RK4 | 0.1 s | +3.4 × 10⁻¹⁶ | +1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ |
| Semi-implicit Euler | 1.0 s | −2.0 × 10⁻⁶ | 0.0 |
| Velocity Verlet | 1.0 s | +1.3 × 10⁻⁸ | −3.7 × 10⁻¹⁶ |
| RK4 | 1.0 s | −1.9 × 10⁻¹¹ | −6.8 × 10⁻¹³ |

Over one spin, RK4 is the most accurate for energy. The two symplectic methods conserve angular momentum to rounding level even at dt = 1 s. That is expected: for forces that point at Earth's centre plus equal-and-opposite pair forces, these methods conserve angular momentum exactly (from memory, verify; confirmed in this run). RK4 does not.

The long-run picture is different. Over 10 orbits at dt = 2 s (guide-computed), measured against the spin kinetic energy. Each "orbit" here is 2,902 steps (5,804 s, the orbital period rounded to whole steps). Sampling at exact multiples of 5,804.8 s instead shifts Verlet's entries, because its error oscillates, but not the pattern:

| Method | Energy error after orbits 1, 2, 3 … 10 (fraction of spin KE) | Angular momentum after 10 orbits |
|---|---|---|
| Velocity Verlet | +2.0e-6, +5.1e-6, +5.6e-6, +2.7e-6, −2.4e-6, −2.1e-8, +3.5e-6, +5.8e-6, +4.7e-6, +1.5e-6 | +9.4 × 10⁻¹⁶ |
| RK4 | −5.2e-8, −1.1e-7, −1.6e-7, −2.3e-7, −4.5e-7, −6.5e-7, −7.4e-7, −8.1e-7, −8.5e-7, −8.6e-7 | −1.25 × 10⁻¹⁰ |

Verlet's error is bigger but changes sign and stays in a band. RK4's error is smaller but only ever grows, in one direction. [Certain, guide-computed]

Will RK4's one-way error eventually pass Verlet's band? Textbooks say a non-symplectic method's energy error keeps accumulating over long runs. In this run it has not caught up: after 10 orbits RK4 sits at −8.6 × 10⁻⁷ against Verlet's band of about ±6 × 10⁻⁶. Its growth also slowed after orbit 6. So when, or whether, it overtakes at this time step is not known from the repo's evidence. [Likely that it eventually would; Speculative about when]

**What this means for the repo.** RK4 passes the repo's gates by a huge margin because the time steps are tiny, not because RK4 is structurally suited to the problem. For runs of an orbit or less, RK4 is a fine choice. For multi-day or multi-year operations studies at larger time steps, a symplectic method would be the safer choice [Likely].

Symplectic does not mean exact. Timing (phase) errors still build up, so a symplectic run slowly gets "out of step" with the true motion even while its energy stays honest. [Certain, textbook]

### A7.8 Conservation laws as tests

A **conserved quantity** is one that never changes while the system runs on its own. Two matter here (Chapter A5 builds both from scratch):

- **Energy**, E: kinetic energy (energy of motion) plus gravitational potential energy plus the elastic energy stored in stretched springs.
- **Angular momentum**, H: the "amount of turning", here measured about Earth's centre.

The code computes both (`total_energy()`, lines 319–332; `angular_momentum()`, lines 334–340):

```
E = Σ ½·m_i·|v_i|²  −  Σ μ·m_i / |r_i|  +  Σ ½·k_j·e_j²     (springs only if stretched, e_j > 0)
H = Σ m_i·(x_i·vy_i − y_i·vx_i)
drift = |X(t) − X(0)| / |X(0)|          for X = E or H

r_i = distance of node i from Earth's centre (m);   e_j = stretch of segment j (m)
```

Why should these stay fixed in this model?

- Gravity points at Earth's centre, so it exerts no twisting force (torque) about that point.
- Each spring pulls its two nodes equally and oppositely along the line between them. These pairs cancel in the total torque. The work they do goes into or comes out of spring energy, which E includes.
- There is no friction unless damping is switched on. The code's optional damping is set by a **damping ratio**, ζ (zeta): a dimensionless number where 0 means no damping and 1 ("critical damping") means just enough to stop a single spring-mass from oscillating at all (textbook). `run()` takes it as `damping_ratio` (line 242). Only gate V3 uses it, at 0.05.

So, with damping off, any change in E or H during a run is either integrator error or a bug. [Certain]

The test measures this as **drift**: the change in a quantity that should be conserved, divided by its starting size, |X(t) − X(0)| / |X(0)|.

**Analogy.** An internal audit. Money only moves between accounts. If the grand total changes, someone made a mistake.

Two limits on what such a check proves:

- Zero drift shows the integrator is faithful to the model. It says nothing about whether the model is right. A model with the wrong spring constant conserves energy perfectly.
- The check only works for a closed system. A catch adds mass with its own energy. Damping removes energy on purpose. Section A7.16 shows a real case.

#### Worked example 7.3: what gate V2 measures, and how loose its tolerance is

Gate V2 (`tests/test_tether_dynamics.py` lines 76–94) runs the default model for one orbit at dt = 0.1 s. It requires both drifts to be below 1 × 10⁻³ (0.1%).

Inputs: E0 = −22,821,030,601,227.7 J (`tools/twin/golden.json`, checkpoint 0); H0 = 4.2756 × 10¹⁶ kg·m²/s (same); node masses and positions from section A7.9 (guide-computed).

```
Achieved (guide-computed, 58,048 RK4 steps):
1. E_end − E0 = +0.055 J
2. energy drift = 0.055 / 2.2821e13 = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁵
3. angular-momentum drift = 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵
```

The gate passes by a factor of about 4 × 10¹¹ (1 × 10⁻³ / 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁵), more than eleven orders of magnitude. That looks overwhelming.

Now look at what the total is made of. Split each node's motion into two parts. One is the motion of the **centre of mass** (CoM): the mass-weighted average position of all nodes, which here travels on the orbit (Chapter A2). The other is each node's motion relative to the CoM, here mostly the spin at ω about it, with s_i the node's distance from the hub. The spin parts are (guide-computed):

```
4. spin kinetic energy   = Σ ½·m_i·(ω·s_i)² = 2.885 × 10¹¹ J  -> 2.885e11 / 2.2821e13 = 1.26% of |E0|
5. elastic energy        = Σ ½·k_j·e_j²     = 1.32 × 10⁹ J    -> 0.006% of |E0|
6. V2 allowance          = 0.001 × 2.2821e13 = 2.28 × 10¹⁰ J
7. allowance / spin KE   = 2.28e10 / 2.885e11 = 7.9%
8. allowance / elastic   = 2.28e10 / 1.32e9   = 17 times all stored spring energy
9. spin angular momentum = Σ m_i·ω·s_i² = 7.386 × 10¹³  -> 0.173% of H0
10. H allowance / spin H = 0.001 × 4.2756e16 / 7.386e13 = 58%
```

Almost all of E and H belongs to the orbit of the tether's CoM, not to the spin or the stretching. A 0.1% tolerance on the total would therefore pass a bug that created or destroyed 7.9% of the spin energy, or 58% of the spin angular momentum. [Certain, arithmetic]

The actual drift is superb. The gate is the loose part. Measuring drift against the spin energy, or against the energy of motion relative to the CoM, would make it a much sharper test [Likely].

### A7.9 From a continuous rope to beads and springs

A **lumped-mass model** replaces a continuous body with point masses, called **nodes**, joined by massless springs, called **segments**. Each node "lumps" together the mass of the cable around it. It is also called a bead-and-spring model. [Certain]

**Analogy.** A pearl necklace on elastic thread. The pearls carry the weight; the thread only pulls.

Why do it? A continuous cable obeys a PDE (section A7.2). Seventeen beads give 17 pairs of ODEs, which RK4 can step.

#### The layout

`TetherConfig.n_nodes = 17` (line 66). The number must be odd so that one node sits exactly at the centre, where the hub is (lines 91–92).

```
h   = 2L / (n − 1) = 640 km / 16 = 40 km            node spacing (line 109)
s_i = −L + i·h      for i = 0 … 16                    position along the tether (line 110)
node 0  : s = −320 km, lower tip (Earthward)
node 8  : s =    0 km, hub (centre)
node 16 : s = +320 km, upper tip
```

#### Mass per node

Each node gets the mass of the cable within half a segment on each side of it. The cable is tapered (Chapter A6, section A6.7), so this mass is not the same for every node. The code integrates the taper profile exactly using the **error function**, erf, which is the area under a bell curve (Chapter A6, section A6.8). `_arm_mass_between()` (lines 151–158) does it:

```
A(s)  = A_L · exp[x²·(1 − s²/L²)]               cross-section area (m²), line 149
A_L   = m_p·ω²·L / σ_w                           tip area (m²), line 105
m(a,b) = ρ·A_L·e^(x²)·(L·√π / 2x) · [erf(x·b/L) − erf(x·a/L)]      mass between |s| = a and b

ρ = 1,560 kg/m³ (rev_a.json materials.density_kgm3)
m_p = 5,000 kg (rev_a.json mass_ratio...payload_mass_kg_for_tonnage)
σ_w = working stress, 1.624 × 10⁹ Pa;   x = taper exponent, 1.732584 (Chapter A6; lines 101–104)
```

The centre node's window [0, h/2] exists on both arms, so its fibre mass is doubled. Then the 200 t hub mass is added (lines 118–119).

#### Worked example 7.4: the tip node's mass

Inputs: A_L = 6.01332 × 10⁻⁵ m² (60 mm²), x = 1.732584, x² = 3.001847, ρ = 1,560 kg/m³, L = 320,000 m (all guide-computed from `TetherSim(TetherConfig())`, matching Chapter A6). The tip node's window is |s| from 300 km to 320 km.

```
1. ρ·A_L                = 1,560 × 6.01332e-5         = 0.0938077 kg/m
2. e^(x²)               = e^3.001847                  = 20.12268
3. L·√π / (2x)          = 320,000 × 1.772454 / 3.465168 = 163,681.9 m
4. coefficient          = 0.0938077 × 20.12268 × 163,681.9 = 308,976 kg
5. erf(x·320/320)       = erf(1.732584)               = 0.985724
6. erf(x·300/320)       = erf(1.624297)               = 0.978387
7. difference           = 0.985724 − 0.978387         = 0.007337
8. m_0                  = 308,976 × 0.007337          = 2,266.9 kg
```

The code gives 2,266.93 kg. [Certain, guide-computed]

All 17 masses (guide-computed; the upper arm mirrors the lower):

| Node | s (km) | Mass (kg) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 (lower tip) | −320 | 2,266.9 |
| 1 | −280 | 7,689.6 |
| 2 | −240 | 14,082.1 |
| 3 | −200 | 23,496.3 |
| 4 | −160 | 35,719.5 |
| 5 | −120 | 49,475.1 |
| 6 | −80 | 62,437.3 |
| 7 | −40 | 71,792.3 |
| 8 (hub) | 0 | 275,212.4 = 75.2 t fibre + 200 t hub |
| 9–16 | +40 … +320 | mirror of 7 … 0 |

```
total mass     = 809,130.4 kg
fibre mass     = 809,130.4 − 200,000 = 609,130.4 kg
EQ-6 check     = m_p·2·√π·x·e^(x²)·erf(x) = 609,130.4 kg
```

The lumped fibre mass equals EQ-6 to machine precision. `MORNING_REPORT.md` (line 39) and `rev_a.json` (`conservative_30pct_fiber_mass_t` = 609.1) agree. [Certain]

Exact mass does not mean exact motion. Any wave shorter than about two 40 km segments cannot exist in a 17-node chain. The model also cannot show a local tension peak within one segment. [Certain]

### A7.10 Springs: Hooke's law, EA, and the target-strain choice

Chapter A6 (sections A6.1–A6.2) defines stress, strain and Young's modulus. Here is how the model turns them into springs.

```
stress           σ = T / A                       Pa = N/m²
strain           ε = (d − L0) / L0                dimensionless
Young's modulus  E = σ / ε                        Pa
axial stiffness  EA = E × A                       N   (a property of the cross-section)
spring constant  k = EA / L0                      N/m (a property of one segment)
Hooke + slack:   T = k·(d − L0)  if d > L0,  else T = 0

T = tension (N)   A = area (m²)   d = current node-to-node distance (m)   L0 = rest length (m)
```

**Hooke's law** says a spring's force is proportional to its stretch. **Axial stiffness** EA tells you how hard a given cross-section resists stretching along its length. The **spring constant** k = EA/L0 is the force per metre of stretch for one whole segment, where the **rest length** L0 is the segment's unstretched length. A cable can pull but not push. When it goes loose it carries nothing. That is the **slack** case in `_deriv()` (lines 209–211): `if ext <= 0.0: continue`. [Certain]

**Analogy.** A rubber band. Stretch it and it pulls back harder the more you stretch. Push the ends together and it just goes floppy.

#### The target-strain choice

The model needs a Young's modulus. It does not take one from a datasheet. It picks one, the **effective modulus** E_eff, so that the cable stretches by a chosen amount, the **target strain**, when carrying its design working stress (docstring lines 27–31; line 106):

```
σ_w   = σ·(1 − derate) / SF = 5.8e9 × 0.70 / 2.5 = 1.624 × 10⁹ Pa
E_eff = σ_w / ε_target       = 1.624e9 / 0.005    = 3.248 × 10¹¹ Pa

σ = 5.8 GPa, derate = 0.30, SF = 2.5   (rev_a.json materials)
ε_target = 0.005   (TetherConfig.target_strain, line 79, labelled [Likely])
```

The docstring compares this with "Zylon HM tensile modulus ~2.7e11 Pa, Toyobo datasheet". So the model is about 20% stiffer than that value (3.248 / 2.7 = 1.20). Chapter A6 (Worked example 6.3) shows that with 270 GPa the arm would stretch about 0.60% at working stress instead of 0.50%. Two further cautions:

- `rev_a.json` gives the construction baseline as "Spectra/UHMWPE core + Zylon outer arm (Hoytether architecture)". The model gives the whole tether Zylon's strength and density (`TetherConfig` lines 70–73).
- Target strain is a modelling choice, not a material property. Main has no sweep of how dynamics results change with it. (The unmerged SH-001 memo, described in Section A7.13, brackets it at 0.0025 and 0.01 for its vibration signature only, in its §5.)

Stiffness matters for dynamics because it sets the **wave speed**, how fast a stretch disturbance travels along the cable (textbook c = √(E/ρ); numbers guide-computed):

```
wave speed   c = √(E/ρ) = √(3.248e11 / 1,560) = √2.082e8 = 14,429 m/s
one-way trip along an arm = L / c = 320,000 / 14,429 = 22.2 s
```

#### Pre-strain: starting at equilibrium

**Pre-strain** means building each segment already stretched. Each segment's rest length L0 is chosen so that, at t = 0, it already carries exactly the tension rigid rotation needs (lines 129–132; `_discrete_static_tensions()`, lines 160–174):

```
T_j   = Σ over nodes outboard of segment j of  m_i·ω²·|s_i|       N
L0_j  = h / (1 + T_j / EA_j)                                         m
k_j   = EA_j / L0_j                                                  N/m
EA_j  = E_eff × A(|segment midpoint|)                                N
```

**Outboard** means farther from the hub. Each node needs an inward pull of m·ω²·r to stay on its circle (Chapter A2, section A2.9). A segment must supply that pull for every node beyond it.

#### Worked example 7.5: the tip segment, step by step

Inputs (guide-computed): A_L = 6.01332 × 10⁻⁵ m², x² = 3.001847, E_eff = 3.248 × 10¹¹ Pa, tip node mass m_0 = 2,266.93 kg, ω = 0.0078125 rad/s, h = 40,000 m. Segment 0 runs from s = −320 to −280 km, so its midpoint is at |s| = 300 km.

```
1. 1 − (300/320)²            = 1 − 0.878906 = 0.121094
2. x² × 0.121094             = 0.363505;   e^0.363505 = 1.438362
3. A(300 km)                 = 6.01332e-5 × 1.438362 = 8.6493 × 10⁻⁵ m²
4. EA                        = 3.248e11 × 8.6493e-5 = 2.8093 × 10⁷ N
5. needed tension            = m_0·ω²·L = 2,266.93 × 6.10352e-5 × 320,000
                             = 2,266.93 × 19.53125 = 44,276 N
6. strain                    = 44,276 / 2.8093e7 = 0.001576  (0.158%)
7. rest length L0            = 40,000 / 1.001576 = 39,937.06 m   (stretched by 62.9 m)
8. spring constant k         = 2.8093e7 / 39,937.06 = 703.43 N/m
9. design tension here       = σ_w × A = 1.624e9 × 8.6493e-5 = 140,465 N
10. actual / design          = 44,276 / 140,465 = 31.5%
```

The code agrees on every line (guide-computed). [Certain]

Line 10 is worth noticing. The taper was sized for a 5 t payload at the tip. The default model has no payload attached, so the outer segments carry much less than their design tension: 31.5% at the tip segment, rising to 95.8% next to the hub. The strain is therefore not a uniform 0.5%. It runs from 0.16% at the tip to 0.48% beside the hub. Only with a payload on each tip (the V3 setup) is the strain close to uniform. [Certain, guide-computed]

Across the 16 segments (guide-computed), k runs from 703.4 N/m at the tips to 9,757.5 N/m beside the hub, and EA from 2.81 × 10⁷ N to 3.88 × 10⁸ N. The built-in stretch h − L0 runs the other way: 62.9 m in the tip segments, the smallest, up to 190.6 m in the segments beside the hub, the largest. One whole arm is stretched by about 1.28 km.

### A7.11 The starting state

The model starts in a simple, well-defined condition (docstring lines 33–37; code lines 134–139):

- The tether is a straight line pointing **radially**: along the line from Earth's centre, with the lower tip Earthward.
- The centre of mass (CoM) is on a circular orbit.
- The whole tether rotates rigidly at ω about the CoM.

```
R_com   = (R_E + altitude) = (6,371 + 610) km = 6,981 km           (line 97)
v_orb   = √(μ / R_com) = √(3.986e14 / 6.981e6) = 7,556.3 m/s       (line 135)
x_i(0)  = R_com + s_i,   y_i(0) = 0
vx_i(0) = 0,             vy_i(0) = v_orb + ω·s_i                    (line 139)

R_E = 6,371 km (physics/skyhook_physics.py line 40, mean radius)
```

So the lower tip starts at 7,556.3 − 2,500 = 5,056.3 m/s and the upper tip at 10,056.3 m/s, both in ECI. Chapter A3 (section A3.3) explains why `rev_a.json` stores a different radius, `com_radius_km` = 6,988, which no dynamics code reads.

Because of the pre-strain, this start is an exact balance in free space. With gravity switched on, the only disturbance is the difference in gravity along the tether, the topic of the next section.

One small leftover: an extended body in inverse-square gravity feels slightly more net pull than a point at its centre of mass. Starting the CoM at point-mass circular speed therefore leaves it on a slightly non-circular orbit. Its radius drops from 6,981.000 km to a minimum of 6,979.402 km over one orbit, a 1.6 km range (guide-computed). That is a small, permanent perturbation in every run. [Certain]

---

### A7.12 Gravity in the model, and the gravity gradient

`_deriv()` gives every node its own inverse-square gravity (lines 192–202):

```
a_i = −μ · r_i / |r_i|³          (vector, points at Earth's centre; magnitude μ/|r_i|²)
```

The docstring stresses that this is "NOT the uniform-gradient approximation" (lines 11–12). Each node feels the pull at its own distance. Chapter A3 (section A3.1) builds this law from scratch.

#### The gravity gradient

The lower end of the tether is closer to Earth than the upper end, so it is pulled harder. The difference in gravity across a body is called the **gravity gradient**. Its stretching effect is the same thing that raises ocean tides, so it is also called the **tidal** effect. [Certain]

#### Worked example 7.6: gravity at the two tips and the CoM

Inputs: μ = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² (`rev_a.json` `orbital.mu_earth_m3s2`); R_com = 6,981 km; L = 320 km; ω = 0.0078125 rad/s.

```
1. lower tip  r = 6,981 − 320 = 6,661 km:  g = 3.986e14 / (6.661e6)² = 8.9838 m/s²
2. CoM        r = 6,981 km:                g = 3.986e14 / (6.981e6)² = 8.1790 m/s²
3. upper tip  r = 6,981 + 320 = 7,301 km:  g = 3.986e14 / (7.301e6)² = 7.4778 m/s²
4. lower − CoM = 8.9838 − 8.1790 = 0.8047 m/s²
5. orbital rate n = √(μ / R_com³) = 1.08241 × 10⁻³ rad/s
6. straight-line estimate 2·n²·L = 2 × 1.17161e-6 × 320,000 = 0.7498 m/s²
```

The straight-line estimate is about 7% below the exact lower-tip value at this length (0.7498 against 0.8047). At the upper tip the exact difference is 8.1790 − 7.4778 = 0.7012 m/s², about 6.5% below the estimate instead. Exact per-node gravity captures this lopsidedness. [Certain, guide-computed]

Step 5 introduces the **mean motion** n: the orbit's average angular rate, 2π divided by the orbital period.

There is a second part, and it is easy to get wrong. Picture a tether that simply hangs straight down and turns once per orbit, so it stays still in a frame that moves around the orbit with the CoM. In that frame there is also a centrifugal difference of n²·L along the radial line. Gravity's difference (2·n²·L, step 6) and this centrifugal difference add. The result is the textbook net **tidal acceleration** of 3·n²·L for a hanging radial tether:

```
7. tidal stretch on a HANGING tether   3·n²·L = 3 × 1.17161e-6 × 320,000 = 1.1247 m/s²
```

The Skyhook tether does not hang. It spins at ω measured against the stars, and its spin pull ω²·L already contains that n²·L centrifugal part. To check, redo the sum in the orbiting frame, where the tether turns at only ω − n. Three terms appear there: the inward pull needed to turn at ω − n, the Coriolis push (the sideways push on anything moving in a rotating frame, Chapter A2, section A2.11) and the centrifugal push. Per unit mass at the tip they are (ω − n)²·L, 2n(ω − n)·L and n²·L, and they add up to exactly ω²·L:

```
(ω − n)² + 2n(ω − n) + n²  =  ω²                    (expand the brackets to check)
```

So for the spinning tether the extra load at radial alignment is the gravity difference alone:

```
8. spin pull                         ω²·L  = 6.10352e-5 × 320,000          = 19.531 m/s²
9. tidal extra, straight-line         2·n²·L = 0.7498 m/s²  -> 0.7498 / 19.531 = 3.84%
10. tidal extra, exact gravity (step 4)        0.8047 m/s²  -> 0.8047 / 19.531 = 4.12%
```

So when the tether points straight down, or straight up, the tide adds about 4% to the tension the spin already puts on the tips. With exact gravity it is 4.1% at the Earthward end and 3.6% at the far end (8.1790 − 7.4778 = 0.7012 m/s², from steps 2–3). Using 3·n²·L here would wrongly give 5.8%. The 4% matches the "Gravity-gradient modulation (~4% at this geometry)" in the `catch_and_measure()` docstring (line 353). The model agrees: within 20 s of the first top and bottom passes, the tip-segment tension averages 3.3% and 4.9% above its free-space starting value, with ringing on top (guide-computed). [Certain for the algebra; Likely that ringing explains the spread around 4%]

#### The tide also twists the spin

When the tether is tilted, the tide does more than stretch it. It pulls the lower half toward "straight down" and the upper half toward "straight up". That twisting force is a **gravity-gradient torque**. Over each turn it slows the spin on one part of the swing and speeds it up on another. [Certain, textbook]

A rigid-dumbbell estimate (guide-derived, not in the repo) shows the size. Measure the tether angle θ from the local vertical. Seen from a frame that turns with the orbit, the tether behaves like a pendulum whose potential energy, per unit of rotational inertia, is (3/2)·n²·sin²θ. Energy conservation then gives its turning rate at "straight down" (θ = 0) and at "horizontal" (θ = 90°):

```
11. rate relative to vertical, at radial   = ω − n = 0.0078125 − 0.0010824 = 6.7301e-3 rad/s
12. at horizontal  = √((ω − n)² − 3n²) = √(4.5294e-5 − 3.5148e-6) = 6.4637e-3 rad/s
13. inertial spin at horizontal = 6.4637e-3 + n = 7.5461e-3 rad/s
14. drop = 1 − 7.5461e-3 / 7.8125e-3 = 3.41%    ->  tip speed ≈ 2,500 × 0.9659 = 2,415 m/s
```

#### What the full model shows

Running the default model (gravity on) for 2,000 s gives this tip speed relative to the CoM (guide-computed, dt = 0.1 s):

| t (s) | 0 | 250 | 500 | 700 | 950 | 1,177 | 1,900 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tip speed (m/s) | 2,500.0 | 2,416.5 | 2,496.7 | 2,420.1 | 2,499.8 | 2,411.7 (lowest) | 2,501.3 (highest) |

The tip speed returns to about 2,500 m/s whenever the tether points straight up and down. It dips by up to 3.53% between those moments, close to the dumbbell's 3.41%. The averages are (guide-computed):

| Averaging window | Mean tip speed | vs 2,500 m/s |
|---|---|---|
| One spin, 804.25 s | 2,454.32 m/s | −1.83% |
| Rigid-estimate bottom-to-bottom time, 933.6 s | 2,456.95 m/s | −1.72% |
| The model's own bottom-to-bottom time, 952.1 s | 2,457.78 m/s | −1.69% |
| The golden run's 600 s (`golden.json`) | 2,462.64 m/s | −1.49% |

This is real physics in the model, not a numerical error. With gravity off, the same default model holds 2,500.000 m/s (guide-computed; gate V1 checks the stiffer version). [Certain, as a model output]

**How the repo describes it, and where that is loose.** The `run_measuring()` docstring (lines 259–264) gives "fractional tip-speed modulation of order 1.5*n^2/omega^2 ~ 3%". The arithmetic is 1.5 × 0.01920 = 2.88%. The V1 test docstring (lines 51–56), `MORNING_REPORT.md` (line 38), `docs/glossary.md` ("Gravity-gradient tip-speed modulation", line 24) and a comment in `tools/twin/twin.js` (lines 384–387) say "~±3%". In the model the swing is one-sided: from +0.05% at radial alignment down to −3.53% near horizontal. That is about ±1.8% around a mean that is 1.7–1.8% low, not ±3% around 2,500. [Certain, guide-computed]

The same `run_measuring()` docstring also says "The rotation-average is the quantity that matches v_tip" and that "averaging over an integer number of rotations cancels the periodic exchange". With gravity on, the model contradicts both. The one-spin average is 1.83% low, not equal to v_tip. And the exchange repeats every bottom-to-bottom time (~952 s), not every spin (804 s), so a whole number of spins does not cancel it. This is why V1 had to switch gravity off (section A7.14). [Certain, guide-computed]

The glossary adds that this "implies nominal spin rate must be set slightly above the target release speed". In the model the tip is close to the design speed whenever the tether is radial, which is where catch and release are planned. At the first lowest point it is 2,499.85 m/s. Over the six lowest points of the first orbit it ranges from 2,483.7 to 2,501.2 m/s (guide-computed, dt = 1/60 s). This guide did not isolate the cause; the slightly non-circular orbit of section A7.11 is one candidate [Speculative]. So the mean is low by 1.7–1.8%, but the speed at the release point is low by at most about 0.7% in this run. The glossary claim needs checking against a real release geometry, which may not be exactly radial [Likely].

#### Swing timing

Chapter A2 (Worked example 2.6) and Chapter A3 (Worked example 3.3) show that "straight down" itself turns once per orbit. So the bottom of the swing recurs every 2π/(ω − n) = 933.6 s for a rigid tether, not every 804.25 s.

The full model is slightly slower again, because its average spin is depressed (guide-computed, scanning node 0's distance from Earth):

```
lowest points of the lower tip:   952.1 s, 1,904.8 s, 2,856.3 s    (every ~952 s = 15.9 min)
highest point of the same node:   475.9 s, at 929.93 km altitude (610 + 320 = 930 km)
rigid estimates:  2π/(ω − n) = 933.6 s;   π/(ω − n) = 466.8 s;   half a spin π/ω = 402.1 s
```

So, for the bare tether in this model, the carry from catch at the bottom to release at the top takes about 476 s, not the 402 s that "half a rotation" suggests. [Certain, guide-computed]

**Libration** is the pendulum-like swinging of a tether about the local vertical (`docs/glossary.md`, line 33). The founding document requires libration to be actively damped (`docs/project_instructions.md` §4.5). The spinning rotovator does not swing back and forth like a hanging pendulum. In the dumbbell picture it goes right round, because (ω − n)² = 4.53 × 10⁻⁵ is far larger than 3n² = 3.51 × 10⁻⁶ (guide-computed). The same gravity-gradient torque that drives libration in a hanging tether produces the tip-speed swing above. [Likely]

The model has no Earth oblateness (J2), no air drag at the 290 km lower tip (`rev_a.json` `geometry.tip_altitude_lower_km`), no Sun or Moon, no electrodynamic forces and no Earth rotation. Only spherical point-mass gravity acts.

### A7.13 Natural frequencies, and how they set dt

Pluck a guitar string and it rings at certain pitches. These are its **natural frequencies**. Each comes with a shape of motion, called a **mode**. A chain of beads and springs has as many modes as it has beads in each direction of motion. [Certain]

For this guide, the 17-node chain's stretching (axial) modes were computed from the model's own masses and spring constants, with the spin and gravity left out. The method is an **eigenvalue calculation**: the masses and springs are written as two 17 × 17 tables (matrices), and a standard routine finds the frequencies at which the whole chain can vibrate in step (guide-computed):

```
angular frequencies (rad/s): 0 (whole chain moving together), 0.1153, 0.1571, 0.2349, 0.2652, ... 0.7231
in millihertz, mHz (1 mHz = 0.001 cycles per second): 18.3, 25.0, 37.4, 42.2, ... 115.1
fastest period: 2π / 0.7231 = 8.69 s
```

#### Worked example 7.7: is the time step small enough?

Inputs: fastest angular frequency ω_max = 0.7231 rad/s (above); time steps from section A7.4.

```
dt = 0.1 s :  ω_max·dt = 0.0723;   steps per fastest period = 8.69 / 0.1   = 87
dt = 0.05 s:  ω_max·dt = 0.0362;   steps per fastest period = 8.69 / 0.05  = 174
dt = 1/60 s:  ω_max·dt = 0.0121;   steps per fastest period = 8.69 / 0.01667 = 521
RK4 stability needs ω·dt < ~2.83 (from memory, verify):  dt < 2.83 / 0.7231 = 3.9 s
Verlet needs ω·dt < 2 (from memory, verify):             dt < 2 / 0.7231    = 2.8 s
```

Every repo time step resolves the fastest vibration with 87 to 521 steps. That, together with RK4's high order, is why the energy drift is near 10⁻¹⁵, which is close to the rounding limit of the arithmetic itself. Symplecticity plays no part, because RK4 has none (section A7.7). [Likely for the explanation; Certain for the arithmetic]

#### The same model, listened to (unmerged branch)

An unmerged branch analyses these vibrations in depth (unmerged branch `claude/creative-tether-stethoscope`, `physics/tether_modes.py` and `docs/research/sh001_modal_health.md`, last commit 4074cd7, 2026-10-23). It **linearises** the same 17-node `TetherSim` in the rotating frame: it replaces the full equations with their straight-line approximation for small wobbles about the steady spin, which is what an eigenvalue calculation needs. Two more words: a **bay** is the 40 km stretch between two neighbouring nodes, and **strands** are the parallel fibre lines of a Hoytether (Chapter A6, section A6.15). Its findings, as stated in its "Bottom line" and §3:

- Its four lowest axial lines are 18.4701, 25.0995, 37.4445 and 42.2598 mHz. They agree with the simple calculation above to about 1%.
- If one 40 km bay loses 25% of its strands, those lines drop by up to 2.30%.
- Catching the 5 t payload shifts the same lines by 2.34–8.53%. So the payload is a bigger signal than the damage.
- The damage signature has **converged**, meaning it stops changing as the model is refined to more nodes, only for the lowest four lines per family. Against a 129-node reference, the 17-node axial frequencies themselves are off by 0.41–2.60% for lines 1–4.

The last point is a direct measure of how coarse 17 nodes is. [Certain as reported on the branch; not on main]

### A7.14 The verification gates V1–V4

**Verification** asks "does the code solve its equations correctly?" **Validation** asks "do the equations describe the real world?" A **gate**, in this repo's language, is an automated test that must pass before work is accepted. The repo's four gates are verification. None is validation. [Certain]

The gates live in `tests/test_tether_dynamics.py`. Its docstring says they were "Written BEFORE the implementation" (line 5). CI runs them on every push to `main` or `dev` and on every pull request (a request to merge one branch into another) to `main`, because `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `pytest tests/ -v --tb=short`. All six tests pass on main in about 6 s (guide-computed run). [Certain]

| Gate | Setup | Pass condition | Achieved (guide-computed) | What it does not prove |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| V1 rigid rotor | gravity off, target strain 1e-4, one spin, dt 0.05 s | tip speed and tip acceleration within 1% | 2,500.0000 m/s (error 2.6 × 10⁻¹²); 19.53125 m/s² (error 2.4 × 10⁻¹²) | That a disturbed elastic tether settles to the rigid limit |
| V2 conservation | default, one orbit, dt 0.1 s | energy and H drift < 0.1% | 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁵ and 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ | That spin and elastic energy are accurate (section A7.8) |
| V3 static tension | gravity off, 5 t at both tips, 60 s at damping ratio 0.05 | tension within 5% of σ_w·A | +0.82% at the 140 km segment | Anything about motion |
| V4 catch | default, catch at t = 100 s, track 400 s | ratio finite and > 1 | 1.467 | Any design value (nothing else is asserted) |

#### V1: the rigid-rotor limit

A **rigid rotor** is a spinning body that does not stretch. For it, tip speed and tip acceleration have exact formulas (Chapter A2, Worked example 2.2):

```
ω = v_tip / L = 2,500 / 320,000 = 0.0078125 rad/s
a_tip = ω²·L = v_tip² / L = 2,500² / 320,000 = 19.53125 m/s² = 1.99 g
```

V1 makes the springs 50 times stiffer (target strain 1e-4, so E_eff = 1.624 × 10¹³ Pa), switches gravity off, and averages over one spin using `run_measuring()`. The match is to about 3 parts in 10¹². [Certain]

Two honest notes. First, the start is already an exact equilibrium (section A7.10), so a steady spin is guaranteed if the code is consistent. Even at the default stiffness, gravity off, the mean tip speed matches to 1.2 × 10⁻¹³ (guide-computed). V1 shows the construction is self-consistent and that RK4 holds a steady spin. It does not show convergence from a disturbed state.

Second, the gate was redefined during development. `MORNING_REPORT.md` (line 45) says: "V1 initially failed with gravity on … I changed the *test definition* during development (before any commit; no committed test was modified)", and calls this "the kind of thing that deserves your scrutiny". The reason given is the real gravity-gradient effect of section A7.12, which this guide's runs confirm (−1.83% over one spin with gravity on). [Certain]

#### V2: conservation

Covered in Worked example 7.3. The drift is excellent; the tolerance is loose because the total is dominated by the orbit.

#### V3: the static tension profile

V3 attaches the 5 t design payload to both tips and checks one segment's tension against the continuous design formula T(s) = σ_w·A(s) (`analytic_tension()`, lines 176–178). It asks for the tension "at mid-arm", 160 km. A node sits exactly at 160 km, so the segments at 140 km and 180 km are equally near. `tension_nearest()` (lines 312–317) picks the first, the 140 km segment. [Certain]

#### Worked example 7.8: gate V3 by hand

Inputs: A_L = 6.01332 × 10⁻⁵ m², x² = 3.001847, σ_w = 1.624 × 10⁹ Pa (sections A7.9–A7.10).

```
1. s/L = 140/320 = 0.4375;   1 − 0.4375² = 0.808594
2. x² × 0.808594 = 2.427275;   e^2.427275 = 11.3280
3. A(140 km) = 6.01332e-5 × 11.3280 = 6.8119 × 10⁻⁴ m²
4. analytic tension = 1.624e9 × 6.8119e-4 = 1,106,247 N
5. model tension (guide-computed) = 1,115,269 N
```

A simpler check at the tip segment (300 km) shows where the 1% comes from. With the payload added, the tip node is 7,266.93 kg:

### A7.15 The catch transient and the dynamic load factor

A **transient** is the temporary response to a sudden change, before things settle. A **catch transient** is the ringing of tension in the tether right after a payload is grabbed. The **dynamic load factor (DLF)** is the peak tension during the transient divided by the steady (static) tension the new load would cause. [Certain]

**Analogy.** A bungee jump. On the first stretch the cord overshoots well past where it will finally hang.

#### Where the factor of 2 comes from

Take one mass on one spring whose far end is held fixed: a **single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF)** system. The spring carries T_before. Suddenly the load it must hold rises to T_after. The mass starts at the old stretch and swings about the new one, overshooting by the same amount on the far side:

```
T_peak = T_after + (T_after − T_before) = 2·T_after − T_before
DLF    = T_peak / T_after = 2 − T_before / T_after         (undamped SDOF, sudden load)
```

If the spring starts unloaded (T_before = 0), DLF = 2. Hang 10 kg on a spring by letting it go suddenly: the static load is 98.1 N and the peak is 196.2 N. That is the "SDOF sudden-load limit of 2" cited in `docs/glossary.md` (line 18). [Certain, textbook]

The glossary goes one step further. It says the tether's factor is "physically bounded below" that limit of 2. For one spring that is true. For a chain it is an expectation, not a proven bound. With many modes ringing at once, their contributions to one segment's tension can have mixed signs, so in principle a peak can exceed the single-spring value [Likely]. The model's values so far (up to 1.52) all sit below 2.

#### What the code does

`catch_and_measure()` (lines 344–368) models a perfect catch:

1. Measure the current spin from the tip: ω_now = (tip speed relative to CoM) / L.
2. Add the payload mass to node 0. Its velocity is unchanged, so the payload arrives exactly matching the tip. The docstring calls this an **ideal rendezvous** (line 348): a meeting with zero relative velocity.
3. Set the static reference T_static = (m_tip + m_payload)·ω_now²·L.
4. Step forward and record the largest tension in segment 0.

The tension cannot jump at the instant of the catch, because the spring's stretch has not changed yet. The same spring force now has to bend the path of a node more than three times heavier (7,266.9 kg instead of 2,266.9 kg). So the node curves less sharply, drifts outward and stretches the spring. Only then does the tension rise. [Certain]

#### Worked example 7.9: gate V4, step by step

Inputs: default `TetherConfig()`, gravity on; catch at t = 100 s; payload 5,000 kg (`rev_a.json` `payload_mass_kg_for_tonnage`); dt = 0.05 s; 400 s tracked (`tests/test_tether_dynamics.py` lines 114–121). Intermediate values guide-computed.

```
1. tip speed at t = 100 s         = 2,465.61 m/s     (gravity-gradient dip, section 7.12)
2. ω_now = 2,465.61 / 320,000     = 0.0077050 rad/s  (98.6% of 0.0078125)
3. ω_now²·L = 5.93677e-5 × 320,000 = 18.9977 m/s²
4. T_static = (2,266.93 + 5,000) × 18.9977 = 7,266.93 × 18.9977 = 138,055 N
5. tension just before the catch  = 43,053 N
6. peak segment-0 tension (400 s) = 202,502 N
7. DLF = 202,502 / 138,055         = 1.4668
```

The test prints "[Speculative] First dynamic load factor estimate: peak/static = 1.467" (lines 130–132). It asserts only that the ratio is finite and above 1 (lines 123–124). A value above 10 would be printed as an anomaly, not failed (lines 126–128). Nothing pins 1.467. [Certain]

Compare the SDOF estimate:

```
8. SDOF: 2 − T_before / T_static = 2 − 43,053 / 138,055 = 2 − 0.3119 = 1.688
```

The chain gives less than one fixed spring would, plausibly because the next node is not fixed and some energy runs off into the rest of the chain [Likely].

There is a second way to define the factor: how much the jump in tension is amplified. On that definition the same run gives (202,502 − 43,053) / (138,055 − 43,053) = 1.68, and the SDOF value would be 2. Always state which definition is meant. [Certain, arithmetic]

#### When does the peak happen?

A history of the same run (guide-computed) gives the ratio T / T_static after the catch:

| Time after catch | 1 s | 6 s | 11 s | 21 s | 56 s | 66 s | 106 s | 116 s | 303 s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T / T_static | 0.34 | 1.00 | 1.21 | 1.04 | 0.64 | 1.21 | 1.22 | 0.43 | **1.467** |

The first peak, 1.214, comes 11.2 s after the catch. A fixed-end SDOF estimate puts it at half a period: π/√(k_0/m) = π/√(703.43/7,266.93) = π/0.3111 = 10.1 s. The 1.467 maximum comes much later, 302.95 s after the catch. In an undamped chain, reflected waves keep running back and forth and sometimes add up. [Certain for the numbers; Likely for the explanation]

#### The number depends on how long you watch

Because nothing dies out, the running maximum keeps creeping up (guide-computed, same catch at t = 100 s):

| Tracking window | 30 s | 100 s | 400 s (V4) | 800 s | 1,600 s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DLF, gravity on | 1.214 | 1.236 | 1.467 | 1.467 | 1.522 |
| DLF, gravity off | 1.244 | 1.320 | 1.419 | 1.419 | 1.438 |

Even with no catch at all, the bare tether's tip-segment tension swings between 0.905 and 1.100 of its t = 100 s value over the next 400 s, because of the gravity gradient (guide-computed). That swing sits inside every DLF measured with gravity on.

#### The number depends on when you catch

At t = 100 s the lower tip is 38.3° from straight down and moving away from Earth at 1,367 m/s (guide-computed). That is not where a real catch would happen. The browser twin waits for the bottom of the swing (section A7.16). Repeating that in Python, catching at the first lowest point (t = 952.03 s, tip 0.05° from vertical, dt = 1/60 s) gives (guide-computed):

| Catch timing | 30 s window | 400 s window |
|---|---|---|
| t = 100 s (V4 phase) | 1.214 | 1.467 |
| Bottom of swing (twin phase) | **1.300** | 1.356 |

The 30 s bottom-of-swing value reproduces the twin's reported 1.300 (`tools/twin/VISUAL_QA.md` line 34). [Certain, guide-computed]

**A contradiction to state plainly.** The glossary reads the twin's ~1.30 against V4's ~1.47 as "suggestive of phase-dependence". But the two numbers also use different windows: 30 s in the twin (`twin.js` line 93, `catchTrackDurationS: 30`) and 400 s in V4. Like for like, phase moves the result one way in a 30 s window (1.214 → 1.300) and the other way in a 400 s window (1.467 → 1.356). The glossary's own hedge, "baselines have not yet been verified identical", is right, and this is a concrete reason. [Certain, guide-computed]

#### The number depends on the mesh

The **mesh** is how finely the model cuts the cable, here the node count. A trustworthy answer should stop changing as the mesh is refined. The same V4 run with different node counts (guide-computed):

| Nodes | 9 | 17 | 33 | 65 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DLF | 1.396 | 1.467 | 1.516 | 1.493 |

The result has not settled with mesh refinement. It moves by a few percent either way.

#### What the catch model leaves out

- **Velocity mismatch.** The payload arrives exactly at the tip's velocity. §4.3 of `docs/project_instructions.md` requires relative velocity "within ~1 m/s" over a capture window of "3–10 seconds". Chapter A2 (section A2.3) and Chapter A5 (Worked example 5.1) discuss what a mismatch adds.
- **The shock reel.** §4.3 specifies "a controlled-tension reel that pays out line over several seconds after latch". The model has none. A reel exists precisely to cut the DLF.
- **Damping.** Real materials and joints lose energy, which would cap the late peaks.
- **Throw.** No release is modelled in Python at all.

So the DLF is a property of the event, the model, the window and the definition together, not of the tether alone. The repo's [Speculative] label on 1.467 is correct. [Certain]

Two smaller points. Adding 5,000 kg to an 809,130 kg tether moves the CoM 5,000 × 320 / 814,130 = 1.965 km toward the tip (0.61% of L), matching the "~0.6%" in the docstring (line 354). And no segment goes slack anywhere in the V4 run: the lowest tension is 20.7 kN, in segment 15 (guide-computed). The slack branch of the code is never exercised by any gate.

---

### A7.16 The digital twin in the browser

`tools/twin/` is a 3D, interactive view of the tether that runs in a web browser. Browsers run **JavaScript** (JS), not Python. So the physics was **ported**, meaning rewritten line by line in another language, as `tools/twin/physics.js`. Its header says: "Python is the validated reference; this file must reproduce it, not reinvent it" (lines 2–3). [Certain]

The port is close to literal. `_deriv()`, `_rk4Step()`, `totalEnergy()` and `angularMomentum()` match the Python functions statement by statement (`physics.js` lines 220–398). All Skyhook design inputs come from `params/rev_a.json`: in the browser, `params-loader.js` fetches the file and stops with an error rather than falling back to hardcoded numbers. As in Python, Earth's radius (6,371 km), standard gravity and the simulation knobs (hub mass, target strain, node count) are set in code (`physics.js` lines 13–23, 66 and 78–84).

#### The one deliberate difference: erf

JavaScript has no built-in error function. `physics.js` (lines 32–54) uses the Abramowitz & Stegun 7.1.26 approximation and states its "max abs error 1.5e-7". At x = 1.732584 it returns 0.98572404, against Python's 0.98572405 (guide-computed, a difference of 8.5 × 10⁻⁹). As a result, the JS node masses differ by up to about 0.06 kg, and the JS fibre total is 609,130.429 kg against 609,130.435 kg: 5.9 g lighter. [Certain, guide-computed]

#### The fixed-timestep loop

Screens redraw at varying rates, perhaps 60 or 144 times a second, and slower when the computer is busy. If the physics step followed the frame time, results would change from machine to machine. `twin.js` (lines 428–456) separates the two with a **fixed-timestep accumulator**: a loop that banks the real time each frame and spends it only in fixed-size physics steps. Its comment calls it the "Gaffer accumulator", after the Gaffer On Games website (Glenn Fiedler's "Fix Your Timestep!" article; from memory, verify):

```
STEP = 1/60 s                         fixed physics step (line 429)
each frame:
    dt  = real time since last frame, capped at 0.25 s          (line 439)
    acc = acc + dt × timeWarp                                    (line 443)
    while acc ≥ STEP:  save state; sim.step(STEP); acc = acc − STEP
    alpha = acc / STEP                                           (line 452)
    draw  = previous state + alpha × (current − previous)        (lines 453–456)
```

**Analogy.** A jar of coins. Each frame drops in some "time coins". The physics spends them only in fixed denominations of 1/60 s. Whatever is left over waits for the next frame.

The drawing **interpolates**: it blends the last two physics states by the leftover fraction, so motion looks smooth. This affects only the picture. The physics never reads the frame time (comment, line 447). [Certain]

**Time warp** speeds up simulated time: the buttons give 1×, 10× and 60× (`tools/twin/index.html` lines 46–48).

```
Worked numbers (guide-computed from the code):
at 60×, 60 frames per second:  acc gains (1/60) × 60 = 1 s per frame  ->  60 physics steps per frame
worst case, capped frame:      0.25 s × 60 = 15 s per frame          ->  900 physics steps per frame
```

The 0.25 s cap prevents the **spiral of death** (comment, line 439): one slow frame forces many steps, which make the next frame slow too, and so on.

#### The catch button

The user arms a catch. On every physics step, `maybeHandlePeriapsis()` (`twin.js` lines 307–343) checks node 0's distance from Earth's centre. When that distance stops falling, the tip is at the bottom of its swing. The code calls this **periapsis**, borrowing the orbital word for closest approach (Chapter A3 uses perigee, the Earth-specific form). It then:

1. computes ω_now from the tip speed,
2. adds `designPayloadKg` (5,000 kg) to `sim.m[0]`, exactly as Python's `catch_and_measure()` does,
3. sets the static reference m_0·ω_now²·L,
4. tracks segment 0's peak tension for 30 s of simulated time (`catchTrackDurationS`, line 93), and
5. shows "load factor … (peak/static)" in the **heads-up display (HUD)**, the on-screen text readout of tip speed, tension, catch status and energy drift (`updateHud()`, lines 350–382).

`tools/twin/VISUAL_QA.md` (lines 21–40) records a browser test of this: load factor 1.300. Section A7.15 reproduced it in Python.

Two claims in that QA note do not match the model. It says "periapsis recurs roughly once per ~804s rotation period". In the model the lowest point recurs every ~952 s (section A7.12); 804 s is the spin period relative to the stars. It also says a cold-start catch landed at "t~952-1200s depending on arming phase". The model has no lowest point between 952 s and 1,905 s, so a first catch at 1,200 s cannot be at a lowest point. Running the twin's own detection rule in Python at its 1/60 s step over a whole orbit finds lowest points only at 952.03, 1,904.73, 2,856.18, 3,809.02, 4,760.73 and 5,713.12 s, with no spurious triggers in between (guide-computed). This guide could not reproduce the QA range. [Certain for the model; the origin of the QA figure is unknown]

#### The energy-drift readout, and a jump that is real

The HUD shows energy drift, (E − E0)/E0 in percent, and turns red above 1% (`twin.js` lines 353–354). `VISUAL_QA.md` (lines 60–75) reports that after a catch the readout "jumps to ~1.03% immediately … and stays there", and explains it as the payload's own energy joining the system. That explanation checks out.

#### Worked example 7.10: the 1.031% jump

Inputs (guide-computed at the twin-style catch, t = 952.03 s): tip ECI speed 5,056.9 m/s; tip altitude 289.53 km; μ = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²; R_E = 6,371 km; payload 5,000 kg; E0 = −2.2821 × 10¹³ J (`golden.json` checkpoint 0).

```
1. kinetic energy per kg    = ½ × 5,056.9²                       = 1.27861 × 10⁷ J/kg
2. radius                   = (6,371 + 289.53) × 1,000           = 6.66053 × 10⁶ m
3. potential energy per kg  = −3.986e14 / 6.66053e6              = −5.98451 × 10⁷ J/kg
4. total per kg             = 1.27861e7 − 5.98451e7              = −4.70590 × 10⁷ J/kg
5. payload energy           = −4.70590e7 × 5,000                 = −2.35295 × 10¹¹ J
6. as a fraction of E0      = −2.35295e11 / −2.2821e13           = +0.010310 = 1.031%
```

Before the catch the same readout was 2.2 × 10⁻¹³ % (guide-computed). So the integrator is fine. The drift check simply stops meaning anything once mass enters the system. To stay useful it would need to be reset after each catch or throw. [Certain for the arithmetic]

#### What else the twin shows

- "Peak tension … x allowable" compares each segment's tension with σ_w·A at its midpoint (`twin.js` lines 356–362). For the bare tether at t = 0 the ratios run from 0.32 at the tip segments to 0.96 beside the hub (section A7.10), so the HUD's "peak" starts near 0.96 before any catch.
- The tether's drawn thickness follows the taper (`tools/twin/tether-mesh.js`, radius √(A/π) with A = `analyticTension()/sigmaW`). As an equivalent solid rod, the radius is about 19.6 mm at the hub and 4.4 mm at the tips (guide-computed). A real Hoytether lattice would be wider and mostly empty space. The drawing multiplies width by 8,000 (`tetherWidthExaggeration`, line 68), giving 157 m and 35 m on screen. The HUD says so.
- Earth is held fixed (lines 478–480). The physics frame is inertial, so this does not affect the physics. But the reason given, that Earth's rotation over "tens of minutes" is "a fraction of a degree" (`VISUAL_QA.md` lines 83–85), is wrong. Earth turns about 0.25° per minute (from memory, verify), so tens of minutes is several degrees, and at 60× warp far more.
- `VISUAL_QA.md` (lines 41–45) leaves "60 fps steady at native res" unchecked. The automated test ran with software rendering at 10–50 fps.

### A7.17 golden.json and cross-language verification

Two programs that should agree can be checked against each other. The repo does this with a **golden reference**: a stored set of trusted outputs that a second program must reproduce. [Certain]

#### Making the golden file

`scripts/generate_golden.py` runs the Python model with default settings (gravity on, target strain 0.005) for 600 s at dt = 1/60 s, 36,000 RK4 steps (lines 27–29, 43–62). It writes `tools/twin/golden.json` containing:

- the run's settings (`meta.config`, 12 fields);
- at t = 0, 60, 300 and 600 s: all 68 state values, energy, angular momentum, tip speed and tip acceleration (`snapshot()`, lines 32–40);
- the run-long mean tip speed, 2,462.6407 m/s, and mean tip acceleration, 18.9557 m/s².

Selected values from `golden.json`:

| t (s) | Energy (J) | Tip speed (m/s) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | −22,821,030,601,227.715 | 2,500.000 |
| 60 | −22,821,030,601,227.76 | 2,486.11 |
| 300 | −22,821,030,601,227.72 | 2,430.51 |
| 600 | −22,821,030,601,227.594 | 2,458.17 |

The energy changes by 0.12 J out of 2.28 × 10¹³ J in 600 s. A fresh in-memory re-run of the current Python model (guide-computed, without running the generator, which would overwrite the file) matches the stored states within 1.1 × 10⁻⁷ (metres or m/s) and the mean tip speed to 13 significant figures. So the golden file is current. [Certain]

The generator's docstring calls the mean "rotation-averaged … same averaging methodology as TetherSim.run_measuring" (lines 13–16). But `run_measuring()` ties the cancellation it relies on to "averaging over an integer number of rotations" (lines 263–264), and 600 s is 0.75 of a spin. So 2,462.64 m/s (−1.49%) is a fine number for checking the two programs agree, but it is not the rotation mean (−1.83% over one spin, section A7.12). [Certain]

#### The checker

`tools/twin/verify.mjs` runs `physics.js` in **Node.js**, a program that runs JavaScript outside a browser, for the same 600 s and compares:

```
0. all 12 config fields equal golden.meta.config exactly, or STOP      (lines 59–90)
1. every node's x and y within 0.1% relative of golden
   (1 m absolute where the golden value is near zero)                  (lines 32–33, 41–48)
2. the JS run's own energy and H drift each < 0.1%                     (line 34)
3. mean tip speed within 1% of golden                                  (line 35)
```

If a check fails it prints hints: "check force sign, half-step state reuse in RK4 stages, unit mismatch (m vs km), slack condition. Tolerances were NOT loosened" (lines 206–210).

#### Worked example 7.11: how close the twin really is

Run on main with Node v22.22.0 (guide-computed):

```
verify.mjs output:
  max relative position error   1.571e-10   (t = 60 s, node 0 y)
  max energy drift              6.676e-13 %
  max angular momentum drift    3.181e-13 %
  mean tip speed                JS 2,462.6407 vs Python 2,462.6407 m/s;  error 1.549e-8 %
  PASS
```

Convert to physical sizes (guide-computed separately; the largest distance between the JS and Python positions of any one node):

```
max |JS − Python| position:  0.06 mm at 60 s,  0.25 mm at 300 s,  0.45 mm at 600 s
max |JS − Python| velocity:  1.8 × 10⁻⁵ m/s at 600 s
0.45 mm / 5.6e6 m          ≈ 8 × 10⁻¹¹ relative
```

Now compare with what the gate would allow. Each x and y coordinate is checked on its own, against 0.1% of its own size:

```
x coordinates (5.5 to 7.3 million m):   0.001 × 5.5e6 to 0.001 × 7.3e6 = 5.5 to 7.3 km
y coordinates at 60 s (0.31 to 0.60 million m):                      0.31 to 0.60 km
y coordinates at 600 s (3.9 to 4.5 million m):                       3.9 to 4.5 km
largest elastic stretch in the model (segments beside the hub):      190.6 m  (section 7.10)
smallest (tip segments):                                             62.9 m   (Worked example 7.5)
```

The two programs agree to under half a millimetre after 600 s, about one part in 10¹⁰. The gate would have passed errors of 0.3 to 7 km, depending on the coordinate and checkpoint. (At t = 0 every y is zero and a 1 m floor applies instead, but nothing has moved yet.) Even the tightest of these, about 309 m on node 0's y at 60 s, is larger than the largest spring stretch. The loosest is more than 35 times it. A wrong spring constant could pass it. [Certain for the arithmetic; Likely for the last sentence]

**Where the half-millimetre comes from.** For this guide, the Abramowitz & Stegun erf that `physics.js` uses was patched into a copy of the Python model in memory. The patched Python run and the JS run then agreed exactly, to the last bit, in all 68 state values at 60, 300 and 600 s (guide-computed). So the entire JS–Python difference comes from the one deliberate erf difference, not from the port. [Certain, guide-computed]

#### Why parity matters

**Parity** means two implementations give the same answer. The twin is the picture people see in meetings. If it silently drifted away from the verified Python model, the picture would mislead. Checking parity keeps the picture honest to the reference. Parity is not validity, though. Both programs can agree and both be wrong about the real tether (section A7.14).

#### Limits of the parity check

- **Not in CI.** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` installs Python and runs pytest. It has no Node step, so `verify.mjs` runs only when someone runs it by hand. Nothing detects a stale `golden.json` if `tether_dynamics.py` changes.
- **Narrow coverage.** The golden run is 600 s of a bare tether: no catch, no damping, no tension or velocity comparison. The twin's catch code in `twin.js` is not parity-tested.
- **Loose tolerance.** 0.3 to 7 km on positions, as shown above.
- **Overstated in publicity.** `materials/core.md` (lines 92–96) and `tools/sims/skyhook_program_site.html` (line 937) say the twin is "verified to machine precision". **Machine precision** is the rounding size of a 64-bit number, about 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ (from memory, verify). The measured agreement, 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰, is close to a million times larger. The cause is the erf approximation, as the patched run above shows; with the same erf the two would agree exactly. The 6.7 × 10⁻¹³ % energy figure quoted alongside is the JS run against its own start, not JS against Python. The site also names the reference as `physics/skyhook_physics.py`; the lumped-mass model is in `physics/tether_dynamics.py` (`physics.js` line 2). [Certain]
