### A12.10 The browser platform

#### Three languages in one page

A web page is built from three text languages:

- **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language) is the structure: headings, buttons, a `<canvas>` to draw on.
- **CSS** (Cascading Style Sheets) is the look: colours, fonts, layout.
- **JavaScript** (JS) is the behaviour: code that runs in the browser.

The **DOM** (Document Object Model) is the live tree of page elements that JavaScript can read and change. Analogy: HTML is the skeleton, CSS the clothes, JS the muscles.

A **single-file HTML** tool puts its CSS and JS inside the one `.html` file. It can be emailed and opened with a double-click. `tools/sims/skyhook_program_site.html` (120,509 bytes, 1,493 lines) is one such file. It holds inline CSS and seven inline scripts: a catch-dynamics sketch, a conjunction visualizer, a calculator, a revision log with export, a mission planner, a Monte Carlo panel and glossary navigation [Certain, read].

#### Drawing: canvas 2D, WebGL, three.js

- **Canvas 2D** is a flat drawing surface with commands such as "move to (x, y), line to (x, y)". The program site uses it for the catch sketch, the conjunction view and the Monte Carlo plot (`getContext('2d')` at lines 795, 975 and 1354). `tools/sims/skyhook_frontier.html` uses it for its chart (line 165).
- **WebGL** is the browser's interface to the **GPU** (graphics card) for fast 3D drawing (it is based on OpenGL ES; from memory, verify).
- **three.js** is a JavaScript library that hides WebGL behind friendlier ideas: a scene, a camera, lights and meshes. A **mesh** is a 3D shape built from many small triangles.
- A **shader** is a tiny program that runs on the GPU for every vertex (corner point of a triangle) or pixel. `tools/twin/earth.js` has shaders for the atmosphere's glow and for hiding city lights on the day side.

#### Libraries from the network: CDNs, classic scripts, ES modules, import maps

A **library** is code someone else wrote for reuse. Its **API** (application programming interface) is the set of names and functions it offers to your code. A **CDN** (content delivery network) is a set of public servers that host libraries, so a page can load them by **URL** (web address). Analogy: borrowing a book from a public library. If the library is closed, your page has no book.

There are two ways to load JavaScript, plus one helper:

- A **classic script**, `<script src="...">`, runs the file and leaves its names in one shared global space. three.js loaded this way creates a global name `THREE`.
- An **ES module** uses `import` and `export` to name exactly what it needs. Browsers load modules with `<script type="module">`.
- An **import map** is a JSON block that tells the browser what a bare module name such as `"three"` means.

The repo uses both styles for three.js [Certain, read]:

| Tool | How three.js is loaded | Version | If the CDN is blocked (on main) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tools/sims/skyhook_orbit_theater.html` | classic script from `cdnjs.cloudflare.com` (line 6) | r128 | [Likely, from reading the code] `THREE` is undefined, the script stops at line 46, and the 3D view stays empty; the HTML buttons still show but do nothing |
| `tools/twin/index.html` | import map to `unpkg.com/three@0.160.0` (lines 64-71) | r160 | `twin.js` never runs; the HUD says "loading…" forever |

The **HUD** (heads-up display) is the text panel drawn over the 3D view; in the twin it starts as "loading…" (`index.html` line 42). The fixes-branch commit for the theater (`1bb064c`) describes the old behaviour as "going blank", which supports the table's reading.

Pinning an exact version is good practice: the page will not change under you. Having two versions means two slightly different APIs to know.

Fonts are also borrowed. The program site, the frontier, the field kit and `materials/style.css` load fonts from Google Fonts. Offline, missing fonts fall back quietly to system fonts. Missing three.js breaks the page.

#### Why the twin needs a web server

Double-clicking a file opens it at an address starting `file://`. `fetch()` is the browser's function for downloading a file by URL. Chrome-family browsers refuse to load ES modules or `fetch()` local files from `file://` pages; other browsers vary (from memory, verify). So the twin must be served by a small web server over `http://`. `tools/twin/VISUAL_QA.md` lines 5-7 say: serve the repo root with `python -m http.server` and open `/tools/twin/`.

Python's server listens on **port** 8000 by default (from memory, verify). Here a port is a numbered network "door" on a computer; this is a different meaning from "port" as a translation of code (Section A12.12). **localhost** means "this same computer". Together that gives `http://localhost:8000/tools/twin/`.

The server must start at the repo root, because the twin fetches `../../params/rev_a.json`. Serve only `tools/twin/` and that path leads nowhere. A web server answers every request with an **HTTP status code**: 200-299 mean OK, 404 means "not found". `params-loader.js` (lines 61-66) turns any non-2xx answer into a FATAL message, so the twin shows a FATAL 404 message instead of running. [Certain, from the code]

#### Storage inside the browser

`tools/sims/skyhook_st001_field_kit.html` keeps splice-test pulls, creep readings and its shopping checklist in **localStorage** under the key `st001` (its script runs from line 217 to 312; `load()` and `save()` are lines 222-223). localStorage is a small per-site store in one browser on one computer. Clear the site data and the field data is gone; nothing reaches the repo unless someone copies the kit's Markdown export. The program site's revision log lives only in page memory until downloaded as a **Blob** (bytes in memory handed to the browser as a file; `saveRev`, `dlRev`).

[Certain] `skyhook_frontier.html` and `skyhook_st001_field_kit.html` start directly with `<title>`, with no `<!DOCTYPE html>`. Browsers then use **quirks mode**, an old compatibility mode with slightly different layout rules (from memory, verify).

### A12.11 JSX and React: source code that needs a host

**React** is a JavaScript library that builds a page out of **components**: functions that return pieces of user interface. **JSX** is HTML-like syntax written inside JavaScript, for example `<div style={{ padding: 7 }}>`. Browsers cannot read JSX directly. A **compiler** turns it into plain JavaScript calls such as `React.createElement("div", ...)` (from memory, verify). A **bundler** is a build tool that gathers a program and its libraries into files a browser can load. React **hooks** such as `useState` and `useMemo` store slider values and cache calculations.

Analogy: JSX is sheet music. Before anyone hears it, it needs an orchestra (React) and a conductor (the compiler and bundler).

| File | Imports | Needs to run |

### A12.12 The digital twin, end to end

A **digital twin** is a software copy of a physical system that behaves like it. Here it is a 3D browser view of the spinning tether. [Certain] The Python simulation `physics/tether_dynamics.py` is the validated reference (Chapter A7 explains its 17-node model and its V1-V4 gates). The twin is a JavaScript **port** (a translation into another language) of that model, with a **renderer** (the code that draws the picture) on top. A golden file proves the port matches.

#### How the pieces connect

```
index.html ──import map──> three.js r160 (unpkg.com)
    │
    └─ twin.js  (entry point, ES module)
         ├─ params-loader.js  fetch ../../params/rev_a.json; check 8 fields + payload mass; throw on any problem
         ├─ physics.js        TetherConfig, TetherSim, RK4 step; no window/document, so Node can run it too
         ├─ earth.js          Earth from 3 NASA textures in assets/; procedural (code-drawn) fallback if they fail
         ├─ tether-mesh.js    tube through the node positions, coloured by tension (reads only)
         └─ cameras.js        4 camera presets with smooth damping
```

RK4 is the fourth-order Runge-Kutta step from Chapter A7: it estimates the rate of change four times per step and blends them. Node is introduced in the golden-file section below.

[Certain, read] `physics.js` decides all motion. Everything else reads its state and draws. The one exception is the catch: `twin.js` adds the 5,000 kg payload to the tip node's mass (`sim.m[0] += cfg.designPayloadKg`, line 319), and from then on `physics.js` moves the heavier node. All purely visual numbers (tether width exaggerated ×8000, bloom threshold 0.85, 7000 stars, a 30 s catch-tracking window) live in one object, `VISUAL_CONFIG` in `twin.js` (lines 40-103). They never feed back into the physics.

`params-loader.js` throws an error starting `FATAL:` on a network error, a non-2xx HTTP status, invalid JSON, or a missing field. It checks eight dotted paths (lines 13-22) plus `mass_ratio.integrated_tether_to_payload_both_arms.payload_mass_kg_for_tonnage`. It never falls back to default numbers. `twin.js` catches the error and shows it in the red `#fatal` overlay (lines 105-119). This is Rule 1 enforced in code: no canon, no twin. (Here "Rule 1" is README.md's first rule, "Single source of truth", which is how `params-loader.js` cites it. `CLAUDE.md` numbers its own rules differently: its Rule 1 is "run the tests first".)

The gap on main: if three.js itself fails to load, `twin.js` never starts, so its error handler never runs. The HUD keeps saying "loading…". The unmerged fixes branch adds an `onerror` handler to the script tag in `index.html` that shows a FATAL message naming unpkg.com (commit `525bb09`).

#### The fixed-timestep loop

A **frame** is one redraw of the picture. Browsers redraw a page about 60 times a second on a typical screen (from memory, verify), but not exactly. A slow laptop draws less often. If the physics step followed the drawing rate, results would depend on your laptop. So `twin.js` (lines 428-456) uses a **fixed-timestep accumulator**:

```
STEP  = 1/60 s                         physics step; never changes
dt    = min(real time since last frame, 0.25 s)
acc   = acc + dt * timeWarp            timeWarp is 1, 10 or 60 (buttons in index.html)
while acc >= STEP:
    sim.step(STEP);  acc = acc - STEP
alpha = acc / STEP                     0 to 1: how far into the next step
draw position = previous + (current - previous) * alpha
```

**Time warp** is a multiplier on how much simulated time passes per real second; the twin's buttons offer 1×, 10× and 60×. The last line is **interpolation**: drawing between two computed states so motion looks smooth. It changes only the picture, never the physics. The 0.25 s clamp prevents a "spiral of death" (the code comment's phrase, line 439) after the browser tab sleeps. Without it, one long pause would demand thousands of physics steps in a single frame. That frame would take a long time, so the next frame would demand even more steps, and the page would freeze.

#### Worked example 6: the accumulator in numbers

Inputs: `STEP` = 1/60 s, clamp 0.25 s, warp 1/10/60 (`twin.js` lines 429-445; `index.html` lines 46-48); RK4 uses 4 derivative evaluations per step (Chapter A7); v_tip 2,500 m/s and L 320,000 m (`rev_a.json`).

1. A 25 ms frame at 1×: acc = 0.025 s. One step of 0.01667 s runs. 0.025 − 0.01667 = 0.00833 s is left. alpha = 0.00833 ÷ 0.01667 = 0.5, so the picture is drawn halfway between two states.
2. At 60× and 60 frames per second: each frame adds (1/60) × 60 = 1.0 s of sim time. The loop runs 1.0 ÷ (1/60) = 60 physics steps, which is 60 × 4 = 240 derivative evaluations per frame.
3. After a long tab sleep at 60×: dt is clamped to 0.25 s, so 0.25 × 60 = 15 s of sim time, that is 15 × 60 = 900 steps. Without the clamp, a 10 s sleep would ask for 10 × 60 × 60 = 36,000 steps in one frame.
4. Spin rate ω = 2,500 ÷ 320,000 = 0.0078125 rad/s. One rotation = 2π ÷ 0.0078125 = 804.25 s = 13.40 min.
5. When armed, the catch fires at the next lower-tip **periapsis**: the moment the catching tip (node 0) is closest to Earth's centre. The code watches node 0's distance from Earth's centre and fires on the first step where it stops shrinking (`maybeHandlePeriapsis()`, `twin.js` lines 307-331). Node 0 starts straight below the hub, at 6,981 − 320 = 6,661 km. Armed at t = 0, a Node replica of that trigger driving the repo's own `physics.js` fired first at t = 952.03 s (run this session). At 1× that is 952 ÷ 60 = 15.9 minutes of waiting. At 60× it is 952 ÷ 60 = 15.9 s.
6. The same replica found the next periapses at 1,904.73 s and 2,856.18 s: about 952 s apart, not 804 s. The reason [Likely]: the tip is lowest when the tether points straight down, and "straight down" itself turns once per orbit. The tip must catch up with it. The catch-up period is 2π ÷ (ω − n), where n = v_orb ÷ r is the orbit's turning rate: n = 7,556.3 ÷ 6,981,000 = 0.0010824 rad/s. With the design ω, 2π ÷ (0.0078125 − 0.0010824) = 2π ÷ 0.0067301 = 933.6 s. With the simulated mean tip speed of 2,462.64 m/s (below), ω = 0.0076958 rad/s and the period is 950.1 s, close to the 952 s observed.

Result [Certain, recomputed with `python3 -B` and `node` this session]: 60 steps per frame at 60×, at most 900 per frame, one rotation per 804 s, one lowest-tip pass per about 952 s. `VISUAL_QA.md` lines 37-40 record a first catch at "t~952-1200s depending on arming phase". Only the 952 s end of that range fits the code. The trigger can fire only at a lowest point, and the next one after 952 s is at 1,905 s, so a first catch at 1,200 s cannot happen (Chapter A7, section A7.16, reaches the same conclusion). The same lines say "periapsis recurs roughly once per ~804s rotation period". The twin's own physics contradicts that too: the recurrence is about 952 s. Chapter A7 (section A7.12) finds the same 952 s in the Python model.

#### Camera damping and a real bug

**Camera damping** means moving the camera only part of the way toward its target each frame, so it glides instead of jumping. `cameras.js` does this every frame (lines 72 and 114): `position += (target - position) * (1 - exp(-k * dt))`, with `k = cameraDampingK = 2.5` per second. At dt = 1/60 s the camera closes 1 − e^(−0.0417) = 4.1% of the gap per frame. `VISUAL_QA.md` (lines 21-31) records a bug found on 2026-07-06: at 60× the tracking cameras lost the tether, because they used real time while the tether moved in sim time. The fix passes `dt * timeWarp` (`twin.js` line 476). At 60× and 60 frames per second that is 1 s per frame, so the camera closes 1 − e^(−2.5) = 92% of the gap and keeps up.

#### The golden file: checking one language against another

```
scripts/generate_golden.py   Python model, 600 s at dt = 1/60 s   ->  tools/twin/golden.json
tools/twin/verify.mjs        JS port, same run                    ->  compare
  positions within 0.1% relative (1 m absolute near zero) at t = 0, 60, 300, 600 s
  JS energy and angular-momentum drift < 0.1%;  mean tip speed within 1%
  600 / (1/60) = 36,000 steps
```

A **golden file** is a stored reference output that later runs must match. **Node** (Node.js) is a program that runs JavaScript outside a browser; `.mjs` marks a file as an ES module for Node. `verify.mjs` reads `rev_a.json` directly from disk, so it needs no web server. On failure it prints hints and exits 1. Its header says tolerances are never loosened to pass.

[Certain, `node tools/twin/verify.mjs` run this session with Node v22.22.0, exit 0]: `PASS`. Max relative position error 1.571e-10. Max energy drift 6.676e-13%. Mean tip speed JS 2462.6407 m/s against Python 2462.6407 m/s.

The mean tip speed is (2,500 − 2,462.64) ÷ 2,500 = 1.5% below the 2.5 km/s design value. [Likely] This is the real gravity-gradient effect that Chapter A7 (section A7.12) discusses, not a bug. Both languages agree on it. V1 (gravity off, near-rigid) does recover 2,500 m/s within 1%. And `MORNING_REPORT.md` (line 38) records the same effect: gravity "depresses its rotation-mean ~1.5–2% below the free-space 2,500 m/s". The exact figure depends on the averaging window; 600 s is shorter than one 952 s bottom-to-bottom cycle.

#### Worked example 7: the one deliberate language difference

JavaScript has no built-in `erf` (the error function used in the mass ratio, Chapter A6). `physics.js` (lines 33-54) uses the Abramowitz & Stegun 7.1.26 polynomial, whose stated maximum error is 1.5e-7. Does that matter?

Inputs: σ 5.8 GPa, ρ 1,560 kg/m³, v_tip 2.5 km/s, SF 2.5, derate 0.30 (`rev_a.json`); the A&S coefficients in `physics.js` lines 43-48; `verify.mjs` position tolerance 0.1% (line 32).

1. V_c = √(2 × 5.8 × 10⁹ ÷ 1,560) = 2,726.88 m/s.
2. x = (2,500 ÷ 2,726.88) × √(2.5 ÷ 0.7) = 0.916798 × 1.889822 = 1.732584. x² = 3.001847, e^(x²) = 20.1227.
3. Python `math.erf(x)` = 0.98572405. A&S erf(x) = 0.98572404. Difference 8.5 × 10⁻⁹.
4. Mass ratio = 2√π × x × e^(x²) × erf(x) = 3.5449077 × 1.732584 × 20.122675 × 0.98572405 = 121.8261 in both languages. Relative difference 8.6 × 10⁻⁹.
5. The 0.1% gate is 10⁻³, about 100,000 times larger than that difference.

Result [Certain, recomputed with `python3 -B` this session]: the approximation is far below any tolerance the project uses.

**`scripts/init_repo.sh`** is a one-time setup script (31 lines). `set -euo pipefail` means stop at the first error, treat unset variables as errors, and fail if any part of a pipe fails (from memory, verify). It runs `git init`, `git add .`, a first commit, then `gh repo create skyhook --private ... --push`; its `USERNAME` argument is used only in `echo` lines. ### A12.14 The Excel workbooks

A **workbook** is an Excel file made of **sheets**. Each sheet is a grid of **cells**. A cell holds a value or a **formula** such as `=B3*C4`, which Excel recalculates.

[Certain, openpyxl read-only scan this session]:

| Workbook | Sheets (formula cells) | Total formulas |
|---|---|---|
| `tools/financial/skyhook_financial_model.xlsx` | README (0), Assumptions (0), Design Calcs (81), Phase Budgets (2), Cash Flow & Payback (63) | 146 |
| `tools/financial/skyhook_phase0_plan.xlsx` | Gantt (432), Spend Curve (17) | 449 |
| `tools/financial/skyhook_risk_register.xlsx` | Risk Register (14) | 14 |

How Python uses the model workbook:

- `load_ladder_from_workbook` opens it with `openpyxl.load_workbook(path, read_only=True, data_only=False)` and reads cells B, C, D (Conservative, Baseline, Optimistic) of rows 3-16 on the `Assumptions` sheet. Those cells are typed numbers (that sheet has 0 formulas), for example strength retention 0.7 / 0.85 / 1 in row 3 and construction launch price 2500 / 1500 / 800 $/kg in row 5.
- openpyxl never recalculates formulas (from memory, verify). With `data_only=True` it returns the **cached values**: the results Excel last saved next to each formula. In this file every formula cell comes back as `None`: no saved values exist. So the Python model re-implements the whole formula chain itself (Chapter A9), and `tests/test_finance.py` checks it within 5% against workbook figures recorded in its docstring (Conservative 121.83×, 609 t, $8,741M).
- `Design Calcs` rows 27-31 hold an "ERF AUDIT" block. It checks Excel's own `ERF` against the same A&S 7.1.26 polynomial the twin uses.

Limits [Certain]:

- `docs/program_manifest.md` line 38 describes the model as "4 sheets, 134 live formulas". The repo file has 5 sheets and 146 formulas. The manifest does not record why. [Likely] The manifest indexes the wider project file set, not just the repo (some of its paths, such as `claude/skyhook_rev_b.md`, are not in the repo), so its entry may describe a different copy of the workbook. Section A12.11 found the same kind of mismatch for `skyhook-sim.jsx`.

One more limit: the program site's Monte Carlo uses `Math.random` without a **seed** (a fixed starting value that makes "random" numbers repeatable), so each page load, and each slider move, gives slightly different results. Chapter A8 (section A8.13) derives the stable closed-form value.

### Key takeaways

- One data file (`params/rev_a.json`) is loaded once, at import, by `physics/skyhook_physics.py`. Every Python module shares that one copy; only callers of `load_params()`, such as the `reva` test fixture, get a fresh one.
- Tests compare computed values with stored canon within chosen tolerances. On main: 74 tests, 73 passed, 1 deliberate skip, 2 deprecation warnings.
- You need `pip install pytest openpyxl` and a git checkout. The README's `pip install pytest` gives 6 failures; CI itself hit exactly this on 2026-08-27.
- Four finance analysis scripts (`sensitivity.py`, `demand_sensitivity.py`, `rightsize_sensitivity.py`, `leg_cost.py`) have no tests at all.
- CI runs Python only. Its last step cannot fail on a wrong number; pytest is the real guard.
- The digital twin is a JavaScript port of `physics/tether_dynamics.py`, checked by `verify.mjs` against a Python golden file to about 10⁻¹⁰. That check is manual, not in CI.
- Browser tools need CDNs and, for the twin, a web server at the repo root.
- Hand-copied numbers in browser tools drift. The worst case on main shows a tether 1.79× too heavy. The fixes branch adds canon snapshots with exact-equality tests; its suite gives 88 passed and 2 skipped out of 90, but it is unmerged.
- The JSX "canonical simulator" crashes on load on every branch.

# Part B: Aster

## Chapter B1: Orientation: what Aster is and how to read its numbers

**Main idea:** Aster is one mission-planning math engine with two front ends, a website and a tool server for AI agents, and every number it gives you comes labelled with its unit, its source and how far to trust it, so the first skill to learn is how to read those labels.

### B1.1 Before you start: two label systems

Two labelling systems appear in this guide. Keep them apart.

| System | Used by | Values | What it says |
|---|---|---|---|
| Guide labels | This guide | [Certain], [Likely], [Speculative] | How sure the *guide* is about a sentence |
| Confidence classes | Aster's software | `measured`, `derived`, `assumed` | How *Aster* obtained a number |

- **[Certain]** means a textbook fact, or a fact checked in the repository for this chapter.
- **[Likely]** means supported by evidence but not proven.
- **[Speculative]** means an informed guess.
- "(from memory, verify)" marks a fact the writer recalled rather than read in the repository.

**Evidence base.** The repository was read, unchanged, at commit `cec19e7` (2026-11-04); section B1.2 defines commits and npm. Live tool answers come from the published package `aster-mission-mcp@0.1.0`, the only version on the npm registry, published 2026-07-10 (`npm view`, run 2026-11-06) [Certain]. Its provenance strings name commit `84fefe8`, baked 2026-07-10T19:59:49.784Z. STATUS.md:15 adds that 0.1.0 "was baked from a dirty worktree" (audit L6-3): a **dirty worktree** is a working copy holding changes never committed, so the package may contain code no commit records [Certain that STATUS says so].

`main` is the repository's primary **branch**, the line of commits that counts as the official version. The package **lags** `main`, so every live number below is marked "(0.1.0)". All calls were re-run twice on 2026-11-06 with byte-identical output. Tests were not run: AGENTS.md:169 forbids a documentation agent from running `npm test` or `npm run build`. Test results quoted are recorded results, with dates.

### B1.2 What Aster is

The README gives Aster's identity in one sentence (README.md:3-5):

> Aster plans asteroid missions in the browser and answers mission-analysis questions over MCP — and every number it produces carries its source, its confidence class, and the commit it was computed from.

Take the terms one at a time.

- A **mission planner** estimates whether, when and at what cost a spacecraft could reach a target. Aster works at **screening** level: a fast, simplified first pass that rules targets in or out before anyone does detailed design.
- The **browser app** is a set of web pages. They are static files that GitHub Pages serves from the repository's `docs/` folder (AGENTS.md §9), so the math runs on your own computer, inside the browser [Certain].
- **MCP** (Model Context Protocol) is a standard way for an AI agent to call an outside tool and get a structured answer back (description from memory, verify). The expansion appears in the Slice 16 seal draft (tools/slice16-harness/SEAL_DRAFT.md:83); the README calls the package a "stdio MCP server" (README.md:28). **stdio** means the agent and the server exchange text through the program's standard input and output streams, like two programs joined by a pipe.
- A number's **source**, or **provenance**, is the file, data set or computation it came from.
- A **confidence class** is Aster's three-level label: `measured`, `derived` or `assumed` (mcp/src/envelope/index.ts:1).
- A **commit** is a saved snapshot of the code in **git**, the version-control system. Each commit is named by a **hash**, a fingerprint string computed from its contents, such as `84fefe8` (the first seven characters of a 40-character hash). Citing it lets anyone re-run exactly the code that produced a number. To **merge** a branch is to join its commits into another branch, usually `main`.

#### One core, two interfaces

The browser app and the MCP server run the same math [Certain, README.md:37-51]:

- The npm package ships `dist/src`, which is the compiled `src/v2` core itself, plus a thin adapter layer in `dist/mcp/src` (the `files` list in mcp/package.json). **npm** is the public registry and installer for JavaScript packages, and `npx` downloads and runs one (from memory, verify).
- Invariant INV-027 forbids any math in `mcp/`: "adapters only" (INVARIANTS.md §6).

Think of a restaurant with a dining-room counter and a delivery window, both served by one kitchen. An inspector who checks the kitchen has checked both. In the same way, validation of a porkchop cell (one square of the launch-date grid of section B1.3) in the browser is validation of the matching MCP `explain_cell` answer (README.md:49-51).

The analogy needs the *same* kitchen: both built from the same commit. The published 0.1.0 package was baked in July 2026, while `docs/` was last rebuilt at `adda2ab` (Slice 20 Front A). So "checking one checks both" is exact only for code unchanged in between [Certain that the builds differ; Likely that unchanged math gives the same numbers].

```
answer = core(inputs)                              # src/v2/   (Lambert solver, DLA, vehicle curves)
page   = render(answer)                            # src/v2/app/, src/v2/render/
reply  = envelope(answer, provenance, confidence)  # mcp/src/  (adapters only, INV-027)
```

#### What Aster is not

- **Not a profit oracle.** The original founding document calls Aster "a decision-support system, not a profit oracle" (FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md:14) [Certain].
- **Not a flight-certified mission designer** (FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md:22) [Certain].
- **Not the old prototype.** The first version (V1) is frozen at `/legacy/`. LEGACY.md:90-91 says its "economic and value figures are unsourced and known to be wrong" [Certain].
- **Not yet a round-trip planner.** "Aster plans only the outbound leg" (src/v2/SLICE_20_FOUNDING.md:9). Adding the return leg is the job of Slice 20 (slices and their fronts are defined in Section B1.7). At `cec19e7` only its Front A has merged, and no return-leg code exists yet in `src/v2` or `mcp/src` [Certain, searched with **grep**, a command-line text-search tool]. The porkchop page does offer a "sample-return" mode, but it only adds an assumed departure burn equal to the arrival burn; it computes no return trajectory (src/v2/porkchop/delta-v.ts:43-45) [Certain].

The product changed fast. On 2026-05-15 the vision document said Aster was a 3D visualisation with 1,008 asteroids and "not yet the mission planner" (ASTER_PRODUCT_VISION.md:29,42). The planning capability was built in Slices 9 to 15 (STATUS.md slice table) [Certain].

### B1.3 The five questions Aster answers

| # | Question | What Aster computes | Taught in |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which targets? | A committed catalog of 41,906 near-Earth objects from JPL's Small-Body Database | Chapters B3, B4 |
| 2 | When to launch? | A grid of departure date × time of flight, the **porkchop plot** | Chapters B5, B6 |
| 3 | How much energy? | Launch energy C3 in km²/s², and velocity changes ΔV in km/s | Chapters B6, B7 |
| 4 | How much mass arrives? | Payload from a published launch-vehicle curve, then the rocket equation | Chapter B7 |
| 5 | How far can I trust it? | Confidence classes, provenance, validation, fidelity tiers, refusals | Chapters B4, B8, B10 |

The About page says the same in prose (src/v2/app/about/main.ts:366-372). The V1 founding document put it as one question: "Which object, launched when, at what approximate cost, offers the best mission trade?" (FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md:14).

Five terms from the table and the chain below:

- A **near-Earth object (NEO)** is an asteroid or comet whose orbit comes close to Earth's. The usual cut-off is a closest approach to the Sun under 1.3 AU, where 1 AU is roughly the Earth–Sun distance (section B1.9.3) (cut-off from memory, verify). JPL is NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. By orbit class, Aster's catalog holds 41,698 asteroids and 208 comets: 166 JFC, 36 HTC and 6 ETC, the Jupiter-family, Halley-type and Encke-type comet classes (names from memory, verify) [Certain for the counts, `catalog.classDistribution` in tests/fixtures/v2/nea-catalog-slice9.json, recomputed]. The About page rightly says "near-Earth objects". mcp/README.md:52 says "near-Earth asteroids", forgetting the comets; so does the data file, which files every record under `asteroids` with an `asteroid-` prefix [Certain, counted].
- **ΔV** ("delta-vee") is a change of velocity a spacecraft must make with its engines. It is the currency of spaceflight. Chapter B7 builds the budget.
- **C3** is the launch energy: the square of the speed the spacecraft still has after it has escaped Earth's gravity, called **v∞** ("v-infinity"). Chapter B6 derives it.
- A **Lambert solver** finds the orbit that joins two given positions in a given flight time. Aster's is a clean-room TypeScript version of Izzo's 2014 method (NOTICE:9-14; src/v2/core/lambert/izzo.ts). Chapter B5 builds it.
- A **fidelity tier** is Aster's per-body label, L0, L1 or L2, for how far its simple **two-body** screening can be trusted for that body (`FidelityTier`, src/v2/boundary/tier-assignments.ts:2). "Two-body" means the model lets only one body, the Sun, pull on the asteroid; every other pull is ignored. Chapter B4 explains the tiers.

The questions chain together:

```
target → (departure date, time of flight) → Lambert solve → v∞ → C3 = v∞²
       → payload(C3) from a vehicle curve → ΔV budget → delivered mass
       → wrapped in an envelope {units, confidence, sourceIds, assumptions}, or a refusal
```

#### Why question 5 matters: the Apophis trap

Asteroid Apophis has catalog designation `99942`. It has the lowest minimum C3 of all 41,905 screened bodies (the catalog's 41,906 minus the hyperbolic comet 2015 D1, which cannot be propagated; Chapter B5): 0.000206 km²/s², for a departure on 2028-09-14 and a 212-day flight [Certain, sorted from tests/fixtures/v2/lambert-screen-cache.json; same value from `get_body` (0.1.0)]. Read naively, it is the cheapest target in the catalog.

Aster's own disclosure text says otherwise (src/v2/app/catalog-list/honesty-disclosure.ts:78-85):

- Close approaches to Earth produce near-zero C3 values that are "mathematically valid but operationally meaningless".
- "Apophis at its 2029 close approach is the canonical example."
- Treat any minimum C3 below 0.1 km²/s² "as a flag to inspect the geometry, not a real planning number."

A second warning: the Slice 18 fidelity file puts Apophis in tier L1, with its earliest material Earth encounter on 2028-Sep-12 (tools/slice18-research/tier-sizing-per-body.json, record `99942`). "Material" means the encounter's estimated deflection, carried to the end of the window, adds at least 10⁶ km of drift (`L1_CRITERION`, src/v2/porkchop/tier-disclosure.ts:23-25). This one is a nudge of only 2.6 m/s, but a small nudge grows over years. For an L1 body the website's disclosure reads "Screening for this object is supported through [date]… Arrivals after it are computed from an orbit the encounter invalidates" (src/v2/porkchop/tier-disclosure.ts:119-122). For Apophis that date is 2028-09-12. The "cheapest" window departs two days later and arrives seven months later, both past the boundary [Certain].

A third check is pure arithmetic and geometry. (Julian Dates and TDB are explained in 1.9.5.)

1. 2028-09-14 plus 212 days is 2029-04-14. The `explain_cell` arrival instant is JD 2462240.50080, which is 00:01 TDB on 2029-04-14.
2. The same tier record names a close approach to Earth at "2029-Apr-13 21:46" (TDB, from JPL's close-approach data) as Apophis's largest **perturbation** in the window (`maxDriftEncounter`). A perturbation is a change to an orbit caused by some other body's gravity; this one is estimated at 2,776 m/s. The "mission" arrives about 2¼ hours after that close approach.
3. Compare positions at the arrival instant. Apophis's position is the `explain_cell` arrival state (0.1.0), from Aster's own two-body orbit. Earth's is its committed midnight record, moved forward 69.184 s to the same instant. They are about 45,900 km apart (45,935 km, about seven Earth radii of 6,378 km each, radius from memory, verify), and Apophis moves 5.842 km/s relative to Earth [Certain, recomputed for this guide].
4. The tool's arrival speed relative to Apophis, `vInfArr` = 5.845 km/s, is almost the same number.

So the "spacecraft" stays almost on Earth's own orbit, and Apophis flies past it [Likely, interpretation]. Nor is Apophis rare: 3,163 bodies, 7.5% of those screened, have a minimum C3 below 0.1 km²/s² [Certain, counted from the screening cache].

The published package does not pass these warnings on. `get_body("99942")` (0.1.0) returns the number with no near-zero flag and no tier [Certain, live call]. On `main`, a `nearZeroC3` field exists (mcp/src/tools/near-zero-c3.ts, added in `531eb30` on 2026-10-10) but is unpublished, since 0.1.0 is still the only release, and `mcp/src` has no fidelity-tier handling at all [Certain, grep and npm registry]. So the website warns people more than the tool server warns agents. A user-experience report of 2026-10-22 records this as problem P1, severity HIGH (tools/audit/ux-run-2026-10-22/UX_RUN_PROBLEMS_2026-10-22.md, on the **unmerged branch** `origin/claude/ux-run-2026-10-22`).

### B1.4 The user surfaces

All web paths sit under `https://hudsonclavin-cloud.github.io/asteroid-mining-planner/` (README.md:15-19).

| Surface | Path | What it shows | Code |
|---|---|---|---|
| Front door | `/` | Redirects to the solar-system view | index.html:6,18 |
| Solar-system view and catalog | `/v2/solar-system/` | 3D Sun and planets, the 41,906-body list, screening colours | src/v2/app/solar-system/ |
| Porkchop planner | `/v2/porkchop/` | C3/ΔV grid for one target, DLA overlay, cost card, validation card | src/v2/app/porkchop/main.ts |
| Compare | `/v2/compare/` | Up to five targets side by side | src/v2/app/compare/main.ts; `COMPARE_BODIES_CAP = 5` (src/v2/porkchop/compare-url.ts:12) |
| About | `/v2/about/` | What Aster is, how it was built, validation figures | src/v2/app/about/main.ts |
| Legacy V1 | `/legacy/` | Frozen prototype, hidden from search engines, with a banner | LEGACY.md:88-97 |
| MCP tools | `npx aster-mission-mcp` | Seven tools and four reference resources | mcp/README.md |

The **DLA** (declination of the launch asymptote) is the angle, north or south of Earth's equator, of the direction in which the spacecraft leaves Earth. A launch site can reach only some DLAs cheaply (Chapter B7).

The seven tools are `search_bodies`, `get_body`, `porkchop_scan`, `explain_cell`, `dla_feasibility`, `estimate_mission_cost` and `get_validation_report`. The four resources are `aster://reference/launch-vehicles`, `…/dla-site-bands`, `…/catalog-schema` and `…/dv-stack-model` [Certain, live `tools/list` and `resources/list` calls (0.1.0), and mcp/README.md]. INV-029 caps the set at eight tools; a ninth needs a founding-document amendment (INVARIANTS.md §6).

Three cautions [Certain]:

1. The compare page is built (vite.config.ts:22) and deployed (`docs/v2/compare/`), but the README "Live" table omits it. Two older V2 pages, `/v2/earth-moon/` and `/v2/inner-solar-system/`, are also still built (vite.config.ts:17-18) and present in `docs/v2/`.
2. The live site was not checked against `docs/` for this chapter; the last recorded byte comparison is the 2026-08-01 audit (README.md:21-23). A change counts as live only when a string it introduced is read from the live page; a green **CI** check (continuous integration, GitHub's automatic test and build runs) is not proof (AGENTS.md §9).
3. On 2026-08-23 Hudson recorded two live-site defects (STATUS.md:109,113). The "?" help overlay said right-drag pans, but right-drag orbited the camera. A cold first load showed 30+ seconds of black screen; the ~9 MB catalog took 32.87 s to download, STATUS's [Likely] cause. The pointer code maps the right button to pan (src/v2/app/solar-system/runtime.ts:2033), and its comment credits the "B1" pan work that STATUS dates to 2026-08-12 (STATUS.md:95). So the mapping [Likely] already existed when right-drag misbehaved, which leans toward STATUS's other hypothesis, a browser intercepting the right button. No later browser check is recorded, so neither fix is confirmed.

### B1.5 The honesty layer as a design value

The **honesty layer** is the set of enforced rules that make every number show its unit, its source and how far to trust it, and that make the software refuse rather than guess when a request is outside what it can support.

It starts from one architectural rule: "Truth must never depend on presentation" (V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md:23). The physics code (`core/`) stores real radii and real distances. The display code (`render/`) may enlarge things, but only as a labelled transform on top. **Honest mode** shows real sizes. **Readable mode** may enlarge bodies but "must preserve source provenance and honesty labels" (V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md §4) [Certain].

An **invariant** is a rule that must hold at all times, written down with an ID (INV-…) so tests and reviews can check it. The honesty layer rests on these (INVARIANTS.md §6):

| Invariant | Rule, shortened |
|---|---|
| INV-016 | Every C3 or ΔV carries a fidelity tag saying it is patched-conic (Sun-only dynamics; Limits, item 1), an older idea than Slice 18's tiers (src/v2/SLICE_10_FOUNDING.md:53-55) |
| INV-021 | A vector's **reference frame** (the set of axes its components are measured along; Chapter B2) is established by measurement, never by its label |
| INV-023 | No extrapolation past a launch vehicle's published performance curve |
| INV-024 | Outside astrodynamics libraries are test oracles only, never imported or copied |
| INV-026 | Numbers on a trust page render from one committed data file, not typed-in literals |
| INV-028 | Every tool result is an evidence envelope (section B1.10); "refusal is a result" |
| INV-032 | No **NaN** ("Not a Number", the result of undefined arithmetic such as 0/0) or Infinity may cross the wire |
| INV-033 | No path, commit, count or URL unless confirmed to exist and match |

An **oracle** is an independent, trusted reference used to check answers. Aster's oracles include poliastro, a Python astrodynamics library (description from memory, verify; "Primary oracle: poliastro 0.17", INVARIANTS.md §4), and NASA's published launch-vehicle performance from the Launch Services Program's elvperf tool ("NASA LSP elvperf", tools/slice13-research/elvperf/oracle/oracle-report.md:4; README.md:53-66).

#### The weakest-link rule

A chain is as strong as its weakest link. Aster rates a whole answer the same way:

```
rank:  assumed = 0  <  derived = 1  <  measured = 2       (CONFIDENCE_RANK, mcp/src/envelope/index.ts:90-94)
envelope.confidence = the lowest rank among the provenance entries   (confidenceMin, :123-133)
```

One subtlety matters. The minimum runs over the list of **sources**, not over the numbers inside the answer. So the top level can say `derived` while a number inside says `assumed`. Section B1.10 shows a real case.

#### Three kinds of answer

| Kind | Meaning | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| Value | A computed answer | `value` holds data |
| Negative value | Known not to work | `value` holds `{feasible: false, …}` |
| Refusal | Cannot answer this | `value: null` plus `refusal {code, reason, what_would_help}` |

"Infeasibility is a value, not a refusal" (src/v2/SLICE_15_FOUNDING.md:134, DEC-15-4(g)). The refusal codes are `out_of_envelope`, `not_found` and `insufficient_data`. The last is defined but never emitted (mcp/src/envelope/index.ts:44; HANDOFF.md:58) [Certain].

Two misreadings to avoid:

- `measured` does not mean correct. It describes how a number was obtained, not whether it is right.
- [Certain] in this guide is not the same as `measured` in Aster.

### B1.7 Project vocabulary

Aster is built in **slices**. A slice is a numbered piece of work that ships one working capability end to end. Every slice is meant to follow the same order (.claude/skills/slice-discipline/SKILL.md:12-30; the About page states the same order, src/v2/app/about/main.ts:382):

```
pre-research → decisions (DECs) locked → founding document → dispatches
             → multi-agent audit (math work, before deploy) → deploy
```

| Term | Meaning | Real example |
|---|---|---|
| **Slice** | Numbered increment that ships one capability | Slice 11 = porkchop + ΔV; Slice 17 = Target Compare |
| **Front** | A sub-track inside a slice | Slice 20 "Front A … is not cuttable" (SLICE_20_FOUNDING.md:14) |
| **Founding document** | The slice's written contract, using a §1–§8 template, committed before any implementation dispatch. Not always: the Slice 19 document says it was "Written AFTER the slice's cleanup tier shipped" (SLICE_19_FOUNDING.md:4) | `src/v2/SLICE_11_FOUNDING.md` |
| **Pre-research** | Measuring inputs and reading literature before deciding | scripts under `tools/sliceN-research/` |
| **DEC** | A locked decision with its justification. Drafts say PROPOSED; "Only Hudson converts PROPOSED → locked" (slice-discipline SKILL.md:107-109) | DEC-17-6: compare holds at most five bodies (SLICE_17_FOUNDING.md:214) |
| **OQ** | An open question, status OPEN, SCOPING or CLOSED with a date; closure cites a measurement | OQ-12-1 asked which frame a velocity was in (SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md:43) |
| **INV** | Invariant: a technical rule that must always hold | INV-021, frame by measurement |
| **AMD** | A numbered amendment to a locked decision, added, never overwritten | "AMD-1 — Worker contract (amends DEC-8)" (SLICE_11_FOUNDING.md:190) |
| **Dispatch** | One scoped instruction packet for the executing agent | template in AGENTS.md §6 |
| **Tripwire** | A measurable condition that proves the approach wrong. If it fires: stop, report, no workaround | "A 'create' target that already exists is a TRIPWIRE" (AGENTS.md:132) |
| **STOP gate** | A fixed point where work halts for verification | math changes must "reproduce a known numerical value against an external oracle before committing" (AGENTS.md:68-69) |
| **CUT RULE** | A pre-declared order for dropping scope, each cut recorded | Slice 17 cut its tiers B3–B5 (STATUS.md:62) |
| **Verify-before-lock** | Nothing locks until it reproduces a value against an oracle | "'It looks right' is not verification" (AGENTS.md:95) |
| **Multi-agent audit** | Three independent AI reviews of math code before deploy, then a reconciliation | "a mathematician, an adversary, and an architect" (about/main.ts:394). Slice 20 calls it a "four-lens audit" because it counts the reconciliation as a lens (SLICE_20_FOUNDING.md:185) |

Four points trip up newcomers [Certain]:

- **A DEC is never edited quietly.** Founding documents are additive-only (wrong lines are kept, and corrections are appended as dated amendments); the pre-commit hook counts deleted lines in them (AGENTS.md:112-119).
- **A tripwire is not a STOP gate.** A tripwire is conditional ("run unless X happens"); a STOP gate is positional ("stop after step N") (AGENTS.md:77-78).
- **INV numbers were once reused.** Slice 16's local INV-033 to INV-036 clashed with global numbers. They were mapped to INV-S16-033 to -036 rather than rewritten, and the global numbers 035 and 036 stay skipped (INVARIANTS.md amendments, 2026-08-01 and 2026-10-26).
- **A plan is not a record.** The roadmap planned Slice 18 as "Explain This Cell" and Slice 20 as "Mission View" (strategy/ASTER_ROADMAP_2026-08.md:72-83). The real ones are Screening Fidelity and Return Leg.
