This line supersedes the DRAFT header" (line 370). That is how additive-only files work: the correction is appended and the old line stays.

### B1.8 Who does what: the agent roles

Most of the code and documents were produced by AI agents under one human's control. Three git words help here. To **push** is to send local commits to the shared copy of the repository on GitHub. To **stage** a file is to mark it for inclusion in the next commit. **Recon** (reconnaissance) is read-only investigation that changes nothing. The roles are fixed by AGENTS.md:

| Role | Who | Does | Does not |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hudson** | The owner, Hudson Clavin | Final authority. Locks DECs (slice-discipline SKILL.md:107-109), verifies in the browser, runs the deploy, is the only one who pushes. May override a tripwire or waive a STOP gate; "this is not delegable" (§7) | — |
| **Nova** | "chat Claude: the advisor and dispatch writer" (§5) | Drafts founding documents, research and dispatches | Run commands, touch the repository, declare a DEC locked or an OQ closed "without a measurement or oracle reference" (§5) |
| **Codex** | Code-executing agent (§4) | Runs dispatches, tests and builds; stages files by name; commits | Push, `git add -A`, skip a verification gate |
| **Claude Code** | Docs and read-only recon agent (§3) | Writes documentation; traces code paths | Run builds or tests, write TypeScript, unless acting as executor |

Since 2026-11-04 (DEC-20-13), Claude Code is the executor "whenever Codex is unavailable", under exactly Codex's rules (AGENTS.md:175) [Certain]. A fifth name, Clome, appears in visual gates ("[V] visual (Hudson + Clome)", SLICE_20_FOUNDING.md:242), and STATUS.md:129 mentions its "automation tab" [Likely: an automated browser checker; AGENTS.md does not define it]. Role names stay fixed while the models behind them change; bylines such as "drafted by Nova/Fable 5" record which model filled a role (src/v2/SLICE_15_FOUNDING.md:5) [Likely].

**Git hooks**, scripts git runs automatically before a commit or push, enforce part of this. `.githooks/pre-push` blocks any push without the Hudson-only override `ASTER_PUSH_OK=1`. `.githooks/pre-commit` refuses paths not listed in `.dispatch-scope` and blocks protected paths (AGENTS.md:107-119). The hooks run only in a checkout where `npm ci` or `npm install` installed them; a fresh clone, web editors and the GitHub UI skip them (AGENTS.md:100-105). AGENTS.md:136 calls them "drift-protection, not adversary-proofing". The tracked `.dispatch-scope` at `cec19e7` still lists Slice 18 paths, so it is stale [Certain, file read]. Its last visible change is `4d3267c` (2026-09-21), but that is also the oldest commit in this shallow checkout (a copy that holds only recent history), so the true last change was on or before that date [Certain, git log and `.git/shallow`].

### B1.9 The language of numbers

The rest of this chapter builds the number skills every later chapter needs. It starts from units and ends with reading a full answer from the tool server.

#### B1.9.1 A quantity is a number times a unit

A **physical quantity** is a number multiplied by a **unit**: "5 km" means 5 × (one kilometre). The number alone means nothing. "5 km" and "5 km/s" are different statements.

The **SI** (International System of Units) has seven **base units**: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol) and candela (cd) [Certain, textbook]. **Derived units** are built from them: speed in m/s, acceleration in m/s², energy in joules, J = kg·m²/s².

```
quantity = number × unit                 5 km = 5 × 1000 m = 5000 m
dimension check: both sides of any equation must have the same unit
```

**In Aster** [Certain]. Inside `core/`, positions are stored in metres, velocities in m/s, and time in TDB seconds since J2000 (V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md §3.1; invariant INV-001 "Canonical Units", src/v2/core/invariants/README.md:12). The edges of the system use friendlier units. In four live tool replies (0.1.0; their "envelope" format is section B1.10) the unit strings were: `%`, `au`, `cells`, `count`, `days`, `deg`, `kg`, `km`, `km/s`, `km^2/s^2`, `m`, `m/s`, `mag`, `rad`, `relative error`, `s since J2000 TDB` and `unitless`.

Code names carry their units as suffixes: `Km2S2` (km²/s²), `Kmps` (km/s), `Mps` (m/s), `M3S2` (m³/s²). This matters because modules differ. `src/v2/porkchop/delta-v.ts:5` holds `STATIONKEEPING_DV_KMPS = 0.150`. `src/v2/porkchop/launch-vehicles.ts:61` holds `SPACECRAFT_STATIONKEEPING_MPS = 150`. Same quantity, different units.

Unit mix-ups have destroyed spacecraft. NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 after one team's software used pound-force seconds where another expected newton seconds (from memory, verify).

#### B1.9.2 Prefixes, scientific notation and stored numbers

**Metric prefixes** scale a unit by powers of ten:

```
n (nano) 10⁻⁹   µ (micro) 10⁻⁶   m (milli) 10⁻³   k (kilo) 10³   M (mega) 10⁶   G (giga) 10⁹   T (tera) 10¹²
```

**Scientific notation** writes a number as a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ |a| < 10. Code writes the same thing as `a e n`: `1.32712440018e20` means 1.32712440018 × 10²⁰. It does not mean "e to the 20".

Examples from the repository [Certain]:

- `GM_SUN_M3_S2 = 1.32712440018e20` m³/s², the Sun's gravitational parameter: the gravitational constant G times the Sun's mass (src/v2/core/propagators/keplerian.ts:9; Chapter B3). Since 1 km³ = 10⁹ m³, this is 1.32712440018 × 10¹¹ km³/s².
- M counts the complete laps a transfer makes around the Sun before arrival. For transfers of less than one lap (M = 0, which the README calls single-revolution) the Lambert solver agrees with poliastro to a maximum relative error (defined in 1.9.7) of `3.428650990914828e-14`; multi-revolution velocity magnitudes (sizes, ignoring direction) agree to `3.5979389805439233e-12` (mcp/README.md "Validation"; `get_validation_report` (0.1.0)).
- The screening cache records `totalSolves = 1804638825`, about 1.80 × 10⁹. Its metadata gives departures every 7 days from 2026-01-01 to 2040-12-31 and flight times every 30 days from 182 to 1,826 days. Count grid points like fence posts: whole steps that fit, plus the starting point. The window is 5,478 days; 5,478 / 7 = 782.6, so 782 whole steps fit, giving 782 + 1 = 783 departure dates. For flight times, (1,826 − 182) / 30 = 54.8, so 54 whole steps, giving 55 values (182 to 1,802 days). Then 783 × 55 × 41,905 bodies = 1,804,638,825, exactly the recorded total (tests/fixtures/v2/lambert-screen-cache.json `metadata`; recomputed). Chapter B6 explains the grid.

**Bytes use two systems.** In SI, 1 kB = 1,000 bytes. In the binary system, 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes. The catalog's compressed download is 8,973,203 bytes (STATUS.md:113): 8,973 kB, or 8,763 KiB.

The repository uses "MB" both ways. STATUS.md:113 calls the 52,969,826-byte raw catalog "52.97 MB" (SI). The roadmap calls the 34,499,477-byte screening cache "the 33 MB screening cache" (strategy/ASTER_ROADMAP_2026-08.md:81). That fits only binary units: 32.9 MiB, not 34.5 MB. The cache's own `generatedAt` is 2026-05-30, before the 2026-08-02 roadmap, so it was probably the same file then [Likely; the shallow history cannot show earlier versions]. Check the base before comparing.

**How computers store numbers.** JavaScript numbers are 64-bit **floating-point** values (f64): scientific notation in base 2, good to about 15–16 significant digits. The **GPU** (graphics processor) works in 32-bit floats (f32), good to about 7 (both from memory, verify). The gap between neighbouring storable numbers grows with size. Near 1 AU = 1.495978707 × 10¹¹ m (V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md:47) the gap is 3.05 × 10⁻⁵ m in f64 but 16,384 m in f32, and storing 1 AU in f32 lands 6,764 m off [Certain, computed with numpy; V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md:47-49 quotes the related figures 3.3e-5 m and 1.8e4 m]. So `core/` keeps f64 metres, and the renderer subtracts the camera position before converting to f32, a technique called a **floating origin** (V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md:50-53; Chapter B9).

#### B1.9.3 Distances and speeds: km, AU, km/s

The **astronomical unit** (AU) is the standard yardstick of the solar system. It is roughly the mean Earth–Sun distance and is now a fixed, defined length, set by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in 2012 (from memory, verify):

```
1 AU = 149,597,870,700 m      AU_M,  src/v2/app/solar-system/runtime.ts:74
     = 149,597,870.7  km      AU_KM, src/v2/render/slice9-spatial-partition.ts:78
```

There is no shared AU constant in `core/`. Five files define their own `AU_M` or `AU_KM`: the solar-system and inner-solar-system `runtime.ts` in `app/`, and `slice9-spatial-partition.ts`, `asteroid-cell-renderer.ts` and `spatial-grid.ts` in `render/`. Two more files repeat the bare number [Certain, grep of `src/v2` and `mcp/src`]. Separate copies can drift apart if someone edits only one; a single shared constant cannot.

Useful anchors [Certain, computed from the constants above]:

- Light needs 499 s, about 8.3 minutes, to cross 1 AU (using c = 299,792,458 m/s, from memory, verify).
- A circular orbit at 1 AU moves at √(GM_sun / r) = √(1.32712440018 × 10²⁰ / 1.495978707 × 10¹¹) = 29.78 km/s.
- A car at 100 km/h moves at 100 / 3600 = 0.0278 km/s. Earth's orbital speed is about 1,070 times that.

Apophis's orbit has **semi-major axis** (roughly its average distance from the Sun, Chapter B3) `aKm` = 137,983,836.49 km in the catalog (tests/fixtures/v2/nea-catalog-slice9.json). `get_body` (0.1.0) reports the same number in metres: 137,983,836,494.7 m. Divide the km value by 149,597,870.7 km: **0.922 AU**, a little inside Earth's orbit. The `get_body` envelope also gives its uncertainty, `sigmaA` = 2.4147 × 10⁻⁹ AU. Multiply by the AU in km: 2.4147 × 10⁻⁹ × 149,597,870.7 = 0.361 km, about **361 m** [Certain, recomputed].

#### B1.9.4 Squared units: km²/s² and C3

Squaring a unit squares its scale: (km/s)² = km²/s², and 1 km²/s² = (1000 m)²/s² = 10⁶ m²/s². A unit of m²/s² is a joule per kilogram, so km²/s² measures **energy per kilogram** [Certain, textbook]. It is not an area. Strictly, C3 is twice the orbit's energy per kilogram, not equal to it (Chapter B6) [Certain, textbook].

C3 is the square of the departure excess speed:

```
C3 = v∞²        v∞ = √C3            (Chapter B6 derives it)
```

The square law has a trap. C3 = 100 is four times C3 = 25, but the speed is only twice as large: 10 km/s against 5 km/s.

#### Worked example 1.1: from C3 back to speed

Inputs: a `porkchop_scan` of Apophis for departures 2026-01-01 to 2026-03-01 and flight times 100–300 days on a 5 × 5 grid (`topN` = 3) returned a best cell with `vInfDep` = 8.033724154926526 km/s and `c3` = 64.54072379744993 km²/s² (0.1.0). `explain_cell` for the 2028-09-14, 212-day cell returned `c3` = 0.000206413468465582 km²/s² (0.1.0). The two thresholds are 25 km²/s² (honesty-disclosure.ts:61) and 0.1 km²/s² (src/v2/core/constants/near-zero-c3.ts:5).

1. Square the speed: 8.033724154926526² = 64.54072379744993. This matches the reported C3 to every digit.
2. Apophis: √0.000206413 = 0.014367 km/s = 14.4 m/s, matching the reported `vInfDep` of 0.014367 km/s.
3. The "low C3" cut: √25 = 5.00 km/s.
4. The near-zero flag: √0.1 = 0.316 km/s = 316 m/s.

Result: Apophis's "best window" leaves Earth at about 14 m/s relative speed (14.4 × 3.6 = 52 km/h), slower than a car on a motorway. That is the signature of Earth and Apophis being almost in the same place at the same time, not of a good mission; section B1.3 showed they are only about 45,900 km apart at the arrival instant. The same `explain_cell` reply gives the arrival burn twice. A **rendezvous** burn is the ΔV needed to match the target's velocity on arrival, so the spacecraft stays with it instead of flying past. The reply gives it as `vInfArr` = 5.844705709724418 km/s and as `rendezvous` = 5844.705709724418 m/s. Their ratio is 1000: the same speed in two units.

#### B1.9.5 Time: days, seconds since J2000 and Julian dates

Calendar dates are awkward for arithmetic: months differ in length and leap years add days. Astronomers count days instead. A **Julian Date** (JD) is a continuous day count. Each JD day starts at **noon**, so a JD ending in .5 is a midnight (from memory, verify).

Aster's anchor is **J2000**, JD 2451545.0 (`J2000_TDB_JULIAN_DATE`, src/v2/core/units.ts:1), which is noon on 2000-01-01; the code comment calls it "J2000-TDB-noon" (src/v2/core/units/utc-to-tdb.ts:22).

```
SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86400                                          src/v2/core/units.ts:2
t [s since J2000] = (JD − 2451545.0) × 86400                      jdTdbToSecondsSinceJ2000, units.ts:15-17
TDB − UTC ≈ (TAI − UTC) + (TT − TAI) = 37 s + 32.184 s = 69.184 s   src/v2/core/units/utc-to-tdb.ts:5-28
```

**UTC** is civil clock time. It has **leap seconds**: extra seconds inserted now and then to keep clocks in step with Earth's slightly irregular rotation (from memory, verify). **TDB** (Barycentric Dynamical Time) is a smooth time scale used for orbit calculations. "Barycentric" refers to the **barycentre**, the solar system's centre of mass.

Two more scales sit in the middle of the formula. **TAI** (International Atomic Time) is the count kept by atomic clocks, with no leap seconds. **TT** (Terrestrial Time) is TAI plus exactly 32.184 s (both from memory, verify). Chapter B2 builds all of these properly. Here, note only that TDB and UTC differ by 69.184 s, a fixed offset in Aster valid from 2017-01-01 onward (utc-to-tdb.ts:14-16).

Where the 37 s comes from: TAI − UTC is 37 s, made of a 10 s offset set in 1972 plus 27 leap seconds added since (from memory, verify). The code comment calls the 37 s "leap seconds accumulated since 1972" (utc-to-tdb.ts:7), which is loose. It also labels the 32.184 s "TDB - TAI" (line 8); strictly that is TT − TAI. TDB stays within about 2 ms of TT, which the code ignores (utc-to-tdb.ts:11-12).

#### Worked example 1.2: a 69-second offset and a one-day bug

Inputs: `UNIX_TO_J2000_SECONDS` = 10957.5 d × 86400 = 946,728,000 s and `TDB_MINUS_UTC_SECONDS` = 69.184 (utc-to-tdb.ts:28-31). The committed ephemeris file holds six bodies (Sun, Mercury, Venus, Earth, Moon, Mars), each with 5,479 daily records; Earth's run from JD 2461041.5 to 2466519.5 (src/v2/data/horizons-inner-solar-system-2026-2040.json, `targets.earth.records`; counted). **Unix time** counts seconds from 1970-01-01 00:00 UTC, treating every day as exactly 86,400 s, so leap seconds are left out (from memory, verify).

1. 2026-01-01 00:00 UTC is 1,767,225,600 s of Unix time (Python `datetime`).
2. Subtract the Unix-to-J2000 offset: 1,767,225,600 − 946,728,000 = 820,497,600 s.
3. Add the TDB offset: 820,497,600 + 69.184 = 820,497,669.184 s.
4. Convert to days: 820,497,669.184 / 86,400 = 9,496.50080074 d.
5. Add J2000: 2,451,545.0 + 9,496.50080074 = **JD 2,461,041.50080074** (TDB).

This matches the table in mcp/README.md ("Advertised span vs accepted span"). The tail 0.00080074 d is the 69.184 s.

The Earth file starts at JD 2461041.5, which is TDB midnight on 2026-01-01. UTC midnight on 2026-01-01 falls 69 s after that start, so it is inside. UTC midnight on 2025-12-31 is JD 2461040.50080074, just under a day (0.9992 d) before the start, so it is outside.

Now the bug. To print its span, the 0.1.0 package converts the start JD back to UTC: TDB midnight minus 69.184 s is 2025-12-31 23:58:50.8 UTC. Its `jdTdbToUtcDateString` then keeps the first 10 characters of that text (`.slice(0, 10)`; the function is still on `main` at mcp/src/tools/compute-shared.ts:141-146), giving "2025-12-31". So the package advertises a span starting 2025-12-31. Asked for a departure starting on 2025-12-31, it refused [Certain, live call (0.1.0)]:

> "Departure window 2025-12-31 through 2026-03-01 is outside the committed Earth ephemeris span 2025-12-31 through 2040-12-30."

The advertised first day is itself refused. `main` now computes the bound with `acceptedUtcDateBounds` (compute-shared.ts:149) and advertises 2026-01-01, but that fix is not published.

Read the README's account of this bug with care. The fix commit `0052ecb` (2026-09-23) replaced "2025-12-31" with "2026-01-01" inside the section "recorded 2026-09-22". That section now says the span "renders as `2026-01-01 through 2040-12-30`" while describing the subtraction that made it render 2025-12-31, and warns that following the "2026-01-01" advice is refused, though its own table marks that date accepted (mcp/README.md:56-75; `git show 0052ecb`) [Certain]. The table is right; the prose is not.

The same arithmetic decodes the unit `s since J2000 TDB`: Apophis's `epochTdb` of 830,865,600 s / 86,400 = 9,616.5 d, plus 2,451,545.0, is JD 2,461,161.5, i.e. 2026-05-01 00:00 TDB [Certain, `get_body` (0.1.0); recomputed]. That is the **re-anchor epoch**, the instant at which a body's orbit was reset from Horizons data. 41,539 of the 41,906 catalog records share it, all marked `anchorSource: "horizons-reanchor"`; the other 367 carry 140 other epochs (309 `sbdb`, 58 `stale-unanchored`) [Certain, counted from `elements.epochTdbJd` and `anchorSource` in the catalog fixture].

#### B1.9.6 Significant figures and false precision

The **significant figures** (s.f.) of a number are the digits that carry real information. 19.09 has four. 0.14 has two. When you multiply or divide, keep no more significant figures than the least precise input [Certain, textbook].

Two words often confused:

- **Precision** is how finely a number is written.
- **Accuracy** is how close it is to the truth.

A number can be very precise and badly inaccurate.

#### Worked example 1.3: how big is Apophis, and how many digits does it deserve?

Inputs: H = 19.09 mag for `asteroid-99942` (tests/fixtures/v2/nea-catalog-slice9.json). The size formula D(km) = (1329 / √p) × 10^(−H/5), with default albedo p = 0.14 (src/v2/core/constants/asteroids.ts:9,73-81). Radius in m = D × 500 (asteroids.ts:83-88). Albedo range 0.053–0.166, and 0.14 ± 0.02 (src/v2/app/compare/main.ts:209-219). **Absolute magnitude** H is a brightness scale where larger means fainter. **Albedo** p is the fraction of sunlight a surface reflects. Chapter B4 derives the formula.

1. √0.14 = 0.374166.
2. 1329 / 0.374166 = 3,551.902 km.
3. −H/5 = −19.09 / 5 = −3.818.
4. 10^(−3.818) = 1.52055 × 10⁻⁴.
5. D = 3,551.902 × 1.52055 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.540084 km.
6. Radius = 0.540084 × 500 = 270.0418 m.

The repository stores `estimatedRadiusM = 270.0417833762203`. The recomputation matches it to all 16 digits [Certain]. But those digits are not knowledge:

- The albedo has two significant figures, so the radius deserves about two: **2.7 × 10² m**.
- Because D ∝ p^(−1/2), a relative error in p becomes half that relative error in D: ½ × (0.02 / 0.14) = 7.1%, or ±19 m.
- Across typical bright and dark asteroids (S-complex median p = 0.166, C-complex median p = 0.053, compare/main.ts:217-218), the radius runs from 248 m to 439 m.

The honest statement is "a radius of about 250–440 m, under an assumed albedo". The envelope marks this leaf `assumed`, and the compare page shows sizes as ranges for exactly this reason (DEC-17-4, compare/main.ts:217-222). STATUS.md:127 records the 16-digit outputs as a known finding, "False precision in generated catalog data" (recorded 2026-08-24; the fixture at `cec19e7` still stores 270.0417833762203).

Even computed numbers do not reproduce to all their printed digits. The screening cache stores Apophis's minimum C3 as 0.00020641346871491306 km²/s². The live `explain_cell` recomputation of the same cell gives 0.000206413468465582 (0.1.0). They differ by 1.2 × 10⁻⁹ in relative terms: about nine matching significant figures, not sixteen [Certain, both values read; the cause was not investigated].

Radius versus diameter matters too. 2 × 270.0418 = 540.08 m is the diameter. A Slice 16 grading fixture once expected an answer of "measured diameter of 540.5 m" to be scored as fabricated. It was in fact this diameter, rounded: a relative difference of 7.7 × 10⁻⁴, inside the 10⁻³ tolerance. That case is the one recorded with invariant INV-037 (INVARIANTS.md:242, second amendment of 2026-08-01).

**Aster's display rule for C3** is three significant figures at every display site, in plain notation for 10⁻⁴ ≤ |C3| < 10⁵ and exponential notation outside (formatC3, src/v2/porkchop/format-c3.ts:1-27). The exceptions are the precision readouts (hover, pinned cell, ΔV stack), which keep six decimals.

| Raw value (km²/s²) | `formatC3` output |
|---|---|
| 0.000206413468465582 | `0.000206` |
| 0.000055 | `5.50e-5` |
| 64.54072379744993 | `64.5` |
| 2928.933 | `2930` |
| 25 | `25.0` |

[Certain, a re-statement of `formatC3` run in Node.js, a program that runs JavaScript outside a browser, three times: once by the writer and once in each fact-check.] Note `2930`: its final zero is a placeholder, not a measured digit. Plain notation hides that; 2.93 × 10³ makes it explicit.

#### B1.9.7 Ratios, percentages and percentage points

```
ratio = a / b                       percent = 100 × part / whole
relative error = |x − x_ref| / |x_ref|
percentage points (pp) = p₁ − p₂    relative change = (p₁ − p₂) / p₂
```

Examples [Certain, inputs from the cited files, recomputed]:

- **Compression.** The raw catalog is 52,969,826 bytes and its compressed download is 8,973,203 bytes (STATUS.md:113). The ratio is 52,969,826 / 8,973,203 = 5.90, the "~5.9:1" STATUS quotes. The download is 16.9% of the raw file. Per record: 52,969,826 / 41,906 = 1,264 bytes.
- **A badge that barely discriminates.** 41,422 of 41,905 screened bodies have the LOW-C3 status: 41,422 / 41,905 = 98.8% (status counts in lambert-screen-cache.json). A label that almost everything carries tells you little. The disclosure says LOW C3 is "a necessary condition … but not sufficient" (honesty-disclosure.ts:61-63).
- **Percent versus percentage points.** Slice 16 measured "FULL faithfulness": the share of AI-agent runs that passed every applicable check on relaying Aster's evidence ("FULL = AND of all applicable dimensions", src/v2/SLICE_16_FOUNDING.md:135; Chapter B11). It came out at 23.8% for one model and 32.5% for another (STATUS.md:69). The gap is 32.5 − 23.8 = 8.7 **percentage points** (pp), a plain difference of two percentages. Relative to 23.8% it is 8.7 / 23.8 = **36.6%**. Both describe the same gap. STATUS compares the 8.7 pp against a registered 10 pp threshold (STATUS.md:71; Chapter B11).
- **Relative error.** The Lambert check's 3.43 × 10⁻¹⁴ means agreement to about 13 significant digits (log₁₀ of 3.43 × 10⁻¹⁴ is −13.5). Near zero, though, relative error blows up: dividing by a tiny reference turns tiny absolute changes into huge relative ones [Certain, textbook]. That is plausibly one reason near-zero C3 cells are fragile [Likely].

Always ask "percent of what?" Worked example 1.5 shows two margin policies, 5% and 10%, on different bases.

#### B1.9.8 Logarithms, exponentials and log scales

A **logarithm** answers "what power?": log₁₀(x) is the power of 10 that gives x, so log₁₀(1000) = 3. ln(x) is the power of e ≈ 2.71828 that gives x. On a **logarithmic scale**, equal distances mean equal **ratios**, not equal differences [Certain, textbook].

Logs appear in Aster in three places:

```
Porkchop colour:  t = (ln C3 − ln 1) / (ln 1000 − ln 1), C3 raised to at least 1, t clamped to [0, 1]
                                                       (src/v2/porkchop/colormap.ts:36-44; INVARIANTS.md:37-48)
Asteroid size:    D ∝ 10^(−H/5)   → H larger by 5 means a diameter 10 times smaller
Rocket equation:  m_final = m_initial × e^(−ΔV / (Isp × g0))          (Chapter B7)
```

#### Worked example 1.4: reading the porkchop colour bar

Inputs: `C3_COLOR_MIN` = 1 and `C3_COLOR_MAX` = 1000 km²/s²; colour stops at t = 0.25 → [59, 82, 139] and t = 0.5 → [33, 145, 140] (red, green, blue values; colormap.ts:4-20). INVARIANTS.md:47 lists the verified anchor C3 = 8.78 → [52, 98, 139].

1. Since ln(1) = 0, t = ln C3 / ln 1000 = log₁₀ C3 / 3. For C3 = 8.78: log₁₀ 8.78 = 0.9435, so t = 0.3145.
2. t lies between the stops 0.25 and 0.5. Local position: (0.3145 − 0.25) / 0.25 = 0.2580.
3. Red: 59 + (33 − 59) × 0.2580 = 52.29, rounded to 52.
4. Green: 82 + (145 − 82) × 0.2580 = 98.25, rounded to 98.
5. Blue: 139 + (140 − 139) × 0.2580 = 139.26, rounded to 139.

Result: [52, 98, 139], the documented anchor. Each third of the bar is one factor of ten: C3 = 10, 100 and 1000 sit at t = 1/3, 2/3 and 1. Below 1 km²/s² everything gets the same darkest colour, so Apophis's 0.000206 looks identical to 1.0. INVARIANTS.md:46 also requires the legend to say "logarithmic scale" [Certain; all four anchors recomputed].

#### Worked example 1.5: a 5% margin and an exponential

Inputs, all from `explain_cell` for Apophis, 2028-09-14, 212 days, Falcon Heavy Expendable, Cape Canaveral (0.1.0): `c3` = 0.000206413 km²/s², `rendezvous` = 5844.705709724418 m/s, `stationkeeping` = 150 m/s, `margin` = 292.2352854862209 m/s, `payloadAtC3` = 15009.944990810654 kg, `deliveredMass` = 2024.4703001373962 kg. Constants from src/v2/porkchop/launch-vehicles.ts:57-78: `SCREENING_ISP_S` = 320, `DETERMINISTIC_MARGIN_FRACTION` = 0.05, `G0_MPS2` = 9.80665, and the Falcon Heavy anchors (C3 0 → 15,010 kg; C3 10 → 12,345 kg). **Isp** (specific impulse) measures engine efficiency in seconds; Isp × g0 is the exhaust speed (Chapter B7). **Stationkeeping** is a fixed allowance of small burns for staying with the target. A **margin** is a safety allowance added to the ΔV budget for things the model leaves out. **Interpolation** estimates a value between two known points; "straight-line" (linear) interpolation joins them with a line.

1. Payload by straight-line interpolation: 15,010 + (12,345 − 15,010) × (0.000206413 / 10) = 15,010 − 0.055 = 15,009.945 kg.
2. Margin, 5% of the rendezvous burn only: 0.05 × 5,844.706 = 292.235 m/s. Stationkeeping is not margined.
3. Total ΔV: 5,844.706 + 150 + 292.235 = 6,286.941 m/s.
4. Exhaust speed: 320 × 9.80665 = 3,138.128 m/s.
5. Exponent: 6,286.941 / 3,138.128 = 2.00340; e^(−2.00340) = 0.134875.
6. Delivered mass: 15,009.945 × 0.134875 = **2,024.47 kg**.

Result: the tool's 2024.4703001373962 kg is reproduced exactly [Certain, recomputed for this guide and twice more in fact-checking]. Three lessons:

- The tool prints 17 significant figures from a representative Isp of 320 s, itself a stand-in for a 300–350 s engine class (launch-vehicles.ts:56). Two or three figures are justified [Likely].
- The porkchop page shows both policies: its cost card uses this 5% rule (src/v2/app/porkchop/main.ts:463-466), while its ΔV-stack readout takes 10% of a subtotal of injection, rendezvous, departure and stationkeeping (`DV_MARGIN_FRACTION = 0.10`, src/v2/porkchop/delta-v.ts:6,47-48; INV-016c). Here the 10% rule gives at least 0.10 × (5,844.7 + 150) = 599.5 m/s, twice the 292.2 m/s above, before injection is even counted. Ask which percentage applies to which number.
- This cell is the near-zero **degeneracy** from section B1.3 and Worked example 1.1: a special case that is mathematically valid but physically meaningless. The arithmetic is right; the mission is not real.

### B1.10 Reading an evidence envelope

Every MCP tool answers with an **evidence envelope**: a JSON object that wraps the answer with its sources, confidence and limits (INV-028).

**JSON basics.** `{ }` holds an object: a set of `"key": value` pairs. `[ ]` holds a list. A value is a string in quotes, a number, `true`, `false`, `null` (nothing), an object or a list.

The envelope's shape is fixed in mcp/src/envelope/index.ts:1-63 [Certain]:

```
EvidenceEnvelope = {
  envelope_version: "1",  tool,  as_of?,  value (null only for a refusal),
  confidence: "measured" | "derived" | "assumed",
  provenance: [SourceRef, …],  assumptions: [string, …],  validity_envelope: string,
  coverage?: {returned, total, selection_rule},
  refusal?:  {code, reason, what_would_help}
}
Quantity leaf = { value, units, frame?, confidence?, sourceIds? }
SourceRef     = repo {path, commit} | external {name, url?, retrieved} | computation {method, code}
                (every SourceRef also carries its own confidence, and an optional id)
```

A `?` marks an optional field. A **leaf** is a single number with its labels.

| Field | Read it as |
|---|---|
| `value` | The answer, or `null` for a refusal |
| `units` | The unit of that leaf; convert before comparing |
| `confidence` (leaf) | How this number was obtained |
| `confidence` (top) | The weakest of the sources in `provenance` |
| `sourceIds` | Pointers into `provenance` by `id` |
| `provenance` | Where each source lives: file path and commit for repository sources; name and retrieval date for external ones |
| `assumptions` | Plain-language premises the answer rests on |
| `validity_envelope` | The range inside which the answer is supported |
| `coverage` | How much of the full result you were shown |
| `as_of` | Date of the input data (set only where launch-vehicle data is used: `estimate_mission_cost` answers and vehicle-curve refusals) |

The builder enforces four rules (mcp/src/envelope/index.ts:102-247) [Certain]:

- A value envelope needs at least one provenance entry.
- Every number must be finite: no NaN or Infinity (INV-032). Every unit string must be non-empty.
- When an envelope cites more than one source, every leaf must carry its own `confidence` and `sourceIds`.
- Every `sourceIds` entry must match a provenance `id`. A dangling pointer, one that points at nothing, throws an error.

#### Worked example 1.6: reading `get_body("99942")` (0.1.0)

1. **Find the leaf.** `"estimatedRadius": {"value": 270.0417833762203, "units": "m", "confidence": "assumed", "sourceIds": ["catalog-boundary"]}`. Read it as "about 270 m, assumed" (Worked example 1.3).
2. **Follow the pointer.** The provenance entry with `id` `catalog-boundary` gives path `src/v2/boundary/slice9-nea-catalog.ts` and a commit string beginning `84fefe8…`, then "(build-baked package commit; per-path granularity unavailable outside a git checkout; baked 2026-07-10T19:59:49.784Z)". Under `npx`, the commit names the package build, not the last change to that file. And because 0.1.0 was baked from a dirty worktree (STATUS.md:15), even the build commit is not a complete description of the code that ran.
3. **Compare the levels.** The top-level `confidence` is `derived`. Yet 15 of the 17 leaves say `assumed`; only `minC3` and `minC3TofDays` say `derived`. The reason is the weakest-link rule of 1.5: it runs over the two provenance entries, both `derived`, not over the leaves. **Always read the leaf.**
4. **Read the assumptions.** The first says: "Physical-parameter confidence is assumed because the Slice 9 catalog boundary does not distinguish measured/derived/assumed per field." So even H and the orbital elements are `assumed`. This is a blanket label, not a statement that each was guessed.
5. **Check what is missing.** There is no `as_of`, no near-zero-C3 flag and no fidelity tier, though `minC3` is 0.000206 km²/s².

The `explain_cell` reply of Worked example 1.5 shows the same pattern: top level `derived`, but `deliveredMass` `assumed` and `payloadAtC3` `measured` [Certain]. Its seven provenance entries are six `derived` and one `measured` (`launch-vehicles`), and the minimum of those is `derived`. [Likely] the leaf labels follow their inputs: delivered mass rests on the assumed stationkeeping and margin, while the payload comes from a published (measured) curve. The `porkchop_scan` of Worked example 1.1 carried `coverage: {returned: 3, total: 25, selection_rule: "lowest departure C3 among feasible cells"}`: you saw 3 of 25 cells, because that call asked for `topN` = 3. The tool's **schema**, its published rules for valid inputs, sets the default at 10 and allows up to 50.

**A refusal** looks like the 2025-12-31 reply in Worked example 1.2: `value: null`, `refusal.code: "out_of_envelope"`, a `reason`, and `what_would_help`. It still carries six provenance entries. It is a result, not a crash.

A reading checklist:

```
1. value null?        → read refusal.code, reason, what_would_help
2. units              → convert before comparing (m vs km, m/s vs km/s)
3. leaf confidence    → not just the top level
4. sourceIds          → provenance path and commit (build-baked under npx)
5. assumptions, validity_envelope, coverage, as_of
6. sanity flags       → C3 below 0.1 km²/s²? date past the body's fidelity boundary?
```

### Limits and known problems

Aster's numbers can be trusted as far as their labels say, and no further. Each item below is a place where you must do checking the labels do not yet do.

1. **Screening is not mission design.** The math is **patched-conic** and two-body: it treats the trip as a chain of separate one-attractor problems (Earth's gravity near Earth, the Sun's in between) and ignores every other pull [Certain, textbook; Chapters B3, B5]. LOW C3 is necessary, not sufficient; arrival ΔV, stay time and return ΔV are excluded (honesty-disclosure.ts:61-63), and 98.8% of screened bodies carry the badge.
2. **No body is certified for the whole window.** The only tiers are L0, L1 and L2 (src/v2/boundary/tier-assignments.ts:2), and none of them vouches for the full 2026–2040 window. Slice 18 counts: L0 11, L1 10,150, L2 31,745, totalling 41,906 (tools/slice18-research/tier-sizing-per-body.json). Of the L2 bodies, 31,050 are simply "unmeasured"; only 7 were measured, and those exceed the bound Aster can certify [Certain, sub-reasons counted]. Two-body drift measured 0.46 to 330 million km across 17 asteroids (src/v2/porkchop/tier-disclosure.ts:31-33). Chapter B4.
3. **Near-zero C3 is a trap.** 3,163 bodies have minimum C3 below 0.1 km²/s². Their windows look cheapest; their delivered masses are correct arithmetic for missions that do not exist.
4. **The agent surface lags the website.** Published 0.1.0 has no near-zero flag, no fidelity tiers (none in `mcp/src` either), a self-contradicting lower date bound, and build-level commits. `mcp/package.json` on `main` still says 0.1.0, and the npm registry holds no later version, so the fixes on `main` are unpublished [Certain, registry query 2026-11-06]. The 2026-10-22 UX report records the same gap as P1 (unmerged branch).
5. **Top-level confidence hides leaf detail.** It summarises sources, not numbers (Section B1.10).
6. **Envelope rules are partly unmet.** DEC-15-4 says `frame` is "required for any vector component or angle" (src/v2/SLICE_15_FOUNDING.md:109). Yet `explain_cell` emits twelve **state-vector** components (x, y, z of position and velocity, for Earth and the target) without one (mcp/src/tools/explain-cell.ts:346-362; live reply); only its DLA stage carries `frame: "ICRF/equatorial"`. `as_of` appears only on `estimate_mission_cost` answers and vehicle-curve refusals (estimate-mission-cost.ts:174; compute-shared.ts:230). The `explain_cell` reply of Worked example 1.5 uses the same dated curve but shows the date only as `asOf: "2024-02-29"` inside its vehicle stage. `get_body` has no date at all, although DEC-15-4(h) asks for data age and names the catalog as a dated snapshot (SLICE_15_FOUNDING.md:134).
7. **False precision.** Data and replies print 16–17 significant figures from 2–4-figure inputs (STATUS.md:127, recorded 2026-08-24 with no remedy chosen; the fixture at `cec19e7` is unchanged). Even the same C3 computed twice agrees to only about nine figures (1.9.6). Round when you read.
8. **Sizes are assumed.** Albedo 0.14 drives every radius; typical dark-to-bright albedos move Apophis between about 248 and 439 m.
9. **Time is simplified.** UTC to TDB is a fixed 69.184 s, right from 2017 until the next leap second, and is copied inline outside the core module (src/v2/app/porkchop/main.ts:190-200; compute-shared.ts:136,144).
10. **Spans differ by surface.** Earth file 2026-01-01 to 2040-12-31 (TDB); screening cache 2026-01-01 to 2040-12-31 (`metadata.screeningWindow`); porkchop departures to 2040-01-01 (src/v2/porkchop/grid-span.ts:6-7); MCP on `main` 2026-01-01 to 2040-12-30; the 3D solar-system view 2026-11-01 to 2027-03-31 (src/v2/data/*-rolling.json; STATUS.md:43). "2026–2040" can mean several things.
11. **Prose drifts behind code.** STATUS lags HEAD by 39 commits; V1-era documents read as current; the README omits the compare page; mcp/README.md's dated bug record was edited after the fix and now contradicts its own table (Worked example 1.2). Trust code and committed data.
12. **This chapter's own limits.** Tests were not run; the last recorded run is 109/109 files and 360/360 tests on 2026-11-04 (tools/slice20-research/front-a/frontA-REPORT.md:36-41). CI does not run the MCP package tests (.github/workflows/ci.yml; tools/run-tests.mjs:25). The live site was not fetched.

### Key takeaways

- Aster is one math core (`src/v2`) behind two interfaces, web pages and an MCP tool server; checking one checks both, as long as both are built from the same code (the published 0.1.0 package is not). It answers five chained questions: which target, when, how much energy, how much mass, how trustworthy.
- The honesty layer puts units, sources, confidence classes, assumptions and refusals on every number. A refusal is a result.
- `measured` > `derived` > `assumed` describes how a number was obtained, not whether it is right. Read the leaf, not only the top level.
- Slices, founding documents, DECs, OQs, INVs, AMDs, tripwires and STOP gates are the process vocabulary. Hudson decides; Nova drafts; Codex or Claude Code executes.
- A number is a value times a unit. Convert before comparing; km²/s² = (km/s)².
- JD days start at noon; J2000 = JD 2451545.0; in Aster TDB − UTC = 69.184 s.
- Keep only the significant figures the inputs justify; 16 printed digits are not 16 known digits. Percentage points are differences; log scales show ratios.
- Apophis's 0.000206 km²/s², the lowest C3 in the catalog, is not a real mission. The labels and flags exist to catch exactly that.

The second pass also corrected one figure: the first had compared Apophis with Earth's midnight record, 69 s before the arrival instant, and so gave 44,415 km instead of 45,935 km.

## Chapter B2: Space and time: coordinate frames, time scales and ephemerides

**Main idea:** Every position Aster uses is three numbers measured from a stated origin, along stated axes, at a stated instant on a stated clock, and the project's hardest-won lesson is that you confirm those statements by measuring the numbers, not by trusting their labels.

### B2.1 Why space and time come first

A number such as "x = 108,098,089 km" means nothing by itself. To use it you need four facts:

1. Where zero is (the origin).
2. Which way the axes point.
3. The unit.
4. The moment it refers to, and which clock measured that moment.

Get any one wrong and everything built on top is wrong too: Lambert arcs (the transfer paths between two positions, Chapter B5), the launch energy **C3** (the square of the speed a spacecraft has left over after escaping Earth, in km²/s²) and porkchop plots (Chapter B6), launch declination (Chapter B7) and the 3D view (Chapter B9). Worse, the output usually still looks plausible.

Aster makes these choices once, in its core, and converts everything else at the edges (`V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md` §3.1 and §3.1.1; `src/v2/core/units.ts`). [Certain]

| Question | Aster's answer | Where it is fixed |
|---|---|---|
| Unit of length | metre (m) | `V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md` §3.1 |
| Unit of velocity | metre per second (m/s) | same |
| Unit of time | TDB seconds since J2000 | same; `units.ts` |
| Root frame | `FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ICRF` | `src/v2/core/frames/ids.ts` |
| Number type | 64-bit floating point ("f64", also called a **double**) | `V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md` §3.1.1 |

The data files arrive in other units: kilometres, km/s and Julian Dates. The **boundary layer** (`src/v2/boundary/`) is the code that reads outside data. It converts units once, on the way in, so every state the core stores is in metres, m/s and TDB seconds. The core enforces this: `assertCanonicalState` rejects any state object carrying a key such as `positionKm`, `velocityKms` or `jdTdb` as an INV-001 failure (`src/v2/core/invariants/assertions.ts:17-28, 91-110, 152-157`). [Certain] A few core helpers that work on scalars accept km/s directly; `dlaDegFromVInf` is one, and its comment says so (`src/v2/core/lambert/dla.ts:14-16`).

This chapter spends its time where the code spends it. The code relies on:

- one root frame, plus pure translations to reach planet-centred frames;
- one rotation that matters, by the obliquity angle;
- one time offset, 69.184 s;
- one interpolator, cubic Hermite;
- one rule, **INV-021**: a frame is something you measure, not something you read off a label.

A note on project labels used below. An `INV-nnn` is a numbered **invariant**, a rule the code must always satisfy, listed in `INVARIANTS.md`. A `DEC-n-m` is a locked design decision and an `OQ-n-m` an open question, both recorded in the founding document of slice n (a **slice** is one planned unit of work; Chapters B1 and B12 explain the process).

### B2.2 Vectors: numbers that have a direction

#### Components and magnitude

A **scalar** is a single number with a unit, such as a mass of 5 kg. A **vector** is a quantity that has both a size and a direction. In three dimensions we write a vector as three **components**, one along each of three agreed axes.

Analogy: "3 blocks east, 4 blocks north, 0 floors up." Those three numbers are useless until you know where you started and which way "east" is. That is the whole subject of this chapter in one sentence.

```
r = (x, y, z)                        components, metres
|r| = sqrt(x² + y² + z²)             magnitude (length), metres
r̂ = r / |r|                          unit vector: length 1, no unit
a + b = (ax + bx, ay + by, az + bz)
a − b = (ax − bx, ay − by, az − bz)
k·a  = (k·ax, k·ay, k·az)            scaling by a number k
```

The **magnitude** is Pythagoras' theorem applied twice. A **unit vector** keeps only the direction.

Tiny example: r = (3, 4, 0) m. Then |r| = sqrt(9 + 16 + 0) = 5 m, and r̂ = (0.6, 0.8, 0).

A **position vector** points from the origin to an object. A **velocity vector** is the rate of change of position; its magnitude is the **speed**. Position and velocity together, six numbers, make a **state vector**. A state vector is enough to predict where a body goes next under gravity (Chapter B3).

In Aster:

- `CanonicalState` (`src/v2/core/types.ts:13-19`) holds `positionM {x, y, z}`, `velocityMps {x, y, z}`, a `frame` tag and `tdbSeconds`. Every state carries its frame and its time. The founding rule is "Reference frames are explicit values, never implicit globals" (`V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md` §3.2). [Certain]
- The Lambert code uses a tuple form `[x, y, z]` with helpers `add`, `sub`, `scale`, `dot`, `cross`, `norm` and `normalize` (`src/v2/core/lambert/vec3.ts:9-45`). These are the textbook formulas above, written in TypeScript. [Certain]
- Every ephemeris record in `src/v2/data/` is seven numbers: `[JD_TDB, x, y, z, vx, vy, vz]`, in km and km/s. [Certain]

One fact matters more than any other here. **The magnitude of a vector does not change when you turn the axes. The components do.** A 30 km/s speed is 30 km/s in every orientation, but its z-component can be 0 in one set of axes and 12 km/s in another. Section B2.11 shows how this fact produced a real bug risk in Aster and the rule that now guards against it.

#### The dot product

The **dot product** multiplies two vectors and gives a scalar. It measures how much the two vectors point the same way.

```
a · b = ax·bx + ay·by + az·bz = |a| |b| cos θ
θ = the angle between a and b
v · ẑ = vz          (ẑ = (0, 0, 1)): the component of v along +Z
```

Intuition: the dot product is the shadow one arrow casts along the other. Walk 10 m along a path at 60° to north and you have gone 10 × cos 60° = 5 m north.

- θ < 90°: the dot product is positive.
- θ = 90°: it is zero. The vectors are **perpendicular**.
- θ > 90°: it is negative.

Tiny example: a = (1, 0, 0) and b = (1, 1, 0). Then a · b = 1. Since |b| = √2, cos θ = 1/√2 = 0.7071, so θ = 45°.

In Aster:

- The **declination of the launch asymptote (DLA)** is the angle between the direction a spacecraft leaves Earth and Earth's equatorial plane (Chapter B7). Aster computes `DLA = asin(vZ / |v|)` (`src/v2/core/lambert/dla.ts:19-29`). The ratio vZ/|v| is the dot product of the unit vector v̂ with ẑ. It is the sine of the angle between v and the XY-plane. [Certain]
- The camera tests check that two directions agree by requiring `dot >= cos(2°)` (`tests/v2-runtime-camera-presets.test.mjs:62-67`). [Certain]

#### The cross product

The **cross product** multiplies two vectors and gives a third vector, perpendicular to both.

```
a × b = (ay·bz − az·by,  az·bx − ax·bz,  ax·by − ay·bx)
|a × b| = |a| |b| sin θ
a × b = −(b × a)                 order matters
x̂ × ŷ = ẑ                        defines a right-handed set of axes
```

Its direction follows the **right-hand rule**: curl the fingers of your right hand from a toward b, and your thumb points along a × b. Analogy: turn an ordinary screw in the direction that carries a toward b, and the screw moves along a × b.

Axes for which x̂ × ŷ = ẑ are called **right-handed**. Every frame in Aster is right-handed. The right-hand rule gives wrong answers in left-handed axes.

The orbital use: the **specific angular momentum** h = r × v (units m²/s) is perpendicular to the plane in which a body orbits. Its direction is the **orbit pole**. Chapter B3 develops orbits; here we only need the pole as a direction.

In Aster:

- `izzo.ts:96` and `lambert-multi-rev.ts:63` take the cross product of the unit vectors along r1 and r2 (`cross(i_r1, i_r2)` and `cross(iR1, iR2)`) to find the plane of a transfer orbit. [Certain]
- The Slice 12 DLA oracle once produced a **false FAIL** because of how it measured angles. It used `acos(a · b)`, which has a double-precision floor of about 1.2×10⁻⁶ deg, right at the 1×10⁻⁶ deg pass bar. The metric was changed to the stable form `atan2(|a × b|, a · b)`, bar unchanged (`src/v2/SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md`, OQ-12-3 closure correction). [Certain]

Why `acos` fails for small angles: cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2. For θ = 10⁻⁸ rad, θ²/2 = 5×10⁻¹⁷, smaller than the gap between 1 and the next double below it. The cosine rounds to exactly 1 and `acos` returns 0. The `atan2` form reads the angle from the sine instead and returns the true 5.73×10⁻⁷ deg. [Certain]

#### Worked Example 2.1: Earth's state today, taken apart

**Inputs.**

- Earth record at JD 2461350.5 (2026-11-06 00:00 TDB) in `src/v2/data/horizons-inner-system-rolling.json`. Earth is Sun-centred (`center: "@sun"`) and the file declares `"frame": "ICRF/J2000"`.
  - r = (108,098,089.691, 93,175,755.627, 40,389,378.563) km
  - v = (−20.881183, 19.827284, 8.595781) km/s
- 1 AU = 1.495978707×10¹¹ m = 149,597,870.7 km (`V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md` §3.1.1).

**Step 1: distance from the Sun.**

```
x² = 1.168520×10¹⁶   y² = 8.681721×10¹⁵   z² = 1.631302×10¹⁵   (km²)
sum = 2.199822×10¹⁶ km²
|r| = sqrt(2.199822×10¹⁶) = 148,317,970.4 km
|r| / 1 AU = 148,317,970.4 / 149,597,870.7 = 0.99144 AU
```

**Step 2: speed.**

```
vx² = 436.024   vy² = 393.121   vz² = 73.887   (km²/s²)
sum = 903.032
|v| = sqrt(903.032) = 30.0505 km/s
```

**Step 3: angle between position and velocity (dot product).**

```
x·vx = −2.257216×10⁹   y·vy = 1.847422×10⁹   z·vz = 3.471783×10⁸
r · v = −6.261560×10⁷ km²/s
cos θ = −6.261560×10⁷ / (148,317,970.4 × 30.0505) = −0.0140487
θ = acos(−0.0140487) = 90.805°
```

The velocity is almost perpendicular to the radius, as expected for a near-circular orbit. The small negative dot product means the distance is shrinking. That fits Earth heading toward its closest approach to the Sun, which falls in early January (from memory, verify).

**Step 4: orbit pole (cross product).**

```
hx = y·vz − z·vy = 800,918,388.7 − 800,811,670.7 =        106,718.0 km²/s
hy = z·vx − x·vz = −843,378,008.4 − 929,187,504.2 = −1,772,565,512.6 km²/s
hz = x·vy − y·vx = 2,143,291,501.1 + 1,945,620,012.2 = 4,088,911,513.2 km²/s
|h| = 4,456,589,039.9 km²/s
ĥ = h / |h| = (0.0000239, −0.3977404, 0.9174980)
```

**Step 5: how far is the pole from the file's +Z axis?**

```
ĥ · ẑ = 0.9174980
angle = acos(0.9174980) = 23.437°
```

**Result.** Earth is 0.991 AU from the Sun, moving at 30.05 km/s. Its orbit pole is tilted **23.437°** from the data's +Z axis. So the file's XY-plane is not the plane of Earth's orbit. Section B2.5 explains why: the axes are tied to Earth's equator, not to its orbit. Section B2.6 shows this pole sits 0.0027° from the rotated ecliptic pole. [Certain: recomputed for this guide]

### B2.3 Coordinate systems and reference frames

A **coordinate system** is an origin plus three perpendicular axes plus a unit. A **reference frame** adds the physical meaning: what the origin sits on, what the axes are tied to, and, for anything that moves, the instant at which you read it. **Coordinates** are the numbers a frame assigns to a point.

Analogy: a street address measured from city hall. A neighbouring city measures from its own city hall. Its street grid may also be turned. To compare addresses you must shift the origin, turn the grid, or both.

An **inertial frame** is one whose axes do not rotate relative to the distant stars and whose origin is not accelerating. Newton's laws hold in it without extra "fictitious" forces. The origin may move at constant velocity; "inertial" does not mean "standing still". [Certain] A Sun-centred frame is only nearly inertial, because the Sun itself is pulled around by the planets (Section B2.4).

Aster names six frames (`src/v2/core/frames/ids.ts:1-16`). [Certain]

| Frame ID | Origin | Axes | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ICRF` | Sun | ICRF (equatorial) | the root: planets, Lambert, the 3D scene |
| `FRAME_GCRS_EARTH` | Earth's centre | ICRF-parallel | the Moon |
| `FRAME_MARS_J2000_ICRF` | Mars | ICRF | Phobos, Deimos |
| `FRAME_JUPITER_J2000_ICRF` | Jupiter | ICRF | the four Galilean moons |
| `FRAME_SATURN_J2000_ICRF` | Saturn | ICRF | seven Saturn moons |
| `FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ECLIPTIC` | Sun | ecliptic | a tag on asteroid orbital elements only |

The founding document fixes how frames are used (`V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md` §3.2): [Certain]

- Transforms are pure functions with the shape `transform(state, fromFrame, toFrame, tdbSeconds) -> state`.
- A round trip A → B → A must return the input within 10 × `Number.EPSILON` relative error (about 2.2×10⁻¹⁵). This is **INV-004**.
- INV-004 applies to heliocentric inputs. A small native state (a moon near its planet) translated by a large vector loses precision to rounding, "by design of the bound".

`transformCanonicalState` (`src/v2/core/frames/transform.ts:184-301`) enforces this loudly. It throws an INV-004 failure if the state's label does not match `fromFrame`, if the time is not finite, if the frame pair is not supported, or if an anchor body's state is missing or mislabelled (`transform.ts:63-79, 120-134, 190-213`). [Certain]

Doc lag: `src/v2/core/frames/README.md` still describes a two-frame "Slice 1 Frame Set". Trust `ids.ts` and `transform.ts`. [Certain]

### B2.4 Where is zero? Heliocentric, geocentric, barycentric, planet-centred

#### The four kinds of origin

- **Heliocentric**: origin at the centre of the Sun.
- **Geocentric**: origin at the centre of the Earth.
- **Barycentric**: origin at the **centre of mass** of a group of bodies. The **Solar System Barycentre (SSB)** is the centre of mass of the whole Solar System.
- **Planet-centred**: origin at a planet, convenient for its moons.

The Sun does not sit still at the SSB. The Sun and planets all orbit their common centre of mass. Jupiter alone drags the Sun around that point by about one solar radius.

```
r_cm = Σ mᵢ rᵢ / Σ mᵢ          mᵢ in kg, rᵢ in m
```

Tiny two-body example: Jupiter's mass is about the Sun's divided by 1047, and Jupiter orbits at about 5.2 AU (both from memory, verify). The Sun–Jupiter barycentre then sits about 5.2 AU / 1048 ≈ 742,000 km from the Sun's centre. The Sun's radius in Aster is 696,000 km (`src/v2/core/constants/bodies.ts:42`), so that is about 1.07 solar radii.

#### Changing origin is a translation, and it needs a time

To move between two frames with the same axes, subtract the new origin's position. Subtract its velocity too.

```
r_P/B = r_P/A − r_B/A          position of P seen from B
v_P/B = v_P/A − v_B/A          velocity of P seen from B
```

Here r_P/A means "position of point P, measured in frame A". Three common mistakes:

- **Forgetting velocity.** Translating position but not velocity gives a body the wrong motion.
- **Forgetting time.** The new origin moves, so you need its position at the same instant.
- **Mixing frames.** You can subtract two positions only if both are in the same frame at the same time.

#### What Aster does

Every supported transform in `transform.ts` is a translation: it adds or subtracts the anchor body's heliocentric position **and** velocity at the requested TDB time (`transform.ts:232-301`). There is no rotation matrix anywhere in `src/v2/core/frames/`. The graph is a star with the heliocentric frame at its centre. [Certain]

```
                    FRAME_GCRS_EARTH
                           |
FRAME_MARS_J2000_ICRF — FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ICRF — FRAME_JUPITER_J2000_ICRF
                           |
                    FRAME_SATURN_J2000_ICRF
```

`FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ECLIPTIC` is in no supported pair. In the 3D view, the anchor states come from Hermite-interpolated planet series wired up at `src/v2/app/solar-system/runtime.ts:862-876`.

The ephemeris files state each body's origin with a Horizons **center code**. I read every target in `src/v2/data/`: [Certain]

| Body | `center` | `origin` | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sun | `@ssb` | `ssb` | Sun relative to the SSB |
| Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn | `@sun` | `heliocentric` | relative to the Sun |
| Moon | `500@399` | `geocentric` | relative to Earth's centre |
| Phobos, Deimos | `500@499` | `mars-centered` | relative to Mars |
| Galilean moons | `500@599` | `jupiter-centered` | relative to Jupiter |
| Saturn moons | `500@699` | `saturn-centered` | relative to Saturn |
| Mars (Mars-system file only) | `500@10` | `heliocentric` | relative to the Sun's body centre |

The numbers 10, 399, 499, 599 and 699 are **NAIF IDs**, the numeric body codes of NASA's navigation software system (from memory, verify), for the Sun, Earth, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn (`bodies.ts:41-92` stores the same IDs). Reading "500@" as "body centre of" is a Horizons convention (from memory, verify). The fixture's "earth" is the geocentre, NAIF 399, not the Earth–Moon barycentre (`STATUS.md:205`).

Ingest decides the frame tag by string matching on these hints (`src/v2/boundary/horizons.ts:270-291`). "JUPITER-CENTERED", "SATURN-CENTERED" and "MARS-CENTERED" map to the planet frames. "GCRS", "EARTH-CENTERED" or "GEOCENTRIC" map to `FRAME_GCRS_EARTH`. Everything else, including the SSB-centred Sun, defaults to `FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ICRF`. [Certain]

Two consequences:

- The Sun is tagged heliocentric although its numbers are barycentric. The C2 verdict calls this a "chip-honesty footnote" that affects origin, not orientation (`tools/frontb-2026-08-11/C2_FRAME_VERDICT.md`, Verdict). [Certain]
- `FRAME_GCRS_EARTH` borrows the name of the Geocentric Celestial Reference System (GCRS). It is a geocentric origin with ICRF-parallel axes reached by plain subtraction. A full GCRS also includes small relativistic corrections, which Aster ignores (from memory, verify). At screening fidelity the difference is negligible. [Likely]

#### Worked Example 2.2: moving the Moon from Earth-centred to Sun-centred

**Inputs** (all at JD 2461350.5, 2026-11-06 00:00 TDB, from `src/v2/data/horizons-inner-system-rolling.json`):

- Moon, geocentric (`500@399`): r = (−385,187.309, −20,647.587, −31,886.365) km; v = (0.047059, −0.901493, −0.469234) km/s.
- Earth, heliocentric: r and v from Worked Example 2.1.
- Sun, relative to the SSB (`@ssb`): r = (−154,005.640, −697,784.613, −287,851.406) km.
- Sun radius 696,000 km (`bodies.ts:42`).

**Step 1: Moon distance from Earth.**

```
|r_moon/earth| = sqrt(385,187.309² + 20,647.587² + 31,886.365²) = 387,056.0 km
```

**Step 2: translate to heliocentric (this is `FRAME_GCRS_EARTH → FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ICRF`).**

```
x: −385,187.309 + 108,098,089.691 = 107,712,902.382 km
y:  −20,647.587 +  93,175,755.627 =  93,155,108.040 km
z:  −31,886.365 +  40,389,378.563 =  40,357,492.197 km

vx: 0.047059 + (−20.881183) = −20.834124 km/s
vy: −0.901493 +  19.827284  =  18.925790 km/s
vz: −0.469234 +   8.595781  =   8.126547 km/s
```

**Step 3: how far is the Sun from the SSB today?**

```
|r_sun/ssb| = sqrt(154,005.640² + 697,784.613² + 287,851.406²) = 770,376 km
770,376 / 696,000 = 1.107 solar radii
```

**Result.** The Moon is 387,056 km from Earth and, after the translation, about 148.0 million km from the Sun. Its heliocentric velocity is Earth's velocity plus the Moon's own 1.017 km/s geocentric velocity; on this date the two point partly against each other, so the Moon's heliocentric speed is 0.754 km/s below Earth's. The Sun's own centre is 770,376 km (1.1 solar radii) from the barycentre. "Heliocentric" and "barycentric" are different origins, and here they differ by more than the Sun's radius. [Certain: reproduced for this guide, and again independently]

Over the whole 2026–2040 file, the Sun–SSB distance ranges from 93,279 km to 1,159,704 km, 0.13 to 1.67 solar radii (recomputed for this guide).

### B2.5 Which way do the axes point? Equatorial versus ecliptic

#### Two natural planes in the sky

Space has no "up". Astronomers pick axes from two natural planes.

- Project Earth's equator outward onto the sky and you get the **celestial equator**. The point straight above Earth's North Pole is the **north celestial pole**.
- The plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun is the **ecliptic**. Seen from Earth, it is the yearly path of the Sun against the stars. Its pole is the **ecliptic pole**.
- The two planes cross along a line. One end of that line, the direction of the Sun at the March equinox, is the **vernal equinox** (from memory, verify).
- The angle between the two planes is the **obliquity of the ecliptic**, written ε. It equals the tilt of Earth's spin axis relative to its orbit, and it is also the angle between the two poles.

Analogy: two sheets of paper joined by a hinge along the equinox line, opened 23.4° apart.

#### The two frames Aster meets

| | Equatorial (ICRF / J2000) | Ecliptic (J2000) |
|---|---|---|
| XY-plane | Earth's mean equator | Earth's mean orbit plane |
| +X | vernal equinox | vernal equinox (the same line) |
| +Z | north celestial pole | ecliptic north pole |
| Aster ID | `FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ICRF` | `FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ECLIPTIC` |
| Where it appears | all five production ephemeris files; Lambert; DLA; the 3D scene | asteroid orbital elements |

Both definitions are frozen at an **epoch**, a reference instant. Here the epoch is **J2000.0**, 2000-01-01 12:00 TT (Section B2.8). A freeze is needed because Earth's axis slowly wobbles. This **precession** traces a circle over roughly 26,000 years (from memory, verify), so "the equator" changes with date.

The **International Celestial Reference Frame (ICRF)** is the modern realisation of the equatorial axes. It is tied to the positions of distant quasars (from memory, verify). It differs from the J2000 mean equator by the "~17 mas frame bias" that DEC-12-2 discloses (`src/v2/SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md:82`). An **arcsecond** (″) is 1/3600 of a degree, and a **milliarcsecond** (mas) is a thousandth of that, so 17 mas is about 5×10⁻⁶ degrees. [Certain that the repo states this]

Do not confuse the words. "J2000" names an **epoch**, not a plane. Both "J2000 equatorial" and "J2000 ecliptic" exist, so a label that just says "J2000" has not told you the plane.

#### The obliquity in Aster

There is exactly one definition in `src/v2` (`src/v2/core/units.ts:4-5`): [Certain]

```
ARCSECONDS_TO_RADIANS = π / (180 × 3600)
J2000_ECLIPTIC_OBLIQUITY_RAD = 84381.448 × ARCSECONDS_TO_RADIANS
  = 0.40909280422232897 rad = 23.4392911°
sin ε = 0.3977771559     cos ε = 0.9174820621
```

A grep of non-test TypeScript under `src/v2` finds `84381` only in `units.ts:5`, `23.4` only in a comment at `dla.ts:11`, and `0.409` nowhere (re-run on `cec19e7`). So no hidden second copy of the angle exists. [Certain]

84381.448″ is the classic J2000 value (IAU 1976). The newer IAU 2006 value is 84381.406″ (both from memory, verify). The 0.042″ difference (about 2×10⁻⁷ rad) is negligible for every quantity in this repo. [Likely]

#### Who uses which axes

- Horizons is asked for `REF_SYSTEM=ICRF` and `REF_PLANE=FRAME`, meaning equatorial axes (`tools/slice20-research/ephemeris-roll/MANIFEST.md:77-88`; `tools/slice2-research/interpolation-report.md`, "Horizons API Parameters"). Every production file declares `"frame": "ICRF/J2000"`. [Certain]
- JPL's Small-Body Database (**SBDB**) publishes orbital elements in J2000 **ecliptic** orientation (`src/v2/boundary/slice7-fixture-spec.md:165`). All 41,906 records of the committed catalog carry the element tag `FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ECLIPTIC`, and ingest refuses any other tag (count of `elementsFrame` over the 41,906 entries of `tests/fixtures/v2/nea-catalog-slice9.json`, made for this guide; `src/v2/boundary/slice9-nea-catalog.ts:301-306`). [Certain]
