The step that turns an ICRF anchor into ecliptic elements is not under `src/v2`. It is in the research tool `tools/slice7-research/state-to-elements.mjs`: `rotateEquatorialToEcliptic` (lines 55-61) applies Rᵀ (Section B2.6) to position and velocity (lines 80-81) before deriving the elements, "so the returned elements round-trip through the existing propagator unchanged" (lines 77-79). That tool carries its own copy of 84381.448″ (`tools/slice7-research/keplerian-propagate.mjs:5`). [Certain that the code exists] Which catalog records went through it, and which kept SBDB's own elements, is Chapter B4's subject.

**Project check.** In the 2026–2040 file, Earth's largest |z| in the stored equatorial axes is 60,466,270 km, about 0.4 AU. After rotating into ecliptic axes (Section B2.6) the largest |z| is only 14,099 km. Earth's orbit lies in the ecliptic, as it should. The small residual grows steadily, from a yearly maximum of 9,622 km in 2026 to 14,099 km in 2040. That steady growth is the real orbit plane slowly drifting away from the frozen J2000 ecliptic (the ecliptic itself precesses by roughly 0.47″ per year, from memory, verify; 0.47″ × 1 AU ≈ 340 km per year). The geocentre's monthly wobble around the Earth–Moon barycentre is a smaller part: removing it changes the yearly maxima by only about 100–420 km. [Likely] (recomputed for this guide; which assumes an Earth/Moon mass ratio of 81.3, from memory, verify)

### B2.6 Rotation matrices: turning the axes

#### What a rotation matrix does

A **rotation matrix** is a 3×3 grid of numbers that re-expresses the same physical vector in a turned set of axes. The arrow does not move. Only its description changes.

Analogy: turn your head and an object that was "ahead" is now "to the left". The object stayed put.

To multiply a matrix by a vector, take each row of the matrix, dot it with the vector, and that gives one output component.

The rotation from ecliptic to equatorial axes turns by ε about the shared X-axis (the equinox line):

```
[x_eq]   [1     0        0   ] [x_ecl]
[y_eq] = [0   cos ε   −sin ε ] [y_ecl]
[z_eq]   [0   sin ε    cos ε ] [z_ecl]

x_eq = x_ecl
y_eq = y_ecl·cos ε − z_ecl·sin ε
z_eq = y_ecl·sin ε + z_ecl·cos ε
```

Properties of any rotation matrix R:

```
Rᵀ R = I         (Rᵀ = transpose: swap rows and columns; I = identity)
R⁻¹ = Rᵀ         undoing a rotation = transposing it
det R = +1       (det = determinant; a reflection would give −1)
|R v| = |v|      lengths never change
```

So equatorial to ecliptic uses Rᵀ: flip the signs of the two sin ε entries.

Order matters when you chain rotations. Rotating about X then Z is generally not the same as Z then X. [Certain]

#### Where Aster rotates

The same three lines of arithmetic appear in three places under `src/v2`. [Certain] (A fourth copy, run in reverse, lives in the research tool `tools/slice7-research/state-to-elements.mjs`; see Section B2.5.)

| Where | What is rotated | When it fires |
|---|---|---|
| `src/v2/core/propagators/keplerian.ts:87-95` (`rotateEclipticToEquatorial`) | every propagated asteroid position and velocity | always, exactly once per state |
| `src/v2/boundary/horizons.ts:298-307` (`rotateEclipticJ2000ToIcrf`) | ingested Horizons vectors | only if the canonical frame is heliocentric and the frame hint contains "ECLIPTIC" |
| `src/v2/app/solar-system/runtime.ts:262-270` (`rotateEclipticDirectionToIcrf`) | one camera aim direction | once, to build a constant |

The propagator **composes** two rotations. It first turns the orbit's own plane into ecliptic axes using the angles Ω, i and ω (`rotatePerifocalToEcliptic`, `keplerian.ts:63-85`; Chapter B3 explains those angles). Then it applies the obliquity rotation. The code comment states the intent: "rotating the ecliptic result through the J2000 obliquity exactly once" (`keplerian.ts:146-148`). The result is tagged `FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ICRF`. [Certain]

`STATUS.md:305` records a Slice 18 audit that found "the obliquity rotation verified applied exactly once, in the correct direction (i=0 orbit pole matches the independently computed rotated ecliptic pole to 1.2e-16)". Its artifacts are "not in version control", so this guide cannot re-check that run. [Likely]

The ingest branch is dormant for production data. All five files in `src/v2/data/` say "ICRF/J2000". Only the frozen test fixture `tests/fixtures/v2/horizons-earth-moon-30d.json` says "Ecliptic of J2000.0", and it feeds the old `/v2/earth-moon` route (`src/v2/boundary/slice1-earth-moon.ts:8`). [Certain]

#### Worked Example 2.3: the "top-down" camera direction

**Inputs.** ε = 84381.448″ (`units.ts:5`). Rotation formula (`runtime.ts:262-270`, identical to `horizons.ts:298-307`). Camera-angle formulas `polar = acos(y)`, `azimuth = atan2(z, x)` (`directionToOrbitState`, `runtime.ts:468-485`).

**Step 1: the angle.**

```
ε = 84381.448 × π / (180 × 3600) = 0.4090928042 rad = 23.4392911°
sin ε = 0.3977772     cos ε = 0.9174821
```

**Step 2: the matrix.**

```
R = [1      0           0     ]
    [0   0.9174821  −0.3977772]
    [0   0.3977772   0.9174821]
```

**Step 3: check it is a rotation.** The diagonal of Rᵀ R is 1 and cos² ε + sin² ε = 0.8417733 + 0.1582267 = 1.0000000. The off-diagonal terms cancel: cos ε·(−sin ε) + sin ε·cos ε = 0. So Rᵀ R = I and det R = 1.

**Step 4: rotate ecliptic north, (0, 0, 1) in ecliptic axes.**

```
x = 0
y = 0 × cos ε − 1 × sin ε = −0.3977772
z = 0 × sin ε + 1 × cos ε =  0.9174821
```

This is exactly `TOP_DOWN_ECLIPTIC_NORMAL_ICRF` (`runtime.ts:359-363`): ecliptic north written in equatorial coordinates.

**Step 5: turn it into camera angles.** The camera rig measures its polar angle from scene +Y, a rig convention (`sphericalToCartesian`, `runtime.ts:407-418`).

```
polar   = acos(y) = acos(−0.3977772) = 113.439°   (= 90° + 23.439°)
azimuth = atan2(z, x) = atan2(0.9174821, 0) = 90°
```

**Step 6: compare with Earth's measured pole.** Worked Example 2.1 found ĥ = (0.0000239, −0.3977404, 0.9174980). Their dot product is 0.99999999891, an angle of 0.0027°.

**Result.** The top-down camera is placed along (0, −0.398, 0.917) from its target and looks back down that line (`runtime.ts:1722-1742` places it; `runtime.ts:1808` aims it). So it looks down the ecliptic pole from the north side. That direction is 23.44° away from scene +Z (celestial north). Earth's orbit pole, computed straight from the data, agrees with this direction to 0.0027°. [Certain: recomputed for this guide]

#### Why a wrong rotation is so dangerous

Rotations keep lengths. So every magnitude check passes whether or not you rotated correctly. Only the components reveal the error.

Here is the error that DEC-12-2 rejects (`src/v2/SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md:79-83`). Take Earth's stored velocity on 2026-03-21 and wrongly apply R again, as if the equatorial numbers were ecliptic (computed in Worked Example 2.7). The velocity's signed angle to the equatorial plane moves from −23.43° to −46.87°. On 2034-06-22, near a solstice, the same mistake moves it by only about 0.005° (recomputed for this guide). An error that is huge on one date and invisible on another is exactly the kind that spot checks miss. [Certain]

### B2.7 Time scales from scratch: UTC, TAI, TT, TDB

#### Why there is more than one clock

Planets move fast. Earth moves at about 30 km/s (Worked Example 2.1). A one-second error in time is a 30 km error in Earth's position. So "what time is it?" needs a precise answer, and there are several.

- The **SI second** is defined by a fixed number of oscillations of caesium atoms (from memory, verify).
- **TAI** (International Atomic Time) is a pure count of SI seconds kept by atomic clocks. It never jumps.
- **UTC** (Coordinated Universal Time) is civil time. It is TAI minus a whole number of seconds. The gap grows by one each time a **leap second** is inserted, which happens now and then so that UTC stays within 0.9 s of Earth's slightly irregular rotation (from memory, verify). Since 2017-01-01 the gap has been 37 s: an initial 10 s offset set in 1972 plus 27 leap seconds (from memory, verify). The comment at `utc-to-tdb.ts:7` calls all 37 s "leap seconds accumulated since 1972"; the total is right, the wording is loose.
- **TT** (Terrestrial Time) is TAI + 32.184 s exactly, a smooth time scale for Earth-based astronomy (from memory, verify).
- **TDB** (Barycentric Dynamical Time) is the time argument of JPL's planetary ephemerides. It differs from TT only by small periodic relativistic terms. The repo puts these "< 2 ms peak" (`utc-to-tdb.ts:11-12`); the amplitude is about 1.7 ms (from memory, verify). The same file's header (lines 5-6) says "below the millisecond level", which contradicts its own line 11.

**Why astronomers use TDB.** Equations of motion need a uniform clock. A leap second is a jump in UTC. A 1-second jump at 30 km/s would put a 30 km step into Earth's track. TDB is smooth, and it is the clock Horizons uses when asked for `TIME_TYPE=TDB` (`MANIFEST.md:77`).

Analogy: UTC is a wall clock that someone nudges now and then to keep it in step with sunrise. TAI, TT and TDB are stopwatches nobody touches.

#### Aster's conversion

```
TAI = UTC + ΔAT            ΔAT = 37 s for dates from 2017-01-01 (utc-to-tdb.ts:7, 14-16)
TT  = TAI + 32.184 s
TDB ≈ TT                   (periodic difference < 2 ms, ignored)
TDB − UTC ≈ 37 + 32.184 = 69.184 s      TDB_MINUS_UTC_SECONDS (utc-to-tdb.ts:28)
```

`utcStringToTdbSeconds` (`src/v2/core/units/utc-to-tdb.ts:33-56`) accepts `YYYY-MM-DD` (taken as UTC midnight), `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss` and the same with `Z`. It throws on text it cannot parse. Then: [Certain]

```
tdbSeconds = unixSeconds − 946,728,000 + 69.184
```

Here **Unix time** (or POSIX time) is the count of seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00 UTC that computers use. The constant 946,728,000 s is the gap from the Unix epoch to J2000 noon (Worked Example 2.4).

Tiny example: 2026-01-01 00:00:00 UTC is 2026-01-01 00:01:09.184 TDB. If you ignored the offset, Earth would be drawn about 69.184 s × 30.05 km/s ≈ 2,079 km from where it really is.

What to notice in the code: [Certain]

- **A comment says TDB where it means TT.** `utc-to-tdb.ts:8` reads "TDB - TAI ≈ 32.184 s (constant offset)". Strictly, 32.184 s is TT − TAI, and TDB ≈ TT. The numbers are unaffected.
- **The constant is copied.** The literal `69.184` is re-typed in seven code lines in five other files: `src/v2/app/ui-overlay/overlay.ts:153`, `src/v2/app/porkchop-smoke/main.ts:33`, `src/v2/app/compare/main.ts:104`, `src/v2/app/porkchop/main.ts:175` and `:197`, and `mcp/src/tools/compute-shared.ts:136` and `:144`. The comment at `utc-to-tdb.ts:14-16` tells maintainers to update only `TDB_MINUS_UTC_SECONDS` after a new leap second. That would leave the copies stale.
- **The live clock.** The 3D view computes `TDB_AT_UNIX_EPOCH = utcStringToTdbSeconds('1970-01-01T00:00:00Z')` = −946,727,930.816 s and then `nowTdbSeconds = Date.now()/1000 + TDB_AT_UNIX_EPOCH` (`runtime.ts:228-230`). `Date.now()` is Unix time, which does not count leap seconds (from memory, verify).
- **Old dates are wrong by whole seconds.** The unit test pins 2000-01-01T12:00:00Z to exactly 69.184 s (`tests/v2-lambert/utc-to-tdb.test.mjs:33-37`). In 2000 the true TT − UTC was 64.184 s, because ΔAT was then 32 s (from memory, verify). The test checks the formula, not the physics. Every date Aster computes with is after 2017, so this does not affect results.
- Leap seconds are planned to be dropped by about 2035 (from memory, verify). If one is added before then, every copy above must change.

Time zones play no part. Everything is UTC or TDB. [Likely: a grep of `src/v2` and `mcp/src` finds no local-time date calls]

### B2.8 Julian Date and date arithmetic

#### One number line for time

Calendar arithmetic is awkward. Months have different lengths, and leap years come and go. Astronomers avoid this with the **Julian Date (JD)**: a running count of days, with a decimal fraction, from an epoch in 4713 BC (from memory, verify). Each JD day starts at **noon**, not midnight (from memory, verify). So a JD ending in .5 is a midnight.

The reference epoch used everywhere in Aster is:

```
J2000.0 = JD 2451545.0 = 2000-01-01 12:00 (TT/TDB)       J2000_TDB_JULIAN_DATE (units.ts:1)
t_J2000 [s] = (JD − 2451545.0) × 86400                     jdTdbToSecondsSinceJ2000 (units.ts:15-17)
MJD = JD − 2400000.5                                        Modified Julian Date (from memory, verify)
```

The last line defines the **Modified Julian Date (MJD)**, which moves the zero to a midnight and shortens the number; Aster's code does not use it. A JD must carry a time-scale tag. JD(TDB) and JD(UTC) for the same instant differ by 69.184 s = 0.000800741 day.

Converting a calendar date to JD (the Meeus algorithm, from memory, verify; it matches every fixture date I checked):

```
if M ≤ 2:  Y ← Y − 1,  M ← M + 12
A = floor(Y / 100)
B = 2 − A + floor(A / 4)
JD = floor(365.25 × (Y + 4716)) + floor(30.6001 × (M + 1)) + D + B − 1524.5
```

D may carry a fraction of a day. The 3D view runs the reverse algorithm for the date labels on its **HUD** (head-up display: the text overlaid on the scene) (`julianDayToGregorianDate`, `runtime.ts:610-634`). That version has no branch for dates before 1582, which no Aster date needs.

#### Why the core counts seconds, not Julian days

A JD near 2.46 million stored as a double has a resolution of about 4.7×10⁻¹⁰ day, which is **40 microseconds**. Seconds since J2000 (about 8.5×10⁸ s today) resolve to about **0.12 microseconds**. The core converts JDs to seconds once, at ingest (`horizons.ts:343`). [Certain: the resolutions recomputed for this guide] Precision is a good reason for that design; the founding document states the unit choice without giving this reason. [Likely]

The same concern drives a detail in `utc-to-tdb.ts:18-23`. Building a JD as "2451545.0 + small" and then subtracting 2451545.0 again throws away digits. This is called **catastrophic cancellation**: subtracting two nearly equal large numbers leaves few correct digits. The code instead goes straight from Unix seconds to seconds since J2000 with one exact constant.

A visible trace of JD granularity: fixture JDs are written to 9 decimals, so Io's one-hour step reads (2461345.541666667 − 2461345.5) × 86400 = 3600.0000268 s (checked in `horizons-jupiter-system-rolling.json`). At Io's orbital speed of about 17 km/s (from memory, verify) that is under a metre of motion, so it is harmless. [Certain]

#### Worked Example 2.4: today as a Julian Date and as TDB seconds

**Inputs.** Date 2026-11-06 00:00:00 UTC. `J2000_TDB_JULIAN_DATE = 2451545.0`, `SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86400` (`src/v2/core/units.ts:1-2`). `UNIX_TO_J2000_DAYS = 10957.5`, `TDB_MINUS_UTC_SECONDS = 69.184` (`src/v2/core/units/utc-to-tdb.ts:28-31`).

**Step 1: calendar to JD.** Y = 2026, M = 11, D = 6. M > 2, so no shift.

```
A = floor(2026 / 100) = 20
B = 2 − 20 + floor(20 / 4) = 2 − 20 + 5 = −13
floor(365.25 × (2026 + 4716)) = floor(365.25 × 6742) = 2,462,515
floor(30.6001 × (11 + 1)) = floor(367.2012) = 367
JD = 2,462,515 + 367 + 6 + (−13) − 1524.5 = 2,461,350.5
```

This is the JD of the calendar label "2026-11-06 00:00". It matches the fixture record at JD 2461350.5.

**Step 2: Unix epoch to J2000 noon.** From 1970-01-01 to 2000-01-01 is 30 years containing 7 leap days, so 30 × 365 + 7 = 10,957 days. Add half a day to reach noon: 10,957.5 days. Then 10,957.5 × 86,400 = 946,728,000 s.

**Step 3: the offset.** TDB − UTC = 37 + 32.184 = 69.184 s.

**Step 4: TDB seconds.** Unix time of 2026-11-06T00:00Z is 1,793,923,200 s.

```
tdbSeconds = 1,793,923,200 − 946,728,000 + 69.184 = 847,195,269.184 s
```

**Step 5: back to JD(TDB).**

```
JD(TDB) = 2,451,545.0 + 847,195,269.184 / 86,400 = 2,451,545.0 + 9,805.500800741
        = 2,461,350.500800741
```

**Step 6: check.** (2,461,350.500800741 − 2,461,350.5) × 86,400 = 69.184 s. Done in double precision, this subtraction actually returns 69.18401 s. The extra 14 microseconds is rounding in the stored JD, the 40-microsecond resolution explained in the subsection just above.

**Result.** UTC midnight on 2026-11-06 is JD(TDB) 2461350.500800741, or 847,195,269.184 TDB seconds since J2000. The fixture sample labelled JD 2461350.5 is TDB midnight, 69.184 s earlier. [Certain: recomputed for this guide]

#### Worked Example 2.5: the one-day slip at the edge of the span

A TDB midnight written as a UTC date lands 69.184 s before midnight, on the previous day. That small offset caused a real, visible contradiction in the published MCP server (Aster's tool server for AI agents, Chapter B10).

**Inputs.** First and last records of `src/v2/data/horizons-inner-solar-system-2026-2040.json`: JD(TDB) 2461041.5 and 2466519.5. Formulas `jdTdbToUtcDateString` and `utcMidnightToJdTdb` (`mcp/src/tools/compute-shared.ts:129-146`), using 946,728,000 and 69.184. Live calls to the published `aster-mission-mcp@0.1.0`, which was baked on 2026-07-10 at commit `84fefe8` and lags main.

**Step 1: first sample to seconds.**

```
(2461041.5 − 2451545.0) × 86400 = 9496.5 × 86400 = 820,497,600 s (TDB)
```

**Step 2: to UTC.**

```
820,497,600 − 69.184 + 946,728,000 = 1,767,225,530.816 Unix s
= 2025-12-31T23:58:50.816Z  →  date label "2025-12-31"
```

The last sample, by the same steps, is 2040-12-30T23:58:50.816Z, label "2040-12-30".

**Step 3: feed the labels back as UTC midnights.**

```
"2025-12-31" → JD(TDB) 2461040.500800741 < 2461041.5   outside the data: refuse
"2026-01-01" → JD(TDB) 2461041.500800741 ≥ 2461041.5   inside: accept
"2040-12-30" → JD(TDB) 2466518.500800741 ≤ 2466519.5   inside: accept
"2040-12-31" → JD(TDB) 2466519.500800741 > 2466519.5   outside: refuse
```

**Step 4: what the published package does.** A `porkchop_scan` starting on 2025-12-31 returns code `out_of_envelope` with reason: "Departure window 2025-12-31 through 2026-03-01 is outside the committed Earth ephemeris span 2025-12-31 through 2040-12-30." The message refuses a date it names as inside the span (live tool reply saved while writing this guide). [Certain]

**Step 5: what main does.** `acceptedUtcDateBounds` (`compute-shared.ts:149-160`) checks Step 3. If the lower label's UTC midnight falls before the first sample, it moves the label one day later. On main the advertised window is therefore 2026-01-01 through 2040-12-30. [Likely: read in code, not run on main]

**Result.** The accepted MCP window is 2026-01-01 to 2040-12-30 (UTC midnights), although the data run from 2026-01-01 to 2040-12-31 (TDB midnights). The compare page guards against the same trap. Its anchor must be 2461041.500800741 (UTC midnight), never 2461041.5. The wrong anchor "flips columns 0 and 730" of the date grid (`src/v2/porkchop/compare-data.ts:55-66`). [Certain]

### B2.9 Ephemerides: timetables for planets

#### What an ephemeris is

An **ephemeris** (plural **ephemerides**) is a table of where bodies are at listed times. Aster's tables also list velocities. Analogy: a train timetable that gives each train's position and speed at every station stop, but not between stops.

Aster does not compute planet orbits itself. It downloads state vectors from NASA/JPL's **Horizons** service (the `source` field of every file is "NASA/JPL Horizons API") and commits them to the repo. Horizons draws on JPL's numerically integrated planetary ephemerides, the "DE" series (from memory, verify). Asteroids are different: Aster propagates them from orbital elements (Chapter B3, Chapter B4).

Each file has the same layout: `{source, frame, timeScale, units, targets: {body: {targetId, center, origin, records: [[jdTdb, x, y, z, vx, vy, vz], ...]}}}`. All five production files declare `frame "ICRF/J2000"`, `timeScale "TDB"`, and units km, km/s and "TDB Julian Date". [Certain]

### B2.10 Reading between the rows: Hermite interpolation

#### The problem

The 3D view needs Earth's position at, say, 14:37 on some day. The table only has midnights. **Interpolation** estimates a value between known samples.

**Linear interpolation** joins two samples with a straight line. Planets do not move in straight lines, so the midpoint of the chord cuts inside the curved path.

**Cubic Hermite interpolation** uses four facts: the positions **and** the velocities at both ends. It fits the unique cubic curve that matches all four. Because the table gives velocities, Hermite can bend the curve the right way.

```
u = (t − t0) / Δt      ∈ [0, 1]          Δt = gap between the two samples, s

h00 = 2u³ − 3u² + 1        h10 = u³ − 2u² + u
h01 = −2u³ + 3u²           h11 = u³ − u²

p(t) = h00·p0 + h10·Δt·v0 + h01·p1 + h11·Δt·v1                      position, m
v(t) = (h00'·p0 + h10'·Δt·v0 + h01'·p1 + h11'·Δt·v1) / Δt           velocity, m/s
```

The primes are derivatives with respect to u: h00' = 6u² − 6u, h10' = 3u² − 4u + 1, h01' = −6u² + 6u, h11' = 3u² − 2u (`src/v2/core/interpolators/hermite.ts:12-45`). The velocity is the exact time-derivative of the position curve, so the two always agree. [Certain]

The error of cubic Hermite shrinks with the fourth power of the gap: halve Δt and the error falls about 16-fold. A textbook bound is Δt⁴/384 × the largest fourth derivative of position (from memory, verify).

Tiny example, a falling ball with p = 5t² m. Take p0 = 0, v0 = 0, p1 = 5, v1 = 10, Δt = 1 s. At u = 0.5: h00 = 0.5, h10 = 0.125, h01 = 0.5, h11 = −0.125. So p = 0.5 × 5 − 0.125 × 10 = 1.25 m, exactly 5 × 0.5². Linear interpolation gives 2.5 m.

#### What Aster's interpolator does

`interpolateBodyStateSeries` (`hermite.ts:82-122`): [Certain]

1. If the requested time equals a sample time, return that sample unchanged.
2. Otherwise scan for the two samples that bracket the time and interpolate between them.
3. If no pair brackets it, call `failInvariant` with the body's invariant ID (INV-008 for the Sun, inner planets and Moon, INV-009 Jupiter system, INV-010 Saturn system, INV-011 Mars moons; `bodies.ts:187-209`). `failInvariant` throws an `AssertError` (`src/v2/core/invariants/runtime.ts:58-76`).

It never **extrapolates**, that is, guesses beyond the ends of the table. Two limits are visible in the code. Its own comment says the two samples are assumed, not checked, to share a frame and body (`hermite.ts:47-51`). And the bracket search is a straight scan from the first sample (`hermite.ts:96-108`), so lookups late in a long table take longer. Linear interpolation is forbidden in core paths; it is allowed only for screen-only render effects (`V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md` §3.7).

#### How good is it? The Slice 2 measurement

Slice 2 measured the error before trusting it. Daily samples over 2026-05-01 → 2026-07-30 were interpolated to 270 in-between times per body and compared against Horizons truth at 6-hour spacing (`tools/slice2-research/interpolation-report.md`). Each **cutover bar**, the error allowed before the interpolator is trusted, was set to 3 × the measured maximum, rounded up to a clean number (report, "Recommendation"). [Certain]

| Body | Max linear error (km) | Max Hermite error (km) | INV-008 bar (km) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sun | 0.209 | 0.00000354 | 0.00002 |
| Mercury | 58,500 | 20.05 | 100 |
| Venus | 10,721 | 0.182 | 1 |
| Earth | 5,448 | 0.0907 | 0.5 |
| Moon | 2,918 | 4.98 | 20 |
| Mars | 2,861 | 0.00893 | 0.05 |

Bars are stored in metres in `INV008_BARS_M` (`bodies.ts:95-105`); the other systems' bars are in `INTERPOLATION_ERROR_BARS_M` (`bodies.ts:152-161`). I re-ran the measurement from the committed inputs (recomputed for this guide). It reproduces the table: Earth matches every printed digit, and the Sun matches to three significant figures. [Certain]

Note the ruling of 2026-10-26: INV-008..011 "enforcement is at test time, in the named interpolation tests, rather than in production runtime code" (`INVARIANTS.md:248-251`). The running app does not check interpolation accuracy live; the guarantee comes from these measurements. [Certain]

#### Worked Example 2.6: one Hermite step by hand

**Inputs** (x-components only), from `tools/slice2-research/data/daily-earth.json`, samples at JD 2461161.5 and 2461162.5 (2026-05-01 and 05-02 TDB):

- p0x = −114,970,771.918717 km, v0x = 18.76926328 km/s
- p1x = −113,332,642.373326 km, v1x = 19.14950118 km/s
- Truth at the midpoint, JD 2461162.0, from `tools/slice2-research/data/truth-earth.json`: x = −114,155,813.72092 km
- Basis functions from `hermite.ts:20-26`

**Step 1: where in the gap.** Δt = 86,400 s and u = 0.5.

**Step 2: basis values.**

```
h00 = 2(0.125) − 3(0.25) + 1 = 0.5
h10 = 0.125 − 2(0.25) + 0.5 = 0.125
h01 = −2(0.125) + 3(0.25) = 0.5
h11 = 0.125 − 0.25 = −0.125
```

**Step 3: combine.**

```
x = 0.5·p0 + 0.125·Δt·v0 + 0.5·p1 − 0.125·Δt·v1
  = 0.5·(p0 + p1) + 10,800·(v0 − v1)            (0.125 × 86,400 = 10,800 s)

0.5·(p0 + p1) = −114,151,707.146 km             (this alone is the linear answer)
10,800 × (18.769263 − 19.149501) = 10,800 × (−0.380238) = −4,106.569 km
x = −114,151,707.146 − 4,106.569 = −114,155,813.715 km
```

**Step 4: compare with truth.**

```
Hermite − truth (x) = −114,155,813.715 − (−114,155,813.721) ≈ +0.006 km
linear  − truth (x) = −114,151,707.146 − (−114,155,813.721) = +4,106.6 km
```

Doing the same for y and z, the full 3D miss is 0.0076 km (7.6 m) for Hermite and 5,423 km for linear.

**Result.** Midway between two daily samples, Hermite puts Earth within about 8 m of Horizons' own answer. A straight line misses by about 5,400 km. The velocity term, 10,800 × (v0 − v1), is what bends the curve. [Certain: recomputed for this guide]

### B2.11 Measure the frame at the consuming boundary: INV-021 and DEC-12-2

#### The principle

INV-021 reads: "Any quantity derived from the *components* (not magnitude) of a Lambert output vector must have its reference frame established by numerical measurement at the consuming boundary before first use — never inferred from a label or doc comment" (`INVARIANTS.md:67`; `src/v2/SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md:37`). [Certain]

The **consuming boundary** is the place in the code where the numbers are actually used, here the DLA computation. "Measurement" means a numerical test whose result differs sharply between the candidate frames.

The stated rationale has two parts:

- Magnitudes are frame-invariant (Section B2.2). Validating C3 to machine precision said nothing about which axes the components were in.
- "The 2026-07-01 halo bug demonstrated that frame-labeling errors survive multiple recons while producing plausible-looking output." In that bug, planet marker dots were drawn offset by "−camLocal" because scene-relative and camera-relative coordinates were confused (`INVARIANTS.md:96-105`, commits `5c9451e`, `dc44751`).

Analogy: two people read the same map, one with north at the top and one with north at the bottom. They agree on every distance and disagree on every direction. Checking distances will never reveal the problem.

#### The story, in order

1. **The label.** The Slice 11 summary in `INVARIANTS.md:28-29` labels `vInfDep` and `vInfArr` (the departure and arrival excess velocities, Chapter B5) "heliocentric ECLIPTIC". A pre-lock research summary proposed rotating by the obliquity before computing DLA (`INVARIANTS.md:56-61`). [Certain]
2. **The probe (OQ-12-1, closed 2026-07-01).** Before writing DLA, the team sampled Earth's velocity from the porkchop worker's own long-span file at four epochs in 2027. |vZ| reached 11.715 km/s (2027-10-01). In an ecliptic frame Earth's vZ would be about 0 at every epoch. Verdict: the components are ICRF/equatorial. The asteroid side agrees, because `propagateKeplerianStateVectors` rotates asteroid states into ICRF before Lambert, so both Lambert inputs share one frame (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md:43-46`). [Certain]
3. **The ruling (DEC-12-2, locked).** DLA = arcsin(vInfDepZ / |vInfDep|) with no rotation. The decision lives in one function, `dlaDegFromVInf` (`src/v2/core/lambert/dla.ts`), whose comment says applying the rotation "would introduce up to ~23.4 deg of silent error" and to read OQ-12-1 "before 'fixing' this". DEC-12-2 requires unit tests that pin four cases: a vector in the equatorial plane gives 0°, pure +Z gives +90°, a known 45° case, and a vector below the guard gives null (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md:79-83`). The guard is 1×10⁻³ in the input's unit, which is 1 m/s for km/s inputs (`dla.ts:14-17`). [Certain]
4. **The Slice 11 erratum (2026-07-02).** A note under AMD-7 says "the frame label above is incorrect for vector components" (`src/v2/SLICE_11_FOUNDING.md:259`). Oddly, AMD-7's own text (lines 247-257) names no axes: it says "heliocentric" (an origin) but never "ecliptic". The label it corrects lived in `INVARIANTS.md`'s summary, or in an earlier draft whose history is not available locally. [Likely]
5. **The 2026-08-01 correction (audit L2-3).** `INVARIANTS.md:228-230` states that the "heliocentric ECLIPTIC" label "is wrong and is superseded by measurement" and that "no ecliptic→equatorial obliquity rotation may be introduced anywhere in the Lambert/DLA path". The wrong lines still stand at lines 28-29 because the file is additive-only: corrections are appended, never edited in. [Certain]
6. **The 2026-09-22 refinement.** 11.715 km/s was a four-epoch sample, not a span maximum. Re-measured over the whole file through the production ingest, the span maximum is 11.89731636992642 km/s at JD 2461120.5 (2026-03-21 TDB). The ratio |vZ|max / |v|max is 0.392650878065271, against sin ε = 0.3977771559319137. The span minimum is 0.001467 km/s at a solstice, 2034-06-22 (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md:179`; `tools/slice12-research/data/earth-vz-span-max.json`). I reproduced all three numbers from the committed file (recomputed for this guide). [Certain]
7. **External check of the shipped path.** The M=1 path (transfers with one full revolution, Chapter B5) was compared with an **oracle**, an independent reference implementation, here the poliastro Python library, over 921 porkchop cells: largest angular separation 5.74×10⁻¹³ deg, largest |ΔDLA| 5.61×10⁻¹³ deg, against bars of 1×10⁻⁶ deg (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md`, OQ-12-3 closure correction). [Certain]

Why |vZ|/|v| should sit near sin ε: Earth's velocity lies in the ecliptic. When it points along the line of steepest tilt, which happens near the March and September equinoxes, the fraction of it along equatorial Z is sin ε. The ratio above, 0.3927, is a little lower than 0.3978 because it divides by the year's top speed (30.300 km/s, near perihelion) instead of the same day's speed (Worked Example 2.7 uses the same-day speed).

#### Worked Example 2.7: measuring the frame yourself

**Inputs.**

- Earth record at JD 2461120.5 (2026-03-21 TDB), `src/v2/data/horizons-inner-solar-system-2026-2040.json`: v = (−0.468308, −27.443964, −11.897316) km/s.
- sin ε = 0.3977772, cos ε = 0.9174821 (Worked Example 2.3).
- Live MCP result (published 0.1.0, lags main): `dla_feasibility` for Apophis (99942), departure 2026-11-06, 200-day flight, M=0, Cape Canaveral.
- Cape Canaveral band GREEN for |DLA| ≤ 28.5° (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md`, OQ-12-2). GREEN is Aster's verdict that the site reaches that DLA directly from its lowest orbit (Section B7.8).

**Step 1: speed.**

```
|v| = sqrt(0.468308² + 27.443964² + 11.897316²) = 29.915491 km/s
```

**Step 2: signed angle to the stored XY-plane.**

```
vz / |v| = −11.897316 / 29.915491 = −0.397698
asin(−0.397698) = −23.434°
```

If the stored axes were ecliptic, this would be about 0°. It is almost exactly −ε. The axes are equatorial.

**Step 3: undo the tilt with Rᵀ and look again.**

```
z_ecl = −y·sin ε + z·cos ε
      = −(−27.443964)(0.3977772) + (−11.897316)(0.9174821)
      = 10.916582 − 10.915574 = 0.001008 km/s
```

In ecliptic axes Earth's vertical speed is about 1 m/s, essentially zero. Across all 5,479 samples, the largest |vz| after this rotation is 0.0038 km/s (recomputed for this guide).

**Step 4: the forbidden step.** Apply R once more to the already-equatorial vector.

```
z' = y·sin ε + z·cos ε = −10.916582 + (−10.915574) = −21.832156 km/s
asin(−21.832156 / 29.915491) = −46.869°
error = −46.869 − (−23.434) = −23.435°
```

That is the "up to ~23.4°" of silent error DEC-12-2 rejects. The magnitude |v| is unchanged by the extra rotation, so no magnitude test would notice.

**Step 5: a real DLA from the published server.** The call returned DLA 6.523193364549625°, `frame "ICRF/equatorial"`, |v∞| = 10.79902305921471 km/s, verdict GREEN with margin 21.976806635450373° (live tool reply saved while writing this guide; an independent repeat call returned identical values). Work backwards to the vZ it implies, and check the margin:

```
vZ = |v∞| × sin(DLA) = 10.799023 × 0.1136054 = 1.226827 km/s
margin = 28.5° − 6.523193° = 21.976807°
```

**Result.** The stored axes are equatorial by measurement: on 2026-03-21 Earth's velocity is −23.434° from the stored XY-plane and about 0° from the ecliptic. A second rotation would shift declinations by 23.4° on this date. The published server's Apophis DLA of 6.52° is consistent with its stated frame and its GREEN verdict. [Certain: recomputed for this guide; MCP call made on 2026-11-06]

### B2.12 The C2 frame verdict: what the 3D view's axes are

INV-021 governs Lambert outputs. The 3D view needed its own answer. A batch of work called Front B asked for a **recon**, a read-only investigation by a fresh agent session, to establish it from the code. The verdict file is `tools/frontb-2026-08-11/C2_FRAME_VERDICT.md`; it landed as `c90b4f6` according to `STATUS.md:93`. [Certain]

> "(i) Frame: Heliocentric J2000 equatorial (ICRF) axes — Horizons vectors passed through unrotated; no ecliptic rotation applied to any rendered position; scene +Z = ICRF/celestial north."

The evidence chain, in short:

- All shipped files declare "ICRF/J2000". The only ingest rotation needs "ECLIPTIC" in the hint, so it does not fire.
- Positions are only scaled from km to m, translated to the focus body, and copied into the scene component by component, "no swizzle" (axes not reordered).
- Nothing rotates the scene or the position-bearing groups.
- `camera.up` is never set, so the default +Y "up" of Three.js (the 3D graphics library the view is built on, Chapter B9) is a camera-rig convention, not a statement about the sky.
- Asteroid states enter ICRF through the propagator's single obliquity rotation.

The subtle part is the top-down view. Its aim is `TOP_DOWN_ECLIPTIC_NORMAL_ICRF` (Worked Example 2.3). So in the top-down view you look down the **ecliptic** pole, and the planets' orbits appear nearly flat. But the scene's axes stay **equatorial**, and scene +Z is tilted 23.44° from your line of sight. The verdict notes that the very need to rotate (0, 0, 1) by the obliquity confirms that the scene axes are not ecliptic. [Certain]

`STATUS.md:93` makes the caveat binding: "copy must not conflate the two." The shipped chip says: "Frame — heliocentric J2000 equatorial (ICRF); +Z is celestial north. The top-down view looks down the ecliptic pole; the axes stay equatorial" (`runtime.ts:1024`). The corner axis triad shows +X as the vernal equinox and +Z as celestial north, "deliberately NOT labeled 'up' and NOT the ecliptic pole" (`src/v2/render/axis-triad.ts:1-18`). [Certain]

Three cautions:

- Line numbers in the verdict refer to commit `7a3622d`. On `cec19e7` they have drifted; for example the constant moved from `runtime.ts:335-339` to `359-363`.
- The verdict is about positions and scene axes. It is not about planet spin axes, which are drawn wrong (see Limits).
- An older note in `V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md` (§13 Known Limitations, Slice 8.5, line 1468) calls the rig's +Y "ICRF north". The C2 verdict and the current code say ICRF north is scene +Z. Trust the verdict and the code. [Likely that the older note is wrong or describes an earlier rig]

### B2.13 Coverage windows: what happens outside the table

#### The 3D view

The view's **coverage** is the stretch of time for which every loaded series has data. It is the intersection: the latest first sample and the earliest last sample (`runtime.ts:855-860`). [Certain]

```
timeMin = max over all series of (first sample time)
timeMax = min over all series of (last sample time)
```

On `cec19e7` that is 2026-11-01 → 2027-03-31 TDB (`STATUS.md:43`; data read directly).

What the view does with time (`runtime.ts:1883-1887, 2295-2297`; `src/v2/app/solar-system/ephemeris-status.ts`): [Certain]

- In live mode, every frame sets the displayed time to `clamp(now, timeMin, timeMax)`. Scrubbing is clamped the same way. **Clamping** means pinning a value to the nearest end of an allowed range.
- Inside coverage the HUD reads "LIVE".
- Past the end it reads "NOT LIVE · clamped to 2027-03-31 TDB", shows the amber warning "Current time is past this view's ephemeris coverage (ends 2027-03-31 TDB). Positions are shown for 2027-03-31, not now.", and appends " (clamped, not now)" to the date line. The test `tests/v2-ephemeris-hud.test.mjs:58-61` pins this text.
- Within 14 days of the end (`COVERAGE_ENDING_NOTICE_SECONDS = 14 × 86400`), the coverage line adds "(coverage ends 2027-03-31 TDB — refresh due)".

Because the app clamps first, it never asks the interpolator for a time outside the table, so the fatal INV-008..011 error is never hit in normal use.

#### Porkchop, compare and MCP

These pages refuse instead of clamping. A departure window outside the Earth span is rejected (`src/v2/porkchop/compare-data.ts:270-285`, DEC-17-10, "Validation, not clamping"); the MCP server returns `out_of_envelope` (Worked Example 2.5). The porkchop page's own departure grid runs from 2026-01-01 to 2040-01-01 UTC (`src/v2/porkchop/grid-span.ts:6-7`). [Certain]

Asteroid positions come from a formula, not a table, so they have no table edge. Their limits are about orbit quality and are covered in Chapter B4.

The previous rolling window ended 2026-10-16. After that date the site's front page showed NOT LIVE (`src/v2/SLICE_19_5_FOUNDING.md:455-461`; `MANIFEST.md`, "Window"). The roll was committed as `6cc5d9b` on 2026-11-03, and the deploy tree was rebuilt with the new files in `33461b1` an hour later ("build(docs): rebuild after ephemeris roll"). The live site changes only when that tree is pushed, so the NOT LIVE period ended at the next push after 2026-11-03. [Certain for the commits; Likely for the push timing, which local git does not record]

An unmerged branch, `origin/claude/ux-run-2026-10-22`, records that all four rolling files end 2026-10-16, so the view opens outside coverage (`tools/audit/ux-run-2026-10-22/UX_RUN_PROBLEMS_2026-10-22.md` on that branch, problem P3, a run against the old main at `6575d0d`; read for this guide with `git show`). It matches main as it stood on 2026-10-22: the previous window ended 2026-10-16 and the roll came on 2026-11-03 (`MANIFEST.md:8-9`). It is obsolete on main now. All four files end 2027-03-31, and so do all four built copies in the deploy tree on main (`docs/assets/horizons-*-rolling-*.json`, first and last JD 2461345.5 and 2461495.5, read for this guide). [Certain for main]

`STATUS.md` disagrees with itself: line 43 gives the new window, while line 55 still says "common coverage ends 2026-10-16 TDB". Line 55 was true when Slice 19.5 closed on 2026-11-02 and was overtaken the next day. [Certain]

#### Worked Example 2.8: today's coverage arithmetic

**Inputs.** Rolling window JD 2461345.5 → 2461495.5 (`src/v2/data/horizons-*-rolling.json`). Daily cadence 86,400 s (`bodies.ts:163-185`). `COVERAGE_ENDING_NOTICE_SECONDS = 14 × 86400` (`ephemeris-status.ts:22`). The reverse JD algorithm `julianDayToGregorianDate` (`runtime.ts:610-634`). Today, JD 2461350.5 (Worked Example 2.4).

**Step 1: window length and sample count.**

```
2461495.5 − 2461345.5 = 150 days
daily samples = 150 + 1 = 151        (both ends included)
```

For the long span: 2466519.5 − 2461041.5 = 5,478 days, so 5,479 samples.

**Step 2: turn JD 2461345.5 into a date** with the runtime's algorithm.

```
shifted = 2461345.5 + 0.5 = 2461346.0;  z = 2461346,  f = 0
alpha = floor((2461346 − 1867216.25) / 36524.25) = floor(16.27) = 16
a = 2461346 + 1 + 16 − floor(16/4) = 2461359
b = a + 1524 = 2462883
c = floor((2462883 − 122.1) / 365.25) = 6742
d = floor(365.25 × 6742) = 2462515
e = floor((2462883 − 2462515) / 30.6001) = floor(12.03) = 12
day = 2462883 − 2462515 − floor(30.6001 × 12) + 0 = 368 − 367 = 1
month = e − 1 = 11;   year = c − 4716 = 2026      →  2026-11-01 00:00 TDB
```

The same steps for 2461495.5 give c = 6743, d = 2462880, e = 4, so 2027-03-31.

**Step 3: is today inside?** 2461345.5 ≤ 2461350.5 ≤ 2461495.5. Yes, so the HUD reads LIVE. (The UTC-midnight JD, 2461350.5008, is also inside.)

**Step 4: days left.** 2461495.5 − 2461350.5 = 145 days.

**Step 5: when does the notice start?** When timeMax − now ≤ 14 days, that is from JD 2461481.5, which is 2027-03-17 TDB.

**Result.** The 3D view is live for 145 more days. It shows "refresh due" from 2027-03-17 and goes NOT LIVE after 2027-03-31 unless someone re-runs the roll commands in `MANIFEST.md:24-39`. [Certain: recomputed for this guide]

### Limits and known problems

Each item says what the limit is, why it matters, and where the evidence is.

#### Data coverage

- **The 3D view runs on a treadmill.** It knows planet and moon positions only for 2026-11-01 → 2027-03-31 TDB. Refresh is manual and the payload grows linearly with span: about 7.0 MB for 151 days, about 72 MiB to 2030 (`MANIFEST.md`, "Ruling"). After 2027-03-31 the front page will show NOT LIVE with frozen positions unless someone re-runs the roll. The 3D view is a cached table, not a live model. The structural fix is deferred to Slice 22. [Certain]
- **The two spans cannot cover for each other.** The long-span file reaches 2040, but DEC-11C-5 forbids merging it into the 3D view, and it lacks the outer planets and moons anyway. The view therefore cannot be scrubbed before 2026-11-01 or after 2027-03-31. The roll also left a gap: the old window ended 2026-10-16 and the new one starts 2026-11-01, so 2026-10-17 → 2026-10-31 was never in any rolling file. [Certain]
- **"Outside the table" behaves differently by layer.** The core interpolator throws a fatal error. The 3D view clamps and labels it NOT LIVE. Porkchop, compare and MCP refuse. Nothing extrapolates silently, but a reader must know which layer they are looking at. [Certain]
- **Old routes run on frozen fixtures.** `/v2/earth-moon` uses a 30-day ecliptic test fixture (2026-03-01 → 2026-03-31) and `/v2/inner-solar-system` a 90-day one (2026-05-01 → 2026-07-30). They step through samples and never show today's sky (`src/v2/boundary/slice1-earth-moon.ts:8`; `src/v2/app/inner-solar-system/loader.ts:14`). [Certain]

#### Time

- **A fixed 37 s TAI − UTC offset.** The UTC → TDB offset is hard-coded and valid only from 2017-01-01. It ignores the < 2 ms periodic TDB − TT term. A future leap second must be edited into the canonical constant and the seven copied literals (Section B2.7). `STATUS.md:305` mentions "two independent UTC→TDB implementations", which undercounts the copies. [Certain]
- **Date labels mix scales at the edges.** A TDB midnight shown as a UTC date falls on the previous day. The published MCP 0.1.0 still advertises "2025-12-31 through 2040-12-30" and refuses 2025-12-31; the same string appears in the `validity_envelope` of its `dla_feasibility` answer (live tool reply saved while writing this guide). Main fixes the label (Worked Example 2.5). `mcp/README.md:53-79` describes both states in one section: line 53 and lines 58-61 already give the fixed label, while lines 63-77 describe the unfixed behaviour and say "Not fixed here". That is confusing. [Certain]

#### Frames

- **J2000 axes, not axes of date.** DLA and all frames use the J2000 mean equator. The ~17 mas ICRF frame bias, precession and **nutation** (a small periodic nodding of Earth's axis on top of precession, from memory, verify) are ignored, and Earth's daily rotation is not modelled at all. DEC-12-2 states precession drift as "≤ ~0.2°" over 2026–2040. A rough estimate of precession in declination, about 20 arcsec per year from J2000 to 2040-12-31 (from memory, verify), gives up to about 0.23°. The "~" covers it; it is a wording nit, not a defect. At screening fidelity (degree-level DLA) none of this matters. [Likely]
- **Planet poles and Saturn's rings are drawn wrong.** The render tilts (Mars 25.19°, Saturn 26.7°; `runtime.ts:92-94`) turn a mesh whose pole sits on local +Y about scene +X, in a frame whose north is +Z. Spin axes and the ring plane end up 59–115° off (`src/v2/SLICE_19_5_FOUNDING.md:338-350`). This is a clash between a Y-up graphics habit and a Z-up astronomy frame. The view says so on screen: "Planet spin axes and Saturn's ring plane are not oriented correctly yet" (`runtime.ts:988-990`). The fix is routed to Slice 22 (OQ-19.5-3, `src/v2/SLICE_19_5_FOUNDING.md:452`). The C2 verdict covers positions and scene axes, not body orientations. [Certain]
- **Mixed origins in the "heliocentric" scene.** The Sun mesh is placed at its SSB-relative position while planets are Sun-centred (`runtime.ts:1792-1803`). The Sun is drawn 0.68–0.77 million km (0.98–1.11 solar radii) from the planets' true origin in the current window, so the drawn Earth–Sun distance can be off by at most 773,318 km / 149,597,870.7 km = 0.52% of 1 AU (recomputed for this guide). The constants README even calls the SSB "heliocentric origin" (`src/v2/core/constants/README.md`, body table). At solar-system zoom this is invisible. [Certain]
- **"earth" is the geocentre.** It wobbles around the Earth–Moon barycentre every month, by about 4,700 km (from memory, verify). Its instantaneous orbit pole therefore swings by a few thousandths of a degree: between 0.0016° and 0.0059° from the J2000 ecliptic pole across the current rolling window. The slow drift of the real orbit plane adds about 0.0036° in 2026 (recomputed for this guide). Together they explain why Worked Example 2.1 found 23.437° rather than exactly 23.439°. The wobble also makes two-body propagation of the geocentre drift badly, which `STATUS.md:205` notes; the screening layer interpolates Earth instead. [Likely]
- **`FRAME_GCRS_EARTH` is a simplified GCRS.** It is a translation only, without relativistic corrections (from memory, verify). Negligible here, but not a full implementation. [Likely]
- **The obliquity is a convention.** 84381.448″ is the classic J2000 value; IAU 2006 gives 84381.406″ (from memory, verify). Negligible for every repo quantity. [Likely]

#### Interpolation

- **Accuracy is checked in tests, not in the running app.** Ruling R1 (2026-10-26) puts INV-008..011 enforcement in the interpolation tests. The bracket samples' frame and body agreement is "enforced by convention — no runtime check" (`hermite.ts:47-51`). The guarantee is the cutover measurement, which for INV-008 covered one 90-day window in 2026 (Section B2.10). [Certain]
- **Error bars are per body, not per date.** They were measured on one window and assumed to hold elsewhere. [Likely that they do, given the 4–6× margins]

#### A wrong field in a committed measurement

`tools/slice12-research/data/earth-vz-span-max.json` has a field `perCalendarYearMaxAbsVzKmPerSec` that is not a per-year maximum. Each value is |vZ| on 31 December of that year: for 2026 it reads 1.878 km/s, while the true 2026 maximum is 11.897 km/s on 2026-03-21. The cause is at `tools/slice12-research/measure-earth-vz.mjs:130`. It compares `absVz` in m/s with `prior.absVzKmS` in km/s, so every sample overwrites the last. The headline span maximum and the 2027 maximum are computed correctly elsewhere in the script. [Certain]

The artifact records the file's SHA-256 hash as `c91f4e50da0e6fc5...` and its size as 7,510,022 bytes; `SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md:179` repeats the hash prefix. The checked-out file is 7,214,102 bytes with hash `b278dd5567f3...`. The difference, 295,920 bytes, equals the file's line count. Converting its line endings to Windows-style CRLF reproduces the recorded hash and size exactly (re-checked twice for this guide). The data did not change. A byte hash depends on how the checkout stores line endings; a Windows checkout with Git's CRLF conversion would produce exactly this. [Certain for the arithmetic; Likely for the cause]

#### Evidence trail

Local git history is shallow; it starts at 2026-09-21. Commits cited before then (`57e4cba`, `c90b4f6`, `7a3622d`, `5c9451e`, `dc44751`) are cited here as "recorded in" the named documents, not as inspected. Numbers from the MCP server come from the published 0.1.0 package (baked 2026-07-10 at `84fefe8`), which lags main. [Certain]

### Key takeaways

- A position is meaningless without four facts: origin, axis directions, unit and time on a named clock. Aster fixes them once: metres, m/s, TDB seconds since J2000, `FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ICRF`.
- Magnitudes survive any rotation; components do not. That is why checking C3 or speeds can never prove a frame.
- Changing origin is a translation of both position and velocity at the same instant. Every Aster frame transform is translation-only.
- Equatorial and ecliptic axes share +X and differ by a 23.4392911° turn about it. Aster's data are equatorial (ICRF). Only asteroid elements are ecliptic, and the propagator rotates them exactly once.
- TDB − UTC = 69.184 s since 2017. A TDB midnight is 23:58:50.816 UTC the day before, which caused a real off-by-one-day label in the published MCP server.
- Julian Dates make date arithmetic subtraction. The core converts them to seconds since J2000 for precision.
- Cubic Hermite interpolation uses velocities as well as positions. Halfway between daily samples it puts Earth within about 8 m; a straight line misses by about 5,400 km.
- INV-021: measure a vector's frame where it is used. The Earth |vZ| probe (11.9 km/s, not ~0) settled DEC-12-2: no rotation in the DLA path.
- The 3D scene's axes are equatorial; the top-down view looks down the ecliptic pole. Copy must keep the two apart.
- The 3D view covers 2026-11-01 → 2027-03-31 TDB and clamps outside it. The planning tools use the 2026–2040 data and refuse outside it: on main the MCP server accepts departures 2026-01-01 → 2040-12-30 (UTC), and the porkchop page's grid runs 2026-01-01 → 2040-01-01.
