## Chapter B3: Orbits around the Sun and the near-Earth asteroid population

**Main idea:** Aster turns six numbers and a date into an asteroid's position at any other date by assuming that only the Sun pulls on it, and the project's job is to know, body by body, how long that assumption stays true.

### B3.1 What this chapter is for

Every **porkchop plot** (a chart of launch cost over departure date and flight time), every **C3** (launch energy per kilogram) and every transfer arc in Aster needs two things (Chapters B5 and B6): where Earth is at departure, and where the asteroid is at arrival. The two come from different machinery. [Certain]

- **Earth** is read from a JPL table and interpolated between rows (Chapter B2). In `src/v2/porkchop/porkchop.worker.ts:139` the Earth state comes from `interpolateBodyStateSeries('earth', ...)`.
- **The asteroid** is computed from its orbit. Two lines later (`porkchop.worker.ts:141`) the target state comes from `propagateKeplerianStateVectors(bodyElements, tdbSeconds)`, defined in `src/v2/core/propagators/keplerian.ts`.

The MCP server (`mcp/src/tools/compute-shared.ts:91-93`) and the 3D scene's asteroid worker (`src/v2/app/solar-system/asteroid-propagation-worker.ts:31`) call the same core function. [Certain]

This chapter builds up what that function needs: gravity, orbit shapes, the six orbital elements, and Kepler's equation. It then describes the near-Earth population in Aster's catalog, why the method drifts from reality, and how Slice 18 measured that drift and turned it into fidelity tiers L0, L1 and L2. Frames and time scales are in Chapter B2; sizes and orbit quality in Chapter B4; Lambert's problem in Chapter B5.

### B3.2 Gravity around the Sun

#### Newton's law

Every mass pulls on every other mass. The pull gets weaker with the square of the distance. This is **Newton's law of universal gravitation**. [Certain]

Analogy: a light bulb spreads its light over a sphere. Twice as far away, the sphere has four times the area, so each patch gets a quarter of the light. Gravity "spreads" the same way.

```
F = G · M · m / r²            force between Sun and asteroid
a = F / m = G · M / r²        acceleration of the asteroid (its own mass m cancels)
μ = G · M                     the Sun's gravitational parameter

F   force                              [N]
G   gravitational constant ≈ 6.674e-11 [m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻²]   (from memory, verify)
M   mass of the Sun                    [kg]
m   mass of the asteroid               [kg]
r   Sun–asteroid distance              [m]
μ   gravitational parameter            [m³ s⁻²]
```

Two things follow.

- **The asteroid's mass does not matter.** It cancels out. No asteroid mass appears anywhere in `keplerian.ts`. A pebble and a mountain on the same path move the same way. [Certain]
- **Only the product G·M matters.** It is called the **gravitational parameter**, written **μ** ("mu") or **GM**. Watching planets move measures μ to about 10 or 11 significant figures. G on its own is known only to about 5 (from memory, verify). So orbit codes carry μ, never G and M separately. [Certain as textbook fact]

#### The project's value

```
GM_SUN_M3_S2 = 1.32712440018e20  m³/s²        src/v2/core/propagators/keplerian.ts:9
```

It is the only solar GM in the core. The porkchop grid derives its kilometre form from it rather than retyping it: `MU_SUN_KM3_S2 = GM_SUN_M3_S2 / (METERS_PER_KILOMETER ** 3)` (`src/v2/porkchop/grid-compute.ts:9`). One number, one place, is a good habit. [Certain]

Tiny illustration. At 1 AU (defined in Section B3.3) the Sun's pull is:

```
μ / r² = 1.32712440018e20 / (1.495978707e11)²  =  5.93e-3 m/s²
```

That is about 1/1,654 of the 9.81 m/s² you feel standing on Earth. It is still enough to bend Earth's path into a closed loop once a year.

**Misconception:** "An orbiting body is weightless because there is no gravity up there." No. An orbiting body is falling all the time. It moves sideways fast enough that it keeps missing the Sun.

#### A label that is wrong

The comment on line 8 of `keplerian.ts` reads "IAU 2015 nominal heliocentric GM". The Slice 18 math-layer audit found the label wrong and the value fine: IAU 2015 nominal is 1.3271244e20, and the value behind Horizons (DE441) is about 1.32712440041e20. The repo's value differs from DE441's by 1.7e-10 relative (`tools/slice18-research/MATH_LAYER_AUDIT.md` L2; `audit-3-results.json`, `checks.constants.gmSun`). The fix is open as OQ-18-5 and deferred, because `src/v2/core/*` is a protected path (`SLICE_18_FOUNDING.md` §5, §8). [Certain]

The audit and OQ-18-5 both call the repo's value "DE430". From memory (verify), 1.32712440018e20 is the older DE405 value, and DE430/DE440/DE441 use about 1.32712440041e20. If so, the "DE430" label is off too. [Likely]

The effect is tiny. Two ways to measure it, both run for this chapter, give:

| What changes | Shift at JD 2468342.5 (433, 99942, 101955) | Script |
|---|---|---|
| Same elements, propagated with each GM | 1.22 to 1.39 km | recomputed for this guide |
| Elements re-derived from each body's Horizons anchor state with each GM, then propagated with that GM | 4.5 to 6.1 km | recomputed for this guide |

The second is closer to what a full switch would mean, because a changes too (vis-viva, Section B3.7). Neither reproduces the audit's "~15 km", which shows no steps. Either way it is negligible next to the drift in Section B3.17. [Likely]

### B3.3 The astronomical unit and the circular orbit

#### The AU

The **astronomical unit (AU)** is a fixed length, roughly the average Earth–Sun distance. It is defined as exactly 149,597,870,700 m (IAU 2012; from memory, verify). It is a convenient ruler for the inner solar system. [Certain]

Aster's core never uses it. Core state is in metres, metres per second and TDB seconds since J2000 (INV-001, `src/v2/core/invariants/README.md`). Field names such as `positionAu` and `velocityAuPerDay` are on a forbidden list (`src/v2/core/invariants/assertions.ts:17-28`). [Certain]

The AU appears only as repeated local literals for display, camera sizing, the screen precompute and research scripts. `AU_M = 149_597_870_700` is in `src/v2/app/solar-system/runtime.ts:74`, `src/v2/app/inner-solar-system/runtime.ts:16` and `src/v2/render/asteroid-cell-renderer.ts:52`. `AU_KM = 149_597_870.7` is in `src/v2/render/spatial-grid.ts:16`, `src/v2/render/slice9-spatial-partition.ts:78`, `tools/build/precompute-lambert-screen.mjs:81` and research scripts. They all agree. [Certain]

**Misconception:** "1 AU is the Earth–Sun distance today." No. Earth's distance varies from about 0.983 AU to about 1.017 AU over a year (from memory, verify). Those two numbers come back in Section B3.14 as class boundaries.

#### The circular orbit

On a circle, gravity supplies exactly the inward pull the circle needs. Set the gravitational acceleration equal to the **centripetal acceleration** v²/r:

```
μ / r² = v² / r        →   v_circ = √(μ / r)
T = 2π r / v_circ      →   T = 2π √(r³ / μ)

v_circ  circular speed [m/s];  r  radius [m];  T  period [s]
```

Analogy: a ball on a string. A shorter string needs a faster swing to stay taut. Inner orbits are faster.

#### Worked Example 3.1: one year at 1 AU with the repo's GM

Inputs:
- μ = 1.32712440018e20 m³/s² (`src/v2/core/propagators/keplerian.ts:9`)
- r = 1 AU = 1.495978707e11 m (`src/v2/app/solar-system/runtime.ts:74`)

Steps:

```
r³        = (1.495978707e11)³                    = 3.3479e33 m³
r³ / μ    = 3.3479e33 / 1.32712440018e20         = 2.5227e13 s²
√(r³/μ)   =                                        5.0226e6 s
T         = 2π × 5.0226e6                        = 3.15582e7 s
T in days = 3.15582e7 / 86,400                   = 365.256898 d

v_circ    = √(1.32712440018e20 / 1.495978707e11) = √(8.8713e8) = 29,784.7 m/s = 29.7847 km/s
v_escape  = √2 × v_circ                          = 42.12 km/s
```

Result: 365.256898 days and 29.78 km/s (recomputed for this guide). [Certain]

Compare with Earth's real sidereal year, about 365.25636 d, and its mean speed, about 29.78 km/s (both from memory, verify). The gap is 0.00054 d, or 1.5 parts per million. Earth's own mass explains almost all of it. For two bodies the period depends on G·(M_Sun + M_Earth+Moon), not G·M_Sun alone, and the Earth–Moon mass is about 3.04e-6 of the Sun's (from memory, verify). That raises μ by 3.04e-6 and shortens the period by half as much: 365.256898 × (1 − 1.52e-6) = 365.25634 d. Planetary pulls and Earth's a not being exactly 1 AU account for the last few hundred-thousandths of a day. [Likely]

Note what does *not* matter: the shape of Earth's orbit. The third law (Section B3.4) depends on a only, so a slightly elliptical orbit has the same period as a circle of radius a.

### B3.4 Kepler's three laws

Johannes Kepler found the first two rules in Tycho Brahe's observations of Mars (published 1609) and the third by comparing the planets (published 1619) (dates from memory, verify). Newton later showed that all three follow from inverse-square gravity. [Certain]

1. **First law: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus.** Not at the centre. (Section B3.6 defines the ellipse and its foci.)
2. **Second law: equal areas in equal times.** The line from the Sun to the body sweeps out area at a constant rate. So the body moves fast when close and slowly when far.
3. **Third law: T² ∝ a³.** The square of the period is proportional to the cube of the orbit's size, with the same constant for everything that orbits the Sun.

```
Law 2:  dA/dt = h / 2 = constant,   h = |r × v|            h: specific angular momentum [m²/s]
Law 3:  T² = (4π² / μ) · a³    →    T[years] ≈ (a[AU])^1.5     a: semi-major axis [m]
```

The second law is **conservation of angular momentum**. Analogy: a figure skater pulls in her arms and spins faster. An asteroid near perihelion is the skater with her arms in.

Tiny illustrations of the third law: a = 4 AU gives T = 4^1.5 = 8 years. A body with a = 1.5874 AU takes 2 years.

**Misconceptions.**
- "Heavier bodies orbit faster." No. The asteroid's mass is not in the law.
- "Law 2 means constant speed." No. The rate of sweeping area is constant; the speed changes all the time.

In the code, the third law appears as the **mean motion** n = √(μ/a³) (`keplerian.ts:210`), the average angular rate in radians per second (Section B3.9).

### B3.5 Conic sections: the four possible orbit shapes

Slice a cone with a flat plane and you get one of four curves. These are the **conic sections**. Every orbit of one body around another, with nothing else pulling, is one of them. [Certain]

Picture in words. Shine a torch at a wall.
- Straight on, the patch of light is a **circle**.
- Tilt the torch and it becomes an **ellipse**, a stretched closed loop.
- Tilt further, until the edge of the beam runs parallel to the wall, and the patch never closes. That is a **parabola**.
- Tilt further still and it flares open. That is a **hyperbola**.

A single number, the **eccentricity e**, says which one you have:

| Conic | Eccentricity | Energy (Section B3.7) | Meaning for an orbit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Circle | e = 0 | negative | bound, constant distance |
| Ellipse | 0 < e < 1 | negative | bound, returns forever |
| Parabola | e = 1 | zero | just escapes |
| Hyperbola | e > 1 | positive | unbound, passes once |

The **conic equation** describes all four, with the Sun at the **focus**:

```
r(ν) = p / (1 + e cos ν)
p = a (1 − e²) = h² / μ

r   distance from the Sun [m]
ν   true anomaly: the angle at the Sun from the closest point to the body [rad] (3.10)
p   semi-latus rectum: the distance r at ν = 90° [m]
```

The number p is the **semi-latus rectum**: the Sun distance when the body is 90° past its closest point. It is the one length that all four conics share.

Tiny illustration: a = 1, e = 0.5 gives p = 0.75. Then r(0°) = 0.75/1.5 = 0.5, r(90°) = 0.75 and r(180°) = 0.75/0.5 = 1.5.

#### Where conics live in Aster

- `sampleOrbitEllipse` (`keplerian.ts:161-193`) draws orbit lines with exactly this equation. It steps ν around the circle and computes r. It is render-only; the audit did not cover it (`MATH_LAYER_AUDIT.md`). [Certain]
- The propagator accepts **only ellipses**. `validateKeplerianElements` (`keplerian.ts:47-62`) throws a `RangeError` unless every element is finite, a > 0 and 0 ≤ e < 1. There is no parabolic or hyperbolic branch. [Certain]
- The catalog has exactly one body that fails this test: comet C/2015 D1 (SOHO), with e = 1.003535566834499 and a = −8.390 AU (`tests/fixtures/v2/nea-catalog-slice9.json`). A negative a is what a hyperbola's formula gives (Section B3.7). [Certain]

Until the Slice 18 close-out, that one body's throw "took the whole compare page down" (`src/v2/porkchop/propagation-guard.ts:8-9`). That file now asks first. `assessPropagation` runs the same checks in the same order as the propagator but returns a value instead of throwing. Users see: "Aster cannot propagate this object. Its eccentricity is 1.0035, which is not an elliptical orbit. No transfer windows are computed." The 3D scene draws it frozen at its anchor position (`asteroid-propagation-worker.ts:30-41`). [Certain]

**Misconception:** "Hyperbolic means fast." Not exactly. It means unbound: the body has more than enough energy to escape and will not come back.

### B3.6 Ellipse geometry: a, e, q, Q and b

Almost every catalog body is on an ellipse, so it pays to know the ellipse well.

Analogy: push two pins into a board, loop a string around them, and pull a pencil around inside the loop. You draw an ellipse. Each pin is a **focus**. The Sun sits at one focus. Move the pins apart and the ellipse gets more stretched.

- **Semi-major axis a**: half the longest diameter. It sets the orbit's size, its period (Section B3.4) and its energy (Section B3.7).
- **Eccentricity e**: how stretched the ellipse is, from 0 (circle) towards 1 (a very thin loop). It describes shape, not size.
- **Perihelion distance q**: the closest the body gets to the Sun.
- **Aphelion distance Q**: the farthest it gets.
- **Semi-minor axis b**: half the shortest diameter.

```
q = a (1 − e)        Q = a (1 + e)        a = (q + Q) / 2
b = a √(1 − e²)      c = a · e            (c: distance from the ellipse's centre to the focus)
```

Real catalog bodies at their 2026-05-01 elements (`tests/fixtures/v2/nea-catalog-slice9.json`; period from the repo GM; a check script written for this guide):

| Body | a (AU) | e | q (AU) | Q (AU) | Period (d) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 433 Eros | 1.4582 | 0.2229 | 1.1332 | 1.7833 | 643.2 |
| 99942 Apophis | 0.9224 | 0.1911 | 0.7461 | 1.0987 | 323.6 |
| 101955 Bennu | 1.1260 | 0.2037 | 0.8966 | 1.3553 | 436.4 |
| 163693 Atira (the class's namesake) | 0.7410 | 0.3222 | 0.5022 | 0.9797 | 233.0 |
| 2000 SG344 | 0.9775 | 0.0669 | 0.9120 | 1.0429 | 353.0 |

These five quantities are what Aster's population logic is built on. q and Q decide the orbit class (Section B3.14). Q ≥ 4.95 AU marks a Jupiter-crossing orbit in Slice 18. The constant is named `JUPITER_PERIHELION_AU` (`tools/slice18-research/tier-sizing.mjs:33`): an orbit whose aphelion reaches Jupiter's closest distance to the Sun, about 4.95 AU (from memory, verify), can meet Jupiter. a and e decide the co-orbital tag (Section B3.16).

#### Eccentricity bands

`eccentricityBandForBody` (`src/v2/core/constants/asteroids.ts:90-104`) sorts bodies into four **eccentricity bands**:

| Band | Rule | Catalog count |
|---|---|---|
| A | e < 0.1 | 1,007 |
| B | 0.1 ≤ e < 0.2 | 3,657 |
| C | 0.2 ≤ e < 0.3 | 5,757 |
| D | e ≥ 0.3 | 31,485 |

Counts are from the fixture (a check script written for this guide). Three in four catalog bodies have e ≥ 0.3, far more stretched than any planet's orbit. The bands feed the Slice 8 accuracy bars (INV-013, 3.12) and the catalog index check in `createAsteroidCatalogIndex`. [Certain]

**Misconception:** "a is the average distance." It is the average of q and Q. The time-averaged distance is a(1 + e²/2), larger, because the body lingers far out (from memory, verify). And a and e are independent: a small orbit can be very stretched.

### B3.7 Energy and the vis-viva equation

A body on an orbit has **kinetic energy** (from its motion) and **potential energy** (from its position in the Sun's gravity). Per kilogram of asteroid, their sum is the **specific orbital energy** ε. With only the Sun pulling, ε never changes. [Certain]

```
ε = v²/2 − μ/r = −μ / (2a)                      specific energy [J/kg = m²/s²]
v² = μ (2/r − 1/a)                              the vis-viva equation
a  = 1 / (2/r − v²/μ)                           the same equation, solved for a

v  speed relative to the Sun [m/s];  r  distance from the Sun [m];  a  semi-major axis [m]
```

The **vis-viva equation** ("living force", an old name for kinetic energy) gives the speed anywhere on an orbit from just two numbers: where you are (r) and how big the orbit is (a). [Certain]

Three things fall out of it:

- **The sign of ε gives the conic.** Negative means bound (ellipse). Zero means parabola. Positive means hyperbola, and then the last formula returns a negative a. That is why 2015 D1 has a = −8.39 AU (Section B3.5).
- **Fast at perihelion, slow at aphelion.** Apophis moves at 37.6 km/s at perihelion and 25.6 km/s at aphelion. Eros moves at 30.9 and 19.7 km/s (recomputed for this guide; catalog elements).
- **Direction does not matter.** At a given r and a the speed is the same whichever way the body is heading.

**Misconception:** "Negative energy is unphysical." No. Zero is defined at infinite distance, at rest. A bound body has less than that, so its energy is negative.

In the repo, the inverse form is how the catalog's elements were made. `cartesianToElements` (`tools/slice7-research/state-to-elements.mjs`) takes one position and velocity from **JPL Horizons** (JPL's online ephemeris service, Chapter B2). It computes a from vis-viva (line 95), then the other elements (`src/v2/core/asteroid-catalog.md`, "Element Derivation"). The Slice 9 re-anchor script imports it (`tools/slice9-ingestion/reanchor-stale-subset.mjs:4`). Two checks agree: [Certain]

- The Slice 18 sanity gate round-tripped this conversion to 9 cm in the worst case (`tools/slice18-research/NEA_DRIFT_MEASUREMENT.md` §1).
- For this chapter, running `cartesianToElements` on the anchor states stored in the fixture for 433, 99942 and 101955, with the repo GM, returned each fixture `aKm` with zero difference (recomputed for this guide).

### B3.8 Placing the orbit in space: i, Ω and ω

Size and shape (a and e) are not enough. The ellipse also has to be tilted and turned into place in three dimensions. That needs a **reference plane** and a **reference direction**.

Aster stores asteroid elements in the **J2000 ecliptic** frame. The reference plane is the plane of Earth's orbit, frozen at the year-2000 epoch, and the reference direction is the **vernal equinox**. The frame id is `FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ECLIPTIC`. `createAsteroidCatalogIndex` rejects any body stored in another frame (`asteroids.ts:130-134`). Chapter B2 explains the frame itself. [Certain]

Picture in words. A large round table is the ecliptic. An arrow painted on it points to the equinox. The asteroid's orbit is a hula hoop, tilted and resting partly above and partly below the table.

- **Inclination i**: the hoop's tilt against the table, from 0° to 180°. Below 90° the body goes round the same way as the planets (**prograde**). Above 90° it goes the other way (**retrograde**).
- **Longitude of the ascending node Ω** (capital omega): the hoop cuts the table along a straight line, the **line of nodes**. The **ascending node** is the point where the body climbs up through the table. Ω is the angle from the painted arrow to that point, measured anticlockwise as seen from above.
- **Argument of perihelion ω** (small omega): the angle, measured inside the hoop in the direction of motion, from the ascending node to perihelion. It says which way the ellipse's "nose" points within its own plane.

```
i ∈ [0, π]     Ω, ω ∈ [0, 2π)        radians in code: iRad, omRad (Ω), wRad (ω)
```

Real values (`nea-catalog-slice9.json`, converted to degrees):

| Body | i | Ω | ω |
|---|---|---|---|
| 433 Eros | 10.83° | 304.27° | 178.92° |
| 99942 Apophis | 3.34° | 203.90° | 126.68° |
| 163693 | 25.62° | 103.87° | 252.93° |
| 2000 SG344 | 0.11° | 191.76° | 275.56° |

Apophis's hoop is almost flat on the table. 2000 SG344's is flatter still.

**Misconceptions.**
- "i is measured from Earth's equator." Not for Aster's stored elements. It is measured from the ecliptic. The code converts to the equatorial ICRF frame only at the very end (Section B3.12).
- "Ω and ω always exist." No. At i = 0 there is no node line, and at e = 0 there is no perihelion. `cartesianToElements` then sets Ω = 0 (no node) or ω = 0 (no perihelion) and measures the remaining angle from a fallback direction (`state-to-elements.mjs:98-124`). Near those cases the conversion is badly conditioned: the audit found round-trip errors up to 7.2 km at e = 0.999, i = 1e-6°, ν = 179.5°, and at most 2.6 cm everywhere else (`MATH_LAYER_AUDIT.md` L1). [Certain]

### B3.9 Timing: the epoch, mean motion and mean anomaly

Five elements fix the ellipse and its orientation. The sixth says where the body is on it, and the **epoch** says when.

- **Epoch t₀**: the instant at which the elements are valid. Think of it as the timestamp on a photograph.
- **Mean motion n**: the body's average angular rate around the Sun, one full turn (2π radians) per period.
- **Mean anomaly M**: an imaginary clock hand that turns at the steady rate n. It reads 0 at perihelion and 2π one period later.

```
n = √(μ / a³)                    mean motion [rad/s]          keplerian.ts:210
M(t) = M₀ + n · (t − t₀)         mean anomaly [rad]           keplerian.ts:211

M₀  mean anomaly at the epoch (field maRad)
t₀  epoch, TDB seconds since J2000 (field epochTdbSeconds)
```

Analogy: a runner goes round an oval track, fast on one side and slow on the other. A metronome ticks once per lap. The metronome tells you what fraction of the lap's time has passed. It does not tell you where the runner is. M is the metronome.

Tiny illustrations (repo GM): a 1 AU orbit has n = 1.991e-7 rad/s. Eros has n = 1.1306e-7 rad/s, which matches the value quoted in `SLICE_18_FOUNDING.md` §2.

#### The six classical elements together

| Element | Symbol | Code field | What it fixes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Semi-major axis | a | `aM` (metres) | size, period, energy |
| Eccentricity | e | `e` | shape |
| Inclination | i | `iRad` | tilt of the plane |
| Longitude of ascending node | Ω | `omRad` | swing of the plane |
| Argument of perihelion | ω | `wRad` | direction of the nose |
| Mean anomaly at epoch | M₀ | `maRad` | where the body is at t₀ |
| Epoch | t₀ | `epochTdbSeconds` | when the other six are valid |

The interface is `AsteroidOrbitalElements` (`src/v2/core/constants/asteroids.ts:15-23`); `keplerian.ts:16` calls it `KeplerianElements`. The fixture stores `aKm` and `epochTdbJd`. The boundary loader converts them once, with `kilometersToMeters` and `jdTdbToSecondsSinceJ2000` (`src/v2/boundary/slice9-nea-catalog.ts:396-404`). [Certain]

#### Where the catalog's epochs come from

The catalog's elements come either from the **JPL Small-Body Database (SBDB)**, which publishes each body's elements at its own epoch, or from re-deriving them out of a Horizons state at a common date (**re-anchoring**). As a result almost every body shares one epoch (fixture, a check script written for this guide): [Certain]

| `anchorSource` | Bodies | Epoch |
|---|---|---|
| `horizons-reanchor` | 41,539 (99.12%) | JD 2461161.5 = 2026-05-01 00:00 TDB |
| `sbdb` | 309 | each body's own SBDB epoch |
| `stale-unanchored` | 58 | old SBDB epochs, not re-anchored |

There are 141 distinct epochs in all. The common epoch is (2461161.5 − 2451545.0) × 86,400 = 830,865,600 s after J2000.

Re-anchoring matters. In Slice 7, Bennu's error after 90 days fell from 6,739,444 km to 4,236 km once its elements were re-derived at the window start instead of its stale SBDB epoch of 2011-01-01 (`src/v2/core/invariants/INV-012.md`; the 2011 date is in `src/v2/core/asteroid-catalog.md:61`). Re-anchoring resets the drift clock. It does not stop drift (Section B3.17). [Certain]

**Misconception:** "M is a direction in space." No. It is elapsed time, written as an angle. Nor is the epoch a discovery date; it is the validity time of the elements.

### B3.10 Three anomalies: M, E and ν

An **anomaly** here is an old astronomer's word for an angle that locates a body on its orbit. There are three, and the code needs to move between them.

Picture in words. Draw the ellipse. Around it draw a circle of radius a, centred on the ellipse's centre (not on the Sun). This is the **auxiliary circle**. From the body, draw a line straight across, perpendicular to the long axis, until it meets the circle.

- **True anomaly ν** (nu): the real angle, measured at the Sun, from perihelion to the body. This is where the body actually is.
- **Eccentric anomaly E**: the angle, measured at the ellipse's centre, from perihelion to the point on the circle. It is a helper angle that makes the algebra solvable.
- **Mean anomaly M**: the clock angle from Section B3.9.

```
r      = a (1 − e cos E)                          distance from the Sun
x_pf   = a (cos E − e),   y_pf = a √(1 − e²) sin E     position in the orbit's own plane, Sun at origin
tan(ν/2) = √((1 + e)/(1 − e)) · tan(E/2)          E to ν
M      = E − e sin E                              E to M (Kepler's equation, 3.11)
```

On a circle (e = 0) all three are equal. They separate as e grows.

Tiny illustration, e = 0.5 and M = 60° (recomputed for this guide): E = 88.64°, ν = 118.82° and r = 0.988 a. A sixth of the period has passed (60/360), but the body has swept a third of the way round (118.8/360). It is still near perihelion, where it moves fast.

**Misconception:** "ν is close to M." Only for small e. In that illustration they differ by 59°.

### B3.11 Kepler's equation and Newton's method

#### The problem

The clock gives M. The position needs E. They are linked by **Kepler's equation**:

```
M = E − e sin E          (elliptic Kepler's equation; angles in radians)
```

Going from E to M is easy: plug in. Going from M to E is not. There is no formula that isolates E using ordinary algebra and functions. It has to be solved numerically. [Certain]

#### Newton's method

**Newton's method** finds where a function crosses zero. Make a guess. Draw the tangent line to the curve at the guess. Slide down that tangent to where it crosses zero. That crossing is the next guess. Repeat.

Analogy: you stand on a foggy hillside and want to reach sea level. You cannot see it, but you can feel the slope under your feet. Pretend the hill keeps that exact slope, and walk to where that straight slope would meet sea level. Then feel the slope again and repeat. Each guess lands closer, because near the answer a curve looks almost straight.

```
f(E)  = E − e sin E − M          we want f(E) = 0
f'(E) = 1 − e cos E              the slope; always > 0 when e < 1
E_next = E − f(E) / f'(E)        one Newton step
```

Near the answer, Newton's method converges **quadratically**: the number of correct digits roughly doubles with each step. Chapter B8 covers the method in general.

#### What the repo does

`solveKeplerEquation` (`src/v2/core/propagators/keplerian.ts:106-133`): [Certain]

1. Rejects non-finite input and any e outside [0, 1) (lines 111-115).
2. Wraps M into (−π, π] with `normalizeSignedAngleRadians` (line 119).
3. Starts at E₀ = M if e < 0.8. Otherwise it starts at +π (M ≥ 0) or −π (M < 0) (line 120).
4. Takes Newton steps. It stops when the size of a step is at most 1e-12 rad (lines 117 and 127). Note that this is a test on the step, not on the leftover error f(E).
5. Gives up after 50 iterations and throws an `Error` rather than return a wrong answer (lines 118 and 132).

A 1e-12 rad step, multiplied by a ≈ 1.5e11 m, is about 15 cm along the orbit. The answer is usually far better than that, because the step before stopping is already tiny: the leftover error ends near 1e-15 rad, about 0.15 mm (Worked Example 3.2).

Tiny illustration (recomputed for this guide; same algorithm): e = 0.9, M = 10°, starting from π. The steps are 1.6, 0.5, 0.19, 0.033, 9.2e-4, 7.1e-7 and 4.2e-13 rad, reaching E = 48.80° in seven iterations. In the last three the exponent roughly doubles each time. That is quadratic convergence.

#### Worked Example 3.2: why the starting guess matters at high eccentricity

Inputs:
- the published solver (`dist/src/v2/core/propagators/keplerian.js` in `aster-mission-mcp@0.1.0`, whose logic is identical to `keplerian.ts:106-133` on main; the package was published 2026-07-10 and can lag main);
- the audit's sweep grid, copied from `tools/slice18-research/audit-1-core.mjs:120-123`: 12 eccentricities from 0 to 0.9999, each with 1,440 values of M starting at −π;
- 2017 UR52's catalog elements: a = 353.30419 AU, e = 0.9964262210658009, i = 108.223°, M₀ = 0.00811235 rad (`nea-catalog-slice9.json`).

Step 1: run all 12 × 1,440 = 17,280 solves. Result: 0 throws.

Step 2: measure the leftover error |E − e sin E − M|. The worst raw value is 6.283185307179586, which is exactly 2π. It occurs at e = 0, M = −π. The solver wraps −π to +π (step 2 above) and correctly returns E = π. The harness then compares π with the unwrapped −π: π − (−π) = 2π. This is an artefact of the test harness, not of the solver.

Step 3: wrap the leftover error into (−π, π] before taking its size. The worst value becomes 1.776e-15 rad (at e = 0.1, M = 2.80998). That confirms the audit's prose figure of 1.8e-15 rad (`MATH_LAYER_AUDIT.md` §2.7).

Step 4: count the most Newton iterations needed over 1,439 values of M, with the repo's start against a naive start E₀ = M:

| e | Repo start: max iterations (failures) | Naive E₀ = M: failures to converge in 50 |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 5 (0) | 0 (max 5) |
| 0.9 | 9 (0) | 0 (max 8) |
| 0.99 | 11 (0) | 38 |
| 0.999 | 14 (0) | 22 |
| 0.9999 | 17 (0) | 51 |

Step 5: a real body. 2017 UR52 is retrograde (i = 108°), with q = a(1 − e) = 353.30419 × 0.0035738 = 1.26263 AU and a period of a^1.5 ≈ 6,641 years. At its M₀ the repo's start converges in 10 iterations to E = 0.346604740736 rad (the naive start, here, in 11).

Result: Newton's method reaches machine precision, about 1.8e-15 rad. The switch to ±π for e ≥ 0.8 is what keeps it inside the 50-iteration cap near e = 1. A naive start fails dozens of times per 1,439 values at e ≥ 0.99. (Verified for this guide, and re-run independently for the fact-check, which also confirmed that a re-implementation of the repo's start returns the identical E in all 17,280 cases.) [Certain]

One honesty note. The committed artifact `tools/slice18-research/audit-1-results.json` still records `worstResidualRad = 6.283185307179586`, and `audit-1-core.mjs:129` still computes the unwrapped value. `MATH_LAYER_AUDIT.md` §2.7 says this was "self-caught and corrected", and `STATUS.md:305` reports the corrected 1.8e-15, but the correction never reached the committed file. The claim is true; the artifact does not show it. [Certain]

### B3.12 Two-body propagation as implemented in `keplerian.ts`

#### The idea

**Propagation** answers the question "where is it at time t?" **Two-body propagation**, also called **Keplerian propagation**, assumes only the Sun pulls on the asteroid. Then the ellipse never changes. Only the clock hand M moves. The method does not step through time; it jumps straight to any date. [Certain]

Analogy: draw the ellipse on a sheet of paper and mark the body on it (perifocal step). Turn the sheet to aim its nose (ω), tilt it (i) and swing it round (Ω). Then describe the result from a different wall of the room (the obliquity rotation).

#### The steps in `propagateKeplerianStateVectors` (`keplerian.ts:195-259`)

```
0. validate: all seven numbers finite, a > 0, 0 ≤ e < 1           (else RangeError)
1. Δt = t − t₀                                                  [s, TDB]
2. n = √(μ/a³);   M = M₀ + n·Δt                                 (μ defaults to GM_SUN_M3_S2, line 203)
3. E = solveKeplerEquation(M, e)
4. perifocal position:  x = a(cos E − e),   y = a√(1−e²) sin E,   z = 0
   perifocal velocity:  vx = −a n sin E / (1 − e cos E),   vy = a n √(1−e²) cos E / (1 − e cos E)
5. rotate perifocal → J2000 ecliptic by Ω, i, ω  (rotatePerifocalToEcliptic, lines 64-85)
     q11 = cosΩ cosω − sinΩ sinω cos i     q12 = −cosΩ sinω − sinΩ cosω cos i
     q21 = sinΩ cosω + cosΩ sinω cos i     q22 = −sinΩ sinω + cosΩ cosω cos i
     q31 = sinω sin i                      q32 = cosω sin i
6. rotate ecliptic → equatorial about x by the obliquity 84381.448″ = 23.4392911°
     (rotateEclipticToEquatorial, lines 87-95; constant in src/v2/core/units.ts:4-5)
7. return position [m] and velocity [m/s]; metadata r, n, M, E
```

The **perifocal frame** is the orbit's own frame: x points at perihelion, y lies in the orbit plane 90° ahead, z points along the angular momentum. Two details are worth noticing. [Certain]

- **ν is never computed** on this path. Position and velocity come straight from E. True anomaly appears only in the render-side `sampleOrbitEllipse`.
- **The obliquity rotation is applied exactly once.** Elements go in as ecliptic; states come out in heliocentric ICRF, wrapped with the frame id `FRAME_HELIO_J2000_ICRF` by `propagateKeplerianState` (`keplerian.ts:261-274`). The audit checked this by propagating an i = 0 orbit: its pole must come out as the ecliptic pole rotated by the obliquity, (0, −sin ε, cos ε). It matched to 1.2e-16, which would catch a missing, doubled or reversed rotation (`MATH_LAYER_AUDIT.md` §2.1).

#### Worked Example 3.3: 433 Eros from six numbers to a state, and against JPL truth

Inputs:
- Eros's elements, `tests/fixtures/v2/nea-catalog-slice9.json` → `asteroids['asteroid-433'].elements`: a = 218,150,587.690 km (1.458246609 AU), e = 0.22288929294611265, i = 10.828550°, Ω = 304.26801°, ω = 178.91644°, M₀ = 40.683253° = 0.7100567134 rad, epoch JD 2461161.5.
- μ = 1.32712440018e20 m³/s² (`keplerian.ts:9`).
- 1 AU = 149,597,870,700 m (`src/v2/app/solar-system/runtime.ts:74`).
- JPL truth: `tests/fixtures/v2/nea-drift-truth-2026-2046.json` → `targets['433'].records`.

**Step 1: mean motion.**

```
a  = 2.1815058769e11 m
a³ = 1.0381716e34 m³
μ/a³ = 1.32712440018e20 / 1.0381716e34 = 1.2783285e-14 s⁻²
n  = √(1.2783285e-14) = 1.1306319e-7 rad/s
```

**Step 2: period.** P = 2π/n = 5.5572333e7 s = 643.19830 d = 1.7609810 Julian years. Kepler's third law in the simple form gives a^1.5 = 1.458246609^1.5 = 1.7609477. The two differ only because the simple form assumes a "year" of 365.25 d, whereas a 1 AU orbit with this GM takes 365.256898 d (Worked Example 3.1). Indeed 1.7609477 × 365.256898 = 643.198 d. [Certain]

**Step 3: perihelion, aphelion, class.**

```
q = a(1 − e) = 1.458246609 × 0.777110707 = 1.1332191 AU
Q = a(1 + e) = 1.458246609 × 1.222889293 = 1.7832742 AU
```

a > 1 AU and 1.017 < q < 1.3 AU, so Eros is an Amor (Section B3.14). The catalog says `AMO`.

**Step 4: advance the clock 100 days.**

```
Δt   = 100 × 86,400 = 8.64e6 s
n·Δt = 1.1306319e-7 × 8.64e6 = 0.9768659649 rad
M    = 0.7100567134 + 0.9768659649 = 1.686922678 rad  (96.65355°)
```

This is already inside (−π, π], so wrapping changes nothing.

**Step 5: solve Kepler's equation.** e < 0.8, so E₀ = M.

| Iteration | f(E) | f'(E) = 1 − e cos E | Step f/f' | New E (rad) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | −2.213881e-1 | 1.0258251854 | −2.158147e-1 | 1.902737337970552 |
| 2 | 5.092539e-3 | 1.0726348720 | 4.747691e-3 | 1.897989647173226 |
| 3 | 2.376189e-6 | 1.0716336137 | 2.217352e-6 | 1.897987429820991 |
| 4 | 5.19e-13 | 1.0716331457 | 4.84e-13 | 1.897987429820507 |

The fourth step is below 1e-12, so the loop stops: E = 1.897987429820507 rad = 108.7466693°. The published `solveKeplerEquation` returns the identical number.

In row 4, f is the difference of numbers near 1.9 that agree to 12 digits, so its digits beyond the third are rounding noise. The repo wraps M through a modulo (step 2 of Section B3.11), which changes M's last bit: with the wrap f = 5.187e-13, without it 5.189e-13 (recomputed for this guide). The final E is identical either way.

**Step 6: true anomaly.**

```
√((1+e)/(1−e)) = √(1.222889 / 0.777111) = 1.2544464
tan(E/2)       = tan(0.948994) = 1.3954127
tan(ν/2)       = 1.2544464 × 1.3954127 = 1.7504705
ν              = 2 × atan(1.7504705) = 120.5235068°
```

The body is 120.5° past perihelion, while the clock says only 96.7°.

**Step 7: distance from the Sun.**

```
cos E = −0.3213844
r = a(1 − e cos E) = 2.1815058769e11 × (1 + 0.2228893 × 0.3213844)
  = 2.1815058769e11 × 1.0716331 = 2.337774e11 m = 1.562705401 AU
```

This equals |r| returned by `propagateKeplerianStateVectors`.

**Step 8: speed from vis-viva.**

```
2/r − 1/a = 8.5551469e-12 − 4.5839895e-12 = 3.9711574e-12 m⁻¹
v² = μ × 3.9711574e-12 = 5.2702199e8 m²/s²
v  = 22,956.959 m/s = 22.95695948 km/s
```

This equals |v| from the propagator. At perihelion the same formula gives 30.9407 km/s, and at aphelion 19.6619 km/s.

**Step 9: energy is conserved.** At the epoch, v²/2 − μ/r = −304,176,214.750 J/kg, which equals −μ/(2a). Propagating to JD 2468342.5 and recomputing changes it by 2e-16 to 4e-16 relative, depending only on how the squares are summed (recomputed for this guide). That is rounding noise: one or two units in the last place of a double.

**Step 10: compare with JPL truth.** Propagate the catalog elements to the truth sample dates and subtract the JPL positions:

| Truth record | Date (JD) | Distance from truth |
|---|---|---|
| 17 | 2461160.5 (one day before the epoch) | 0.289 km |
| 278 | 2462987.5 (+5 years) | 69,523 km |
| 1043 (last) | 2468342.5 = 2045-12-28 | 269,854 km |

Result. Eros is an Amor with a 643.2-day period. Newton's method converged in four steps. The two-body state is 0.3 km from JPL one day off its epoch and about 270,000 km off after 19.7 years. All three distances match the committed Slice 18 artifact to every digit shown: `tools/slice18-research/nea-drift-results.json` → `bodies['433'].B_catalogElements` holds 0.289278365010197, 69523.28488048373 and 269854.18252183317. (Reproduced by a check script written for this guide.) [Certain]

The arithmetic is perfect and the answer still drifts. That gap is the subject of 3.17.

#### What the propagator is held to

Several invariants touch this code. They measure different things, so do not mix them up.

| Invariant | What it bounds | Value | Where enforced |
|---|---|---|---|
| INV-005 | relative drift of energy and angular momentum | < 1e-9 per orbit (two-body) | documented in `src/v2/core/invariants/README.md`; no runtime check exists (see Limits) |
| INV-012 (Slice 7) | position error vs Horizons, 90 days, 18-body sample | 100,000 km (`ASTEROID_KEPLERIAN_ERROR_BAR_M`, `asteroids.ts:11`) | `assertKeplerianError` (`assertions.ts:188-217`), test time |
| INV-013 (Slice 8) | the same, stratified by eccentricity band, 200 bodies | A 35,613 / B 52,970 / C 37,688 / D 43,758 km | `tests/v2-slice8-cutover.test.mjs` only (bars in `INV013_BARS_KM`, `tools/slice8-ingestion/slice8-cutover-sample.mjs:4`) |

Sources: `src/v2/core/invariants/INV-012.md`, `INV-013.md`, `INVARIANTS.md` amendment 2026-10-26 R1. [Certain]

The measured conservation over 2026–2046 for five real bodies is energy ≤ 7.1e-14 and angular momentum ≤ 3.7e-15 relative (`tools/slice18-research/audit-1-results.json`, `checks.conservation`). The worst case is 2017 UR52, at e = 0.996. Against INV-005's 1e-9: 1e-9 / 7.1e-14 ≈ 1.4e4 for energy and 1e-9 / 3.7e-15 ≈ 2.7e5 for angular momentum, so about four and five orders of magnitude inside. [Certain] (The audit took the largest deviation over 501 dates, while INV-005 is stated per orbit. For this propagator the two framings agree: every date is computed afresh from the same elements, so rounding error does not pile up from one orbit to the next. [Likely])

INV-012's worst sampled body was the main-belt asteroid Hygiea at 35,313 km (2.83× margin), in a Slice 7 sample that predates the NEO-only catalog (`INV-012.md`). The key point: **INV-012 and INV-013 are 90-day visualization bars.** They say nothing about a 20-year screening span. [Certain]

Speed matters for this choice. The Slice 7 design estimated about 1,008 bodies × 60 frames per second ≈ 60,000 propagations per second (`src/v2/core/asteroid-catalog.md`, "Runtime Scale"). A method that jumps straight to any date costs the same small amount for every date; one that must step through time costs more the further it goes. The estimate is [Certain]; that speed drove the choice is [Likely], since the document records the rate, not the reasoning.

### B3.13 Period and synodic period

The **period** P is the time for one lap (Section B3.4). The **synodic period** S is how often Earth and the asteroid return to the same relative arrangement. It sets how often launch windows repeat (Chapter B6). [Certain]

```
1/S = |1/P_Earth − 1/P_asteroid|
```

Using P_Earth = 1 year and P = a^1.5 (recomputed for this guide):

| Semi-major axis | Synodic period |
|---|---|
| 1.05 AU | 14.2 years |
| 1.02 AU | 34.2 years |
| 1.01 AU | 67.5 years |
| 2000 SG344 (a = 0.9775 AU) | 28.7 years |
| 433 Eros (a = 1.458 AU) | 2.3 years |

The more Earth-like the orbit, the rarer the realignments. When one comes, the asteroid lingers near Earth for a long time. That is good for missions (low launch energy) and bad for prediction (Earth's pull acts for a long time). Section B3.16 returns to this.

### B3.14 Near-Earth objects and the four classes

#### Definitions

A **near-Earth object (NEO)** is an asteroid or comet whose perihelion distance is q < 1.3 AU. A **near-Earth asteroid (NEA)** is an NEO that is an asteroid. The four standard NEA classes are **Atira** (also called IEO), **Aten**, **Apollo** and **Amor**. They use Earth's perihelion (about 0.983 AU) and aphelion (about 1.017 AU) as boundaries. (Definitions and thresholds from memory, verify against JPL/CNEOS.) [Likely]

```
Atira (IEO):  a < 1.0 AU   and  Q < 0.983 AU          entirely inside Earth's orbit
Aten  (ATE):  a < 1.0 AU   and  Q > 0.983 AU          mostly inside, reaches out across it
Apollo (APO): a > 1.0 AU   and  q < 1.017 AU          mostly outside, dips in across it
Amor  (AMO):  a > 1.0 AU   and  1.017 < q < 1.3 AU    outside, comes close but never crosses
```

Picture Earth's orbit as a ring drawn on the table. An Atira's loop sits wholly inside the ring. An Aten's loop is mostly inside and pokes out. An Apollo's loop is mostly outside and dips in. An Amor's loop comes up close to the ring from outside without touching it.

**Misconceptions.** "NEO means it will hit Earth": no, it describes orbit shape only. "Atens stay inside Earth's orbit": no, that is Atiras. "A class is permanent": no, elements change (Section B3.17), so a body near a boundary can cross it.

#### Aster's catalog

The catalog is 41,906 bodies from the SBDB query API with `sb-group=neo`. Every record has `neo = true` (`nea-catalog-slice9.json`, `selectionSource` and `catalog` blocks). [Certain]

| Code | Class | Bodies |
|---|---|---|
| APO | Apollo | 23,757 |
| AMO | Amor | 14,516 |
| ATE | Aten | 3,387 |
| IEO | Atira ("Interior Earth Object") | 38 |
| JFC | Jupiter-family comet | 166 |
| HTC | Halley-type comet | 36 |
| ETC | Encke-type comet | 6 |

Aster does **not** compute these classes. The label is copied from SBDB at ingestion. No threshold code exists in `src/v2`. The `AsteroidOrbitClass` type lists `'MBA' | 'APO' | 'ATE' | 'AMO'` plus any string, so `IEO` arrives as a plain string (`asteroids.ts:6`). [Certain]

#### Worked Example 3.4: classifying six bodies, and spotting a bad record

Inputs: each body's a and e from `nea-catalog-slice9.json` (2026-05-01 elements for all six); the thresholds above (from memory, verify).

Method: q = a(1 − e) and Q = a(1 + e), then apply the four rules.

| Body | a (AU) | e | q = a(1−e) | Q = a(1+e) | Rule result | Catalog label |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 163693 | 0.740960 | 0.322166 | 0.502248 | 0.979671 | a < 1, Q < 0.983 → Atira | IEO |
| 99942 Apophis | 0.922365 | 0.191143 | 0.746061 | 1.098669 | a < 1, Q > 0.983 → Aten | ATE |
| 101955 Bennu | 1.125981 | 0.203698 | 0.896621 | 1.355341 | a > 1, q < 1.017 → Apollo | APO |
| 433 Eros | 1.458247 | 0.222889 | 1.133219 | 1.783274 | a > 1, 1.017 < q < 1.3 → Amor | AMO |
| 2000 SG344 | 0.977457 | 0.066924 | 0.912042 | 1.042873 | a < 1, Q > 0.983 → Aten | ATE |
| 2008 TC3 | 3.096109 | 0.059711 | 2.911237 | 3.280981 | q > 1.3 → **not an NEO** | APO |

One check by hand, for Apophis: q = 0.922365 × (1 − 0.191143) = 0.922365 × 0.808857 = 0.746061 AU, and Q = 0.922365 × 1.191143 = 1.098669 AU.

Result: the first five agree with SBDB. The sixth does not. A body with q = 2.91 AU cannot be an Apollo, or an NEO at all; that orbit sits in the main asteroid belt. (Recomputed for this guide.) [Certain]

Applied to the whole catalog, the rules disagree with 91 SBDB labels (recomputed for this guide):

| SBDB label → rule result | Bodies |
|---|---|
| APO → AMO | 46 |
| AMO → APO | 28 |
| AMO → not an NEO (q just at or above 1.3) | 9 |
| APO → ATE | 6 |
| APO → not an NEO | 2 (2008 TC3 and 2014 AA) |

Most of these are boundary cases. Of the 89 mismatches outside the last row, 79 sit within 0.02 AU of the boundary they cross and 86 within 0.05 AU. The largest is 2024 FQ5, labelled APO but with a = 0.85 AU (recomputed for this guide). SBDB computed its labels from SBDB's own elements at another epoch, and a body near q = 1.017 AU can fall either side after re-anchoring [Likely]. The last row is different, and the Limits section comes back to it.

### B3.15 MOID and potentially hazardous asteroids

The **minimum orbit intersection distance (MOID)** is the smallest distance between two orbits, treated as fixed curves in space, ignoring where the bodies actually are on them. Analogy: the closest gap between two roads. Whether two cars meet depends on timing as well.

A **potentially hazardous asteroid (PHA)** has an Earth MOID of at most 0.05 AU and an absolute magnitude H of at most 22.0, roughly 140 m across or larger (from memory, verify; H is explained in Chapter B4). [Likely]

In Aster: [Certain]

- V2 computes **no MOID**. A search of `src/v2` for "moid" finds nothing. The only MOID code is the legacy V1 `src/physics/orbital/moid.ts`, a sampling approximation over 120 × 120 points. Its header says "Accuracy ~0.01 AU (see DEVLOG.md)". `DEVLOG.md` ("Phase 2 — Burn Simulator", item 1) adds that sampled MOID is "systematically overestimated (never underestimated)" and says "Do not use for hazard assessment." Nothing in `src/v2` imports from `src/physics`.
- The `pha` flag is copied from SBDB. 2,545 of 41,906 bodies carry `pha = true` (6.07%): APO 2,178, ATE 199, AMO 160, IEO 8 (recomputed for this guide).
- 33 of those PHAs have H > 22 (H ranges 14.08 to 22.57). That conflicts with the definition above. Aster does not recompute the flag, so this is a question about SBDB's definition, not an Aster calculation. [Speculative]

**Misconceptions.**
- "PHA means it will hit." No. It means "close orbit and large enough to matter".
- "MOID is the closest approach." No. Actual approaches are never closer than the MOID and are usually much farther.

### B3.16 Earth-like and co-orbital asteroids

Some asteroids have orbits that are near-twins of Earth's. They are the cheapest to reach, because a spacecraft leaving Earth barely has to change its velocity to match theirs (low launch energy C3, Chapter B6). They are also the hardest to predict, because they spend long stretches near Earth (Section B3.13), where Earth keeps nudging them. Relative to Earth such bodies can trace tadpole, horseshoe or quasi-satellite paths (from memory, verify). [Likely]

Aster's definition of **co-orbital** (`src/v2/SLICE_10_FOUNDING.md:59` and OQ-7; `tools/build/precompute-lambert-screen.mjs:92-94` and `:226-229`):

```
e ≤ 0.1   AND   i ≤ 5°   AND   |a − 1 AU| ≤ 0.05 AU (7,479,893.535 km)
```

A chapter script recomputed this test on all 41,906 fixture records. Exactly 130 pass (APO 84, ATE 43, AMO 3). The shipped cache `docs/lambert-screen-cache.json` flags the same 130, with an empty symmetric difference. Its `catalogFixtureSha256` (f88028d2…) equals the fixture's own hash, so both came from the same catalog (recomputed for this guide). [Certain]

Example, 2000 SG344: e = 0.066924 ≤ 0.1; i = 0.1131° ≤ 5°; |0.977457 − 1| = 0.022543 AU ≤ 0.05 AU. Co-orbital.

How wrong does two-body screening go for these bodies? Slice 10 compared Aster's departure excess speed with NASA's NHATS service (its study of human-accessible near-Earth asteroid targets; expansion from memory, verify) for 36 co-orbitals (`tools/slice10-research/coorbital-drift-detail.json`, `summary`). NHATS also builds patched-conic transfers (`SLICE_10_FOUNDING.md:296`), so the comparison isolates the asteroid's position. The founding document attributes the gap to "Keplerian propagation of osculating elements diverging from integrated N-body orbits" (`:59`). That NHATS places the asteroid on JPL's integrated orbit is implied there, not stated. [Likely] The measured numbers are: [Certain]

- median deviation 0.0487 km/s;
- maximum 1.125 km/s, for 2000 SG344;
- 6 above 0.1 km/s, 1 above 1.0 km/s, 0 above 2.0 km/s.

The tolerance is 0.1 km/s for stable targets and 2.0 km/s for co-orbitals (`SLICE_10_FOUNDING.md:292`), "calibrated to the measured maxima with margin, NOT derived from a theoretical error model". The flag is a caution only: co-orbitals are tinted cyan (`src/v2/render/asteroid-screening-color.ts:55-56`) and explained in `src/v2/app/catalog-list/honesty-disclosure.ts`.

A wording point: that disclosure says both screens "use patched-conic propagation" (`honesty-disclosure.ts:71`). Strictly, the propagation is two-body Keplerian; "patched conic" names a way of building a transfer. `SLICE_10_FOUNDING.md:59` says it more clearly: Keplerian propagation "diverging from integrated N-body orbits". [Likely]

### B3.17 Why two-body propagation drifts

#### Osculating elements

At any instant, a real asteroid has one position and one velocity. There is exactly one ellipse around the Sun alone that matches both. These are the **osculating elements** ("osculating" means "kissing": the ellipse touches the real path at that instant). [Certain]

The planets keep bending the real path. So the kissing ellipse changes slowly over time. Two-body propagation freezes it at the epoch and follows the frozen ellipse forever. The gap between the frozen ellipse and the real path is the **drift**, or **model error**. [Certain]

Three things cause it:

1. **Steady tugs** from the planets, above all Jupiter.
2. **Sudden kicks** at close approaches to Earth, Venus or Mars.
3. **Small non-gravitational forces**: comet outgassing, and for small asteroids the **Yarkovsky effect**, a tiny thrust from uneven re-radiation of absorbed sunlight as heat (from memory, verify).

#### Small errors in a grow along the track

Suppose a is off by a small amount Δa. Kepler's third law then makes n slightly wrong, and the body slowly runs ahead of or behind where it should be:

```
Δn / n = −(3/2) · Δa / a
along-track error  Δs(t) ≈ (3/2) · n · Δa · t          grows linearly with time
```

#### Worked Example 3.5: why Aster draws no uncertainty ribbon (DEC-18-2)

Mission View, an animated arc with an uncertainty ribbon, was the plan before Slice 18. Measurement removed the ribbon (`SLICE_18_FOUNDING.md` §2, DEC-18-2). Here is why.

Inputs:
- Eros's 1-sigma uncertainty in a: `sigmaA` = 1.5722e-10 AU (`nea-catalog-slice9.json`).
- n = 1.13063e-7 rad/s (Worked Example 3.3).
- Horizon t = 10 Julian years.
- Measured drift for Eros at +10 years: 238,268 km (`nea-drift-results.json`, `bodies['433'].A_primaryAnchor.fwd_10y_km`).

Steps:

```
Δa = 1.5722e-10 AU × 149,597,870.7 km/AU = 0.0235198 km
t  = 10 × 365.25 × 86,400 = 3.15576e8 s
Δs = 1.5 × 1.13063e-7 × 0.0235198 × 3.15576e8 = 1.2588 km
ratio = 238,268 km / 1.26 km ≈ 1.9e5
```

Result: the element uncertainty moves Eros about 1.26 km in ten years. The founding document records 1.259 km and marks it `[UNVERIFIED-IN-REPO]` because it is derived, not produced by a committed artifact; a check script written for this guide reproduces it. The model drift is about 190,000 times larger. Across the 17 measured NEAs the founding document puts the gap at 5.6 to 8.4 orders of magnitude. A ribbon built from element sigmas would have been "a false precision claim wearing an honesty costume" (`SLICE_18_FOUNDING.md` §2). [Certain]

The lesson: **drift is model error, not orbit uncertainty.** JPL may know an orbit very well and Aster's two-body copy can still be wrong by millions of kilometres.

#### The close-approach kick

When an asteroid passes close to a planet, the planet bends its path. Slice 18's instrument estimates the velocity change δv from the closest-approach distance and speed (`SLICE_18_FOUNDING.md` DEC-18-6; `tools/slice18-research/dv-scope.mjs`):

```
tan(θ/2) = μ_p / (d · v²)         δv = 2 · v · sin(θ/2)
added drift ≈ δv × (time remaining to JD 2468342.5)

μ_p  planet's GM [km³/s²]        d  closest-approach distance [km] (CAD "dist")
v    relative speed [km/s] (CAD "v_rel")      θ  bend angle in this formula
```

**CAD** is JPL's close-approach data service. A modest kick early in a 19-year window carries the whole way, which is why the instrument multiplies by time remaining instead of looking at distance alone. Using distance alone gave a scope estimate of 6.3% of the catalog; δv × time remaining gave 24.3% (DEC-18-6). [Certain]

The planet GMs live only in that research script, for example Earth 398,600.435507 km³/s² (`dv-scope.mjs:31-32`). The shipped delta-v code uses 398,600.4418 (`src/v2/porkchop/delta-v.ts:3`), a harmless 1.6e-8 difference. [Certain]

#### What Slice 18 measured

Front B compared Aster's two-body states with JPL's integrated orbits from 2026-01-01 to 2045-12-28, weekly, for 20 bodies: 17 NEAs and 3 comets (`tests/fixtures/v2/nea-drift-truth-2026-2046.json`: 1,044 records each from the NASA/JPL Horizons API; the audit names DE441 as the ephemeris behind it, `MATH_LAYER_AUDIT.md` L2). [Certain]

**Planets set a floor.** As two-body orbits over 2026–2040, Mercury drifted at most 71,364 km, Venus 173,767 km and Mars 120,455 km (`tools/slice18-research/TWO_BODY_DRIFT_MEASUREMENT.md` §3). Earth's geocentre drifted 17.2 million km, an artefact of its monthly wobble around the Earth–Moon centre of mass. Its derived ellipse has a period 0.432 d short, and 0.432 d × 29.7847 km/s × 86,400 s/d = 1.11 million km per orbit, close to the measured 1.154 million km at +1 year (§6; recomputed for this guide). [Certain]

**Real NEAs drift far more.** Maximum drift over the window for the 17 NEAs (`tools/slice18-research/nea-drift-results.json`; `NEA_DRIFT_MEASUREMENT.md` §2, §5): [Certain]

| Band | Bodies |
|---|---|
| below 10⁵ km | none |
| 10⁵ to 10⁶ km | 2: 2010 KD (462,290 km), 433 Eros (620,080 km) |
| 10⁶ km or more | 15 |
| of which above 10⁸ km | 3: 2012 UE34 (164.4 M), 2026 BX8 (269.4 M), 99942 Apophis (325.8 M km) |

The three comets were kept separate: 12P 10.3 M, 3D 17.2 M and 323P 396.5 M km. The 17 were chosen to be extreme and varied, so these are not catalog rates (`NEA_DRIFT_MEASUREMENT.md`, limitation 1).

**Close approaches dominate.** Apophis passes 38,011 km from Earth's centre on 2029-04-13 at 7.42 km/s. Its drift grew at about 44,000 km per year before and about 226 million km per year after, roughly 5,200 times faster. Passes at 5 million km or more made no measurable difference (`NEA_DRIFT_MEASUREMENT.md` §4). [Certain]

**Elapsed time does not predict drift. Encounter crossings do** (§6). Even for planets, the same elapsed time gave up to 12× different drift depending on the anchor epoch (Venus at 5 years: 47,680 km against 4,057 km; `TWO_BODY_DRIFT_MEASUREMENT.md` §5). [Certain]

**Orbit quality does not predict drift.** The **Spearman rank correlation** (a score from −1 to +1 for how well one ranking predicts another) between JPL's condition code U (Chapter B4) and 5-year drift was 0.03 (§7). U describes how well JPL knows the orbit, which this measurement cannot test, because JPL's solution was the truth (limitation 3). [Certain]

**Drift saturates.** Apophis's maximum separation is 3.258e8 km, about 2.18 AU, which is roughly the size of the orbits themselves (recomputed for this guide). Once the predicted body is on the wrong side of the Sun, the error cannot keep growing. [Certain]

**Misconception:** "Error grows smoothly with time." No. It steps up at encounters.

### B3.18 From drift to fidelity tiers: Slice 18's L0, L1 and L2

#### The idea

Slice 18 asked one question: how wrong is Aster's own arithmetic? Its answer is that the evidence cannot certify any body as trustworthy throughout the screening window, so there is no such tier and every body gets an honest label instead (`SLICE_18_FOUNDING.md` §1, DEC-18-3, DEC-18-10). The **disclosure unit is a date**, not a distance: a body's limit is stated as the date its screening stops being supported. [Certain]

Each body gets one **fidelity tier** in `tools/slice18-research/tier-sizing-per-body.json`, served as `docs/tier-sizing-per-body.json` (byte-identical, 10,880,177 bytes) and loaded by `loadTierAssignments` in `src/v2/boundary/tier-assignments.ts`, which refuses any file without exactly 41,906 records (`:64-66`). [Certain]

| Tier | Meaning | Members | Count |
|---|---|---|---|
| **L0** | does not exist, or cannot be propagated | 9 bodies whose Horizons ephemeris ends at a verified Earth impact; 3D/Biela, a comet that broke up in the 1840s–50s (historical record, not ephemeris-verified); 2015 D1, the hyperbolic comet | 11 |
| **L1** | supported only until a dated close approach | bodies with at least one **material** encounter: its δv, carried to the window's end, adds ≥ 10⁶ km of drift | 10,150 |
| **L2** | Aster cannot bound the error, or has not measured it | 206 comets + 482 Jupiter-crossers (Q ≥ 4.95 AU) = 688 "structurally blind" (the catalog's other 2 comets, 3D/Biela and 2015 D1, are in L0); 31,050 unmeasured; 7 measured but unbounded | 31,745 |

Total 41,906. These figures hold **at the 10⁶ km threshold, against the 2026-09-11 CAD snapshot** (`SLICE_18_FOUNDING.md` §9 C-4 and C-6; recounted from the per-body records for this chapter). The same document holds two older tables (DEC-18-10 and C-1); they are superseded and should not be quoted. [Certain]

Why "structurally blind"? CAD returns non-Earth approaches only out to 0.15 AU from Venus, 0.10 from Mercury, 0.25 from Mars and 0.28 from Jupiter, and nothing for Saturn in the window (DEC-18-9). A body that reaches Jupiter's distance can have a large Jupiter encounter that CAD will never report. [Certain]

Why 10⁶ km? Because a separate measurement found that at 10⁶ km of drift the best transfer window moved in 3 of 15 tested cells, and at 10⁵ km in none. The provenance sentence is shown wherever the threshold appears (`THRESHOLD_PROVENANCE` in `src/v2/porkchop/tier-disclosure.ts`). Against the 17 measured bodies the instrument agrees on 7, under-predicts 10 and over-predicts 0 (DEC-18-6). [Certain] It never called a body material when measurement said it was not. So L1 is built to be a lower bound on the number of materially degraded bodies; DEC-18-6 calls this one-sidedness "a design property, not a statistic", and any change that allows over-prediction counts as a regression. That it holds beyond those 17 is [Likely].

L1 is fragile. At 0.5 × 10⁶ km it would hold 13,172 bodies; at 2 × 10⁶ km, 6,469. 1,063 bodies sit within ±10% of the cutoff. Four bodies changed tier between two CAD snapshots because JPL revised its close-approach rows (C-4, C-5). [Certain]

#### What the user sees

`tier-disclosure.ts` holds the sentences, filled only from the artifact. Examples (verbatim):

- L1: "Screening for this object is supported through [DATE]. A close approach to [BODY] on that date changes its orbit by an estimated [δv] m/s. Arrivals after it are computed from an orbit the encounter invalidates."
- L2 unmeasured: "… Two-body propagation over the screening window drifted 0.46 to 330 million km across the 17 asteroids that were measured. This object was not among them."

The "0.46 to 330 million km" is 462,290 km and 325,803,827 km rounded (`nea-drift-results.json`). [Certain]

On the porkchop page, `src/v2/porkchop/support-boundary.ts` splits cells for L1 bodies. A cell is unsupported if and only if its arrival is at or after the encounter:

```
arrival JD = depJD + tofDays                      arrivalJd()
unsupported ⇔ arrival JD ≥ encounter.jd           isArrivalAfterEncounter()
boundary TOF at a departure = encounter.jd − depJD   boundaryTofDaysAtDeparture()
```

Unsupported cells get a dark wash and a dashed boundary curve. They are never hidden, because "not assessed" and "no opportunity" are different claims (DEC-18-7). [Certain]

The boundary is the **earliest** material encounter, ratified 2026-09-21. For 2,352 of the 10,150 L1 bodies an earlier material pass comes before the largest one (§8 addendum). [Certain]

#### Worked Example 3.6: Apophis across 2029, and its L1 boundary

Inputs:
- Apophis's elements: a = 0.92236498 AU, e = 0.19114293, epoch JD 2461161.5 (`nea-catalog-slice9.json`).
- JPL truth: `nea-drift-truth-2026-2046.json` → `targets['99942']`.
- CAD rows for 99942 at Earth: `tools/slice18-research/cad-wide/cad-all-0.3.json` (fetched 2026-09-11T04:27:49Z).
- μ_Earth = 398,600.435507 km³/s²; window end JD 2468342.5 (`dv-scope.mjs`).
- Tier record: `tier-sizing-per-body.json` → `records['99942']`.
- Cache row: `docs/lambert-screen-cache.json` → `asteroid-99942`.

**Step 1: class and period.** Q = 0.922365 × 1.191143 = 1.098669 AU > 0.983 and a < 1, so Aten (Worked Example 3.4). P = 323.56 d.

**Step 2: drift of the catalog's own elements against truth** (recomputed for this guide):

| Truth date (JD) | Meaning | Distance from truth |
|---|---|---|
| 2462238.5 | last weekly sample before the flyby | 33,583 km |
| 2462245.5 | first sample after, 7 days later | 1,200,935 km (×35.8) |
| 2462609.5 | one year later | 226,796,788 km |
| 2467110.5 | maximum | 3.258e8 km (2.18 AU) |

**Step 3: the instrument on three Earth passes** (recomputed for this guide):

(a) 2027-12-29: d = 43,923,794 km, v = 14.685521 km/s.

```
tan(θ/2) = 398,600.4355 / (43,923,794 × 14.685521²) = 4.2078e-5
δv = 2 × 14.685521 × sin(atan(4.2078e-5)) = 1.2359e-3 km/s = 1.24 m/s
time remaining = 5.6794e8 s;   added = 1.2359e-3 × 5.6794e8 = 701,912 km   < 10⁶: not material
```

(b) 2028-09-12 04:11: d = 38,381,694 km (0.2566 AU), v = 7.894359 km/s.

```
tan(θ/2) = 398,600.4355 / (38,381,694 × 7.894359²) = 1.6664e-4
δv = 2 × 7.894359 × sin(atan(1.6664e-4))
   ≈ 2 × 7.894359 × 1.6664e-4             (small angle: sin(atan x) ≈ x)
   = 2.6310e-3 km/s = 2.63 m/s
time remaining = (2468342.5 − 2462026.6746) × 86,400 = 5.4569e8 s
added = 2.6310e-3 × 5.4569e8 = 1,435,723 km   ≥ 10⁶: MATERIAL
```

(c) 2029-04-13 21:46: d = 38,011.5 km, v = 7.422539 km/s.

```
tan(θ/2) = 398,600.4355 / (38,011.5 × 7.422539²) = 0.19033;   θ = 21.553°
δv = 2 × 7.422539 × sin(10.777°) = 2.7757 km/s = 2,776 m/s
time remaining = 5.2722e8 s;   added = 2.7757 × 5.2722e8 ≈ 1.463e9 km
```

These match the artifact: `encounter.dvKmS` = 0.002631035645 and `maxDriftEncounter.dvKmS` = 2.775704395. Pass (b) is the earliest material one, so it is the L1 boundary: "supported through 2028-09-12 … 2.6 m/s", with the 2029 flyby named as the largest perturbation (2,776 m/s). (The founding document's §8 calls pass (b) "~0.27 AU"; the CAD row gives 0.2566 AU.)

A cross-check with the textbook hyperbolic-flyby formula uses the speed far from Earth, v∞, instead of the speed at closest approach (from memory, verify):

```
e_hyp = 1 + d · v∞² / μ = 1 + 38,011.5 × 5.841356² / 398,600.4355 = 4.2539     (d = closest approach)
bend  = 2 · asin(1 / e_hyp) = 27.19°
δv    = 2 · v∞ / e_hyp = 2 × 5.841356 / 4.2539 = 2.746 km/s
```

That is about 1% below the instrument's 2,776 m/s. So the δv is sound, but the instrument's θ (21.6°) is not the true bend angle; the measurement document quotes "~28°" (§4).

The CAD file itself confirms that `v_rel` is the speed at closest approach. Energy conservation on the flyby hyperbola gives v∞ = √(v_rel² − 2μ/d) = √(7.422539² − 2 × 398,600.4355 / 38,011.5) = 5.84136 km/s, which equals the same row's `v_inf` to every digit shown. The same holds for passes (a) and (b) (recomputed for this guide). [Certain]

**Step 4: test two porkchop cells** against `encounter.jd` = 2462026.674559:
- departure JD 2461900.5, TOF (time of flight) 120 d → arrival 2462020.5 < boundary → supported. The boundary TOF at this departure is 2462026.6746 − 2461900.5 = 126.17 d.
- departure JD 2461950.5, TOF 200 d → arrival 2462150.5 ≥ boundary → unsupported.

**Step 5: the catalog's headline number.** The cache's best Apophis window departs 2028-09-14 (JD 2462028.5) with TOF 212 d and C3 = 2.06e-4 km²/s². Arrival = 2462028.5 + 212 = 2462240.5, which is 2029-04-14 00:00 TDB. The flyby's closest approach is JD 2462240.407 (2029-04-13 21:46), so arrival is 0.093 d, about 2.2 hours, later. All five of the cache's best windows depart between 2028-05-18 and 2028-09-14 and arrive between 2029-04-11 and 2029-04-16, so all five arrive after the 2028-09-12 boundary.

Its stored arrival excess speed is 5.8447 km/s (`bestWindows[0].vInfArr`). That is within 0.004 km/s of CAD's `v_inf` for the flyby, 5.8414 km/s: the "rendezvous" is really Apophis passing Earth at its flyby speed.

Result. Apophis's two-body screen is good to tens of thousands of kilometres until 2029 and wrong by hundreds of millions afterwards. Its L1 boundary is 2028-09-12, about 213 days before the drift actually breaks (§8 follow-up), so the boundary is conservative. Every one of its best cached windows lies in the unsupported region. The near-zero C3 is the close-approach degeneracy (C3 < 0.1 km²/s², `src/v2/core/constants/near-zero-c3.ts`; Chapter B6): the "transfer" amounts to staying in Earth's orbit while Apophis flies by. The numbers are [Certain]; that reading is [Likely].

One disagreement to note. `NEA_DRIFT_MEASUREMENT.md` §10 explains why Apophis's best window did not move under measured drift by saying it "departs 2028, arriving *before* the 2029 encounter". The cached best window checked here arrives about 2 hours *after* closest approach. §10 used the live 200 × 100 grid, whose best cell was not re-checked here. A likely reason the C3 barely moved anyway: two hours after a 2.78 km/s kick, the position has shifted only about 2.78 km/s × 8,000 s ≈ 22,000 km. [Likely]

#### The MCP server does not carry the tiers

The published `aster-mission-mcp@0.1.0` (2026-07-10, older than Slice 18) returns, for `get_body` on 99942, only `inv014Tier: "visualization-tier"` and no L0/L1/L2 field (live reply to this chapter's call, repeated for the fact-check). That Slice 9 label is a 90-day validity tier whose encounter check covered only 2026-05-01 to 2026-07-30. `mcp/src` on main has no tier code either; the unmerged branch `origin/claude/ux-run-2026-10-22` records the gap as problem P1. Agents get fewer caveats than browser users. [Certain]

### Limits and known problems

#### The model itself

- **Sun-only gravity.** Measured maximum drift over 2026–2045 is 0.46 to 330 million km across 17 NEAs, and the evidence supports no "trustworthy throughout" tier (DEC-18-10). For an L1 body, every cell arriving after its first material encounter is computed on an orbit that encounter invalidates. A porkchop can look crisp and still describe the wrong place. [Certain]
- **Ellipses only.** The propagator refuses e ≥ 1, so 2015 D1 cannot be screened (Section B3.5). [Certain]
- **The δv instrument under-predicts.** It missed 10 of 17 measured bodies: five Jupiter-crossers whose Jupiter passes CAD cannot see (CAD stops at 0.10–0.28 AU from the other planets and has no Saturn rows), and five that, in OQ-18-2's words, "drift secularly with no encounter at all, and are unexplained" ("secular" means steady and cumulative rather than sudden; OQ-18-2 is deferred). So L1 is built to be a lower bound, and its date is model-derived, not measured: for Apophis about 213 days early (`dv-scope-results.json`; `SLICE_18_FOUNDING.md` §8 follow-up 2, DEC-18-9). [Certain]
- **Tier counts move.** L1 depends on the CAD snapshot date and the 10⁶ km threshold, so every L1 figure must name both (C-4, C-5). [Certain]
- **Short horizon, small sample, JPL as truth.** Both instruments stop at 2045-12-28; the field `at_2046_01_01_km` and a comment in `dv-scope.mjs:31` misname that date (C-7). Only 20 bodies were measured, chosen to be extreme, so the 31,050 "unmeasured" L2 bodies have no error figure. And only model error was measured, never solution error (`NEA_DRIFT_MEASUREMENT.md`, limitations 1 and 3). [Certain]
- **Co-orbitals.** The most accessible targets are the least well modelled, up to 1.125 km/s off NHATS (Section B3.16). N-body propagation is deferred. [Certain]
- **The visualization tier can mislead.** INV-014's "visualization-tier" is a 90-day label whose encounter check covered only 2026-05-01 to 2026-07-30, Earth and Venus, at 0.05 AU. Apophis and Bennu carry it, yet both are L1 (Bennu's boundary is a 2037-02-11 Earth pass, `tier-sizing-per-body.json`). The MCP package shows only this tier (Section B3.18). [Certain]

#### Data problems

- **Two likely impactors are not in L0.** 2008 TC3 and 2014 AA are labelled APO by SBDB, but their re-anchored elements are main-belt orbits (a = 3.096 and 3.205 AU, q = 2.911 and 2.640 AU). Their SBDB records carry 1-day data arcs (`dataArcDays: 1`; 575 and 8 observations) and H = 30.72 and 30.95, inside the nine verified impactors' H range of 29.12–33.58 (DEC-18-5). Both are tiered L2 "unmeasured", with transfer windows computed; the published MCP gives 2008 TC3 a minimum C3 of 47.53 km²/s² (this chapter's `get_body` call). From memory (verify), both hit Earth soon after discovery: 2008 TC3 over Sudan on 2008-10-07, 2014 AA over the Atlantic around 2014-01-02. If so, DEC-18-5's claim that "nine is the complete NEA-class set" of non-existent objects is wrong. That claim rests on a mechanism: a destroyed object "cannot supply" a 2026 Horizons state, so it stays `stale-unanchored`. DEC-18-5 marks it [Likely] because "the ingestion path has not been traced" (OQ-18-3, deferred). [Likely]
  - The repo already saw one symptom. The Slice 9 derived-fields diagnostic records that 2008 TC3 was "stored `D` but re-anchored `e = 0.0597`" and read it as a stale band label, not as a bad orbit (`tools/slice9-diagnostic/SLICE_9_A2B_DERIVED_FIELDS_DIAGNOSTIC.md:64`). [Certain]
  - Outside evidence, not repo evidence: Horizons API queries made while fact-checking this chapter (2026-11-06). With the re-anchor script's command form `';<designation>'` (`reanchor-stale-subset.mjs:64-77`), Horizons returned a 2026-05-01 state, not an error, for 2008 TC3, for 2014 AA, and even for 2018 LA. Yet in September the Slice 18 truth fetch, with the same command form, got "No ephemeris for target "(2018 LA)" after A.D. 2018-JUN-02" (`nea-drift-truth-2026-2046.json`, `findings.S_nonExistentCatalogBodies`). Today's 2008 TC3 state is 0.98 AU from the Sun; the fixture's anchor is 2.93 AU. So whether Horizons returns a post-impact state depends on when or how it is asked. The mechanism DEC-18-5 relies on is not safe. [Likely]
- **No MOID; classes and PHA flags are not recomputed.** 91 SBDB labels disagree with the class rules applied to the shipped elements, and 33 PHAs have H > 22 (Sections B3.14, B3.15). [Certain]
- **Destroyed objects still rank.** L0 bodies still compete in minimum-C3 lists, so a "best" target can be a mission to nothing (OQ-18-1, deferred). [Certain]
- **Null turns into zero at ingestion.** `assertFiniteNumber` in `src/v2/boundary/slice9-nea-catalog.ts:166-172` applies `Number(value)`, and `Number(null)` is 0, which is finite. 2015 D1's `maRad` is null in the fixture, the only null element in the catalog. It is refused anyway (for its negative a), but "expected finite" promises more than the check does. [Certain] The null itself probably comes from `cartesianToElements`: for e > 1 its factor √((1 − e)/(1 + e)) (`state-to-elements.mjs:129`) is the square root of a negative number, which is NaN in JavaScript, and `JSON.stringify` writes NaN as null. [Likely]

#### Documentation and code gaps

- **INV-005 has no runtime check.** The README names `assertPropagationDrift`, but a search of `src/v2`, `tests` and `mcp/src` finds it only in that README. Conservation is checked by `tests/v2-core-keplerian.test.mjs:141` (a 90-day test on Vesta) and by the Slice 18 audit. The repo's own sanity audit already flagged this as A2-F06 (`tools/audit/sanity-69472a3/ASTER_AUDIT_REPORT.md:918`). [Certain]
- **Provenance slips with no numerical effect:** the GM_SUN comment (OQ-18-5, Section B3.2), two Earth GMs (Section B3.17), and the 2π still in the committed Kepler audit artifact (Worked Example 3.2). [Certain]
- **Documents disagree about epochs.** `STATUS.md` (DEC-18-3 text) and `TWO_BODY_DRIFT_MEASUREMENT.md` §5 say each asteroid carries "one fixed SBDB element epoch". The fixture is 99.1% Horizons-re-anchored to one common epoch (Section B3.9). `NEA_DRIFT_MEASUREMENT.md` limitation 6 agrees with the fixture. [Certain]
- **A misprint.** `TWO_BODY_DRIFT_MEASUREMENT.md` §6 prints Earth's derived a as "0.998198 AU". 149,477,893.6 / 149,597,870.7 = 0.999198 AU, which gives the stated period of 364.818 d; 0.998198 would give 364.270 d (recomputed for this guide). [Certain]
- **A sentence that over-reaches.** The "measured-but-unbounded" sentence ("…it exceeds the bound Aster can certify") is shown for Eros (620,080 km) and 2010 KD (462,290 km), whose drift stayed below the 10⁶ km threshold, and DEC-18-10 says no certified bound exists. [Likely]
- **An unbound literal.** The "0.46 to 330 million km" in `tier-disclosure.ts:31-32` and `:214-216` is typed by hand. No committed test ties it to `nea-drift-results.json` (a search of `tests/` finds no "0.46" or "330"). INV-026 says trust-surface numbers must render from a committed artifact, "never from literals in component code"; the 2026-10-26 clarification X4 accepts a constant only "when a committed test binds it to the provenance artifact" (`INVARIANTS.md`). The values do agree today. [Likely]
- **Stale status lines.** `STATUS.md` still calls the Slice 18 close-out branch "NOT yet merged", but `propagation-guard.ts` and `support-boundary.ts` are on main at `cec19e7`. [Certain]
- **Reproducibility and cost.** The Slice 18 scripts hardcode Windows paths (`tier-sizing.mjs:27`; `dv-scope.mjs:21-28`), and the 10.9 MB tier artifact loads eagerly on the solar-system (catalog), porkchop and compare pages (`STATUS.md:340`, open item). [Certain]
- **This chapter's own limits.** The clone is shallow, so older commit hashes could not be checked. The repo's tests and build were not run (AGENTS.md). MCP numbers come from version 0.1.0, which lags main.

### Key takeaways

- Only the product μ = GM matters. Aster uses μ_Sun = 1.32712440018e20 m³/s² from one constant in `keplerian.ts`; its comment's "IAU 2015" label is wrong but the value is fine.
- Six elements (a, e, i, Ω, ω, M₀) plus an epoch fix an orbit. a and e give size and shape; i, Ω, ω place it; M₀ and the epoch say where the body is and when.
- Kepler's equation M = E − e sin E has no algebraic solution. Aster solves it with Newton's method, a 1e-12 rad step tolerance and a ±π start for e ≥ 0.8, to about 1.8e-15 rad.
- Two-body propagation jumps straight to any date and conserves energy to better than 1e-13 (worst 7.1e-14 over 2026–2046). It is fast and arithmetically exact, but physically wrong as soon as planets matter.
- NEOs have q < 1.3 AU. Atiras, Atens, Apollos and Amors are defined by a, q and Q. Aster copies these labels and the PHA flag from SBDB and computes no MOID.
- The maximum two-body drift measured for 17 real NEAs over 2026–2045 is 0.46 to 330 million km. It is driven by close approaches, not by elapsed time and not by orbit quality.
- Slice 18 turned that into tiers: L0 11, L1 10,150, L2 31,745 (at 10⁶ km, 2026-09-11 CAD snapshot). L1 bodies carry a dated support boundary on the porkchop.
- Two likely impactors (2008 TC3, 2014 AA) appear to have slipped past L0, and the MCP server shows none of the tiers.
