## Chapter B7: Leaving Earth: launch geometry, launch vehicles and mission cost

**Main idea:** A porkchop cell becomes a mission only when three more questions have answers (can a rocket from this launch site leave in the right direction, how much mass can a real rocket throw to this departure energy, and how much of that mass survives the spacecraft's own burns), and Aster answers each one only as far as its sources allow and refuses where they stop.

Chapter B6 produced a grid of departure energies (C3). This chapter pins one cell and asks what flying it would take. It starts with a rocket on a spinning Earth and ends with the porkchop page's "Mission cost" card, every line of which you will recompute by hand.

Evidence base: the repository at commit `cec19e7`, read-only. Small check scripts written for this guide recompute values from repository inputs; they are working files, not part of the repository. Live numbers come from the published MCP package `aster-mission-mcp@0.1.0` (published 2026-07-10, so it can lag `main`). A few grid cells were recomputed by calling that package's own grid function directly (scripts written for this guide); those results carry the same lag caveat. One source is an unmerged branch. It is labelled where used.

---

### B7.1 Toolkit refresher

Three tools from school mathematics carry this chapter.

- **Angles.** 180° = π radians. The function arcsin (inverse sine) returns angles only from −90° to +90°. That is exactly the range of a declination (north/south angle), which is why arcsin appears in the DLA formula.
- **Vectors.** A velocity has three components (vx, vy, vz) and a magnitude |v| = √(vx² + vy² + vz²). The angle a vector makes above a flat plane is arcsin(component perpendicular to the plane ÷ magnitude).
- **Exponentials and logarithms.** e ≈ 2.718. ln is the natural logarithm, the inverse of e^x. The function e^(−x) falls fast: e^(−1) ≈ 0.368 and e^(−2) ≈ 0.135. The rocket equation lives here.

One word appears on every page of this chapter. **Δv** ("delta-v") is a change in velocity that an engine must supply. Mission designers add up Δv the way a traveller adds up fares: it is the currency of spaceflight.

| Quantity | Unit used in Aster | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| Excess speed, v∞ | km/s | Lambert output, DLA |
| C3 (speed squared) | km²/s² | launch-vehicle curves |
| Spacecraft Δv | m/s (cost card) or km/s (Δv stack) | budgets |
| Mass | kg | payload, delivered mass |
| Specific impulse | s | rocket equation |

Watch the switch: the cost card works in m/s, the Δv stack in km/s (`src/v2/app/porkchop/main.ts`, for example lines 879 and 983). [Certain]

---

### B7.2 Earth's spin gives a free eastward push

A rocket on the pad is not at rest. Earth turns once per **sidereal day** (one rotation relative to the stars), so the pad moves east with the ground. The speed depends on the **latitude** φ, the angle of the site north or south of the equator.

```
v_rot = (2π · R_E / T_sid) · cos φ
  R_E   = Earth equatorial radius = 6378.137 km   (the repo's 6578.137 km parking radius minus 200 km)
  T_sid = sidereal day ≈ 86,164.09 s           (from memory, verify)
  φ     = launch-site latitude (deg)
  v_rot = eastward ground speed (km/s)
```

Computed for this guide:

| Site | Latitude | v_rot |
|---|---|---|
| Equator | 0° | 0.465 km/s |
| Cape Canaveral | 28.5° | 0.409 km/s |
| Vandenberg | 34.7° | 0.382 km/s |

A low orbit needs about 7.8 km/s sideways. Launching east banks about 0.4 km/s of it for free. Launching west must first cancel that speed. Think of jumping off a moving walkway: jump with the motion and you land faster; jump against it and you land slower.

Two misconceptions to drop now:

- "The spin lifts you." No. It supplies part of the horizontal speed only.
- "Every launch gets the same bonus." No. The bonus scales with cos φ and depends on direction. A polar orbit has no eastward motion at all, so a polar launch cannot use the bonus and must even cancel it. A due-west launch ends 2 × v_rot worse off than a due-east one.

[Certain] Aster never computes v_rot: no Earth-rotation rate appears in `src/v2/` or `mcp/src/` (searched for this guide). [Likely] The effect is already inside the published vehicle curves of Section B7.13, which are Florida queries; elvperf does not say which launch direction each query assumed. The section is here because it explains why launch sites and directions matter at all.

---

### B7.3 Inclination, and why latitude sets a floor

An orbit lies in a flat plane through Earth's centre. **Inclination** *i* is the tilt of that plane against the equator.

| Inclination | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 0° | equatorial | orbit stays over the equator |
| 0°–90° | **prograde** | moves eastward, with Earth's spin |
| 90° | **polar** | passes over both poles |
| 90°–180° | **retrograde** | moves westward, against the spin |

At the moment of launch the rocket is in its orbital plane. That plane passes through Earth's centre and through the launch site. So the plane must reach at least as far north as the site. An orbit tilted only 10° never rises above 10°N, so a rocket at 28.5°N cannot be in it.

Analogy: a hula hoop passing through the centre of a ball. To touch a dot painted at latitude 30°, the hoop must be tilted at least 30°.

Spherical trigonometry turns this into a formula. The **launch azimuth** A is the compass heading of the rocket's flight, measured from north (90° = due east).

```
cos i = cos φ · sin A          (non-rotating Earth)
  i = orbit inclination (deg)
  φ = launch-site latitude (deg)
  A = launch azimuth from north (deg)

Minimum inclination: sin A = 1 (A = 90°, due east)  →  i_min = φ
```

[Certain, textbook; the repository uses the same relation as a cross-check in `src/v2/core/lambert/feasibility.ts`, Vandenberg comment.]

Two misconceptions:

- "You can't reach orbits steeper than your latitude." Backwards. Steeper is easy: turn the azimuth away from east. Shallower is the impossible direction without an extra manoeuvre.
- "The latitude is the inclination." Only for a due-east launch.

---

### B7.4 Range-safety corridors and Aster's two launch sites

The formula in Section B7.3 says what geometry allows. **Range safety** says what the authorities allow. Each launch site may fly only a set of azimuths, its **azimuth corridor**, chosen so spent stages and failed rockets fall into the ocean, not onto towns. The usable inclinations are what geometry and the corridor both allow.

Analogy: a runway could point many ways, but noise rules forbid flying over the city.

Aster stores each site as a `LaunchSite` object in `src/v2/core/lambert/feasibility.ts` (lines 1–52). The two sites are Cape Canaveral in Florida and Vandenberg Space Force Base (SFB) in California:

| Field | Cape Canaveral | Vandenberg SFB | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `latitudeDeg` | 28.5 | 34.7 | metadata only |
| corridor (in comments) | Az 35–120° | Az 158–201° | source of the limits |
| `iMinDeg` | 28.5 | 70 | GREEN band edge |
| `iMaxDeg` | 57 | 104 | metadata only |
| `dlaCeilingDeg` | 57 | 90 | AMBER/RED band edge |

Sources, as cited in the file and in `src/v2/SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md` (OQ-12-2, AMD-12-1): the NASA Space Shuttle overview (1988), a US patent (4,368,578) and a Vandenberg site profile. [Certain]

Three ideas make the table readable.

**Why Vandenberg's minimum is 70°, not 34.7°.** A due-east launch from Vandenberg would fly over land, so it is prohibited. The corridor starts at Az 158°, which gives about 70°. The `iMinDeg` comment says so: "due-east is PROHIBITED (overflight), which is WHY iMinDeg (70) far exceeds latitudeDeg (34.7)". [Certain]

**Why the ceiling is `min(i, 180° − i)`.** An orbit at 104° is retrograde. It reaches a highest latitude of 180° − 104° = 76°, the same as a 76° prograde orbit. A tilt beyond 90° buys nothing in north–south reach. So the field the classifier uses is the **declination ceiling**, the largest coverage `min(i, 180° − i)` over every inclination the corridor allows. Vandenberg's corridor crosses Az 180° (due south, polar, i = 90°), and a polar orbit reaches every latitude. Its ceiling is therefore 90°. [Certain, `feasibility.ts` lines 10–20; AMD-12-1]

**Why latitude is "metadata only".** The classifier reads only `iMinDeg` and `dlaCeilingDeg`: "latitudeDeg and iMaxDeg are metadata and deliberately NOT classification inputs" (`feasibility.ts` line 68). At Cape the minimum inclination equals the latitude only because due east is allowed there, a "coincidence" that hid a bug (Section B7.8). [Certain]

#### Worked Example 7.1: from corridor edges to inclinations

Inputs: Cape latitude 28.5°, corridor 35–120°; Vandenberg latitude 34.7°, corridor 158–201° (`feasibility.ts`, lines 24–50). Formula from Section B7.3.

Step 1, the cosines of the latitudes: cos 28.5° = 0.87882 and cos 34.7° = 0.82214.

Step 2, each corridor edge:

| Site, azimuth | sin A | cos i = cos φ · sin A | i | coverage min(i, 180−i) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cape, 90° | 1.00000 | 0.87882 | 28.50° | 28.50° |
| Cape, 35° | 0.57358 | 0.50407 | 59.73° | 59.73° |
| Cape, 120° | 0.86603 | 0.76108 | 40.44° | 40.44° |
| Vandenberg, 158° | 0.37461 | 0.30798 | 72.06° | 72.06° |
| Vandenberg, 180° | 0.00000 | 0.00000 | 90.00° | 90.00° |
| Vandenberg, 201° | −0.35837 | −0.29463 | 107.14° | 72.86° |

Step 3, compare with the sourced limits: Cape 57°, Vandenberg 70° and 104°. The spherical values sit about 2–3° higher (59.73 vs 57, 72.06 vs 70, 107.14 vs 104). The southerly Cape edge (120°) has no sourced inclination in the repository. The founding doc names the cause: a "rotating-Earth azimuth correction, same ~2-3 deg class as Cape's 59.7→57" (AMD-12-1). [Certain that the doc says this]

Step 4, test that explanation with a toy model written for this guide (not repository code). The rocket flies ground heading A; adding the site's eastward spin must give the 200 km circular speed, 7.784 km/s. The inertial heading tilts toward east:

| Site, ground azimuth | Inertial azimuth | Inclination (toy model) | Sourced value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cape, 35° | 37.47° | 57.69° | 57° |
| Cape, 120° | 118.50° | 39.43° | none sourced (compare the MGS "~39°", Section B7.9) |
| Vandenberg, 158° | 155.39° | 69.98° | 70° |
| Vandenberg, 201° | 198.37° | 105.02° | 104° |

[Likely] The toy model lands within about 1° of all three sourced limits. That supports the doc's explanation: corridors are ground azimuths, and Earth's spin bends the inertial heading east. The model uses the surface spin speed and the 200 km orbital speed together, so it is a sketch, not a launch-azimuth calculation.

Result: Cape can reach about 28.5–57° and Vandenberg about 70–104°, including polar. The 107° row shows why raw `iMaxDeg` must never be compared with a declination: its coverage is only 72.86°.

---

### B7.5 From parking orbit to escape: the hyperbola and v∞

Recap from Chapters B5 and B6. Lambert's problem gives the Sun-centred velocity the spacecraft needs as it leaves Earth's neighbourhood. Subtract Earth's own velocity and you get the **departure excess velocity** v∞,dep: the velocity left over after the spacecraft has climbed out of Earth's gravity. Its squared magnitude is C3.

```
v∞,dep = v_spacecraft,helio − v_Earth,helio      (vector, km/s)
C3     = |v∞,dep|²                                (km²/s²)
```

Real departures happen in two steps. The rocket first reaches a low circular **parking orbit**, which in Aster is 200 km up (`LEO_PARKING_RADIUS_KM = 6578.137` in `src/v2/porkchop/delta-v.ts`). At the right moment it fires once more and enters an **escape hyperbola**, an open orbit that never comes back. Far from Earth the hyperbola straightens into a line called the **asymptote**. The spacecraft travels along it at v∞,dep.

Analogy: a sling. You whirl the stone in a circle (the parking orbit) and let go at the right instant, so it flies off along a chosen line (the asymptote).

The key fact for the rest of this chapter: the escape hyperbola lies in the same plane as the parking orbit. So the asymptote direction must lie in that plane too. [Certain, textbook]

The code computes the subtraction above literally. The browser grid subtracts Earth's velocity from each Lambert branch's departure velocity `v1` (`src/v2/porkchop/grid-compute.ts`, lines 113–115). The MCP cost tool does the same with `selectedBranch.v1` and the ephemeris Earth state (`mcp/src/tools/estimate-mission-cost.ts`, lines 160–166). [Certain]

---

### B7.6 DLA, the declination of the launch asymptote

Astronomers locate a direction in the sky with two angles. **Declination** is the angle north (+) or south (−) of the celestial equator, the sky's copy of Earth's equator. **Right ascension** is the angle around the equator. Treat v∞,dep as a direction and it has both.

The **declination of the launch asymptote (DLA)** is the declination of v∞,dep: how far north or south of Earth's equatorial plane the spacecraft must head.

```
DLA = arcsin( v∞,z / |v∞| )          (deg, −90 to +90)
  v∞,z = component along Earth's north pole (equatorial frame), km/s
  |v∞| = magnitude of v∞,dep, km/s
  Guard: |v∞| < 1e-3 km/s (1 m/s), or any non-finite input  →  DLA = null
```

A toy example. Take v∞ = (2.0, 1.0, 1.5) km/s. Then |v∞| = √(4 + 1 + 2.25) = √7.25 = 2.6926 km/s. The ratio 1.5 / 2.6926 = 0.55709, and arcsin(0.55709) = 33.85°. The same vector has C3 = 7.25 km²/s². (recomputed for this guide)

In the code this is `dlaDegFromVInf(vx, vy, vz, epsilonMag = 1e-3)` in `src/v2/core/lambert/dla.ts` (lines 19–30). It clamps the sine to [−1, 1] against rounding. The null guard exists because a vector of almost zero length has no meaningful direction: dividing by a tiny magnitude turns rounding noise into a random angle. [Certain]

**The frame matters.** The formula needs the z-axis to point along Earth's rotation pole: an **equatorial frame**. The pole of Earth's orbit (an **ecliptic frame**) is tilted about 23.4° from it. Aster's state vectors are already ICRF (the International Celestial Reference Frame, Chapter B2), which is equatorial-aligned, so `dlaDegFromVInf` applies no rotation. The project established this by measurement, not by trusting a label.

A probe sampled Earth's velocity from the fixture at four epochs in 2027 and found |vZ| = 11.715 km/s; in an ecliptic frame Earth's vZ would stay near 0 (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md` OQ-12-1; `dla.ts` lines 1–17; `INVARIANTS.md` INV-021). A later re-measurement over the whole fixture found a larger span maximum, 11.897 km/s, which strengthens the same verdict (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md` §8, 2026-09-22 entry). The pre-research summary told the team to rotate by the obliquity. Doing so "would introduce up to ~23.4 deg of silent error" (`dla.ts` comment). Chapter B2 tells that story in full. [Certain]

**Where DLA is computed.** In the browser, the grid is solved in a **web worker**, a background thread that keeps the page responsive (Chapter B9). The page's own code runs on the **main thread**. DLA is computed in the worker, once per converged Lambert branch, because only there do the vector components exist (`src/v2/porkchop/grid-compute.ts` line 121). It crosses to the main thread as one extra number, with non-finite values turned into `null` (`porkchop.worker.ts` lines 80–83). Verdicts are assigned on the main thread, so changing the site picker never re-runs Lambert. [Certain, `SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md` DEC-12-5; in `src/v2/porkchop/porkchop-view.ts` the site feeds only the readouts and the contour levels, lines 695 and 1066–1079]

**Disclosed approximations.** DLA uses the J2000 equator, not the equator of the launch date. **Precession**, the slow wobble of Earth's rotation axis, shifts the equator by at most about 0.2° over 2026–2040. The ICRF frame bias is about 17 milliarcseconds (a milliarcsecond is 1/3,600,000 of a degree), which is negligible. Both are disclosed, not corrected (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md` DEC-12-2). [Certain]

**Validation.** Against poliastro (a Python astrodynamics library) on the shipped multi-revolution path, the largest DLA difference over 921 cells was 5.61 × 10⁻¹³°, against a bar of 10⁻⁶° (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md` OQ-12-3 closure correction; `tools/slice12-research/data/dla-oracle-m1-vectors.json`). Chapter B8 covers oracles. [Certain]

Misconceptions:

- "DLA is the latitude of the launch pad." No. It is a property of the trajectory: where it wants to go.
- "If the magnitudes match an oracle, DLA is validated." No. Magnitudes are identical in every frame. Only components reveal the frame (INV-021).

---

### B7.7 Why the DLA must be reachable: i ≥ |DLA|

Put Sections B7.5 and B7.6 together. The asymptote lies in the parking-orbit plane. A plane tilted at inclination *i* contains directions with declinations from −*i* to +*i*, and no others. The launch time chooses where that plane's tilt points around the pole, because Earth turns under the sky during the day. So a direct departure with no extra steering needs:

```
i_parking ≥ |DLA|                     (prograde case; in general min(i, 180° − i) ≥ |DLA|)
Free:     |DLA| ≤ iMinDeg             the site's lowest orbit already contains the asymptote
Possible: |DLA| ≤ dlaCeilingDeg       some orbit the corridor allows contains it
```

[Certain, `feasibility.ts` lines 58–60; NASA Trajectory Browser guide cited in OQ-12-2]

It is an inequality. Low declinations are the easy side: every tilted plane contains them. From Cape, a DLA of 20° needs i ≥ 20°, and the 28.5° minimum orbit already contains it. It costs nothing. A DLA of 45° needs i ≥ 45°, so the rocket must fly a more northerly azimuth to raise the inclination.

Analogy: a hoop tilted 30° touches every latitude from 30°S to 30°N. A dot at 10°N is always on some such hoop. A dot at 50°N never is.

**The project's headline misconception.** Several documents wrote this inequality backwards, as "|DLA| ≥ latitude". The "Hard rule" bullet in `tools/slice12-research/DLA_RESEARCH_SUMMARY.md` §1 says exactly that, now under an ERRATUM box: "The inequality above is INVERTED ... LOW declinations are the free/optimal side". The same box says the wrong line "propagated three times before being contained". The founding doc calls the AMD-12-1 dispatch draft "the third resurrection" of the error, after the 2026-07-01 catch in the handoff and plan documents and audit finding M-E (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md` §8 and the AMD-12-1 execution note). [Certain]

Why is the inverted version tempting? The summary's §4 solves for the azimuth giving an inclination of exactly |DLA|: S = cos(DLA) / cos(φ), solvable only if |S| ≤ 1, which fails when |DLA| < φ. But nobody needs i to equal |DLA|; any i ≥ |DLA| works. The formula answers "does a plane with exactly this tilt pass over my site?", not "can I reach this declination?" That §4 still has no erratum. Do not quote it as method. [Certain that the text says this; the diagnosis is mine, Likely]

---

### B7.8 The band verdicts: GREEN, AMBER, RED and null

Aster turns the inequality into four screening verdicts. The function is short enough to read whole (`feasibility.ts`, lines 73–85):

```
classifyFeasibility(dlaDeg, site):
  null   if dlaDeg is null or not finite
  GREEN  if |DLA| ≤ iMinDeg                  direct from the site's lowest orbit
  AMBER  if iMinDeg < |DLA| ≤ dlaCeilingDeg   direct, but the inclination must be raised
  RED    otherwise (|DLA| > dlaCeilingDeg)    beyond the corridor: dogleg required
```

| Verdict | Cape Canaveral | Vandenberg SFB | Plot-readout badge |
|---|---|---|---|
| GREEN | \|DLA\| ≤ 28.5° | \|DLA\| ≤ 70° | "Direct" |
| AMBER | 28.5° < \|DLA\| ≤ 57° | 70° < \|DLA\| ≤ 90° | "Raised inclination" |
| RED | \|DLA\| > 57° | never (ceiling is 90°) | "Dogleg req." |
| null | no DLA | no DLA | no badge |

Badge labels: `FEASIBILITY_BADGE_LABEL`, `src/v2/porkchop/porkchop-view.ts` lines 135–139, used by the plot's readouts (line 417). The cost card's badge prints the class name itself, "GREEN" or "AMBER" (`main.ts` line 831). On the plot, the overlay draws green contour lines at ±`iMinDeg` and red lines at ±`dlaCeilingDeg` on the signed DLA field (`buildDlaContourLevels`, lines 249–262). [Certain]

The MCP tool adds an **angular margin** (`marginDeg`): how many degrees the cell sits inside (+) or outside (−) its active band edge. It uses `iMinDeg` for GREEN cells and `dlaCeilingDeg` otherwise: `marginDeg = band − |DLA|` (`mcp/src/tools/compute-shared.ts`, `siteVerdictRows`, lines 270–300). [Certain]

#### Worked Example 7.2: verdicts for three real cells

Inputs: site bands from `feasibility.ts`. DLA values from live `dla_feasibility` calls on `aster-mission-mcp@0.1.0` (lags `main`; outputs saved while writing this guide).

**Cell A: 99942 Apophis, departure 2028-06-01, 300 days, M = 0.** The tool returned DLA = 40.41329720789109° and |v∞,dep| = 1.5706 km/s.

- Cape: 40.413 > 28.5 and 40.413 ≤ 57, so AMBER. Margin = 57 − 40.413 = +16.587°. Tool: `marginDeg` 16.58670279210891.
- Vandenberg: 40.413 ≤ 70, so GREEN. Margin = 70 − 40.413 = +29.587°. Tool: 29.58670279210891.

**Cell B: 2020 FK3, departure 2026-12-26, 465 days, M = 1.** DLA = 82.20409518257004°.

- Cape: 82.204 > 57, so RED. Margin = 57 − 82.204 = −25.204°.
- Vandenberg: 70 < 82.204 ≤ 90, so AMBER. Margin = 90 − 82.204 = +7.796°.

**Cell C: the same FK3 date and flight time, M = 0.** DLA = 23.82°, with |v∞,dep| = 27.12 km/s. GREEN at both sites.

Result: the hand classification matches the tool on every row (recomputed for this guide). Cells B and C share a date and flight time but are different trajectories; M counts full revolutions around the Sun (Chapter B5). The M = 1 arc leaves slowly (C3 0.757) but steeply north. The M = 0 arc leaves at a moderate 23.8° but very fast. A verdict belongs to a branch, not a date pair. [Certain for the numbers. The classification step is the same at `main`: the package's compiled `dla.js` and `feasibility.js` match `dla.ts` and `feasibility.ts` line for line (compared for this guide). The Lambert inputs could still differ, because the package lags.]

**A bug this model fixed.** Before amendment AMD-12-1, GREEN meant |DLA| ≤ latitude, and Vandenberg was stored as `{latitudeDeg 34.7, iMaxDeg 100.4}`. Its RED band was unreachable, since |DLA| never exceeds 90°. A Phase E audit (finding H-1) found 1,502 of 17,477 Apophis cells misclassified with Vandenberg selected (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md` AMD-12-1). [Certain] By the band edges, the only cells whose class changed are those with 34.7° < |DLA| ≤ 70°: AMBER under the old model, GREEN under the new. A recount confirms it: on the page's 200 × 100 grid (2026–2040 departures), the M = 1 family has exactly 17,477 converged Apophis cells, and exactly 1,502 of them lie in that band (recomputed for this guide; 0.1.0 package grid function). [Certain that the recount gives these numbers; Likely that they are the audit's cells]

Misconceptions:

- "AMBER means infeasible." No. It is reachable directly, at a payload cost (Section B7.10).
- "GREEN at Vandenberg is as cheap as GREEN at Cape." No. A 70° orbit gets far less help from Earth's spin (Section B7.2). The verdict is geometry only.
- "null means GREEN." No. null is a separate state for cells with no DLA, reachable only at C3 below about 10⁻⁶ km²/s² (`SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md` §8, "Null-band (fourth) display state").

`feasibility.ts` lines 70–71 add a duty for every caller: "callers must surface a disclosure that this classifies screening feasibility only, not day-specific launch geometry" (INV-016d). The next section shows why. [Certain]

### B7.9 Day-of-launch geometry: the Mars Global Surveyor example

The band edges assume launch at the best instant of the day, on either side of the corridor. Real missions need a **launch period** (an opportunity every day for weeks), each day with a usable **launch window** of some minutes. Away from the best instant, the parking plane must be steeper than |DLA| to contain the asymptote, and some days only one side of the corridor works. [Likely, standard mission-design practice (from memory, verify)]

The repository's example, shown on the porkchop page under the site picker (`main.ts` line 730, the INV-016d disclosure): "MGS launched from Cape with DLA 36.5 deg (nominally AMBER) yet required a dogleg because its daily window forced the southerly azimuth side, where the effective ceiling is only ~39 deg." Its source is the MGS Mission Plan, §3 (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md` OQ-12-2). Mars Global Surveyor launched in November 1996 on a Delta II (from memory, verify). [Certain that the repo says this]

**A puzzle the repo leaves open.** 36.5° is below 39°. The southerly ceiling alone therefore does not force a dogleg.

[Speculative] Worked Example 7.1's toy model puts Cape's southerly edge (ground Az 120°) at 39.43°, close to "~39 deg". The repository does not say which corridor MGS's launch pad used, so this agreement may be a coincidence. Either way, the stated mechanism needs one more step. [Speculative] The likely step is the window: with a ceiling only about 3° above the DLA, the plane contains the asymptote only near one instant each day, and a daily window of useful length needs more inclination than that. The repository does not state this. Check the MGS Mission Plan before teaching a mechanism.

Analogy: a train that stops for one second. You can board it only if you stand in exactly the right place at exactly the right moment.

Lesson for reading Aster: a GREEN or AMBER verdict says the geometry is possible in principle. It does not promise a launch period.

### B7.10 Plane changes, doglegs and the two-regime model

What if |DLA| is beyond the ceiling? The spacecraft must still end up in a plane that contains the asymptote. Some engine must rotate the plane.

A **plane change** is a burn that turns the velocity vector sideways without changing its size. A **dogleg** is a plane change made during ascent: the rocket flies the allowed azimuth, then turns. For an impulsive turn through angle Δi at speed v:

```
Δv_plane = 2 · v · sin(Δi / 2)
  v  = orbital speed where the burn happens (km/s); 200 km LEO: 7.784 km/s
  Δi = plane rotation (deg)
```

[Certain, textbook; confirmed as item 10 in `tools/slice13-research/literature/3d-verification-record.md`]

At LEO speed this is brutal (recomputed for this guide):

| Δi | Δv_plane |
|---|---|
| 1° | 0.136 km/s |
| 10° | 1.357 km/s |
| 28.5° | 3.832 km/s |

For scale, escaping Earth from the same orbit costs 3.224 km/s (Section B7.11). A 28.5° turn at LEO costs more than leaving Earth. Analogy: turning a car at motorway speed needs enormous sideways grip; at walking pace it is trivial.

Aster prices plane changes with a **two-regime model** (`SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md` DEC-13-3 and OQ-13-2; `INVARIANTS.md` INV-016d amendment):

| Regime | What happens physically | What Aster charges | What the card says |
|---|---|---|---|
| GREEN | nothing to change | 0 | "none (GREEN)" |
| AMBER | the launch flies a steeper azimuth; geometry does the plane-matching | 0 m/s, disclosed | "0 m/s (modelled; launch-geometry, AMBER)" |
| RED | brute-force dogleg needed | no number at all | headline "Not feasible at screening fidelity"; dogleg line "exceeds site capability" |

Card strings from `main.ts` lines 800–906. [Certain]

**Why zero for AMBER.** The evidence anchor is a lunar-mission result from JPL's DESCANSO series: a 21-day launch period from a 28.5° parking orbit cost about 71.7 ± 29.7 m/s in total (`3d-verification-record.md` item 9). That is tiny next to a dogleg. Option (b), a flat payload derate of "3–5%", was rejected because it would be "a number without a source" (OQ-13-2). [Certain]

Two cautions belong here.

1. The founding doc and the INV-016d amendment describe AMBER plane-matching as "~1 m/s-per-degree". A later audit note says that figure is **unsourced**: the evidence gives only the 71.7 m/s total, for a lunar transfer, and says it is "not a liftable formula for interplanetary DLA pricing" (`INVARIANTS.md`, Slice 19.5 note, audit B5-F06). The shipped AMBER text now states only the qualitative claim. Do not teach the per-degree number. [Certain]
2. "Zero added Δv" is not "zero cost". A raised inclination gets less help from Earth's spin, so the rocket lifts less. The shuttle-era figure, used only as order-of-magnitude context, is about 500 lb (227 kg) of payload per degree between 28.5° and 57° (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md` OQ-12-2). Later copy admits it: "a payload penalty for this launch site and vehicle still applies" (`porkchop-view.ts` line 1500) and "Delivered mass excludes that payload penalty; Aster does not model it." (`main.ts` line 837). An AMBER delivered mass is knowingly optimistic by an unquantified amount. [Certain]

**Why a verdict, not a number, for RED.** The evidence anchor is NASA's IXPE launch. A second-stage dogleg removed the 28° inclination of a due-east Cape ascent, and with the booster-recovery reserve the capacity fell from more than 14 t to "a little more than a ton" (`3d-verification-record.md` item 8, citing Spaceflight Now, December 2021). That is a loss of about 1 − 1/14 = 93%. An early research pass had quoted 330 kg, which was IXPE's own mass (`SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md` §8). IXPE flew on a Falcon 9 (from memory, verify). [Certain for the repo figures]

DEC-13-3 adds that "a precise-looking 2v·sin(Δi/2) charge at LEO speed would misprice the AMBER regime by ~3 orders of magnitude". Check it. One degree at 7.784 km/s costs 136 m/s. Against the doc's own ~1 m/s per degree the ratio is 136 = 10^2.13: two orders of magnitude, not three, and the denominator is unsourced anyway. [Likely overstated; recomputed for this guide]

The pre-research summary's payload losses ("Δi=5° → ~0.68 km/s (~14% payload loss)", `DLA_RESEARCH_SUMMARY.md` §2) are uncited, not project numbers. Back-solved through Section B7.12, they imply an Isp near 450–460 s, which is typical of a hydrogen-oxygen upper stage (from memory, verify). [Likely; recomputed for this guide. For example, 1 − exp(−680 / v_e) = 0.14 gives v_e ≈ 4,510 m/s, so Isp ≈ 460 s.]

### B7.11 Injection Δv: from a 200 km parking orbit to a given C3

**Injection** is the burn that takes the vehicle from circular parking-orbit speed to the speed the escape hyperbola needs at its lowest point, its **perigee**. Two formulas from Chapter B3 do the work. Circular speed is √(μ/r). The vis-viva equation for a hyperbola gives the perigee speed as √(C3 + 2μ/r).

```
v_circ = √(μ / r)
v_p    = √(C3 + 2μ / r)
Δv_inj = v_p − v_circ
  μ = 398,600.4418 km³/s²   (Earth's GM)          EARTH_MU_KM3_PER_S2
  r = 6,578.137 km          (200 km altitude)     LEO_PARKING_RADIUS_KM
```

This is `injectionDvFromC3` in `src/v2/porkchop/delta-v.ts` (lines 18–26). [Certain]

Numbers. v_circ = √(398600.4418 / 6578.137) = 7.784262 km/s. 2μ/r = 121.1895 km²/s², so escape speed is √121.1895 = 11.008609 km/s.

| C3 (km²/s²) | v_p (km/s) | Δv_inj (km/s) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 (just escape) | 11.0086 | 3.224 |
| 10 | 11.4538 | 3.670 |
| 20 | 11.8823 | 4.098 |
| 30 | 12.2959 | 4.512 |
| 55 | 13.2736 | 5.489 |

(recomputed for this guide; the v_p column was re-rounded in fact-checking.) The Slice 11 gate values (3.616 km/s at C3 = 8.78 and 35.83 km/s at C3 = 1781.29) and its smoke value (4.599 km/s at C3 = 32.16) are reproduced exactly (`SLICE_11_FOUNDING.md` line 452). [Certain]

Look at the table. Raising C3 from 0 to 10 km²/s² costs only 0.445 km/s, yet √10 = 3.16 km/s of extra speed far away. Speed added deep in a gravity well is worth more energy than speed added far out, because kinetic energy grows with the square of speed. This is the **Oberth effect**. [Certain, textbook]

Misconception: "Δv_inj = √C3 − v_circ." No. You must add the escape energy 2μ/r under the square root first.

### B7.12 The rocket equation from scratch

Everything so far is about velocity. Mass is what costs money. The link is the rocket equation.

A rocket of mass m throws a small mass dm of exhaust backward at **exhaust velocity** v_e, measured relative to the rocket. Momentum is conserved, so the rocket gains speed dv:

```
m · dv = −v_e · dm               (dm is negative: the rocket loses mass)
dv     = −v_e · dm / m
Integrate from full mass m₀ to final mass m_f:
Δv  = v_e · ln(m₀ / m_f)
m_f = m₀ · exp(−Δv / v_e)
```

The ratio m₀/m_f is the **mass ratio**. Engine makers quote **specific impulse** Isp instead of v_e. Isp is v_e divided by **standard gravity** g₀, so it comes out in seconds:

```
v_e = g₀ · Isp
  g₀  = 9.80665 m/s² (exact by definition)        G0_MPS2
  Isp = 320 s (Aster's screening value)            SCREENING_ISP_S
  v_e = 9.80665 × 320 = 3,138.128 m/s
```

Constants: `src/v2/porkchop/launch-vehicles.ts` lines 56–63. The equation is named after Tsiolkovsky, who published it around 1903 (from memory, verify). [Certain]

What fraction survives each burn (recomputed for this guide):

| Spacecraft Δv | m_f / m₀ = exp(−Δv / 3138.128) |
|---|---|
| 1,000 m/s | 0.7271 |
| 2,000 m/s | 0.5287 |
| 3,000 m/s | 0.3844 |
| 4,000 m/s | 0.2795 |

Each extra 1,000 m/s multiplies what is left by the same factor, about 0.727. Δv costs mass exponentially. Analogy: compound interest in reverse; each step takes the same percentage, not the same amount.

**Why 320 s.** DEC-13-5 discloses it "as representative of the 300–350 s class" of **storable bipropellants**: two propellants, fuel and oxidiser, that stay liquid at room temperature, as most deep-space spacecraft carry (from memory, verify). The card's disclosure says "representative of the 300–350 s storable-bipropellant class" (`main.ts` line 928). Electric propulsion (SEP) is out of scope (`SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md` DEC-13-5, §7). The research record lists SEP at 2,000–3,000 s and marks both Isp classes "UNVERIFIED at table level" (`3d-verification-record.md` item 13). [Certain that the repo says this; the class values themselves are Likely]

Misconceptions:

- "Isp is in seconds, so it is a time." It is an exhaust speed divided by g₀.
- "Double the Δv, double the fuel." No. Doubling Δv squares the mass ratio.

### B7.13 Launch-vehicle performance curves: payload versus C3

A **launch vehicle** is the rocket that lifts the spacecraft off Earth. Its **performance curve** gives the largest spacecraft mass it can send to each departure energy C3. Asking for more energy leaves less mass, so the curve always falls. Analogy: a van's rated load drops as you ask it to climb steeper hills.

NASA's Launch Services Program (LSP) publishes these numbers through an interactive query tool, **elvperf**. Each anchor's comment reads "NASA LSP elvperf, as-of 2024-02-29, queried 2026-07-02" (for example `launch-vehicles.ts` line 77; the same facts sit in the header, lines 4–5, and the constants on lines 65–66). The queries were run by hand and the screenshots committed as `tools/slice13-research/elvperf/elvperf-c3-{00,10,20,30,40,55}.png`. Each published point is an **anchor**: one (C3, payload) pair carrying `basis: 'official'` and a source comment, as invariant INV-022 requires. [Certain]

Payload in kg at each C3 in km²/s² (`launch-vehicles.ts` lines 68–187; `SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md` DEC-13-1):

| Vehicle (site) | C3 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 55 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Falcon Heavy Expendable (KSC) | 15,010 | 12,345 | 10,115 | 8,225 | 6,640 | 4,670 |
| Falcon Heavy Recovery (KSC) | 6,690 | 5,130 | 3,845 | 2,740 | 1,805 | 650 |
| Vulcan VC2 (CCSFS) | 5,920 | 4,750 | 3,710 | 2,790 | 1,970 | 945 |
| Vulcan VC4 (CCSFS) | 8,550 | 7,140 | 5,880 | 4,780 | 3,800 | 2,555 |
| Vulcan VC6 (CCSFS) | 10,850 | 9,130 | 7,630 | 6,310 | 5,150 | 3,685 |
| New Glenn (CCSFS) | 7,180 | 4,930 | 2,365 | 120 | — | — |
| Falcon 9 FT ASDS (CCSFS) | 3,310 | 2,220 | — | — | — | — |
| Falcon 9 FT RTLS (CCSFS) | 1,770 | 875 | — | — | — | — |

Facts about the table [Certain]:

- **38 anchors**, all official: 5 × 6 + 4 + 2 × 2. The lock note said "40". A later annotation calls that "an arithmetic slip" (`SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md` §8). The golden test pins 38 (`tests/v2-golden/launch-vehicles.golden.test.mjs`, lines 85–89).
- **Short curves are honest.** Falcon 9 vanishes after C3 = 10 and New Glenn after 30. OQ-13-4 kept both Falcon 9 versions because short curves "show where the vehicle dies".
- **Vulcan VC0 is excluded.** It has one anchor (2,100 kg at C3 = 0), and one point cannot be interpolated.
- **The primary source corrected the research.** Falcon Heavy at C3 = 55 is 4,670 kg (Expendable) and 650 kg (Recovery), not the 4,690 and 660 of a research PDF.
- ASDS (drone-ship landing) and RTLS (return to launch site) say where the Falcon 9 booster lands; flying back costs more propellant, so less payload (from memory, verify).

Two misconceptions with real history:

- "A GTO payload number is a C3 = 20 number." No. A geostationary transfer orbit is still bound to Earth, C3 ≈ −16 km²/s². A research pass made exactly this mislabel with ULA's table. The slice recorded it as its "canonical inverted premise" (`SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md` §8).
- "The curve knows the DLA." No. elvperf's High Energy query takes no declination input (measured 2026-07-02). Every curve is a Florida query: KSC (Kennedy Space Center) or CCSFS (Cape Canaveral Space Force Station), neighbouring sites on the same coast (from memory, verify). So the AMBER model of Section B7.10 is Aster's own, not NASA-calibrated (`SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md` §8).

**An anchor that came and went.** The Slice 13 doc says a "New Glenn C3=5 anchor (`df3225f`)" landed (§8, last entry). The code has none. The golden test explains: `df3225f` added `{ c3: 5, payloadKg: 6360 }` and was "reverted in bcf1738 ('provenance fails INV-022')". The test pins New Glenn at C3 = 5 to the interpolated 6,055 kg, so re-adding 6,360 fails CI (golden test lines 1–18, 49–60; `.github/workflows/ci.yml` line 72). STATUS.md's cleanup queue (item C8) allows a re-land only "with elvperf screenshot + oracle row + DEC-13-1 amendment". Code and tests win; the founding doc was never annotated. [Certain]

### B7.14 Piecewise-linear interpolation, and the refusal to extrapolate

Between two neighbouring anchors, Aster draws a straight line and reads off the value. Doing this segment by segment is **piecewise-linear interpolation**.

```
For C3_k < C3 < C3_{k+1}:
  t     = (C3 − C3_k) / (C3_{k+1} − C3_k)        fraction of the way along the segment
  P(C3) = P_k + t · (P_{k+1} − P_k)
C3 exactly on an anchor            → that anchor's payload
C3 below the first or above the last anchor → BEYOND_CURVE   (never a number)
C3 not finite (NaN, ±∞)            → NON_FINITE_C3
```

This is `payloadAtC3(vehicle, c3)` in `launch-vehicles.ts` (lines 210–239). It returns either a number or a frozen marker object, so TypeScript will not let a caller do arithmetic on a refusal. [Certain]

**Why refuse to extrapolate.** **Extrapolation** extends the line past the last known point, where there is no evidence. INV-023: "extrapolated payload under a credibility headline is exactly the fake precision the tool exists to avoid" (`SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md` §3). The card reads "No published payload data past this C3 — not extrapolating." (`main.ts` line 822). Over MCP the refusal is a first-class answer, code `out_of_envelope`. The README quotes a real one: "falcon-heavy-expendable publishes payload anchors only for C3 0 through 55 km^2/s^2; requested cell is C3=2928.933 km^2/s^2." (`README.md` lines 76–93; built by `curveDomainRefusal`, `compute-shared.ts` lines 218–235). [Certain]

**Which way is the error?** A curve is **convex** if it bends upward like the inside of a bowl. A falling convex curve drops steeply at first and then flattens. A straight chord between two points of a convex curve lies above the curve. So if the true curve is convex between two anchors, linear interpolation overestimates payload there. Analogy: a taut string between two points of a sagging rope runs above the rope.

DEC-13-7 called the curves "convex-looking" and asked for the direction to be measured, not assumed. Section B7.17 shows it was: every measured point came out high. [Certain]

One caution. Convexity here is a property within each segment, not of the whole anchor list. New Glenn's drops are 2,250 kg (C3 0 → 10), then 2,565 kg (10 → 20), then 2,245 kg (20 → 30), so its anchors alone do not bend upward everywhere. The oracle still found its interpolated values high at C3 = 15 and 25. [Certain for the arithmetic; the within-segment shape between anchors is Likely, inferred from the four held-out points]

#### Worked Example 7.3: interpolating real cells

Inputs: anchors from `launch-vehicles.ts`; held-out values from `tools/slice13-research/elvperf/oracle/oracle-actuals.tsv`; the Apophis cell C3 from the live `estimate_mission_cost` call (MCP 0.1.0).

**(a) Falcon Heavy Expendable at the Apophis cell, C3 = 2.46685257512734.** The segment is (0, 15,010) to (10, 12,345).

- t = (2.46685 − 0) / (10 − 0) = 0.246685
- P = 15,010 + 0.246685 × (12,345 − 15,010) = 15,010 − 0.246685 × 2,665 = 15,010 − 657.416 = 14,352.584 kg

The tool returned `payloadAtC3` = 14,352.583788728563 kg. Match.

**(b) New Glenn at C3 = 25.** Segment (20, 2,365) to (30, 120). t = 0.5. P = 2,365 + 0.5 × (120 − 2,365) = 2,365 − 1,122.5 = 1,242.5 kg. elvperf's own answer at C3 = 25 is 1,205 kg. Error = (1,242.5 − 1,205) / 1,205 = 37.5 / 1,205 = +3.11%. Positive, as convexity predicts. The card carries this: "New Glenn: interpolation across the steep C3 20–30 segment overestimates payload by up to ~3.1% (measured, Phase B oracle)." (`main.ts` line 942).

**(c) Refusals.** New Glenn at C3 = 30.1 is above its last anchor, so BEYOND_CURVE. Falcon 9 ASDS at 10.1, also BEYOND_CURVE. Falcon Heavy at −1 is below the first anchor, also BEYOND_CURVE. Falcon Heavy at NaN gives NON_FINITE_C3 at `main`. The published 0.1.0 package returns beyond-curve there, because the NON_FINITE_C3 marker arrived later (commit `4535df9`, 2026-10-14, "refuse non-finite C3 as structured input"). [Certain; recomputed for this guide; re-run against a copy of `main`'s `launch-vehicles.ts`]

### B7.15 The Δv stack: the physics view, and two mission modes

A **Δv budget** (or stack) adds up every velocity change a mission needs. Aster's stack panel assumes impulsive burns, patched conics (Chapter B5) and no gravity assists (disclosure string, `main.ts` line 1016).

```
subtotal = Δv_inj(C3) + Δv_rdv + Δv_dep (sample return only) + Δv_sk
margin   = 0.10 × subtotal
total    = subtotal + margin
  Δv_rdv = |v∞,arr|     rendezvous
  Δv_dep = |v∞,arr|     symmetric-return assumption
  Δv_sk  = 0.150 km/s   stationkeeping allocation
[buildDeltaVStack, src/v2/porkchop/delta-v.ts lines 36–58]
```

Terms:

- **Rendezvous** means matching the asteroid's velocity so you stay with it. The spacecraft cancels the whole arrival excess speed |v∞,arr|; the asteroid's gravity is negligible.
- **Stationkeeping** is a generic allowance for small corrections near the target.
- **Margin** is a budget allowance for unknowns, not a structural safety factor.
- A **one-way rendezvous** ends at the asteroid. A **sample return** must also leave it again.
- The **symmetric-return assumption** prices that departure burn as equal to |v∞,arr|, without computing a return trajectory.

[Certain, `delta-v.ts`; `SLICE_11_FOUNDING.md` DEC-7]

**The mode toggle has a history.** Before Slice 13 the departure line was always on, so the stack silently modelled a sample return. A recon caught it; the fix was a toggle defaulting to one-way (`SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md` OQ-13-1). At `main`, departure is added only for `'sample-return'` (`delta-v.ts` line 45). The published MCP package still ships the old always-on helper, but its tools never call it. [Certain]

**How rough is the return?** An exploratory check of six windows on 433 Eros, 99942 Apophis and 2000 SG344 found the symmetric-return assumption off by 0.08–5.1 km/s, "sometimes too high and sometimes too low" (`src/v2/data/symmetric-return-error.json`, status "exploratory, unvalidated"; shown in sample-return mode, `main.ts` line 1016). Treat sample-return totals as rough. [Certain]

---

### B7.16 Delivered mass and the mission cost card

Now combine the vehicle and the spacecraft. The vehicle throws mass m_LV(C3) onto the departure asymptote. The spacecraft then burns its own propellant for everything after that. What reaches the asteroid is the **delivered mass**:

```
m_delivered = m_LV(C3) × exp( −Δv_sc / (g₀ · Isp) )
Δv_sc = Δv_rdv + 150 m/s + Δv_dep (sample return only) + margin
margin = 0.05 × (Δv_rdv + Δv_dep)        stationkeeping is not margined
  NO injection term
[deliveredMassKg, launch-vehicles.ts lines 241–289; budget assembly, main.ts lines 439–485]
```

[Certain, `SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md` DEC-13-4 and DEC-13-6]

**The double-count guard.** The vehicle's payload-at-C3 already includes the injection burn, because the rocket's upper stage did it. Charging injection to the spacecraft as well is what DEC-13-4 calls "the slice's #1 correctness hazard". The guard is structural: the budget type `SpacecraftDvBudget` has no injection field at all (`launch-vehicles.ts` lines 10–11, 32–41). The card states the split in words: "Launch vehicle provides injection to C3 = … — embodied in payload-at-C3, not a spacecraft ΔV line." (`main.ts` line 912). [Certain]

**The 5% margin.** DEC-13-6 replaced the flat 10% with 5% on "deterministic maneuver lines" (planned burns: rendezvous and departure), anchored to a convention of ECSS, the European space-standards body (European Cooperation for Space Standardization; from memory, verify). The research record states that convention as 5% on analytically derived trajectory manoeuvres (`3d-verification-record.md` item 12). The 150 m/s stationkeeping line is a generic allocation and gets no margin. [Certain that the repo says this]

**Two margins on one screen.** The Δv stack panel below still applies 10% to everything, injection included, and both panels say so (`main.ts` lines 917 and 1021). The card prices a spacecraft on a real rocket; the stack is a vehicle-agnostic physics total. [Certain]

**Input hardening.** After the curve check, `deliveredMassKg` returns `INVALID_INPUT` for an unknown mode, a sample return with no departure line, or any NaN, infinite or negative budget value. A negative Δv would make mass grow: an audit probe turned 10,115 kg into 49,765.70 kg with −5,000 m/s, since 10,115 × exp(5,000 / 3,138.128) = 49,765.70 (guards at `launch-vehicles.ts` lines 258–286; the probe is pinned as a named regression in `launch-vehicles.test.mjs` lines 294–297; Phase F audit MED-2). [Certain]

What the card shows, by state (`main.ts` lines 792–948):

| Cell state | Headline | Delivered row | Extra text |
|---|---|---|---|
| GREEN | delivered mass in kg | the mass | dogleg "none (GREEN)" |
| AMBER | delivered mass in kg | the mass | "Delivered mass excludes that payload penalty; Aster does not model it." |
| RED | "Not feasible at screening fidelity" | "—" | dogleg "exceeds site capability"; stack greyed; payload labelled "Not a delivered-mass estimate" |
| null band (no DLA) | delivered mass in kg | the mass | no badge; dogleg "— (no DLA for this cell)" |
| C3 beyond curve | "No published payload data past this C3 — not extrapolating." | "—" | — |
| Corrupted inputs | "—" | "—" | "invalid cell data" |

A collapsible "Assumptions & sources" block lists the curve source and date, the interpolation rule, Isp 320 s, the mission mode, "arrival wet mass (no dry-mass modeling)", the margin policy and the dogleg regime for this cell (`main.ts` lines 922–943). That is invariant INV-016e. [Certain]

The Target Compare page reuses `deliveredMassKg`, but with a fixed reference budget (1,000 m/s rendezvous for every body) rather than each cell's own arrival speed. Chapter B6 covers that page. [Certain, `src/v2/app/compare/main.ts` lines 134–142 and 1068–1072]

#### Worked Example 7.4: the Apophis cost card by hand

Inputs: live `estimate_mission_cost` for 99942, departure 2028-06-01, 300 days, M = 0, `falcon-heavy-expendable`, `cape-canaveral` (MCP 0.1.0): C3 = 2.46685257512734 km²/s², rendezvous = 4,089.4296336748325 m/s (that is |v∞,arr| = 4.08943 km/s), verdict AMBER. Constants from `launch-vehicles.ts` and `delta-v.ts`.

Step 1, payload from Worked Example 7.3: 14,352.584 kg.

Step 2, the spacecraft budget:

- rendezvous = 4,089.430 m/s
- margin = 0.05 × 4,089.430 = 204.471 m/s (tool: 204.47148168374164)
- stationkeeping = 150 m/s
- Δv_sc = 4,089.430 + 150 + 204.471 = 4,443.901 m/s

Step 3, the rocket equation:

- v_e = 9.80665 × 320 = 3,138.128 m/s
- Δv_sc / v_e = 4,443.901 / 3,138.128 = 1.41610
- exp(−1.41610) = 0.242659

Step 4, delivered mass = 14,352.584 × 0.242659 = 3,482.78 kg. The tool returned 3,482.7792179364897 kg. Match. The cell is AMBER at Cape, so the browser card would add the payload-penalty sentence.

Step 5, the trap. Wrongly add the injection for this C3, 3.335824 km/s (Section B7.11 formula). Then Δv = 7,779.725 m/s, the factor is exp(−2.47909) = 0.083819, and the "delivered mass" is 1,203.0 kg. That is 65% too low. The unit test guards the same trap for Falcon Heavy at C3 = 20 (`launch-vehicles.test.mjs` lines 235–247). It checks the correct answer, 10,115 × exp(−1,725 / 3,138.128) = 5,837.65 kg. Its wrong path adds a round 3,200 m/s injection (not the exact 4,098 m/s for C3 = 20) and gives about 2,106 kg. The test asserts only that production differs from the wrong path by more than 1,000 kg.

Step 6, sample return, by the browser's formula (the MCP tool is one-way only, so no tool check exists): departure 4,089.430 m/s; margin 0.05 × 8,178.859 = 408.943 m/s; Δv = 8,737.802 m/s; factor 0.061766; delivered 886.5 kg.

Step 7, the Δv stack panel for the same one-way cell: 3.336 (injection) + 4.089 (rendezvous) + 0.150 = 7.575 km/s; margin 0.758 km/s; total 8.333 km/s. Its margin, 758 m/s, is 3.7 times the card's 204 m/s, because it is 10% and covers injection too.

Result: every card number follows from two cell inputs (C3 and |v∞,arr|), the vehicle's anchors and four constants (g₀, Isp, the 5% margin and the 150 m/s allocation). The 4.1 km/s arrival burn, with its margin and stationkeeping, leaves under a quarter of the launched mass. (recomputed for this guide; re-run for fact-checking against copies of `main`'s `launch-vehicles.ts` and `delta-v.ts`, which reproduces 3,482.7792179364897 kg, 886.504 kg and 8.332779 km/s.)

CI pins one such case permanently. New Glenn at C3 = 5, one-way, budget {1,500, 150, 75} m/s must give exactly 3,494.511538898568 kg (`tests/v2-golden/launch-vehicles.golden.test.mjs` lines 76–83). [Certain]

Misconceptions:

- "Delivered mass is useful payload." No. It is arrival wet mass: tanks, structure and leftover propellant are all inside it.
- "A 'cost card' gives money." No. Its currency is mass. The MCP tool says why: "No committed cost-per-kg source exists in the Slice 13 model, so costPerKg is omitted rather than invented." (`estimate-mission-cost.ts` line 248).

### B7.17 Validating the curves: the oracle report

Are straight lines good enough? Ask an **oracle**: an independent source of truth, queried at points the model never saw (**held-out** points). For Slice 13 that meant four more elvperf queries at C3 = 15, 25, 35 and 50 (`tools/slice13-research/elvperf/oracle/oracle-report.md`, dated 2026-07-03; values in `oracle-actuals.tsv`). The oracle is recorded as commit `808e709` (OQ-13-5) and tested `launch-vehicles.ts` at `7180593` (report header); neither commit is in this guide's shallow clone, so both hashes are unchecked. The **relative error** of each point is (interpolated − actual) / actual. The **RMS** (root mean square) error is the square root of the average squared error, a typical size that punishes large misses.

The report splits points into two classes. **STRICT** points sit on well-behaved segments and must pass a 5% bar. **OBSERVED** points sit on steep or final segments; they are measured and disclosed, not gated.

| Class | Points | Max error | RMS | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| STRICT | 16 | 1.18% (New Glenn, C3 = 15) | 0.55% | PASS (bar 5%) |
| OBSERVED | 6 | 3.11% (New Glenn, C3 = 25) | 2.10% | disclosed |

All 22 errors are positive, as convexity predicts. Every vehicle missing from an elvperf screenshot also returned BEYOND_CURVE, with no mismatch either way. The values were transcribed from screenshots "by Nova (chat)" (report header). [Certain]

#### Worked Example 7.5: recomputing the OBSERVED summary

Inputs: anchors (`launch-vehicles.ts`) and actuals (`oracle-actuals.tsv`). At C3 = 50 the segment is (40, P₄₀) to (55, P₅₅), so t = 10/15 = 2/3.

| Point | Interpolated | Actual | Error | Error² |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| New Glenn, 25 | 1,242.5 | 1,205 | 3.112% | 9.685 |
| FH Expendable, 50: 6,640 + ⅔(4,670 − 6,640) | 5,326.7 | 5,280 | 0.884% | 0.781 |
| FH Recovery, 50 | 1,035.0 | 1,005 | 2.985% | 8.911 |
| Vulcan VC2, 50 | 1,286.7 | 1,260 | 2.116% | 4.479 |
| Vulcan VC4, 50 | 2,970.0 | 2,940 | 1.020% | 1.041 |
| Vulcan VC6, 50 | 4,173.3 | 4,120 | 1.294% | 1.676 |

Sum of squares = 26.573. Mean = 26.573 / 6 = 4.4288. RMS = √4.4288 = 2.104%. Max = 3.112%. The report says 2.10% and 3.11%. Match. Over all 22 points the RMS would be 1.19%. (recomputed for this guide)

**What this oracle does not cover.** It tests `payloadAtC3` only. It does not test Isp, the margin, |v∞,arr|, DLA or Lambert, and it cannot show elvperf itself is right. The README says the report "covers **cost interpolation only**", yet the same bullet opens "Launch-vehicle delivered-mass interpolation validated" (`README.md` lines 63–66), and the About page repeats "delivered-mass interpolation" (`src/v2/app/about/main.ts` line 289). The wording overstates. Read it as payload interpolation. Chapter B8 covers oracle design in general. [Certain]

### B7.18 The same answers over MCP

Two of the seven MCP tools carry this chapter's logic (Chapter B10 covers the envelope format).

| Tool | Inputs | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `dla_feasibility` | designation, departureDate, tofDays, M (default 0), optional `siteId` | DLA, \|v∞,dep\|, a verdict row per site with `marginDeg` |
| `estimate_mission_cost` | the same plus `vehicleId`; `siteId` optional | C3, payload, one-way budget, delivered mass, optional site verdict |

Sources: `mcp/src/tools/dla-feasibility.ts` lines 24–30; `estimate-mission-cost.ts` lines 30–37. Both solve a one-cell grid. IDs are slugs such as `falcon-heavy-expendable` and `cape-canaveral` (`compute-shared.ts` lines 183–200). Four behaviours differ from the browser. [Certain, from the code and live calls]

1. **One-way only.** "Mission mode is one-way: no departure burn is included."
2. **RED still gets a number.** The tool returns delivered mass with `siteFeasible: false` and the note "delivered mass is still shown". The browser shows "—" (`estimate-mission-cost.ts` lines 252–253; `main.ts` line 906). Found by reading: `siteFeasible` is true only for GREEN or AMBER (line 169), so a cell with no DLA (null band) is also flagged `siteFeasible: false`, with the same "outside the direct-injection screening band" note, although it is not RED. [Certain from the code; not exercised in a live call]
3. **No site, no verdict.** Without `siteId` it says "No launch site selected; site-band feasibility omitted."
4. **M defaults to 0.** The browser's family toggle can show both the M = 0 and M = 1 families (`porkchop-view.ts` line 36, `'both' | 'm0' | 'm1'`). For 2000 SG344, 2027-08-14 + 598 days, the default M = 0 gives C3 = 124.040 and an `out_of_envelope` refusal. M = 1 gives C3 = 0.054 and a delivered mass. An agent must choose M on purpose.

### B7.19 The showcase body and the reproducibility caveat (L3-6)

The porkchop page opens on 2020 FK3, not Apophis (`DEFAULT_BODY_ID`, `main.ts` line 79). OQ-13-3 explains why. A catalog scan found that FK3's "globally cheapest cell (C3 = 0.72 km²/s², departure 2026-12-26, TOF 465 d) is RED at DLA +82.4°". The cheapest-looking deal is infeasible from Cape: the honesty layer at its most visible. The same scan reported a 41,866-body run and 4,641 NEAs (11.1%) with a RED cheapest window. [Certain that the doc says this]

A post-lock annotation then says these figures are "unreproducible from the repository alone". The recon report (`aster-audit-reports/slice13-showcase-recon.md`) is not tracked, and no committed generator reproduces the scan. The figures are "not asserted to be wrong", but "public surfaces should not cite them as validated" (`SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md`, annotation `S16-REMEDIATE-2026-08-01-A`; audit finding L3-6, `tools/audit/REPO_AUDIT_2026-07-31.md`; STATUS.md Slice 13 row). [Certain]

A spot-read for this guide with MCP 0.1.0 at integer inputs (2026-12-26, 465 d, M = 1) gives C3 = 0.7565 km²/s² and DLA = 82.20°, Cape RED (Worked Example 7.2). The page's grid cell is not exactly the integer date. So the fact-check also recomputed the actual 200 × 100 grid cell, departure index 14 (2026-12-26, a fraction of a day after midnight) and flight-time index 17 (464.76 d), on the M = 1 branch, with the 0.1.0 package's grid function (recomputed for this guide). It gives C3 = 0.7178 km²/s² and DLA = 82.40°: the doc's 0.72 and +82.4° to every digit quoted. [Certain for the recompute, with the package-lag caveat] This reproduces one cell. It does not show that the cell is FK3's global minimum, and it does not regenerate the 41,866-body scan or the 11.1% figure.

The same cell hides a second problem behind the RED badge. Even ignoring geometry, it delivers little. The arrival burn is 9,089.6 m/s. With margin 454.5 m/s, Δv_sc = 9,694.1 m/s, the factor is exp(−9,694.1 / 3,138.128) = 0.04554, and 14,808.4 kg of Falcon Heavy payload becomes 674.4 kg (tool: 674.390666001973 kg, flagged `siteFeasible: false`). The lowest-C3 cell is not the cheapest mission. (recomputed for this guide)

The lesson is about evidence. A number without a recoverable source is a claim, not a result.

### Limits and known problems

The models in this chapter are screening models. Each limit below says why it matters. Items found by reading code, rather than named by the repository, say so.

#### Launch geometry

- **Screening, not launch-day geometry.** The bands assume the best instant and either corridor side. A nominally AMBER cell can still need a dogleg (MGS, Section B7.9). There is no right ascension of the asymptote, no arrival declination and no launch-period model (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md` §7). A verdict is not a launch-window guarantee. [Certain]
- **Two sites only.** Cape Canaveral and Vandenberg. No other spaceport and no custom latitude (`SLICE_12_FOUNDING.md` §7; `SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md` §7). [Certain]
- **Florida curves for every site** (found by reading). All eight vehicle curves are KSC or CCSFS queries. `deliveredMassKg` takes no site input, and the site picker changes only the verdict. Choose Vandenberg and a GREEN cell is still priced with a Florida curve, although a 70°+ orbit gets less help from Earth's spin. The only hint is "(KSC)" or "(CCSFS)" in the vehicle list (`site` fields at `launch-vehicles.ts` lines 72–178; `deliveredMassKg` at lines 241–289; picker option text at `main.ts` line 761). [Certain that the code does this; the size of the error is unknown]
- **AMBER is optimistic** by an unmodelled payload penalty, with no NASA calibration behind it, an unsourced "~1 m/s per degree" and an overstated "~3 orders of magnitude" (Section B7.10). [Certain; the overstatement is Likely]

#### Vehicle data and interpolation

- **Always slightly high between anchors**, by up to 3.1% (New Glenn, C3 20–30). [Certain]
- **No number past the curve.** That is deliberate (INV-023), but it means Falcon 9 can price nothing above C3 = 10 and New Glenn nothing above 30. [Certain]
- **Data as of 2024-02-29.** Vehicle availability, retirement and upper-stage versions are not modelled (`SLICE_13_FOUNDING.md` DEC-13-1, §7). [Certain]

#### Spacecraft model

- **One Isp, wet mass, impulsive burns, no money.** Isp 320 s for every spacecraft; arrival wet mass with no dry-mass model; no electric propulsion, gravity losses or gravity assists; no dollar figure. It is a screening number, not a science-payload estimate or a price. [Certain]
- **Rough sample return**: 0.08–5.1 km/s error in an unvalidated check (Section B7.15). [Certain]
- **Margin base is the caller's job.** One unit test prices its sample-return case with the one-way margin base (5% of 1,500 m/s) and gets 4,821.73 kg. The app would use 5% of 2,100 m/s and get 4,775.85 kg. The test checks only the departure factor, and `deliveredMassKg` cannot detect a mismatched base (`launch-vehicles.test.mjs` lines 230–256; `launch-vehicles.ts` lines 262–264; `main.ts` lines 462–466). [Certain]

#### Surfaces and fidelity

- **The cost card does not repeat the L1 caveat.** The page shows it elsewhere, but not on the card. Worked Example 7.6 shows it. [Certain]
- **MCP differs from the browser** (Section B7.18), and package `0.1.0` lags `main`. Three lags were found for this chapter: non-finite C3 is reported as beyond-curve, the old always-on departure helper ships, and `estimate_mission_cost` returns no `nearZeroC3` field. `main` adds that field (`estimate-mission-cost.ts` line 190, commit `531eb30`, 2026-10-10); the live 0.1.0 calls in this chapter carry none. [Certain]
- **A likely strict-compile break in the MCP source at `main`** (found by reading). `buildOneWayMissionCost` checks only `isBeyondCurve` before returning `payloadKg: payload` (`compute-shared.ts` lines 237–268). Since `4535df9` the payload type also includes the `NON_FINITE_C3` marker, and `mcp/tsconfig.json` is `strict` with `noEmitOnError`. A minimal reproduction against an unmodified copy of `launch-vehicles.ts` (recomputed for this guide) fails with TS2322 under `strict`, and did so again when re-run in fact-checking (TypeScript 6.0.2). The real project was not compiled, because AGENTS.md forbids builds here. No CI job would catch it: the root `tsc --noEmit` job uses a non-strict `tsconfig.json` that covers only `src/` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml` lines 33–34). At run time the same path would throw rather than refuse, though converged branches normally carry finite C3. [Likely]

#### Documentation drift

- `tools/slice12-research/DLA_RESEARCH_SUMMARY.md` still says the Lambert v∞ is "heliocentric ECLIPTIC" and that "ONE rotation is required" (§3), and its §4 repeats the inverted test. Only §1 carries errata. It also gives Cape's corridor as 40–115° and Vandenberg's latitude as 34.4°, versus 35–120° and 34.7° in `feasibility.ts`. [Certain]
- `tools/slice12-research/data/earth-vz-span-max.json` has a wrong per-year block. The generator compares a value in m/s with a stored value in km/s (`measure-earth-vz.mjs` lines 129–131), so each "per-year maximum" is the last sample of the year. The committed per-year values are all 1.81–1.98 km/s, impossible as yearly maxima when the span maximum is 11.897 km/s. That headline span maximum is unaffected (independent check; recomputed for this guide). [Certain]
- `src/v2/data/validation-provenance.json` labels the OBSERVED row's scope "all 22 non-absent held-out comparisons", but its 2.10% RMS is over the 6 OBSERVED points (Worked Example 7.5). The STRICT row lists "held-out C3 = 15/25/35/50" in one field and excludes the 40–55 segment in another. [Certain]
- `src/v2/mission/` holds only a README saying mission work "stays frozen"; the real code is in `src/v2/porkchop/` (audit L3-7). The `launch-vehicles.ts` header still says "oracle to quantify" the New Glenn error, which the oracle did in July. `mcp/src/resources/reference.ts` line 152 calls `delta-v.ts` "the older patched-conic stack helper", though the browser shows it as a live panel. The New Glenn C3 = 5 record (Section B7.13) and the showcase figures (Section B7.19) complete the list. [Certain]

#### Worked Example 7.6: a GREEN delivered mass past the L1 boundary

Chapter B4 explained fidelity tiers. 2000 SG344 is tier L1 ("materially-degraded-delta-v"). Its boundary is an Earth close approach on 2027-05-16 03:32 (JD 2461541.6470806), the earliest encounter that materially changes its catalogued orbit (`tools/slice18-research/tier-sizing-per-body.json`, the same file the page loads as `docs/tier-sizing-per-body.json`; `src/v2/boundary/tier-assignments.ts` lines 30–34). `isArrivalAfterEncounter` marks a cell unsupported when depJD + tofDays ≥ the encounter JD (`src/v2/porkchop/support-boundary.ts` lines 45–51).

Inputs: live `estimate_mission_cost` for 2000 SG344, 2027-08-14 + 598 days, M = 1, Falcon Heavy Expendable, Cape (MCP 0.1.0): C3 = 0.05427613298860554, rendezvous = 1,280.5376532060238 m/s, DLA = −26.30°.

1. Arrival = 2027-08-14 + 598 days = 2029-04-03. That is 688 days after the encounter, so the cell is unsupported.
2. Payload = 15,010 + 0.0054276 × (12,345 − 15,010) = 14,995.535 kg.
3. Margin = 0.05 × 1,280.538 = 64.027 m/s. Δv_sc = 1,280.538 + 150 + 64.027 = 1,494.565 m/s.
4. Delivered = 14,995.535 × exp(−1,494.565 / 3,138.128) = 9,313.76 kg. Tool: 9,313.75756221362 kg.
5. Verdict: |−26.30| ≤ 28.5, so GREEN at Cape, with a margin of only 2.20° (`dla_feasibility` for the same inputs returns `marginDeg` 2.2004970341748873).

**What the browser shows (unmerged evidence).** A user-experience report on the unmerged branch `origin/claude/ux-run-2026-10-22` (`tools/audit/ux-run-2026-10-22/UX_RUN_PROBLEMS_2026-10-22.md`, item P2) is not on `main`; it tested the build at commit `6575d0d`, not `cec19e7`. It reports the card showing "9,329 kg delivered to (2000 SG344) GREEN" for a cell labelled "2027-08-14 + 598 d", with a ΔV stack total of 5.118 km/s. A text search of the card found "zero occurrences" of the encounter text. The report says the L1 warning appears "only in the side panel and in the plot's hover/caption text".

**Reproducing 9,329 kg.** The browser label rounds the flight time, and the grid's dates are not whole days. The page's grid has 200 departures from 2026-01-01 to 2040-01-01 and 100 flight times from 182.5 to 1,826.25 days (`main.ts` lines 202–209; `src/v2/porkchop/grid-span.ts`). The cell labelled "2027-08-14 + 598 d" is departure index 23 (JD 2461632.451) with flight time index 25, which is 182.5 + 25 × 1,643.75 / 99 = 597.59 days. Recomputed on the M = 1 branch with the 0.1.0 package's grid function (recomputed for this guide):

- C3 = 0.04848 km²/s², |v∞,arr| = 1.2759 km/s, DLA = −26.65°, GREEN at Cape.
- Delivered mass = 9,329.1 kg; one-way ΔV stack total = 5.118 km/s.
- Arrival JD = 2461632.451 + 597.59 = 2462230.04, which is 688.4 days after the encounter (JD 2461541.647).

Both of the report's numbers match. [Certain for the recompute, with the package-lag caveat; Likely that this is the cell the report pinned]

**Where the caveat is, and is not, at `main`.** The page does show the body's fidelity tier: `renderTierDisclosure` puts a "Fidelity tier L1" panel, with the L1 criterion, near the title in the sidebar (`main.ts` lines 213–243 and 637). The plot view receives the support boundary (`main.ts` line 1051) and its readout prints "Arrival is after this object's … encounter. This cell is computed from an orbit that encounter invalidates." for unsupported cells (`support-boundary.ts` lines 59–64; used at `porkchop-view.ts` lines 1318 and 1490). The cost card itself, `main.ts` lines 735–948, contains no tier or encounter text. [Certain] The MCP envelope has no tier field either. [Certain] So the card, and the MCP tool, print a confident GREEN mass for a cell whose orbit the encounter invalidates. The page-level caveat sits elsewhere on the same screen.

**A second flag the card should raise.** C3 = 0.048 is below the 0.1 km²/s² near-zero threshold (`src/v2/core/constants/near-zero-c3.ts` line 5). By the code, the card's payload row shows a "near-zero C3" badge for any finite C3 below 0.1, unless the viewer has switched on the hide toggle (`main.ts` lines 857–860). The badge's tooltip says such a value "typically indicate[s] close-approach co-location of Earth and the body" and is "not a planning number" (`src/v2/porkchop/near-zero-c3.ts`). [Certain for the code; the badge was not observed, and the UX report does not mention it] At `main` the MCP tool also flags it, through `nearZeroC3.degenerate` (`estimate-mission-cost.ts` line 190); the published 0.1.0 package does not.

### Key takeaways

- Latitude sets the lowest inclination a due-east launch reaches. Range safety then limits azimuths, so Cape reaches 28.5–57° and Vandenberg 70–104°.
- DLA = arcsin(v∞,z / |v∞|), computed in an equatorial frame with no rotation. The constraint is i ≥ |DLA|: low declinations are free.
- GREEN ≤ `iMinDeg` < AMBER ≤ `dlaCeilingDeg` < RED. Latitude and raw `iMaxDeg` are metadata, never thresholds.
- Plane changes at LEO cost about 136 m/s per degree. Aster charges AMBER nothing (disclosed, optimistic) and gives RED a verdict, never a number.
- Payload comes from 38 official elvperf anchors, interpolated by straight lines and never extrapolated. All 22 held-out checks came out slightly optimistic: at most 1.18% on STRICT points and 3.11% on New Glenn's steep segment.
- Delivered mass = payload × exp(−Δv_sc / (g₀ · 320 s)), where Δv_sc excludes injection. The rocket already did that burn.
- The card uses a 5% margin on planned burns. The Δv stack uses 10% of everything. Both are disclosed.
- Numbers need recoverable sources and the right fidelity context. The showcase scan (L3-6) and the L1 gap (Worked Example 7.6) are where Aster currently falls short.
