## Chapter B9: The web app: browser, rendering and deployment

**Main idea:** Aster's website is a folder of static files that the visitor's browser downloads and runs, so every number, dot and label on screen is computed in that browser, and the engineering problems are keeping the screen responsive, drawing very small things honestly, and not making the visitor download too much.

Chapters B5 to B8 covered the mathematics. This chapter covers the machine that shows the results to a person. Chapter B10 covers the other consumer of the same math, the MCP server.

How this chapter was researched: everything was read from the repository at commit `cec19e7` (2026-11-04), read-only. No build or test was run, and no browser was opened, so runtime behaviour is described from the code, not observed. The clone is shallow (175 commits, back to 2026-09-21), so a few older commits the docs cite (`358d379`, `b6b7f92`, `dc19cbd`) cannot be inspected. Two fact-check passes re-read the cited files and recomputed every worked example with independent scripts. Commit dates come from `git log` when the commit is in the clone, and from the repo's own run reports otherwise. [Certain]

### B9.1 The journey of one visit

1. You open `https://hudsonclavin-cloud.github.io/asteroid-mining-planner/`.
2. GitHub Pages returns `docs/index.html`, which only redirects (`index.html:6,18`).
3. The browser loads `/asteroid-mining-planner/v2/solar-system/`: an empty `<div id="app">` plus script tags.
4. It downloads the JavaScript those tags name, such as `solarSystemV2-C6dR6zLr.js`.
5. The JavaScript downloads data: planet positions, the 41,906-body near-Earth catalog (208 of the bodies are comets, section B9.23) and a star catalog (`src/v2/app/solar-system/runtime.ts:834-838`). Alongside them it fetches the screening cache (every body's precomputed cheapest launch windows, Chapter B6) and the tier file (how far each body's orbit can be trusted, Chapter B4), and later a long Earth position file for the porkchop (sections B9.7 and B9.19).
6. It builds a 3D scene with Three.js, starts two background workers and redraws once per display refresh, about 60 times a second on a 60 Hz screen.
7. A separate layer written with Preact draws the catalog panel and honesty labels over the 3D canvas.

The chapter goes bottom up: bytes, pages, code, pixels, then shipping.

### B9.2 Bytes, URLs and static hosting

A **byte** (B) is 8 **bits** and holds one of 256 values. A **file** is a list of bytes. A **URL** is an address: scheme (`https`), host (`hudsonclavin-cloud.github.io`) and path. Think of a postal address and a parcel.

```
1 kB  = 1,000 B      1 MB  = 1,000,000 B     (decimal; used in STATUS.md)
1 KiB = 1,024 B      1 MiB = 1,048,576 B     (binary)
network speeds are in bits per second: bits = 8 × bytes
```

The browser is the **client**. It sends an **HTTP request**. A **server** returns a **response**: a **status code** (200 OK, 404 not found), **headers** (labels about the reply) and a **body** (the bytes). A **static host** only hands out files that already exist; it runs no code per visitor, like a vending machine rather than a kitchen. Aster's site is static, so all of its math runs in your browser. [Certain: `AGENTS.md` §9]

A first-order download model:

```
t_load ≈ n_rt · RTT + 8 · S_wire / B
  RTT round-trip time (s), n_rt round trips before data flows,
  S_wire bytes sent over the network (B), B bandwidth (bit/s)
```

Project hook. On 2026-08-23 the owner measured a cold load of the live site (STATUS.md:113). The catalog alone was 8,979 kB and took 32.87 s:

```
8,979,000 B × 8 = 71,832,000 bit;   71,832,000 / 32.87 s = 2.19 Mbit/s
```

The network conditions were not recorded, so this describes that capture only. [Certain arithmetic]

### B9.3 HTML, CSS and the DOM

**HTML** describes a page's structure. **CSS** describes its appearance. The browser turns the HTML into the **DOM** (Document Object Model), a tree of live objects that scripts can change. HTML is the building plan, CSS the interior design, the DOM the furnished building that JavaScript rearranges.

Aster's HTML holds almost nothing. The landing page body is:

```html
<div id="app"></div>
<script type="module" src="../../src/v2/app/solar-system/main.ts"></script>
```

(`v2/solar-system/index.html:31-32`), plus a style block that makes the page black and turns off scrolling. JavaScript builds everything else. [Certain]

CSS can compute sizes. The **viewport** is the visible area of the browser window. The catalog sidebar uses **`clamp()`**, a CSS function that picks a preferred size but keeps it between a minimum and a maximum (`src/v2/app/catalog-list/panel.ts:536`):

```
width = clamp(320px, 42vw, 400px) = min( max(320, 0.42·W), 400 ) px     W = viewport width
```

`vw` is "percent of viewport width". At W = 1,440 px the sidebar is 400 px; at W = 375 px the 320 px floor wins. Section B9.22 shows why that matters on phones.

### B9.4 JavaScript, the main thread and the frame budget

**JavaScript** is the language browsers run. A page's scripts run on one **main thread**, a single sequence of work that also does layout, painting and input. The browser feeds it through an **event loop**, one task at a time: a click handler, a timer, a finished download. While one task runs, the page cannot repaint. Think of a shop with one cashier.

A display redraws at a fixed **refresh rate**, which sets the **frame budget**:

```
T_f = 1000 ms / f_refresh      60 Hz -> 16.7 ms      120 Hz -> 8.3 ms
```

(60 and 120 Hz are common rates, from memory, verify.) A task longer than the budget skips frames.

Project hooks:

- The 3D view draws in a `requestAnimationFrame` loop, a callback run just before each redraw (`runtime.ts:2309`). [Certain]
- The compare page knowingly blocks the main thread: its comment says the "synchronous N-grid pass (~1.4 s at N=5) blocks the main thread", and `setTimeout(0)` lets a busy message paint first (`src/v2/app/compare/main.ts:1038-1040`). 1,400 / 16.7 ≈ 84 frozen frames. [Likely: a code comment, not a recorded measurement]
- Slice 9 (a **slice** is one numbered unit of project work, Chapter B1) recorded that moving asteroid propagation off the main thread cut 95th-percentile frame time from about 33 ms to about 17 ms on non-overview camera states, measured in a headless browser on Apple Silicon (`src/v2/SLICE_9_FOUNDING.md:77-98`). [Likely: one measurement on one machine]

### B9.5 TypeScript: types for the author, not the browser

**TypeScript** (TS) is JavaScript plus **type annotations** such as `x: number`. A **type checker** warns about mismatches before the code runs. Browsers cannot run TS, so a **transpiler** deletes the annotations and writes plain JavaScript. A spell-checker underlines mistakes; a printer prints regardless.

```ts
// TypeScript source                  // after the types are stripped
function f(x: number): number {       function f(x) {
  return 2 * x;                         return 2 * x;
}                                     }
```

The checker flags `f("3")`. The stripped code still returns 6, because JavaScript converts `"3"` when it multiplies. Types do not exist at run time. [Certain]

Aster splits the two jobs:

| Job | Tool | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Check types, write nothing | `tsc --noEmit` | `package.json` `typecheck:v2`; `tsconfig.json` `"noEmit": true`; CI job `typecheck` |
| Strip types, then bundle | esbuild strips, Rollup bundles, both run by Vite | `vite.config.ts:32-34`, `target: 'es2020'` |

**esbuild** is a fast transpiler; **Rollup** is a bundler (section B9.6). Vite 5 runs both during `npm run build` (from memory, verify); `package-lock.json` installs them as Vite's dependencies (esbuild 0.21.5, Rollup 4.60.2). `tsconfig.json` also sets `"strict": false` (fewer checks, not none), `"isolatedModules": true` (each file translatable alone, as esbuild needs) and excludes the legacy V1 folders. The source HTML points at a `.ts` file; the built `docs/v2/solar-system/index.html:29` points at `/asteroid-mining-planner/assets/solarSystemV2-C6dR6zLr.js`. One more pin: AGENTS.md §4 lists "Use Three.js APIs newer than r128" among the things Codex (the code-executing agent, Chapter B1) must not do, and `package.json` has `three ^0.128.0`. [Certain]

### B9.6 Modules, bundlers and Vite

A **module** is a file that `export`s names and `import`s them from other files. Following every import from a start file gives the **import graph**. A **bundler** walks that graph from each entry point and writes a few optimised files called **chunks**. Aster uses **Vite** (`^5.4.0` in `package.json`, 5.4.21 in `package-lock.json`): `npm run dev` serves source almost directly; `npm run build` bundles with Rollup and esbuild (Vite internals, from memory, verify).

#### Content hashing

A **hash function** turns bytes into a short fingerprint: same bytes, same fingerprint; changed bytes, almost surely a new one. **Content hashing** puts it in the file name:

```
output name = <chunk name> + "-" + hash(content)[:8] + ".js"
public URL  = origin + base + "assets/" + output name
            = https://hudsonclavin-cloud.github.io + /asteroid-mining-planner/ + assets/three.module-CFyvS0yg.js
```

Every hashed name in `docs/assets/` carries an 8-character fingerprint such as `CFyvS0yg`; exactly how the bundler computes it is an internal detail. [Certain for the names]

A browser **cache** keeps downloaded copies. With hashed names it can keep them a long time, because new content always arrives under a new name, like an edition number on a book's spine. Proof in this repo: the frozen legacy bundle is still `legacy-C6NkCVYx.js`, the name `src/v2/SLICE_19_FOUNDING.md:152-153` quoted weeks earlier, even though its HTML page has since moved to `legacy/`. Unchanged bytes, unchanged name. [Certain]

The built HTML also gets **modulepreload** links that fetch shared chunks early and in parallel. The landing page lists six, including `three.module` and `store` (`docs/v2/solar-system/index.html:30-35`). [Certain]

#### Aster's Vite settings (`vite.config.ts`)

| Setting | Value | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `base` (line 7) | `'/asteroid-mining-planner/'` | Every built URL starts with it; code reads it as `import.meta.env.BASE_URL` (`runtime.ts:107`) |
| `publicDir` (8) | `'textures'` | Copied to `docs/` unchanged, including `textures/_staging_v1/` |
| `build.outDir` (10) | `'docs'` | The website is written into `docs/` |
| `emptyOutDir` (11) | `true` | `docs/` is wiped before each build |
| `rollupOptions.input` (13-22) | nine HTML files | A **multi-page app**: each HTML file is its own entry |
| `esbuild.target` (33) | `'es2020'` | The JavaScript dialect emitted |

In this repo **`docs/` is not documentation**; it is the compiled website. Because of `emptyOutDir`, anything there that the build does not regenerate is deleted. AGENTS.md §9 items 3 and 5 say such deletions are expected and that unchanged sources rebuild byte-identically (verified 2026-08-06). [Certain]

The nine inputs are `index.html`, `legacy/index.html` and seven under `v2/`. Besides the legacy page, four do real work: `v2/solar-system`, `v2/porkchop`, `v2/compare` and `v2/about`. The root, `v2/index.html`, `v2/earth-moon` and `v2/inner-solar-system` only redirect, so `src/v2/app/earth-moon/runtime.ts` and `src/v2/app/inner-solar-system/runtime.ts` ship on no page. `v2/renderer-test/` and `v2/porkchop-smoke/` are not inputs at all, so they never reach `docs/`. [Certain]

#### Data, inlining and plugins

**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation, introduced in Chapter B1) is plain text that describes objects and lists; almost all of Aster's data files are JSON. Data enters the build through the pattern `new URL('<relative path>.json', import.meta.url)`; the catalog, for example, is `new URL('../../../tests/fixtures/v2/nea-catalog-slice9.json', import.meta.url)` (`src/v2/boundary/slice9-nea-catalog.ts:160-163`). Vite copies the file to `docs/assets/` under a hashed name, such as `nea-catalog-slice9-BkYibDG0.json`. Very small files are **inlined** instead, written into the JavaScript as **base64** text (a way of writing any bytes using only letters, digits, `+` and `/`): `src/v2/data/symmetric-return-error.json` (1,256 B) sits inside `docs/assets/porkchopV2-BuZQKmsX.js` as a `data:application/json;base64,...` string. (Vite's default inline limit is 4 KiB, from memory, verify. The repo is consistent with it: the 6,499 B `validation-provenance.json` ships as its own file, `docs/assets/validation-provenance-BkAPLf5w.json`.) [Certain that it is inlined: the decoded base64 equals the source file byte for byte]

A **plugin** is extra code that hooks into the build. Aster's four run after the bundle is written (`vite.config.ts:35-96`):

| Plugin | Effect |
|---|---|
| `copy-physics-worker` | `legacy/physics.worker.js` → `docs/legacy/` |
| `copy-lambert-screen-cache` | `tests/fixtures/v2/lambert-screen-cache.json` (34,499,477 B) → `docs/lambert-screen-cache.json` |
| `copy-fidelity-tier-assignments` | `tools/slice18-research/tier-sizing-per-body.json` (10,880,177 B) → `docs/tier-sizing-per-body.json` |
| `copy-nojekyll` | writes an empty `docs/.nojekyll` (section B9.20) |

The two big data files are kept out of the import graph on purpose. For the screening cache, a comment says this fixed a build out-of-memory crash (`panel.ts:68-74`, citing `b6b7f92`, not visible in this clone); the tier file is handled the same way, with no reason recorded beside it. [Likely] Both plugins also add dev-server middleware so `npm run dev` serves the files at the same base path. These copies keep fixed, unhashed names, so the cache safety of hashing does not apply to them. [Certain for the names]

### B9.7 Loading data: fetch, promises and parsing

`fetch(url)` starts a download and returns a **promise**, a placeholder for a value (or error) that arrives later. Inside an `async` function, `await` pauses that function until the promise **settles**; other tasks keep running. `Promise.all([a, b, c])` waits for all three and fails if any fails.

```
t_parallel = max(t_1, …, t_n)          t_sequential = t_1 + … + t_n
```

Like a dinner that cannot start until the last guest arrives. The `max` form is the ideal case. Parallel downloads share the same network link, so when bytes rather than round trips dominate, the total is closer to (total bytes) ÷ (bandwidth) than to the slowest single file. And arrival is not the end: `response.json()` **parses** the bytes into objects on the main thread, at a cost that grows with the decoded size.

Project hooks:

- `mountSolarSystem` begins with one `await Promise.all([...])` over the planet **ephemerides** (tables of positions over time, Chapter B2), the **NEA** (near-Earth asteroid) catalog and the star catalog (`runtime.ts:834-838`). The renderer is created only at line 878. Nothing appears until the slowest download has arrived and been parsed. [Certain]
- The screening cache and tier file downloads start even earlier. `panel.ts` fetches them at module scope (`panel.ts:75, 85`), and `main.ts` imports `runtime.ts`, which imports the overlay, which imports `panel.ts`. Imported modules run before the code that imports them (standard JavaScript module behaviour, from memory, verify), so these two downloads begin before `mountSolarSystem` starts and share the link with the three it waits for. [Certain for the import chain]
- There is no loading indicator before the renderer exists. `src/v2/app/solar-system/` contains none, and the catalog panel's own "loading" empty state (`src/v2/app/catalog-list/empty.ts:15-16`) can only appear after `mountPhaseCOverlay` runs at `runtime.ts:897`, which is after the `Promise.all`. [Certain: code search]
- `src/v2/app/solar-system/main.ts:12` is `void mountSolarSystem(mount);` with no `.catch`. The catalog loader throws on a failed response (`src/v2/boundary/slice9-nea-catalog.ts:489-492`), so a failed download leaves a black page and a console error. [Certain for the code path]
- **The catalog is loaded twice** on the landing page. `runtime.ts:836` loads it for the scene. `mountPhaseCOverlay` (called at `runtime.ts:897`) then calls `ensureCatalogLoaded()` (`src/v2/app/ui-overlay/overlay.ts:109-131`, called at :414), which loads it again unless the store already holds one, and the only `setCatalog` call in the app is inside that function (`overlay.ts:123`). The loader does not remember earlier results (`slice9-nea-catalog.ts:488-496`). The second download may come from the browser cache, but the parse runs twice. [Certain for the code path, which nothing short-circuits; not observed in a browser. It may explain the two catalog rows, 32.87 s and 1.45 s, that STATUS.md:113 left unexplained: Likely.]

How big is a parse? As an order-of-magnitude illustration only, **Node.js** (a program that runs JavaScript outside a browser), v22.22.0 on this sandbox, took about 190-310 ms to `JSON.parse` the 52,969,826-character catalog, 145-180 ms for the screening cache, about 50-65 ms for the tier file and about 21-25 ms for the long Earth file (three independent scripts, three runs each; the spread between runs is the point, not the exact figure). STATUS.md:113 records the browser parse cost as not measured. [Certain for Node; Speculative for phones]

### B9.8 Components and the virtual DOM (Preact)

A UI library lets you describe *what* the screen should show and works out *how* to change the DOM. A **component** is a function that takes inputs (**props**) and returns a tree of **virtual nodes** (VNodes), cheap objects that describe the interface. When state changes, the library calls the component again, compares old and new trees (**diffing**) and patches only the DOM nodes that differ. A stage manager given a new script moves only the props that changed.

```
UI = f(state)
diff work per update   ∝ virtual nodes re-rendered (the whole re-rendered tree is compared)
DOM work per update    ∝ nodes that actually changed
```

The saving is in the second line: comparing cheap JavaScript objects costs far less than touching the real DOM, which can force the browser to redo layout. [Certain: textbook virtual-DOM behaviour]

Aster uses **Preact** (`^10.29.2`), a small library with React's model:

- It calls `h(type, props, ...children)` directly, with no JSX (the HTML-like syntax many React projects use). Example: `src/v2/app/design/components/StatusBadge.ts`.
- Pages mount with `render(h(Page, {}), mount)`: `src/v2/app/porkchop/main.ts:1068`, `compare/main.ts:1301` (which passes `null` instead of `{}`), `about/main.ts:457`.
- Pages use **hooks**, functions that give a component memory between calls: `useState` stores a value, `useEffect` runs code after rendering (for example, to start a download).

The architecture rule is DEC-1 (a DEC is a locked design decision, Chapter B1; `src/v2/SLICE_9_FOUNDING.md` §2, line 19): "Scene stays imperative Three.js… Declarative DOM overlay beside the canvas." **Imperative** code says step by step what to do; **declarative** code says what the result should be. Preact never draws the 3D scene; it draws panels and labels over it. [Certain]

### B9.9 Signals: state that updates its dependents

A **signal** is a box holding a value; code that reads `signal.value` in a tracked context becomes a dependent. A **computed** signal is derived from others and recalculates only when an input changes. An **effect** re-runs when any signal it read changes. It works like a spreadsheet: change A1 and only the formulas that use A1 update.

```
c = g(s_1, …, s_k)       recomputed only if some s_i changed
effect E read {s_i}  ->  E re-runs when any s_i changes
```

Aster uses `@preact/signals` (`^2.9.0`). In `src/v2/app/ui-store/store.ts`, private writable signals hold the state (`mutableSearchQuery`, `mutableSortKey` and others, lines 49-60). Read-only `computed` views are exported (lines 63-72), and changes go through named functions such as `setSort` and `setSearch`. One exception: the layout signal is exported writable (`layoutModeSignal`, line 61), though it also has a setter, `setLayoutMode` (line 199). DEC-2 calls this a "single external store, unidirectional flow" (`SLICE_9_FOUNDING.md:25-29`). The chosen layout is remembered in **localStorage**, a small per-site browser store, under `aster-v2-layout-mode` (`store.ts:37-47`). [Certain]

The catalog chains signals (`src/v2/app/catalog-list/panel.ts:96-171`):

```
catalog + screening index + tier assignments
   └─> allRowsSignal       = computed(buildRowData)            join of three files
         └─> filteredRowsSignal = computed(filter, search, sort)
               └─> one effect in overlay.ts re-renders the Preact tree
```

That effect is coarse: it reads every tracked signal, scroll position included (`trackPanelSignals`, `panel.ts:240-254`), and re-renders the whole overlay (`src/v2/app/ui-overlay/overlay.ts:436-447`). Preact's diff keeps that affordable because only changed nodes reach the DOM. [Likely; not measured] Per-frame camera state stays out of signals by rule: DEC-2 keeps "fast per-frame state (camera easing, tween accumulators)" in "scene-local refs, NOT the reactive graph" (`SLICE_9_FOUNDING.md:25-29`). The likely reason is cost: pushing values through a reactive graph 60 times a second buys nothing. [Likely]

### B9.10 Virtualised lists: showing 41,906 rows

Creating 41,906 real DOM rows would be slow to build and lay out. **Virtualisation** (or **windowing**) creates DOM nodes only for rows near the visible part. It needs a tall empty **spacer** whose height equals all rows stacked (so the scrollbar stays truthful), a **window** of real rows placed at their true positions, and an **overscan** of a few extra rows so fast scrolling shows no gaps. Like a train window: you see a few metres of track, but the railway is all there.

```
H_total = N · h
i_start = max(0, floor(y / h) − b)
i_end   = min(N, ceil((y + V) / h) + b)          rows in DOM = i_end − i_start
  N rows, h row height (px), y scroll offset (px), V visible height (px), b overscan rows
```

Aster's values: h = 56 px (`CATALOG_LIST_ROW_HEIGHT_PX`, `src/v2/app/catalog-list/types.ts:21`), b = 6 (`rowBuffer`, `panel.ts:502`), V = 600 px until the panel measures itself (`panel.ts:58`); after that V is the scroll container's real `clientHeight` (`panel.ts:173-181`). The code also caps y at H_total − V, so the window never runs past the last row (`panel.ts:500-501`). Each row sits at `top = index × 56 px` (`panel.ts:565`) and is keyed by `bodyId` (`row.ts:70-83`). A **key** tells the diff which old row is which new row; index keys would reuse the wrong rows after a sort. [Certain]

#### Worked example 1: how many of the 41,906 rows exist at once

Inputs: `buildRowData` keeps a body only if it has a screening record (by `bodyId`) and a tier record (by designation) (`panel.ts:96-125`), over `tests/fixtures/v2/nea-catalog-slice9.json`, `tests/fixtures/v2/lambert-screen-cache.json` and `tools/slice18-research/tier-sizing-per-body.json`; h, b and V as above.

Step 1, rows. The catalog, the cache and the tier file each hold 41,906 records and every body matches, so N = 41,906 (recomputed for this guide; re-joined independently during fact-checking). The default "ALL" tab applies no class filter, so all of them are listed.

Step 2, spacer: 41,906 × 56 = 2,346,736 px.

Step 3, at the top (y = 0):

```
i_start = max(0, 0 − 6) = 0
i_end   = ceil(600/56) + 6 = ceil(10.71) + 6 = 17         -> 17 rows
```

Step 4, mid-list (y = 1,000,010):

```
floor(1,000,010/56) = 17,857  -> i_start = 17,851
ceil(1,000,610/56)  = 17,869  -> i_end   = 17,875         -> 24 rows
```

(At y = 1,000,000 the bottom edge does not cross a row boundary and the count is 23.)

Step 5, the maximum. A 600 px window can touch at most ceil(600/56) + 1 = 11 + 1 = 12 rows (it may clip one row at the top and one at the bottom), plus 2 × 6 overscan: 24. A sweep over every whole-pixel scroll position agrees (recomputed for this guide). In general the bound is ceil(V/56) + 1 + 12, so a panel that measures 800 px tall holds up to 28 rows and a 900 px one up to 30.

Step 6, the share: 24 / 41,906 = 0.057%.

Result: with the 600 px default, at most 24 row elements exist at once, inside one 2,346,736 px spacer; a taller real panel holds a few more (28 at 800 px, 30 at 900 px). All 41,906 row objects still sit in memory; only the DOM is small. [Certain]

#### The TanStack Virtual discrepancy

The Slice 9 plan names **TanStack Virtual**, a library for exactly this. DEC-1 reads "Preact + Signals + TanStack Virtual" (`SLICE_9_FOUNDING.md:19`), OQ-5 (an OQ is a numbered open question, Chapter B1) is "RESOLVED. TanStack Virtual" (`:129`), and `package.json` lists `@tanstack/virtual-core ^3.15.0`. But nothing imports it: a search of `src/` and of the built `docs/assets/*.js` finds no `tanstack` or `Virtualizer`. The windowing is hand-written at `panel.ts:499-509`. OQ-5's intent (fixed height, stable key, modest overscan) is met; the named library is a declared but unused dependency. [Certain]

### B9.11 Web Workers: heavy work off the main thread

A **Web Worker** is a second JavaScript thread the page starts. It cannot touch the DOM. Page and worker talk only by **messages** (`postMessage` on one side, a `message` event on the other). Messages are normally copied by **structured clone**, a deep copy. A large binary buffer (`ArrayBuffer`) can instead be **transferred**: ownership moves, nothing is copied, and the sender loses access (web platform behaviour, from memory, verify). It is like posting a long calculation to a colleague in another room while you keep serving customers.

```
t_copy ≈ S / r_copy  (grows with size S)        t_transfer ≈ constant
```

Workers do not shrink the total work. They keep the interface responsive while it happens.

| Work | Runs in | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Asteroid positions for the scene | asteroid propagation worker | `src/v2/app/solar-system/asteroid-propagation-worker.ts`, spawned at `runtime.ts:1351` |
| Porkchop grids (landing-page modal and `/v2/porkchop/`) | porkchop worker | `src/v2/porkchop/porkchop.worker.ts`, client `porkchop-client.ts` |
| Compare grids, up to five bodies | main thread | `src/v2/app/compare/main.ts` (731 × 100 cells per body, lines 118-119) |

**The asteroid propagation worker.** The page sends one `init` message with every body's orbit (`runtime.ts:1400-1403`), then `propagate` messages with a target time. The worker runs the Kepler propagator of Chapter B3 for each body on an elliptical orbit (any other body stays at its fixed catalog position, `anchorPositionM`, worker lines 37-40) and answers `propagate-result` with a `Float64Array` of positions in metres, transferring its buffer (`postMessage(..., [positionsM.buffer])`, worker lines 44-52). `buildSlice9RuntimePropagationBodies` includes every catalog body (`slice9-runtime-asteroids.ts:92-105`), so each update moves

```
3 coordinates × 8 bytes × 41,906 bodies = 1,005,744 B
```

by transfer, not copy. [Certain]

**The porkchop worker.** A porkchop plot (Chapter B6) needs thousands of Lambert solves (Chapter B5). INV-018 (an INV is a numbered invariant, a rule that must always hold, Chapter B1) makes it absolute: "Lambert grid computation runs on a Web Worker, never the main thread" (`src/v2/SLICE_11_FOUNDING.md:35`). The contract (`porkchop.worker.ts:13-58`):

| Direction | Message | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| page → worker | `init` | Earth's state series from the long 2026-2040 file |
| worker → page | `ready` | `earthSampleCount` |
| page → worker | `compute-grid` | `bodyId`, `bodyElements`, `gridParams`, `M` (revolution count) |
| worker → page | `grid-result` / `error` | `cells`, `compute_ms` / `reason` |

Three design choices. **One long-lived worker**, created once by `createPorkchopClient` and ended by `dispose()`, which calls `worker.terminate()` (`porkchop-client.ts:27-30, 115-121`; DEC-8, `SLICE_11_FOUNDING.md:123-127`). **One request at a time**: a second throws "Porkchop client already has a compute in flight" (`porkchop-client.ts:100`). **Strip at the boundary**: `stripBranch` drops the velocity vectors `v1` and `v2` and turns a non-finite `dlaDeg` into `null` (`porkchop.worker.ts:73-86`), because NaN would slip past checks that only test for missing values. Recorded speed: 98.5 ms median per body, worst 117 ms over 10 test bodies, on the same 200 × 100 grid the page uses, with a ~150 ms loading-indicator target (`SLICE_11_FOUNDING.md:47`; grid size in `tools/slice11-research/data/lambert-grid-timing.json`). [Certain that it was recorded; Likely that it holds at HEAD]

#### Worked example 2: one click versus the precomputed cache

Inputs: `GRID_PARAMS` (`src/v2/app/porkchop/main.ts:202-209`): departures 2026-01-01 to 2040-01-01 (`src/v2/porkchop/grid-span.ts:6-7`), time of flight (TOF) 182.5 to 1,826.25 d, 200 × 100 cells; spacing `(end − start)/(count − 1)` (`buildLinspace`, `grid-compute.ts:67-74`); cache metadata in `tests/fixtures/v2/lambert-screen-cache.json`: window 2026-01-01 to 2040-12-31, steps 7 d and 30 d, TOF 182 to 1,826 d, `totalSolves` 1,804,638,825, `wallTimeSeconds` 3,137.744173.

Step 1, departure span and step. Fourteen years with leap days in 2028, 2032 and 2036:

```
14 × 365 + 3 = 5,113 d;        5,113 / 199 = 25.69 d per departure step
```

Step 2, TOF step: (1,826.25 − 182.5) / 99 = 1,643.75 / 99 = 16.60 d.

Step 3, cells: 200 × 100 = 20,000 per revolution family. The "both" view sends M = 0 and M = 1, so 40,000 cells, about 2 × 98.5 ms ≈ 0.2 s of worker time. DEC-8 budgets exactly that: "~98ms M=0 + ~98ms M=1 = ~200ms total" (`SLICE_11_FOUNDING.md:126`).

Step 4, the cache. Its window is 5,478 days:

```
nDep = floor(5,478 / 7) + 1 = 783       nTof = floor((1,826 − 182) / 30) + 1 = 55
783 × 55 × 41,905 = 1,804,638,825       = totalSolves exactly
```

The grid comes from the script that built the cache, `tools/build/precompute-lambert-screen.mjs`. It steps departures from 2026-01-01 while the date is at or before 2040-12-31, 7 days at a time, and flight times from 182 d while at or below 1,826 d, 30 days at a time (lines 84-89 and 141-153). 41,905 is one fewer than the catalog: the cache lists 41,422 `low_departure_c3`, 483 `high_departure_c3` and 1 `propagator_failed` body (recomputed for this guide and re-counted in the fact-check). The script counts a solve only after the asteroid's position has been propagated (lines 249-256), so the failed body, 2015 D1, adds none. [Certain: the code and the product agree exactly]

Step 5, the offline rate: 1,804,638,825 / 3,137.744 s ≈ 575,000 solves per second.

Result: the browser solves 20,000 cells per family on demand, off the main thread. The 1.8 billion catalog-wide solves were done once, offline, and ship as a 34.5 MB file the page only reads. [Certain]

### B9.12 Drawing in 3D: pixels, the GPU, WebGL and Three.js

A screen is a grid of **pixels**. A **GPU** (graphics processing unit) colours millions of them in parallel. **WebGL** is the browser's interface to the GPU; it draws into a `<canvas>` element. **Three.js** wraps WebGL in three ideas: a **scene** (a tree of objects with positions), a **camera** (a viewpoint with a **field of view**, FOV, the angle it sees top to bottom) and a **renderer** (which draws the scene from the camera into the canvas). Think of a film set, a camera operator and a film lab, with the shutter pressed 60 times a second.

Every point passes through the same chain of coordinate changes, the **pipeline**:

```
world --(view matrix)--> camera space --(projection matrix)--> clip space
      --(divide by w)--> normalised coords in [-1, 1] --(viewport)--> pixels
```

A **matrix** here is a 4×4 table that rotates, moves or projects points. The **projection** makes far things smaller, which is **perspective**.

| What | Code (`src/v2/app/solar-system/runtime.ts`) | Line |
|---|---|---|
| Renderer | `new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true })` | 878 |
| Camera | `PerspectiveCamera(45, aspect, 1, MAX_CAMERA_DISTANCE_M * 10)`, with `MAX_CAMERA_DISTANCE_M = 15 AU` | 1222-1227, 81 |
| Labels | a `CSS2DRenderer` overlay of ordinary DOM elements | 885 |
| Depth range | `near = max(1, r·1e-4)`, `far = max((r + pan)·10, 5e8)`, recomputed each frame | 1735-1736 |

The **near and far planes** bound what the camera draws. GPU depth precision worsens as far/near grows (from memory, verify), so Aster ties both to the camera's orbit radius r. With no pan and r above 50,000 km (where 10r exceeds 5e8 m), far/near = 10 / 1e-4 = 100,000; panning, capped at 2r (`runtime.ts:1730`), raises it to at most 300,000. Close to a small body the 5e8 m floor on far takes over. The zoom clamp lets the camera come within the body's radius plus 1 km of a focused asteroid (`runtime.ts:828`, applied at :2153). For a 20 m asteroid that is r = 1,020 m, so near = max(1, 0.102) = 1 m and far = 5e8 m, a ratio of 5 × 10^8. Whether that causes visible depth errors was not checked. [Certain arithmetic]

Not everything is 3D. The porkchop plot uses the plain 2D canvas: a 200 × 100 `ImageData` pixel grid, one pixel per cell, scaled up to 1,000 × 500 with smoothing off so each cell stays a crisp block (`src/v2/porkchop/porkchop-view.ts:44-47, 797-830`), and the porkchop page loads no `three.module` chunk. Three.js only draws; every position comes from `src/v2/core/` (Chapters B2, B3 and B8). [Certain]

### B9.13 Apparent size, true scale and markers

**Apparent size** is how many pixels an object spans. It depends on radius divided by distance; a coin at arm's length can cover the Moon. Aster's convention (`computeApparentDiameterPx`, `src/v2/render/asteroid-renderer.ts:66-86`; same in `src/v2/render/halos.ts:102-103`):

```
θ = 2 · atan(R / d)        D_px = θ · H_px / fov
  R radius (m), d distance (m), H_px viewport height (px), fov vertical field of view (rad)
```

**True scale** means drawn sizes and distances follow physical ones. A **marker** is a deliberate minimum-size visibility aid. Aster draws distances and planet radii at true scale and adds labelled markers (`halos.ts`):

```
marker opacity = 0.85 if D_px ≤ 1.5;  falls linearly to 0 at D_px = 4;  0 above 4
marker size    = max(8 px, D_px)      (Saturn's moons: 6 px · sqrt(R / R_smallest))
```

#### Worked example 3: what you see in the top-down view

Inputs: FOV 45° (`runtime.ts:1222`); camera distance `TOP_DOWN_ORBIT_RADIUS_M = 8 AU` (`runtime.ts:99`), which is where the view starts: the initial orbit radius is the top-down state (`runtime.ts:1405`) around the initial focus, the Sun (`runtime.ts:1422`); `AU_M = 149,597,870,700` m (`runtime.ts:74`); radii from `src/v2/core/constants/bodies.ts` (Sun 696,000,000 m, Jupiter 71,492,000 m, Earth 6,378,136.6 m); `EARTH_FOCUS_RADIUS_M = 4e8` m (`runtime.ts:79`); an assumed 900 px viewport height (illustration only).

Step 1, scale factors:

```
45° = 0.7854 rad;   900 / 0.7854 = 1,145.9 px per rad;   d = 8 AU = 1.1968e12 m
```

Step 2, the Sun: θ = 2 · atan(6.96e8 / 1.1968e12) = 1.163e-3 rad, so D = 1.163e-3 × 1,145.9 = 1.33 px.

Step 3, Jupiter: θ = 1.195e-4 rad, D = 0.137 px. Earth: θ = 1.066e-5 rad, D = 0.0122 px. These use d = 8 AU for simplicity. The planets sit a little farther from a camera parked 8 AU above the Sun (Earth about √(8² + 1²) = 8.06 AU), so their true sizes are slightly smaller still.

Step 4, markers: all three are ≤ 1.5 px, so each gets opacity 0.85 and an 8 px marker.

Step 5, zoom to Earth at d = 4e8 m: θ = 2 · atan(6.378e6 / 4e8) = 0.0319 rad, D = 36.5 px. Above 4 px, the marker fades out and the true-scale sphere shows.

Result: in the starting top-down view every body is physically under 1.4 px wide; what you see are 8 px markers. The on-screen chip says so (`runtime.ts:1023`): "Markers — bodies smaller than 4 px on screen get a marker floored at 8 px (Saturn moons use a scaled floor); far-field asteroid points floor at 2.5 px — markers are visibility aids, not sizes". Its numbers are imported constants (`HALO_INVISIBLE_MIN_DIAMETER_PX`, `DEFAULT_MIN_HALO_DIAMETER_PX`, `ASTEROID_POINTS_MIN_SIZE_PX`), so the chip cannot drift from the code. (recomputed for this guide) [Certain]

A small inconsistency found while writing this guide, not mentioned in `halos.md` or `asteroid-rendering.md`: `halos.ts:114` converts pixels back to metres with the pinhole factor `2 · d · tan(fov/2) / H`, while the size formula uses `H / fov`. At 45° the two differ by 0.8284 / 0.7854 = 1.055, about 5.5%. For a perspective camera the pinhole factor is the exact one at the centre of the screen, so the size formula overstates a small body there by about 5% (and understates it near the top and bottom edges; `H / fov` is the average over the height). [Certain arithmetic; Likely immaterial, about 0.1 px at the 2 px threshold]

**Level of detail** (LOD) swaps cheaper drawings for small objects: a shared point cloud, then instanced meshes, then one full mesh for the focused body. **Hysteresis** uses different enter and exit thresholds so a value hovering near one does not flicker, like a thermostat that heats below 19 °C and stops above 21 °C:

```
points -> instanced at D ≥ 2.0, back at D < 1.5;   instanced -> mesh at D ≥ 32, back at D < 28
```

(`asteroid-renderer.ts:27-30`, `classifyAsteroidRenderMode` at :88-113.) The first pair applies to bodies that are not focused; the mesh pair applies only to the focused body, which is never drawn as a point. Detail is keyed to apparent size, not distance (`src/v2/render/asteroid-rendering.md`). [Certain]

### B9.14 Floating-point precision and camera-relative rendering

Computers store most real numbers as **floating point**: a fixed number of binary significant digits (the **significand**) times a power of two (IEEE 754, textbook). GPU buffers use **float32** (24-bit significand, about 7 decimal digits). Every JavaScript number is **float64** (53 bits, about 16 digits). The gap between neighbouring representable numbers, the **ulp**, grows with magnitude:

```
ulp(x) = 2^(floor(log2|x|) − 23)    float32
ulp(x) = 2^(floor(log2|x|) − 52)    float64
```

Like measuring a flea with a ruler marked only in kilometres.

#### Worked example 4: why positions are made relative to a nearby point first

Inputs: scene units are metres (chip "1 unit = 1 m", `runtime.ts:1022`); `AU_M` and `MAX_CAMERA_DISTANCE_M = 15 AU` (`runtime.ts:74, 81`); GPU positions are float32 (`Math.fround`, `asteroid-renderer.ts:418-420`); spacings from `numpy.spacing` (recomputed for this guide; re-run during fact-checking).

Step 1, 1 AU in float32. 1.496e11 lies between 2^37 = 1.374e11 and 2^38 = 2.749e11:

```
ulp = 2^(37 − 23) = 2^14 = 16,384 m
```

Step 2, other distances (`numpy.spacing`; recomputed for this guide):

| Distance | float32 spacing | float64 spacing |
|---|---|---|
| 1 km | 6.1e-5 m | 1.1e-13 m |
| Earth radius, 6.371e6 m | 0.5 m | 9.3e-10 m |
| Moon distance, 3.844e8 m | 32 m | 6.0e-8 m |
| 1 AU | 16,384 m | 3.1e-5 m |
| 15 AU | 262,144 m | 4.9e-4 m |

Step 3, consequence. Absolute Sun-centred positions in float32 would snap to a 16 km grid near Earth's orbit, and a focused asteroid would jitter by kilometres.

Step 4, the fix. **Camera-relative rendering** (a **floating origin**) subtracts a nearby reference point in float64 first and converts only the small difference to float32:

```
render position = float32( p_body(float64) − p_ref(float64) )
```

The textbook reference point is the camera. `src/v2/render/camera-relative.ts` implements exactly that (`subtractCameraRelativeF64`, then `Math.fround`; its comment: "No absolute canonical positions are ever written to the target buffer."). At `cec19e7`, though, the only app file that imports it is `src/v2/app/earth-moon/runtime.ts`, which ships on no page (Section B9.6). [Certain: code search]

The live landing view uses the same idea with a different reference: the orbit **anchor**, the focused body that the camera circles. `asteroid-renderer.ts:385-390` subtracts the anchor in float64 and `:418-420` rounds the difference with `Math.fround`; `runtime.ts:1764-1775` does the same for planets, and the chip comment calls scene distances "anchor-subtracted meters" (`runtime.ts:999`). The focused body therefore sits at the origin, where float32 spacing is finest. A body 6,000 km from the anchor keeps about half-metre precision. [Certain for the code paths]

Why this is enough even though the camera is not at the origin: the camera stays within about 3r of the anchor (orbit radius r, pan capped at 2r, `runtime.ts:1730`), so float32 rounding of that offset is at most about 2⁻²³ × 3r ≈ 3.6e-7 r. One pixel at distance r is about r × fov / H = r × 0.785 / 900 ≈ 8.7e-4 r. The rounding is therefore at most about 3.6e-7 / 8.7e-4 ≈ 0.0004 px, whatever the zoom. [Likely: this guide's estimate, not a repo measurement]

### B9.15 Shaders: thousands of soft dots in one call

A **shader** is a tiny GPU program. A **vertex shader** runs once per point and sets its screen position and, for point clouds, its pixel size (`gl_PointSize`). A **fragment shader** runs once per covered pixel and sets colour and **alpha** (opacity). **Attributes** differ per point (position, colour, size); **uniforms** are shared by all points in a draw. **Additive blending** adds each dot's light to what is already drawn, so overlaps glow. Think of a spray-paint crew with one instruction sheet (uniforms) and a note per dot (attributes).

Aster's asteroid point shader (`src/v2/render/asteroid-points-shader.ts:52-71`; size attribute from `asteroid-renderer.ts:424`):

```
a            = max(1, log10(R + 10))          R = estimated radius (m)         attribute aSize
s_raw        = a · k / z                      k = 1.5e12 (uScale), z = camera-space depth (m)
s_css        = clamp(s_raw, 2.5, min(driver max, 12))      CSS px
gl_PointSize = s_css · DPR                    device px (section 9.16)
```

The fragment shader draws a soft dot, `alpha = (0.7·core + 0.3·halo) · 0.4`, and discards pixels outside the circle (lines 74-93). Blending is additive and depth is not written. Inside the clamps a bigger estimated radius gives a slightly bigger dot, through a logarithm; at the clamps size carries nothing. Point size is a visibility encoding, not a physical size. [Certain]

The starfield is a decorative layer (`src/v2/render/star-renderer.ts:28-31`):

```
star size (CSS px) = clamp(3 + (2.5 − magnitude) · 0.35, 1, 8);    gl_PointSize = size · DPR
```

**Magnitude** is the astronomers' brightness scale (smaller is brighter). Stars are drawn "at infinity": only camera rotation moves them (`star-renderer.ts:23-29`). They come from `tests/fixtures/v2/star-catalog-tycho2-mag75.bin`: a 16-byte header beginning `TYC2BIN0`, version 1, count 40,000, then 28 bytes per star (seven float32: x, y, z, magnitude, r, g, b). 16 + 40,000 × 28 = 1,120,016 B, the file's size (`src/v2/boundary/star-catalog-tycho2.ts`). The name says magnitude 7.5, but the faintest stored star is 7.97; the generator defaults to a limit of 8.1 and keeps the brightest 40,000 (`tools/slice8-5-research/build-star-catalog.mjs:17-18`). [Certain for the measured values]

### B9.16 The device pixel ratio and the NEA legibility fix

A **CSS pixel** is the unit layout uses; a **device pixel** is a physical dot. The **device pixel ratio** (DPR) is device pixels per CSS pixel: often 1 on older monitors, 2 on "Retina" laptops, up to 3 on phones (from memory, verify).

```
size_device = size_css · DPR           area_device = area_css · DPR²
```

A shader that forgets DPR draws its dots half as wide, a quarter of the area, on a DPR-2 screen: two painters told "10 units", one in inches, one in centimetres. Aster reads DPR at mount and on every resize and gives the same value to the renderer, the stars and the asteroid points (`runtime.ts:879, 1217, 1341, 1874-1880`). [Certain]

#### What went wrong and how it was fixed

STATUS.md:91 records "NEA point legibility — FIXED STRUCTURALLY (`358d379`)". (NEA: near-Earth asteroid.) The header of `asteroid-points-shader.ts:11-38` gives four parts:

1. **No pixel-ratio term.** The star shader multiplied by `uPixelRatio`; the asteroid shader did not, which gave the stars "a free 2x linear / 4x area advantage" on DPR-2 screens.
2. **No far-field floor.** The old lower clamp of 1.0 let distant points collapse to one pixel. The floor is now 2.5 CSS px.
3. **The wrong ceiling.** The GPU driver reports its smallest and largest drawable point sizes as **`ALIASED_POINT_SIZE_RANGE`**; the maximum is "typically 255+". That is a **hardware limit**, not a design choice, yet it had been passed straight through as the ceiling, so the 64 px fallback constant (`ASTEROID_POINTS_FALLBACK_MAX_SIZE_PX`) "was never the operative ceiling" and sub-pixel bodies bloomed into haze (shader header lines 27-33; STATUS.md:91 says the driver value "had been overriding the 64 px constant"). The ceiling is now `Math.min(driverMax, 12)` (`runtime.ts:1331-1341`); `resolveAliasedPointSizeRange` falls back to [1, 64] if the driver's answer is unusable (`asteroid-points-shader.ts:114-135`).
4. **Brightness reverted.** "Two brightness retunes produced no perceived change because brightness was never the binding variable." Opacity is back to 0.4 and scale to 1.5e12.

Screening colours were also resaturated so green separates from grey by hue. (C3 is the launch energy of Chapter B6; "low C3" bodies are the cheap ones to leave Earth for.) The dim end of the low-C3 ramp went from `0x206040` to `0x18a060` (`src/v2/render/asteroid-screening-color.ts:15-22`). The 65% starfield default is "optional, not load-bearing" (STATUS.md:91). [Certain as recorded; commit `358d379` is outside this clone]

#### Worked example 5: device-pixel sizes before and after the fix

Inputs: the formula of 9.15 (`asteroid-points-shader.ts:39-47, 62-71`); old behaviour from the header comment (floor 1.0, no DPR, ceiling = driver maximum, taken as 255); `estimatedRadiusM` from `tests/fixtures/v2/nea-catalog-slice9.json` (433 Eros: 14,839.9 m; 2000 SG344: 20.39 m); `AU_M`; DPR = 2; the 40,000 star magnitudes.

Case A, 433 at depth 1 AU:

```
a     = log10(14,849.9) = 4.1717
s_raw = 4.1717 × 1.5e12 / 1.4960e11 = 41.83 CSS px
true apparent diameter = 2·atan(14,839.9 / 1.496e11) × 1,145.9 = 0.00023 px   -> points mode
  (1,145.9 px per rad is the 900 px-high view of Worked example 3)
OLD: clamp(41.83, 1, 255) = 41.83, no DPR      -> 41.8 device px
NEW: clamp(41.83, 2.5, 12) = 12 × 2            -> 24 device px
```

Case B, 2000 SG344 at depth 8 AU:

```
a     = log10(30.39) = 1.4827
s_raw = 1.4827 × 1.5e12 / 1.1968e12 = 1.858 CSS px
OLD: 1.858, no DPR                             -> 1.86 device px
NEW: clamp(1.858, 2.5, 12) = 2.5 × 2           -> 5.0 device px
```

A caveat on OLD: it uses today's scale k = 1.5e12. The header says the build just before the fix had been toned to 1.4e12 (lines 35-36), which would make the old dots about 7% smaller still: 1.73 px for case B and 39.0 px for case A. The comparison below holds either way.

Stars: the median magnitude is 7.32, so 3 + (2.5 − 7.32) × 0.35 = 1.313 CSS px = 2.63 device px; 72.2% of stars are ≤ 1.5 CSS px; the brightest is 4.26 CSS px.

Result: before the fix a small far asteroid (1.86 device px) was smaller than the median star (2.63), while a body far below one pixel could bloom to about 40 px. After it, the far asteroid is 5.0 device px, about 1.9 times the median star, and on this DPR-2 screen no point exceeds 12 × 2 = 24 device px. The shader comment's "typical star ~1.0-1.5 CSS px" matches the measured median of 1.31. (recomputed for this guide; re-run during fact-checking and an independent read of the star file) [Certain arithmetic]

The lesson is diagnostic. The symptom was "too dim"; two fixes turned up brightness and changed nothing, because size was the binding variable. Measure the competing layer before turning a knob. (One stale pointer remains: the comment cites `runtime.ts:1074-1077`, but the code is now at 1331-1341.)

#### The landing view's clock

The solar-system view shows planets where they are *now*, which works only while now lies inside its ephemeris data (Chapter B2). The **HUD** (head-up display, the text laid over the scene; Chapter B2), built by `src/v2/app/solar-system/ephemeris-status.ts`, says `LIVE`; or `NOT LIVE · clamped to <date> TDB` when now is outside coverage and positions freeze at the nearest edge; or `SCRUBBED` when the user moved the time. (TDB is the astronomical time scale and JD the Julian day count of Chapter B2.)

The rolling files `src/v2/data/horizons-*-rolling.json` share one range: Earth's 151 records run from JD 2461345.5 to 2461495.5, which is 2026-11-01 to 2027-03-31 TDB (recomputed for this guide; `timeMin`/`timeMax` are the intersection of all series, `runtime.ts:855-861`). With `COVERAGE_ENDING_NOTICE_SECONDS = 14 × 86,400` (`ephemeris-status.ts:22`):

```
2461495.5 − 2461345.5 = 150 days  (151 daily samples)
"refresh due" note from 2027-03-31 − 14 d = 2027-03-17;   NOT LIVE after 2027-03-31
```

The previous window ran 2026-07-18 to 2026-10-16, with 91 daily planet samples (`tools/slice20-research/ephemeris-roll/roll-REPORT.md`), which is why the unmerged UX run of 2026-10-22 (Section B9.22), run against the old main, found an expired view. #### Design tokens

A **design token** is a named value, such as `status-low-c3 = #3a8d4a`, used instead of a raw literal, like paint codes in a building specification. A **design system** is the full set of tokens and shared components. `src/v2/app/design/tokens.json` (21,955 B) holds 84 colour tokens in one dark theme, 11 spacing values (2-28 px), 8 radii, 6 shadows and 3 font families. [Certain]

The rule, DEC-19.5-4, is that the repo is the authority and meaning-carrying values are imported, never retyped. Its heading still says "PROPOSED", but `SLICE_19_5_FOUNDING.md:440` records it "LOCKED as drafted" (document locked 2026-10-14). The full migration (F4) was routed to Slice 23. [Certain]

#### Contrast ratio

**Contrast ratio** measures text readability against its background, from 1:1 to 21:1. DEC-19.5-6 sets a floor of 4.5:1 for normal text (3:1 at 24 px and above) and a 2 px focus outline. The formula (WCAG 2.x, from memory, verify; it reproduces the repo's numbers). The repo's own checker, `tools/design/contrast.mjs`, does the same steps. It uses 0.03928 as the cutoff where the block below uses 0.04045; no 8-bit channel value c/255 falls between the two, so both give identical ratios:

```
c = channel/255;   c_lin = c/12.92 if c ≤ 0.04045, else ((c + 0.055)/1.055)^2.4
L  = 0.2126 R_lin + 0.7152 G_lin + 0.0722 B_lin              relative luminance, 0..1
CR = (L_lighter + 0.05) / (L_darker + 0.05)
```

#### Worked example 6: why `#3a8d4a` became `#378646`

Inputs: `src/v2/app/design/a11y-overrides.ts` (old `#3a8d4a`, new `#378646`, both under white text, L = 1).

Step 1, channels: R = 0x3a = 58, G = 0x8d = 141, B = 0x4a = 74.

Step 2, linearise: 58/255 = 0.2275 → ((0.2275 + 0.055)/1.055)^2.4 = 0.04231; G → 0.26636; B → 0.06848.

Step 3, luminance: 0.2126 × 0.04231 + 0.7152 × 0.26636 + 0.0722 × 0.06848 = 0.00900 + 0.19050 + 0.00494 = 0.2044.

Step 4, contrast: (1 + 0.05) / (0.2044 + 0.05) = 1.05 / 0.2544 = 4.127, which fails 4.5:1.

The same procedure gives `#378646` → 4.506; `#9a7a3a` → 4.024 and `#907236` → 4.520; and grey hint text on the sidebar `#0f1116`: `#666666` → 3.289, `#7d7d7d` → 4.587 (recomputed for this guide; re-run during fact-checking).

Result: all six ratios stored in `A11Y_OVERRIDES` reproduce to three decimals. Each override lifts a failing colour just above 4.5:1 by changing lightness only (the file's own description: "lightness-only overrides"; HSL hue is unchanged at 0.365 for the green and 0.111 for the amber), so green stays green. The 8 px marker floor and 2.5 px point floor were deliberately left alone. [Certain]

### B9.19 Page weight: decoded versus gzipped

**Compression** rewrites a file into fewer bytes by replacing repeated patterns with short references; **gzip** is the common web format. **Wire bytes** are what crosses the network and set download time. **Decoded bytes** are the size after decompression and set parse time and memory. The **compression ratio** is decoded ÷ wire. **Eager** files load before first paint; **lazy** files load on demand. **Minification** strips whitespace without changing meaning. A vacuum-packed duvet posts quickly and is just as big once opened.

```
r = S_decoded / S_wire;     t_wire ≈ 8 · S_wire / B;     parse time and heap ∝ S_decoded
```

Which data files does each page fetch eagerly? From the code: solar-system = NEA catalog + screening cache + tier file + long Earth file + 4 rolling files + star catalog (`runtime.ts:834-838`, `panel.ts:75, 85`, `overlay.ts:121, 134`); compare = the first four (`compare/main.ts:971-979`); porkchop = catalog + tier file + long Earth file (`porkchop/main.ts:310, 369-370`). STATUS.md:450-454 gives per-page totals for 2026-09-22, and these file sets reproduce its compare and porkchop totals exactly once the tier file's 84 B growth is allowed for (Step 3). Textures are not counted here.

#### Worked example 7: the landing page's data weight at `cec19e7`

Inputs: served sizes from `git cat-file -s cec19e7:<path>` (served copies are the committed LF files, 9.20; the same sizes as the files in this LF checkout, and the deployed copies in `docs/` are byte-identical to their sources); fetch sites as listed above; the one measured wire size, STATUS.md:113.

Step 1, sizes: catalog `tests/fixtures/v2/nea-catalog-slice9.json` 52,969,826; screening cache 34,499,477; tier file 10,880,177; `horizons-inner-solar-system-2026-2040.json` 7,214,102; rolling files 200,060 + 1,295,812 + 3,074,744 + 2,463,346 = 7,033,962; star file 1,120,016.

Step 2, add:

```
52,969,826 + 34,499,477 + 10,880,177 + 7,214,102 = 105,563,582   (compare)
105,563,582 + 7,033,962 + 1,120,016           = 113,717,560 B (solar-system)
52,969,826 + 10,880,177 + 7,214,102            =  71,064,105 B (porkchop)
```

Step 3, reconcile with STATUS.md:450-454 (110,906,873 B on 2026-09-22). The rolling files were rolled from 91 to 151 daily planet samples, 4,223,359 → 7,033,962 B (roll-REPORT.md line 5), and the tier file grew by 84 B (STATUS.md:340 gives 10,880,093 B):

```
7,033,962 − 4,223,359 = 2,810,603;     10,880,177 − 10,880,093 = 84
110,906,873 + 2,810,603 + 84 = 113,717,560 ✓
```

Step 4, compress (zlib 1.3, recomputed for this guide and re-run during fact-checking): solar-system 23,264,943 B at level 6; 24,011,256 B at level 5.

Step 5, pick the level. STATUS.md:113 measured the catalog on the wire at 8,973,203 B. Level 5 reproduces it exactly; level 6 gives 8,471,252 B (recomputed for this guide). So level 5 models the host better, and STATUS's own level-6 totals run low. [Certain for the match; Likely that it keeps holding]

Step 6, catalog ratio: 52,969,826 / 8,973,203 = 5.9.

Step 7, at an assumed 20 Mbit/s link (hypothetical): 24,011,256 × 8 = 192.1 Mbit, so 9.6 s.

Step 8, minify the catalog (Python `json.dumps`, no spaces): 52,969,826 → 36,170,778 B (−31.7%); level-5 gzip 8,973,203 → 7,962,645 B (−11.3%).

Step 9, the code's share: 700,047 B of JS against 113,717,560 B of data = 0.62%.

Result: the landing page's data is 113.7 MB decoded and about 24.0 MB on the wire. Minifying would cut decoded size by a third but wire size by only a tenth. This is the cheap measurement STATUS.md:117 asked for and had not taken. It supports STATUS's [Likely] claim that float digits, not whitespace or key names, dominate the wire. Data, not code, is the weight. [Certain for the sizes; Likely that float digits make up most of the rest]

Cautions and extras:

Yet at `cec19e7` `panel.ts:75` fetches the 34.5 MB screening cache at module scope, which is about 8.8 MB more at gzip level 5 (recomputed for this guide). The capture may have been filtered, the code may have differed in August, the cache may have been served differently, or the total mis-transcribed. Do not quote 9.0 MB as the page's total. [Unresolved]
- **Brotli**, a stronger compression format, was offered and not returned by the host (STATUS.md:113). The remaining levers are leaner data, fewer bodies or lazy loading. STATUS.md:527-528 lists "a per-body payload path" as a next candidate, and the audit rulings route deploy weight to Slice 24, whose row reads "Lean Payload owns the deploy weight and the porkchop data path" (`tools/audit/sanity-69472a3/phase0/RULINGS.md:66`).

### B9.20 Deployment to GitHub Pages

**GitHub Pages** is GitHub's static host. Serving a folder of a branch directly is a **branch deploy**. A **project site** for repository R of user U lives at `https://U.github.io/R/` (from memory, verify), which is why `base` is `/asteroid-mining-planner/`. Aster's Pages serves the committed `docs/` folder on `main`, so the live site is whatever `docs/` held at the last push. Like a printed newspaper, editing the draft changes no printed copies. [Certain: `AGENTS.md` §9]

The sequence is `npm run build` → `git add docs/` → commit → push, and "Hudson approves before `git push`" (`AGENTS.md` §2, "Build and deploy"; Hudson is the owner, Chapter B1). AGENTS.md §9 item 2 says when a change is live:

```
live(change) ⇐ (a) npm run build ∧ (b) a docs/-only commit ∧ (c) Hudson's manual push
             ∧ (d) the change's own string or bundle hash read from the live page, cache disabled
green CI ⇏ live
```

The rule exists because on 2026-08-06 "twelve src/v2 commits sat undeployed behind green CI" (`AGENTS.md:308`). [Certain]

**CI** (continuous integration) runs checks on every push. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` has four jobs on Node 24: `typecheck` (`npx tsc --noEmit`), `build` (`npm run build`), `golden-numbers` and `full-tests`. The build job only proves the build succeeds; its output is discarded. CI never commits or deploys. Its header comment still says "Two gates" and "never builds docs/", which the `build` job contradicts inside the runner. [Certain]

Three details:

- **`.nojekyll`.** Pages normally runs **Jekyll**, a site generator, which skips paths starting with an underscore (from memory, verify), such as `_staging_v1`. The empty `docs/.nojekyll` turns it off (`vite.config.ts:88-94`). [Certain for the file; Likely for the reason]
- **Line endings.** `.gitattributes:9` marks `docs/**` as text with `eol=lf`, and lines 10-13 exempt images and `.bin` files. STATUS.md:430-433 records that the on-disk copies in the owner's checkout (a Windows machine, STATUS.md:13) are larger than what the host serves, so served bytes are measured with `git cat-file -s`. (By git's documented rules `eol=lf` should check text out with LF on any system, from memory, verify; the larger Windows copies are recorded, not explained.) A CRLF copy of the catalog would be larger by exactly its 1,927,737 line breaks. [Certain for the count]
- **Entry bundles at `cec19e7`**: `aboutV2-ca_cBGJA.js`, `compareV2-DpGmp5zP.js`, `porkchopV2-BuZQKmsX.js`, `solarSystemV2-C6dR6zLr.js`, `legacy-C6NkCVYx.js`, from rebuild commit `adda2ab` (Slice 20 Front A step W5, `tools/slice20-research/front-a/frontA-REPORT.md:27`). The live site was not fetched from here, so whether it serves exactly these is unverified.

### Limits and known problems

- **Nothing shows until every eager file loads.** `Promise.all` gates the renderer and there is no loading indicator; a cold load once took 30+ s of black (STATUS.md:113). A first-time reviewer may conclude the site is broken. [Certain for code; Likely still slow on slow links]
- **A failed download leaves a silent black page**, because `void mountSolarSystem(mount)` has no error handler. [Certain]
- **The catalog is parsed twice** on the landing page, doubling the largest parse. [Certain by code path; not observed in a browser]
- **The payload is large, eager and data-dominated**: 113.7 MB decoded, about 24 MB on the wire, 0.6% JavaScript. Porkchop and compare also fetch the full 53 MB catalog to show one to five bodies. Minifying alone saves about 11% of wire bytes. Deploy weight and the porkchop data path are routed to Slice 24, "Lean Payload" (`RULINGS.md:66`), which has no founding document at `cec19e7`; STATUS lists "a per-body payload path" only as a next candidate (STATUS.md:527-528). [Certain]
- **Dead deployed weight**: `docs/_staging_v1` and the unused cloud texture ship anyway. [Certain]
- **The ephemeris expires on 2027-03-31** and is refreshed by hand; it lapsed once already. [Certain]
- **Phones are poorly served**: 82-85% coverage by the sidebar, no `@media` rules (only the `clamp()` widths), no two-finger pan. [Certain by code]
- **No ranking by reachability**, and the text sort puts a high-C3 body first. [Certain]
- **Disclosed rendering errors**: planet spin axes and Saturn's ring plane are wrong; the HUD says so, and the fix (Front G) is routed to Slice 22 (`SLICE_19_5_FOUNDING.md` §9.2). [Certain]
- **The float-precision safeguard is not the documented one.** The live view rounds anchor-relative positions, not camera-relative ones, and the `camera-relative.ts` helper, which has its own test (`tests/v2-slice1-integration.test.mjs:116`), is used on no shipped page. The estimate in Section B9.14 says the anchor method is precise enough; a search of `tests/` found no test of on-screen jitter for the landing view. [Certain for the code; Likely for the adequacy]
- **Point size carries little information**: a logarithmic hint inside the 2.5-12 CSS px clamp and nothing at the clamps; the radius behind it is estimated with an assumed albedo and stored with false precision. [Certain]
- **Residual typed dates**: `2040-01-01` is still a literal in `ui-overlay/overlay.ts:161` and `compare/main.ts:115`, not taken from `grid-span.ts`, so they can drift if the span changes. The Slice 19.5 close routes them to Slice 24 (`SLICE_19_5_FOUNDING.md:579-580`). [Certain]
- **Tokens are not yet the single style source.** [Certain]
- **This chapter's evidence** comes from code reading: no browser, a shallow clone, Node rather than browser timings, and an MCP package (0.1.0) that lags main.

### Key takeaways

- Aster is a static site: GitHub Pages serves the committed `docs/` folder, and all math runs in the visitor's browser.
- TypeScript is checked by `tsc --noEmit` and stripped by esbuild inside Vite; types do not exist at run time.
- Vite builds nine HTML entries into `docs/` under `/asteroid-mining-planner/`, wipes the folder first, and fingerprints file names so caches stay safe.
- The 3D scene is imperative Three.js r128; the panels are declarative Preact driven by signals.
- The 41,906-row catalog keeps only a few dozen rows in the DOM (24 at the 600 px default height) with hand-written windowing; TanStack Virtual is declared but unused.
- Workers carry the heavy work: 20,000 Lambert cells per revolution family per click, and about 1 MB of positions per update, transferred, not copied.
- Positions are made relative to the focused body in float64 before the GPU's float32, whose spacing at 1 AU is 16,384 m.
- The NEA legibility fix was about size, not brightness: a missing pixel-ratio term, a raised floor, and a 12 px ceiling below the driver's hardware maximum.
- Distances and planet radii are true scale; markers and point floors are labelled visibility aids.
- The landing page's data weighs 113.7 MB decoded and about 24 MB on the wire. Data, not code, is the weight problem.
- A change is live only when its own text is read from the live page; green CI is not a deploy.

## Chapter B10: The MCP server and evidence envelopes

**Main idea:** Aster's MCP server lets an AI agent ask the same validated math core that drives the web app, and every answer comes back in an "evidence envelope" that carries each number's units, confidence class, sources and commit, or else a structured refusal that says why the server will not answer and what would help.

Chapters B5 to B8 built the math. Chapter B9 showed how a person sees it in a browser. This chapter is about the other door into the same house: the one an AI agent uses.

That door is called the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**. Aster ships an MCP server as an npm package called `aster-mission-mcp`. An agent such as a chatbot can start it, ask "what is the cheapest window to Apophis?", and get an answer it can check.

The hard part is not the plumbing. It is honesty. A person looking at the website sees labels, colours and warnings. An agent sees only text. If the text says "C3 = 0.0009" with no warning, the agent will repeat it as fact. So the project built a strict wrapper around every number. This chapter explains that wrapper from first principles.

We go in four steps. First the plumbing: processes, JSON, JSON-RPC and MCP itself. Then input checking with schemas. Then the evidence envelope and its three kinds of outcome. Last, shipping: provenance outside git, the dirty-worktree incident, npm packaging, the eval set, and where the published package has drifted from the repository.

Three conventions carry through the chapter:

- Claims carry a label: [Certain] (textbook fact, or verified in this repo), [Likely] (supported but not proven) or [Speculative] (informed guess).
- Facts I recalled rather than read in the repo say "(from memory, verify)".
- Repo paths are relative to the repository root, read at commit `cec19e7` on `main`. Live outputs come from the published package `aster-mission-mcp@0.1.0`, which was published on 2026-07-10 and **lags main**. I say "observed on 0.1.0" for those, and "per source" for behaviour I could only read in main's code. I did not build or run main's server, because the repo's `AGENTS.md` forbids agents like me from running its build and test scripts.

### B10.1 The problem the server solves

Suppose you ask a chatbot "how much can a Falcon Heavy deliver to Apophis?". Without help, it will answer from memory. It may invent a number. It cannot run a Lambert solver in its head.

The fix is to give the agent a calculator it can call. But a calculator that prints bare numbers is not enough for Aster. The project's whole idea is the **honesty layer**: every number must say where it came from and how much to trust it (Chapter B1). The Slice 15 founding document, which set up the server, states the rule plainly: "an agent must never receive a number with less disclosure than a human viewing the site" (`src/v2/SLICE_15_FOUNDING.md` §2, the INV-016 family). [Certain]

So the server has two jobs:

1. Expose the math core to agents through a standard protocol.
2. Wrap every answer so its honesty survives the trip.

The founding document also names the demo. An agent asks for a transfer the launch-vehicle data cannot support, and "watches the tool refuse to extrapolate beyond a sourced launch curve — with the refusal explaining itself. The refusal is the demo." (`SLICE_15_FOUNDING.md` §1). [Certain] Section B10.8 works through that exact refusal.

### B10.2 The plumbing from scratch

#### Processes and text streams

A **process** is a running program. When the operating system starts a process, it gives it three text channels:

- **stdin** (standard input): where the process reads input.
- **stdout** (standard output): where it writes results.
- **stderr** (standard error): a side channel for warnings and diagnostics.

[Certain, textbook]

Think of a clerk behind a hatch. Paper slides in on one side (stdin). Answers slide out the other side (stdout). Complaints go into a separate tray (stderr).

```
process : stdin (stream of bytes) → stdout (stream of bytes), with side output on stderr
```

A **pipe** joins one program's stdout to another program's stdin. In a shell, `echo hello | wc -c` prints `6`: five letters plus a newline character. [Certain]

A program can also start another program as a **child process** and hold both ends of its pipes. That is exactly how an AI host talks to Aster's server. The repo's own eval runner (the script that runs its scripted tool tests, Section B10.13) does it in code: it calls `spawn(...)` on `mcp/dist/mcp/src/index.js` and writes requests into the child's stdin (`mcp/eval/run-eval.ts`, lines 74-77). [Certain]

One rule follows at once. If stdout carries the protocol, nothing else may print there. A stray log line would corrupt the message stream. Diagnostics must go to stderr. The repo learned this: commit `50b9ad9` "suppressed expected git-probe stderr during baked fallback" (`SLICE_15_FOUNDING.md` §8), and `gitCommitForPath` in `mcp/src/resources/repo.ts` (line 42) starts git with `stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'ignore']`. That means: git gets no input, git's stdout is captured into a string for the server to read, and git's stderr is thrown away. Nothing git prints can reach the server's own stdout. [Certain]

#### JSON: data written as text

**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is a way to write structured data as plain text. It has six kinds of value [Certain, textbook]:

| JSON type | Example |
|---|---|
| object (labelled slots) | `{"value": 2.5, "units": "km/s"}` |
| array (ordered list) | `[1, 2, 3]` |
| string | `"km/s"` |
| number | `2.5` |
| boolean | `true`, `false` |
| null (nothing) | `null` |

Think of JSON as a filing cabinet written on one line: folders (objects) with labelled slots (keys).

JSON has one trap that matters a lot here. It has **no NaN and no Infinity**. **NaN** ("not a number") is what a computer produces for things like 0/0. In JavaScript, `JSON.stringify(NaN)` silently produces `null`, and so does `JSON.stringify(Infinity)`. [Certain: I ran both in Node v22.22.0 during this check; `{a: NaN, b: Infinity}` became `{"a":null,"b":null}`.] So a broken calculation can reach the reader as `null`, which looks like "no answer" rather than "bug".

The project turned this into a rule. **INV-032** says "No non-finite numbers cross the wire", because "`JSON.stringify` silently converts NaN/Infinity to `null` — a silent honesty failure" (`SLICE_15_FOUNDING.md` §3, line 40). Section B10.6 shows the two places in code that enforce it. [Certain]

Note also that a JSON number has no units. `4` could be 4 km²/s² or 4 m²/s², a factor of a million apart. Section B10.6 shows how Aster fixes that.

#### Protocols and JSON-RPC 2.0

A **protocol** is an agreed format and order for messages. Both sides must follow it, or they cannot understand each other.

**JSON-RPC 2.0** is a small protocol for calling functions on another program. **RPC** means "remote procedure call". It has three message types (from memory, verify):

- A **request** asks for something. It has a method name, parameters, and an `id` number.
- A **response** answers one request. It repeats the same `id` and carries either a `result` or an `error`.
- A **notification** is a request with no `id`. No reply is expected.

```
request  = { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": n, "method": m, "params": p }
response = { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": n, "result": r }                     (success)
         | { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": n, "error": { "code": k, "message": s } }  (failure)
```

The `id` works like a numbered ticket at a deli counter. The counter calls "ticket 7" when order 7 is ready, so orders can finish in any sequence and still reach the right customer.

Error codes are numbers. The code **−32602** means "Invalid params" in JSON-RPC 2.0 (from memory, verify). Aster uses it through the SDK constant `ErrorCode.InvalidParams` (`mcp/src/tools/porkchop-scan.ts`, line 48). [Likely for the standard meaning; Certain for the repo usage]

An error response is not a crash. It is a normal, structured reply that says "your request was badly formed". Section B10.7 shows a twist: inside MCP, a bad tool argument does not come back as a JSON-RPC `error` object at all. It comes back as a normal `result` that is flagged as an error.

### B10.3 The Model Context Protocol

#### Hosts, clients and servers

**MCP** is a protocol, built on JSON-RPC, that lets an AI application talk to outside programs that offer capabilities. Anthropic introduced it in late 2024 (from memory, verify). [Likely]

Three roles appear [Likely, from the MCP model as I recall it; consistent with the SDK classes the repo uses]:

| Role | What it is | In Aster's world |
|---|---|---|
| **Host** | The AI application the person uses | A chat app or coding agent |
| **Client** | The part of the host that speaks MCP to one server | The SDK's `Client` class, or the eval runner |
| **Server** | A program that offers capabilities | `aster-mission-mcp` |

MCP is plumbing, not an AI model. The model decides what to ask. The server only answers.

#### Tools, resources and prompts

An MCP server can offer three kinds of capability:

- **Tools**: named functions the model may call with arguments. Methods `tools/list` and `tools/call`.
- **Resources**: read-only documents addressed by a **URI** (a name like a web address). Methods `resources/list` and `resources/read`.
- **Prompts**: reusable message templates.

Aster offers seven tools, four resources and no prompts. `mcp/src/index.ts` registers tool modules and one resource module, and nothing else (lines 18-24). [Certain] On 0.1.0, a `prompts/list` request gets the JSON-RPC error −32601 "Method not found", because the server never declares a prompts capability. [Certain, observed on 0.1.0]

Why split tools from resources? Static reference data, such as the table of launch vehicles, never changes between calls. The founding document put it in resources on purpose: "MCP resources exist for static reference data; spending tool slots on lookups wastes both the budget and agent attention" (DEC-15-5, `SLICE_15_FOUNDING.md` line 146). [Certain]

#### The lifecycle of a session

A session runs in a fixed order (from memory of the MCP spec, verify):

1. **initialize**: the client says which protocol version it speaks and what it supports. The server replies with its name, version and capabilities.
2. **initialized**: a notification from the client saying "ready".
3. **Discovery**: `tools/list` and `resources/list`.
4. **Calls**: `tools/call` and `resources/read`, as many as needed.

I ran a handshake against the published package. The server answered with `serverInfo {name: "aster-mission-mcp", version: "0.1.0"}` and capabilities `{resources: {listChanged: true}, tools: {listChanged: true}}`. The `tools/list` reply listed 7 tools, and its `result` object serialises to 20,753 bytes of JSON. That matches the 20,753-byte "cacheable prefix" the Slice 16 study recorded (`src/v2/SLICE_16_FOUNDING.md` lines 162, 326). [Certain, observed on 0.1.0]

The project pins MCP spec version `2025-11-25` and the official TypeScript SDK `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` at exactly `1.29.0` (DEC-15-2; `mcp/package.json` line 40). [Certain] The repo's eval runner sends `initialize` with that version and then goes straight to `tools/call`, with no `initialized` notification (`run-eval.ts` lines 88-95; a grep finds no `initialized` in the file). I did the same with a hand-written line client against 0.1.0, and the server answered every `tools/call`. So this server tolerates the skip, even though a strict client should send the notification. [Certain, observed on 0.1.0 with a check script written for this guide]

#### The stdio transport

A **transport** is the channel the JSON-RPC messages travel through. With the **stdio transport**, the host launches the server as a child process. Each JSON-RPC message is one line of text on the child's stdin or stdout (newline-delimited; from memory, verify).

The repo's eval runner implements exactly this by hand. It writes `JSON + "\n"` to the child's stdin, splits stdout on newlines, matches each response to its request by the numeric `id`, and gives up after 10 seconds (`REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000`, `run-eval.ts` line 51 and lines 156-247). [Certain]

Aster is **stdio-only** by decision DEC-15-3: "Zero hosting surface, zero auth surface, reviewer-runnable offline." A remote transport over HTTP was deferred to a later slice (`SLICE_15_FOUNDING.md` lines 92-93). [Certain]

#### Aster's server in 27 lines

Here is the whole entry point, `mcp/src/index.ts`, trimmed of imports:

```ts
#!/usr/bin/env node
const server = new McpServer({ name: 'aster-mission-mcp', version: '0.1.0' });

registerCatalogTools(server);           // search_bodies, get_body
registerPorkchopScanTool(server);
registerExplainCellTool(server);
registerDlaFeasibilityTool(server);
registerEstimateMissionCostTool(server);
registerGetValidationReportTool(server);
registerReferenceResources(server);     // 4 resources

const transport = new StdioServerTransport();
await server.connect(transport);
```

[Certain, `mcp/src/index.ts` lines 1-27]

The first line is a **shebang**. It tells a Unix shell to run the file with Node.js. Note that the version string `'0.1.0'` is typed here by hand, separately from `mcp/package.json`. Section B10.14 explains why that matters.

One call, end to end:

```
model decides → client sends tools/call { name, arguments }
  → SDK validates arguments against the tool's inputSchema
       (on failure: result { isError: true, content: [{ text: "MCP error -32602: ..." }] }, no envelope)
  → handler computes, builds an envelope
  → toolResult(envelope) returns { structuredContent: envelope,
                                   content: [{ type: "text", text: pretty JSON }] }
```

The `toolResult` function in `mcp/src/tools/common.ts` (lines 8-21) returns the envelope twice. `structuredContent` is the object, for programs. `content[0].text` is the same thing as indented JSON text, for models and people. [Certain]

#### Tool annotations

Each tool also declares four **tool annotations**, which are hints to the host. All seven Aster tools use the same set, `CLOSED_WORLD_TOOL_ANNOTATIONS` (`mcp/src/tools/common.ts` lines 1-6):

| Hint | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `readOnlyHint` | `true` | Does not change anything |
| `destructiveHint` | `false` | Cannot delete or overwrite |
| `idempotentHint` | `true` | **Idempotent**: calling twice has the same effect as calling once |
| `openWorldHint` | `false` | **Closed-world**: uses only its own committed data, never the internet |

I confirmed all four on all seven tools in the live `tools/list`. [Certain, observed on 0.1.0] They are declarations. A host may trust or ignore them; nothing in the protocol enforces them. [Likely]

### B10.4 Schemas: describing acceptable input

#### What a schema is

A **schema** is a machine-checkable description of acceptable data. Think of the printed boxes on a paper form: "date: YYYY-MM-DD", "count: whole number 1 to 50". **Validation** is the clerk who rejects a form with letters in the number box.

**JSON Schema** is the standard, language-neutral way to write a schema in JSON. **zod** is a TypeScript library where you write the schema as code instead. The MCP SDK converts zod schemas into JSON Schema when it answers `tools/list`. [Certain]

Here is a real conversion, observed in the published package's `tools/list`. The zod line in `mcp/src/tools/porkchop-scan.ts` (line 36) is:

```ts
topN: z.number().int().min(1).max(50).default(10)
```

The SDK publishes it as JSON Schema draft-07:

```json
{ "type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 50, "default": 10 }
```

The surrounding object also gets `"additionalProperties": false`, which tells the client not to send any argument the schema does not name. And `z.number().positive()` becomes `"exclusiveMinimum": 0`, meaning "strictly greater than zero". The published schema also names its dialect, `"$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"`. [Certain, observed on 0.1.0]

The advertised schema and the runtime check are not quite the same thing. At run time the SDK checks arguments with the zod schema itself, and a plain `z.object` quietly **drops** unknown keys rather than rejecting them.
