## Chapter B12: Process, governance and infrastructure

**Main idea:** Aster's numbers are only as trustworthy as the process that produced them, so this chapter explains each layer of that process (version control, written slice contracts, git hooks, tests, CI, audits and agent roles), what each layer actually enforces, and where it has drifted from what the documents say.

**Evidence base.** Everything below was read, unchanged, at commit `cec19e7` (the merge of pull request #10, 2026-11-04; the git words in this paragraph are defined in Section B12.2). That checkout is identical to `origin/main` [Certain: `git rev-parse HEAD origin/main`]. No test, build or repository test script was run, because AGENTS.md:169 forbids a documentation agent from running them. Test counts are therefore *recorded* results, quoted with their dates. A few behaviours were demonstrated in a throwaway sandbox outside the repository, never inside it. One live result comes from the published tool package `aster-mission-mcp@0.1.0` (published 2026-07-10), which lags `main`; it is marked "(0.1.0)". Values marked "recomputed for this guide" come from the guide's own check scripts, kept in its working folder, not in the repository.

### B12.1 Why a software project needs process at all

A program is a set of text files that many people, or many AI agents, change over months. Three questions then become hard.

1. *What exactly was the code when this number was computed?*
2. *Who changed what, and was the change allowed?*
3. *Does the code still do what we think it does?*

**Process** is the set of habits and tools that keep those answers checkable. **Governance** is the part of process that says who may decide what. **Infrastructure** is the machinery that runs the checks.

Think of a hospital pharmacy. Every dose is logged (version control), only a pharmacist signs off (roles), the barcode scanner refuses the wrong drug (hooks), and a second pharmacist re-checks high-risk doses (audits). Each layer catches mistakes the others miss.

Aster needs this more than most projects [Certain, files cited]. Its pitch is that every number carries its source, confidence class and commit (README.md:3-5; Chapter B1), and a commit (a saved snapshot of the code, defined in Section B12.2) is a git concept. And most of the typing is done by AI agents directed by one owner, Hudson (AGENTS.md:9-16). The rules in this chapter exist mainly so an agent cannot silently drift.

A few project words appear before their full definitions, so here is a preview. A *slice* is one numbered unit of work, split into *fronts* (Section B12.4). A *dispatch* is one written instruction packet handed to an executing agent such as Codex or Claude Code (Sections B12.4, B12.12). AGENTS.md §7 (line 281) names Hudson "the sole person who pushes to origin", the shared copy of the code on GitHub.

### B12.2 Git from scratch

#### Version control and the content hash

**Version control** is a system that records every saved state of a set of files, so you can compare, restore and audit them. **Git** is the version-control program Aster uses.

Git names every stored thing by a **hash** of its contents. A **hash function** turns any input into a short, fixed-length "fingerprint". Change one byte of the input and the fingerprint changes completely. In practice you cannot work backwards from the fingerprint to the input. (SHA-1, the hash used here, can be attacked by someone who builds two colliding files on purpose, and git uses a hardened variant; from memory, verify. For catching accidents it is ample.)

Analogy: a library catalogue number computed from the text of the book itself. Two identical books get the same number. Change one comma and the number is totally different.

Git's object name (the SHA-1 form used by this repository):

```
id = SHA1( type + " " + size_in_bytes + "\0" + content )
  type    = "blob" (a file), "tree" (a folder) or "commit"
  size    = length of content in bytes, written as decimal text
  "\0"    = one zero byte
  id      = 160-bit number, written as 40 hexadecimal digits
```

A **repository** (repo) is the folder of files plus git's database of every object. Git usually shows only the first 7 hex digits of an id, a **short hash**. Every citation in this guide such as `cec19e7` is one.

#### Worked example 12.1: computing a hash, and the chance of a short-hash clash

*Inputs:* the 6-byte file `hello` + newline (a generic file, not from the repo); the count of objects reachable from `cec19e7` (`git rev-list --objects HEAD | wc -l` = 2,726).

Step 1. Build the header: `"blob 6\0"`. Append the 6 content bytes.

Step 2. SHA-1 of that 13-byte string. Python's `hashlib` gives `ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a`. `git hash-object --stdin` gives the same id [Certain: both run in this session].

Step 3. How likely are two of the 2,726 objects to share a 7-digit prefix? The **birthday approximation** (a standard probability result, from memory, verify) is:

```
P ≈ 1 − exp( −n(n−1) / (2 · 16^k) )
  n = number of objects, k = hex digits shown
```

Step 4. Plug in n = 2,726 and k = 7.
- n(n−1) = 2,726 × 2,725 = 7,428,350.
- 2 · 16^7 = 2 × 268,435,456 = 536,870,912.
- Ratio = 7,428,350 / 536,870,912 = 0.013836.
- P ≈ 1 − e^(−0.013836) = 0.0137, about 1.4%.

Step 5. Check reality: cutting every id to 7 digits finds 0 duplicates [Certain: `cut -c1-7 | sort | uniq -d`].

*Result:* about a 1.4% chance of any clash, and none exists. Git lengthens a short hash when it becomes ambiguous (from memory, verify).

Two consequences matter for Aster.

- **A hash is not encryption.** It hides nothing. It only identifies content.
- **A file cannot contain its own commit hash.** Writing the hash into the file changes the content, which changes the hash. Aster's run reports say exactly this ("a file cannot contain its own commit hash", `tools/slice20-research/front-a/frontA-attempt1-REPORT.md`:2; similar wording at `recon/S20_01-REPORT.md`:2). So a run report points at its own evidence commit indirectly: as "the branch tip" (those two reports), or by naming the commit's *parent* (`ephemeris-roll/roll-REPORT.md`:2, "parent ce4dece").

#### Commits and the commit graph

A **commit** is a saved snapshot of the whole project. It records:
- a pointer to the folder **tree**;
- the hash of one or more **parent** commits;
- an **author**, a date and a **commit message**.

Each commit points back to its parent, so history forms a chain. Where chains split and rejoin, history forms a **directed acyclic graph** (DAG): each arrow points from a commit to an earlier one, and there are no loops. Think of a family tree drawn child → parent.

The most useful question about the graph is "how many commits does B have that A lacks?":

```
ahead(A, B) = number of commits reachable from B but not from A
git command:  git rev-list --count A..B
  --first-parent   walk only the main line (one step per merge)
  --no-merges      skip merge commits
```

Two common misreadings:
- *"A commit stores only the changes."* Conceptually it stores a full snapshot. A **diff** (the list of changed lines) is computed when you ask for one.
- *"The author field tells you who typed the change."* It records whatever identity git was configured with. In Aster, all 166 visible non-merge commits are authored `Hudson Clavin`, and only 38 carry a `Co-Authored-By` trailer naming a Claude model [Certain: `git log --no-merges --format=%an`, trailers]. Git alone cannot tell you which agent made a commit.

#### Branches, `main`, HEAD and tags

- A **branch** is a movable name pointing at one commit. Commit on it and it moves forward.
- **`main`** is the conventional name of the trunk branch.
- **HEAD** means "the commit you are on now".
- A **tag** is a name that never moves.

```
branch : name → commit id   (moves on each commit)
tag    : name → commit id   (fixed)
HEAD   → a branch name (normally) → commit id
```

A branch costs about 40 bytes: one hash. It is a sticky note in a notebook, moved to each new page you write. A tag is a note glued in place.

In Aster, branches are named per task and per slice: `s19-5-close`, `s20-recon`, `s20-eph-roll`, `s20-phase0`, `s20-front-a` (from the merge messages in `git log --merges`). Run reports also name safety tags such as `s20-pre-front-a` and `s20-pre-eph-roll` as rollback anchors (`frontA-LOG.md`:6, `roll-REPORT.md`:10). This checkout holds no tags at all (`git tag -l` prints nothing), so those tags cannot be inspected here [Certain].

#### Merging

A **merge** combines two lines of history.
- A **fast-forward** happens when the target has not moved since the branch started. The target name simply slides forward. No new commit appears.
- A **merge commit** is a new commit with **two parents**: the old tip of the target and the tip of the branch.

```
base = merge-base(main, branch)        latest common ancestor
fast-forward possible  ⇔  base == main tip
merge commit M:  parent1 = old main tip,  parent2 = branch tip
```

A merge commit does *not* mean there was a conflict. It only means a two-parent commit was written.

#### Remotes, push, fetch and pull requests

- A **remote** is another copy of the repository. Aster's is called `origin`, on GitHub.
- **Push** uploads your commits to the remote. **Fetch** downloads its commits. **Pull** is fetch then merge.
- A **pull request** (PR) is a GitHub page asking to merge one branch into another. It shows the diff, the automatic check results and any discussion.

Think of submitting a chapter to an editor, who reviews it before it goes into the printed book.

#### Shallow clones and worktrees

A **clone** is a copy of a repository, normally with its full history. A **shallow clone** downloads only recent history. Commits older than its cut-off are invisible, not missing. A claim about an older commit is *unverifiable* in a shallow clone, not false.

This checkout is shallow: 175 commits, with its root at `4d3267c` (2026-09-21) [Certain: `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` = `true`]. The sanity audit met the same trap. Its early readers marked "roughly forty STATUS.md hashes unverifiable" until a session ran `git fetch --deepen=2000` and recovered "the 873 commits of history the default shallow clone hides" (`tools/audit/sanity-69472a3/ASTER_AUDIT_REPORT.md` §1).

A **worktree** is a second working folder that shares one repository database. `/home/user/aster-guide` is one: its `.git` file points into another checkout's `.git/worktrees/` folder [Certain]. A side effect is worth knowing. The *local* branch named `main` in that shared database is stale at `6575d0d` (2026-10-13), while `origin/main` is `cec19e7`. In this chapter, "main" always means `origin/main`.

#### PR #10, the merge you are reading

`cec19e7` is "Merge pull request #10 from hudsonclavin-cloud/s20-front-a", 2026-11-04 10:18 −0500. Its parents are `01e4bb7` (old main) and `9b792bb` (branch tip). It brought in 19 commits [Certain]:

- one evidence commit, `a296efc` ("docs(research): Slice 20 Front A run evidence");

Across those commits, 52 files changed, with 1,039 lines added and 402 deleted (`git diff --shortstat 01e4bb7 cec19e7`). The largest share of the deletions, 178 of 402 (44%), is inside `docs/`, the generated build tree, where deletions on rebuild are expected (AGENTS.md §9 rule 3). Most of the rest are in `src/` (144) and `tests/` (79), where Front A rewrote tests and moved badge code into shared components; 1 is in STATUS.md [Certain: `git diff --numstat 01e4bb7 cec19e7`, summed by top-level folder].

#### A merge is a deploy

GitHub Pages serves the committed `docs/` folder on `main` (Chapter B9). So merging a PR that contains a rebuilt `docs/` *is* a deploy: "a merge before CI finishes is a deploy before CI" (Slice 20 §7; CI is the automatic check server of 12.9). AGENTS.md §9 rule 2 gives the condition for a change to count as live. In it, `npm run build` runs the project's build script through **npm**, the package manager that comes with **Node.js** (the program that runs JavaScript outside a browser); `npm run <name>` runs a script listed in `package.json`.

```
LIVE  ⇔  built (npm run build)
       ∧ docs/ committed in an artifacts-only commit
       ∧ pushed / merged to main by Hudson
       ∧ content-verified in a cache-disabled browser
```

The rule itself says "(c) Hudson's manual push"; since 2026-10-28 that step reaches `main` as a PR merge, hence "pushed / merged". Step (a) is "run by Hudson unless a dispatch carries an explicit §3 waiver" (AGENTS.md:313-318). A green check is not on that list. AGENTS.md §9 records why: on 2026-08-06, "twelve src/v2 commits sat undeployed behind green CI".

#### Branches that are not on main

- **PR #1, the K2 Momentum Bank prototype**, is not part of `main` (K2 is an Aster idea that asks whether an inbound payload's Earth-arrival v∞ fits Skyhook's catch envelope; Section C1.10). Slice 20 §2 lists it as "`origin/claude/k2-momentum-bank`, `8cb8d54`, tools-only, CI green, open" and says it is to be "merged before Front B". Commit `8cb8d54` is absent from this clone and is not an ancestor of `cec19e7` [Certain]. Whether the PR is still open on GitHub cannot be checked from here [Likely open].
- **UNMERGED BRANCH `claude/ux-run-2026-10-22`.** One commit, `ae2efb4` (2026-10-22, author "Claude"), adding a UX problems report with screenshots. It is 1 commit ahead of `main` and 125 behind [Certain: `git rev-list --left-right --count`]. Anything quoted from it must carry that label.

#### Commit messages

AGENTS.md:65 requires `type(scope): description`; its own example is `feat(slice12): add DLA per-cell computation`. A real one from Front A is `0078621`, `test(boundary): count Slice 9 tiers from records`. All 166 visible non-merge subjects follow the form, and 157 include a scope [Certain: a **regular expression**, or regex (a text-matching pattern), run over `git log --no-merges --format=%s`]. The types used are `fix` 54, `docs` 50, `build` 15, `test` 14, `feat` 12, `refactor` 9, `strategy` 4, `research` 3, `chore` 3, `data` 1 and `ci` 1.

The other commit rules (AGENTS.md:60-65) each protect history. Stage files by name, never `git add -A` or `git add .`, so no stray file rides along. Make one logical change per commit, so any change can be reverted alone. Never push from a Codex dispatch, never use `--no-verify`, and never `--amend` a pushed commit, so a cited hash keeps meaning the same thing.

### B12.4 The slice lifecycle and founding documents

#### What a slice is

A **slice** is one numbered unit of project work with a defined scope. Slice 20 is "Return Leg". Slice 19.5 was "Honest Front Door". A slice is split into **fronts** (parallel workstreams such as "Front A") and **phases**. A **dispatch** is one written instruction packet handed to an executing agent.

A **founding document** is the slice's constitution. It is written before the work, and it says what counts as done, what may be cut and what evidence each claim needs. Think of a construction charter signed before ground is broken, with a change-order log at the back.

#### The lifecycle

The in-repo skill `.claude/skills/slice-discipline/SKILL.md`:12-30 calls this order "non-negotiable":

1. **Pre-research.** Measure the inputs before deciding anything: literature plus scripts in `tools/sliceN-research/`.
2. **DECs locked.** Each decision is justified, ideally citing the pre-research.
3. **Founding doc** committed before any implementation dispatch.
4. **Dispatches**, atomic, phase by phase.
5. **Multi-agent audit** on math-layer work, before deploy.
6. **Deploy**: build, commit `docs/`, push, verify live.

Slice 20 followed it closely [Certain: `git log` and `tools/slice20-research/`]:

| Step | Slice 20 evidence | Commit / PR |
|---|---|---|
| Read-only recon | `S20_01-REPORT.md` | `4b75726`, PR #6 |
| Literature pass ("leads, unverified") | `S20_02_return_leg_perplexity.md` | `00ee6d2`, PR #8 |
| Verification, run twice | `S20_03…`, `S20_03b…` | `00ee6d2`, `fa89896`, PR #8 |
| Founding doc DRAFT | `src/v2/SLICE_20_FOUNDING.md` | `b78622e`, PR #8 |
| Hudson's rulings, lock record in §9.1 | +33 lines, 0 deleted | `297242a`, PR #9 |
| Front A executed | 17 commits + evidence | PR #10 |
| Audit before deploy (Front B) | not yet run | — |

Not every slice did. Slice 18 "ran dispatch-first, with DEC-18-1 through DEC-18-4 held only in STATUS"; its founding doc "was created retroactively to correct that" (STATUS.md:141-145). Slice 19 likewise "ran recon → dispatches and did NOT produce a founding doc before implementation" (`src/v2/SLICE_19_FOUNDING.md`:29-30). Both records are honest about the miss.

#### The structure of a founding document

Recent founding docs (Slices 19.5 and 20) use nine sections:

| § | Content |
|---|---|
| 1 | Purpose and scope, with out-of-scope items and their destination slices |
| 2 | Inputs and pre-research |
| 3 | Decisions (DECs) |
| 4 | Open questions (OQs), each with a default |
| 5 | Cut rule: what to drop, in order, if hours run out |
| 6 | Fronts and their gates |
| 7 | Acceptance criteria |
| 8 | Entry and exit conditions, and a size estimate |
| 9 | Amendments and corrections: "Append only. Never edit above this line." |

The skill's own template (SKILL.md:37-71) still has a different eight-section layout (§5 "Locked DECs", §8 "engineering record"). Template and practice have drifted apart [Certain].

#### DRAFT, PROPOSED, RULED, LOCKED

An AI-drafted founding doc starts as **DRAFT**, and its decisions are marked **PROPOSED**. Once Hudson has decided a DEC it is **RULED**; when the whole document is approved it is **LOCKED**, and from then on changes are amendments only. Only Hudson rules and locks; "a model never writes 'LOCKED'" (skill lines 104-109, and the anti-pattern list at 151-153). Because the document is additive-only (Section B12.7), locking cannot rewrite the header. It adds a dated line at the bottom. Slice 20 line 3 still reads "STATUS: DRAFT — not locked", while §9.1 line 370 says "this founding document is LOCKED as of 2026-11-04. This line supersedes the DRAFT header, which stays unedited under the additive rule."

The reading rule follows: **for a founding doc, the bottom governs.** A reader who stops at §3 will think every DEC is still PROPOSED.

Prose dates and git dates can also differ. Slice 19.5 §9.1 records Hudson's Phase 0 ruling as "2026-10-14" and says the document "is LOCKED as of 2026-10-14", but the commit that landed that record, `361ddba`, is dated 2026-10-24 [Certain]. Meanwhile work was already landing under the ruling, for example `a697963` "rebuild after S19.5 FIX1" (2026-10-14) [Certain: `git log --first-parent`]. The DRAFT had been committed first (`6575d0d`, 2026-10-13), so "founding doc before dispatches" held; only the lock record lagged. STATUS.md:141 records a related Slice 18 lesson, after Nova-supplied prose dates proved wrong: "git's own dates govern from here." Read strictly, that would date the 19.5 lock to 2026-10-24 [Likely interpretation].

### B12.5 Naming decisions: DEC, OQ, INV and AMD

Stable identifiers let anyone point at one exact rule months later.

| Prefix | Meaning | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DEC** | A **decision**: PROPOSED, RULED or LOCKED | `DEC-<slice>-<n>` | DEC-20-13 |
| **OQ** | An **open question**, with a default answer until ruled | `OQ-<slice>-<n>` | OQ-20-8 (GM_EARTH value and source) |
| **INV** | An **invariant**: a project-wide technical rule that must never be violated | `INV-<nnn>`, global | INV-024 (external libraries serve only as validation references, "oracles", 12.6) |
| **AMD** | A numbered **amendment** that changes a locked DEC | `AMD-<n>`, with an "amends DEC-X" pointer | Slice 11 AMD-1 "amends DEC-8" |

The rules are not perfectly uniform. Slice 11 uses bare `DEC-1`…`DEC-10`, plus `DEC-11C-1`… for a sub-phase (`src/v2/SLICE_11_FOUNDING.md`:79-147). Invariants carry letter suffixes (INV-016c, -016d, -016e). Slice 16 has local invariants namespaced `INV-S16-033`…`036` (INVARIANTS.md:223-226) [Certain].

#### Amendment discipline

A locked decision is never quietly edited. AGENTS.md §4 lines 194-195 forbid modifying a DEC "without recording it as an amendment in the founding doc's §5a with the 'amends DEC-X' marker pattern". `src/v2/SLICE_11_FOUNDING.md` §5a shows the pattern: "The locked DEC text in §5 is preserved unchanged; this section records the deltas with explicit 'amends DEC-X' pointers." Later slices use other spellings for the same idea, such as Slice 20's "DEC-20-3 … (amends DEC-17-10 additively)".

It works like a bank ledger. You never rub out a wrong entry. You add a correcting entry, and the original stays visible.

#### When identifiers collide

Recorded collisions [Certain, sources cited]: **INV-014** had two meanings, so ruling R2 split it into INV-014a and INV-014b (INVARIANTS.md:253). **Slice 16 reused INV-033…036** locally while global INV-033 and INV-034 existed; the local ones were mapped, not rewritten, to INV-S16-033…036. **"F2"** names three different findings (STATUS.md cleanup C16). And the index row for INV-017…020 still says "no partial renders" (INVARIANTS.md:194), which the sanity audit (V6) found does not match INV-019; the fix (Slice 19.5 item C5) is routed to Slice 24.

The INV-037 number choice shows the discipline at work (INVARIANTS.md:240). The next free global number was 035. But Slice 16 documents use bare "INV-035" and "INV-036" for local rules. So "035 and 036 are therefore skipped as ambiguous-on-sight, and INV-037 is the first unambiguous global number. Skipping two integers is cheaper than a reference a reader must disambiguate by file location."

### B12.6 Verify-before-lock, tripwires and STOP gates

#### Verify-before-lock

AGENTS.md §2 (lines 92-96) sets the rule, called **verify-before-lock**:

> No measurement, threshold, or DEC gets locked until independently verified against an oracle or an independent measurement. "It looks right" is not verification. "It reproduces value X against oracle Y within tolerance Z" is.

An **oracle** is a trusted external reference whose answer you compare against, for example the poliastro Python library for Lambert solutions, the orbit that joins two positions in a given time (INV-024; Chapter B5 covers Lambert's problem and Chapter B8 covers oracles in depth). The same section asks for "at least two independent recon passes before a DEC is written". A **recon** is a read-only investigation.

```
pass  ⇔  |x_aster − x_oracle| ≤ tolerance
```

Slice 20's lock record (§9.1, lines 364-365) adds a rule for external facts: "an external number a DEC rests on needs two agreeing verification runs, or its primary source opened directly by Hudson or Clome."

Why two runs? If one run wrongly confirms a claim with probability p, two *independent* runs both do so with probability p². Runs that share a cause of error are not independent. A simple model: with probability ρ the second run just repeats the first run's verdict, and otherwise it errs independently:

```
P(both wrong) = p · ( ρ + (1 − ρ) · p )
  ρ = 0  →  p²   (fully independent)
  ρ = 1  →  p    (the same mistake twice; no gain)
```

In this model ρ is exactly the correlation coefficient between the two runs' "wrong" indicators: the covariance is P(both wrong) − p² = ρ·p·(1 − p), and each indicator's variance is p·(1 − p) [Certain: algebra]. With an illustrative p = 0.1: ρ = 0 gives 0.01, ρ = 0.5 gives 0.1 × (0.5 + 0.5 × 0.1) = 0.1 × 0.55 = 0.055, and ρ = 1 gives 0.1 [the numbers are illustrative, Speculative as a model of real research runs]. Asking the same research tool twice sits nearer ρ = 1, which is why the rule also accepts a primary source opened by a person.

The rule earned its place. The S20_03 verification prompt was run twice in fresh threads, and the runs disagreed on 2 of 16 items (Slice 20 §9.1):
- **#10 Hayabusa2:** run 2 found 11.8 km/s inertial (Prabhu et al. 2022).
- **#14 Keck 2012 Earth-arrival C3:** run 1 said UNVERIFIABLE, run 2 said CONFIRMED.

Hudson resolved #14 by opening slide 31 of the primary presentation himself on 2026-11-04. The values the DECs actually rest on were confirmed by both runs from different primary sources. They come from **NHATS**, NASA's study of human-accessible near-Earth asteroid targets (expansion from memory, verify; see Chapter B3): an entry-speed criterion of ≤ 12 km/s at 125 km altitude, an 8-day minimum stay at the asteroid, and separate outbound and return Lambert legs.

#### STOP gates and tripwires

Dispatches use two control devices, and each dispatch must say which one it uses ("Know which the dispatch uses", AGENTS.md §2 lines 67-79; `.claude/skills/dispatch-writer/SKILL.md`:113-131).

- A **STOP gate** is positional: "STOP after step N. Hudson verifies X." The run cannot pass it, however well the steps went. Math-layer changes stop until an oracle value is reproduced. UI changes stop for Hudson's browser check before `npm run build`.
- A **tripwire** is conditional: "run to completion; stop ONLY if `<measurable condition>` fires." Conditions must be measurable, "never vibes". When one fires, the final report replaces "next steps" with "what I found and why I stopped".

```
conditional tripwire:  continue(step k)  ⇔  not fired(k)
positional STOP gate:  continue(step k)  ⇔  Hudson approved(k − 1)
```

Think of a climber's turnaround time. You choose it at base camp, while calm, so you cannot argue past it at altitude.

Two Slice 20 examples [Certain]:

- **A tripwire that did not fire.** Front A's W4-0 recon was to halt above 40 badge construction sites. It found 9 badge or colour sites, 2 `C3Value` calls and 4 raw C3 formatter sites, "below the 40-site halt threshold" (`frontA-REPORT.md`:135-137), so work continued.
- **A tripwire that did fire.** The first Front A attempt reported "FRONT-A: STOPPED(a)" (`frontA-attempt1-REPORT.md`). PR #8 had merged the founding DRAFT before Hudson committed the lock record. So `main` (`d2f7f68`) held a 338-line doc with no "LOCKED as of 2026-11-04" line, and the working tree held an uncommitted 33-line lock edit. The run did not "help" by committing a protected file. It stopped, wrote its evidence, and named its files "attempt1" so a relaunch would not trip AGENTS §2.1 rule 8 ("A 'create' target that already exists is a TRIPWIRE"). PR #9 then landed the lock (`297242a`) and the evidence (`43adf6b`), and the second attempt passed.

Stopping is not failure. The stop *was* the safety system working.

### B12.7 Git hooks: turnstiles at the door

#### What a hook is, and when it runs

A **git hook** is a script git runs automatically at a fixed moment. `pre-commit` runs before a commit is recorded. `pre-push` runs before an upload. If the script exits with a nonzero **exit code** (a program's numeric "status" when it finishes; 0 means success), git cancels the action.

A hook is a turnstile that only lets you through if your ticket checks out. But a turnstile exists only at the entrance where someone installed it. Three conditions must all hold:

```
hook runs  ⇔  core.hooksPath points at the hook folder (Aster: .githooks)
            ∧ the hook file is executable (git mode 100755, not 100644)
            ∧ the user did not pass --no-verify
```

**`core.hooksPath`** is a git setting naming the folder git looks in for hooks. It is a *local* setting, so it never travels with a clone. Git ignores `.githooks/` completely unless that setting points at it [Certain: demonstrated in the sandbox below].

Git records a **file mode** for every tracked file. In the mode `100755`, "100" marks a regular file (from memory, verify). "755" is a Unix permission triple: 7 = read 4 + write 2 + execute 1 for the owner, and 5 = read 4 + execute 1 for everyone else. A `100644` file has no execute bit, and git skips a non-executable hook with only a hint.

#### How Aster installs its hooks

`package.json`:10 defines `"prepare": "node tools/setup-hooks.mjs"`. npm runs `prepare` during `npm ci` and `npm install`, the two commands that install a project's libraries (from memory, verify; `npm ci` is described in Section B12.9). The script is 13 lines (`tools/setup-hooks.mjs`):

1. Run `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree`.
2. If that succeeds, run `git config core.hooksPath .githooks` and print `setup-hooks: configured core.hooksPath = .githooks`.
3. Wrap both in `try { … } catch { }`, so any error is swallowed: "npm prepare also runs outside a checkout; installation must remain successful."

Both hooks are committed executable: `git ls-files -s .githooks` shows `100755` for each [Certain]. The history is short and instructive:

| Date | Commit | Change |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-22 | `f7b19e7` | pre-commit counts deletions with `--numstat`; guarded set widened (C17) |
| 2026-10-26 | `e5cdc9d` | `prepare` script added: hooks install in every clone (DEC-19.5-7) |
| 2026-10-28 | `0741fee` | both hooks marked executable (DEC-19.5-7) |

Before `e5cdc9d` and `0741fee`, the hooks did nothing in a fresh clone: "'Hook-enforced' is false in any clone" (ASTER_AUDIT_REPORT.md §8). The audit explains why nobody noticed: "On Windows the exec bit is not modelled, which is why it works on one machine". That machine was presumably Hudson's Windows checkout (STATUS.md:13 names `C:\Users\hudso\…` as the canonical repo) [Likely].

#### The pre-push hook

`.githooks/pre-push` is 9 lines. If the environment variable `ASTER_PUSH_OK` equals `1`, it exits 0. Otherwise it prints "PUSH BLOCKED … pushing is Hudson's manual act" and exits 1. An **environment variable** is a named setting passed to a program by the shell that starts it.

That is all it does. It does not look at what is being pushed. Its message names a `git hpush` alias, which is not defined anywhere in the repository (`git config --get alias.hpush` prints nothing here) [Certain]. Older run reports tell Hudson to run `ASTER_PUSH_OK=1 git hpush` (for example `tools/frontb-2026-08-11/RUN_REPORT.md`:142), so the alias presumably lives in Hudson's own git configuration [Likely].

#### The pre-commit hook, line by line

`.githooks/pre-commit` is 75 lines of POSIX shell script. A **shell** is the command-line language that starts programs and joins their output; "POSIX" means the portable subset every Unix-like system understands. Here is what each part does [Certain: file read].

| Lines | What happens |
|---|---|
| 2-3 | List staged paths: `git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACMRD` (added, copied, modified, renamed, deleted; letters from memory, verify). Nothing staged → exit 0. |
| 4-6 | If `ASTER_PROTECTED_OK=1`, exit 0 at once, before any check. |
| 7-11 | If `.dispatch-scope` is missing: "COMMIT BLOCKED … (fail-closed)", exit 1. |
| 12-28 | Helpers: strip a trailing carriage return and surrounding spaces from each scope line; print a hex hint when a path only matches after that clean-up. |
| 30-37 | For each staged path (except the scope file itself): if it is `src/v2/core/*`, `.githooks/*`, `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`, print "BLOCKED protected path". |
| 38-48 | Otherwise the path must match a scope line as a shell `case` pattern. Blank and `#` lines are skipped. No match: "BLOCKED out-of-scope path". |
| 64-73 | For guarded documents, count deleted lines with `git diff --cached --numstat`; any deletion: "BLOCKED: N deletion line(s)". |
| 74 | Any block: "Commit rejected", exit 1. |

#### `.dispatch-scope`: the work permit

**`.dispatch-scope`** is a plain-text allowlist, one path pattern per line. Every dispatch writes it first, listing exactly the files that dispatch may commit (AGENTS.md §2.1 rule 2). It is a contractor's permit naming the rooms they may enter.

```
allowed(f)  ⇔  f == ".dispatch-scope"
            ∨ ( f ∉ Protected  ∧  some scope line p matches f as a shell case pattern )
no .dispatch-scope file  ⇒  every commit blocked   ("fail-closed")
```

**Fail-closed** means that when the guard cannot decide, it refuses. The opposite, **fail-open**, would silently disable the check whenever the file went missing.

Two matching details catch people out [Certain: AGENTS.md §9 rule 4; sandbox]:
- In a shell `case` pattern, `*` also crosses `/`. So `docs/*` matches `docs/v2/porkchop/index.html`.
- A bare `docs/` matches nothing, because a pattern without a wildcard must equal the whole path.

The guard has caught real slips. In Front A, "one initial `.dispatch-scope` typo was rejected by the hook and corrected without override" (`frontA-LOG.md`:21). The report names it: the scope listed `src/v2/porkchop/porkchop-view.ts` under the wrong folder, `src/v2/app/porkchop` (`frontA-REPORT.md`:169-172). The ephemeris roll shows the normal rhythm instead: one scope per commit, each "restored with `git checkout -- .dispatch-scope` after commit" (`roll-REPORT.md`:25).

Two quirks [Certain]:
- **The committed scope file is stale.** `.dispatch-scope` is tracked (blob `44535f4`) and holds a Slice 18 scope: a comment "S18 — founding doc §9 C-5 …" and three Slice 18 paths. Dispatches overwrite it locally and restore it afterwards, as above. So in a fresh clone the fail-closed branch never fires; an agent that forgets its scope inherits three old paths instead of a refusal. A changed scope file can also ride along in a commit by mistake. The UNMERGED BRANCH `claude/ux-run-2026-10-22` shows this: its one commit, `ae2efb4`, also changes `.dispatch-scope` [Certain: `git show --stat ae2efb4`; not on main].
- **Paths with spaces would be split.** Line 30 loops `for f in $STAGED`, which splits on whitespace. No tracked path (of 1,212) contains a space today [Certain]. The usual failure would be a block, the safe direction, because a split fragment matches no exact scope line [Likely: a broad wildcard scope line could still let a fragment through].

#### Protected paths

Four **protected paths** are always blocked for agents: `src/v2/core/*` (the math core), `.githooks/*` (the guards themselves), `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` (the rulebooks). Listing them in `.dispatch-scope` does not help; the protected check runs first. Only Hudson's override passes them.

Founding documents are *not* on that list. Slice 20 calls its own file a "protected path; Hudson hand-commits" (line 4; the [P] gate at line 243 says the same), but that is policy, not mechanism. The hook only counts deletions in founding docs (next section). An in-scope, purely additive edit to a founding doc commits without any override [Certain: sandbox step "additive append to SLICE_20_FOUNDING.md, in scope, no override (exit 0)"]. Front A's attempt-1 report says the lock commit "needs `ASTER_PROTECTED_OK`"; mechanically, it did not.

#### The additive-only guard and `git diff --numstat`

Some documents may only be *added to*, never trimmed. The **additive-only guard** is the part of the hook that enforces this (pre-commit line 66). It covers:
- `INVARIANTS.md`;
- every `SLICE_*_FOUNDING.md` at the repo root (where `SLICE_17_FOUNDING.md` lives);
- every `src/v2/*_FOUNDING.md`. Because `*` crosses `/`, this also reaches files *inside* `src/v2/founding-drafts/`, but only those whose names end `_FOUNDING.md` (today just `DOSSIER_FOUNDING.md`). The hook's comment (lines 59-60) says "src/v2/founding-drafts/ is covered", which overstates it: the folder's other four files, such as `DECISIONS_2026-07-07.md`, are not guarded [Certain: every tracked path classified with the hook's own `case` patterns];
- every `src/v2/*_LOCKED.md`.

**`git diff --numstat`** prints one line per file: `<added> <deleted> <path>`, or `- - <path>` for binary files. With `--cached` it describes what is staged for the next commit. The hook sums the deleted column and blocks if the sum is above 0:

```
D(doc) = Σ deleted  over numstat lines where deleted ≠ "-"
block  ⇔  D(doc) > 0        (unless ASTER_PROTECTED_OK=1)
```

STATUS.md is deliberately absent: "it is the living file and is rewritten every session" (hook comment, line 63). Two important documents are also absent, by pattern rather than by choice: `V2_FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md` (the source of INV-001…013) and `FOUNDING_DOCUMENT.md` match none of the guarded patterns [Certain: classification re-run over `git ls-files` with the patterns of line 66].

#### Worked example 12.2: why the hook counts with numstat, not with a text pattern

*Inputs:* a three-bullet Markdown list with the middle bullet deleted (a sandbox file, `old.md` → `new.md`); the old hook pattern `^-[^-]` (quoted in the hook's comment, lines 50-55); the real commits `297242a` and `9b792bb`.

Step 1. In a unified diff, a deleted line is shown with a leading `-`. A deleted bullet `- INV-B delete me` therefore appears as `-- INV-B delete me`. The diff header also contains a line starting `---`.

Step 2. Count with the old pattern `^-[^-]` ("a dash, then one character that is not a dash"). The deleted bullet's second character is a dash, so it does not match. The header's second character is a dash too. Count = **0**. The deletion is invisible. (The same pattern also misses a deleted *blank* line, which a diff shows as a lone `-` with no second character at all [Certain: `printf -- '-\n' | grep -c '^-[^-]'` gives 0].)

Step 3. Count with `^-` ("any line starting with a dash"). It matches the header and the deletion. Count = **2**. This is sound only if you know to expect exactly one header line per file.

Step 4. Count with `^- ` ("dash, then space"). The deleted bullet starts `--`, so no match. Count = **0**.

Step 5. Ask git: `git diff --no-index --numstat old.md new.md` prints `0 1 old.md => new.md`. Deleted = **1**, the truth [Certain: all four counts re-run during fact-checking].

Step 6. Apply numstat to two real commits.
- The Slice 20 lock record `297242a`: `33 0 src/v2/SLICE_20_FOUNDING.md`. D = 0, so it passes. The file grew from 338 lines at `d2f7f68` to 338 + 33 = 371 lines at `cec19e7`, which matches `wc -l` [Certain].
- The DEC-20-13 amendment `9b792bb`: `2 0 AGENTS.md`. Purely additive.

*Result:* only numstat, or `^-` with the header as the one expected line, proves a change additive. The hook's own comment says it best: "git reports deletions as a number, so there is no pattern left to get wrong."

This exposes a small error in a run report. Front A's report says its additive proof for AGENTS.md was `Select-String '^- '` and that it "printed only `--- a/AGENTS.md`" (`frontA-REPORT.md`:116-117). The pattern `^- ` cannot match that line. On the real commit, `grep -c '^- '` gives 0, while `grep '^-'` prints exactly `--- a/AGENTS.md` [Certain]. The recorded command or its output is wrong, most likely a slip from `^-` to `^- ` [Likely]. The amendment is additive either way.

The guard has held. In the visible history, 17 commits touched 7 guarded documents, adding 1,406 lines and deleting 0 [Certain: `git log --numstat` over the visible history, root commit excluded, re-run during fact-checking]. The sanity audit reports zero deletions in every guarded document across 923 commits (ASTER_AUDIT_REPORT.md:92, 96-97), a figure that cannot be re-checked in this shallow clone.

AGENTS.md is protected but *not* additive-guarded. That gap mattered once: the `fab7c22` rewrite deleted 31 lines and lost three standing rules, which PR #3 restored (Section B12.3).

#### Overrides: drift protection, not security

Two environment variables override the hooks: `ASTER_PROTECTED_OK=1` for commits and `ASTER_PUSH_OK=1` for pushes. AGENTS.md §2.1 rules 1-3 say only Hudson uses them, per command, never saved in a profile.

The hooks catch honest slips, not a determined person: `git commit --no-verify` and unsetting `core.hooksPath` both bypass them. AGENTS.md:136-138 says so: "hooks are drift-protection, not adversary-proofing … using them against these rules is itself a violation, is loud in history". It is a "Staff only" sign, not a locked door.

The code is broader than the prose in one place. AGENTS.md:121-122 calls `ASTER_PROTECTED_OK=1` an override "for protected paths and additive amendments", but hook lines 4-6 exit before *any* check, scope included. In the sandbox, an out-of-scope file under `src/v2/core/` committed with the override set [Certain]. Hudson's sanctioned sequence writes an exact `.dispatch-scope` first (`frontA-attempt1-REPORT.md` command block), but the hook would not notice if he skipped it.

#### What the sandbox showed

Byte-identical copies of both hooks (sha256 prefixes `c0017c858c15` and `25a61bb11549`, matching the repo's files) were run in a throwaway repository with git 2.43.0 on Linux. The script, written for this guide, was run three times, each in a fresh sandbox (researcher, writer, fact-checker). The outputs were identical apart from git's own per-run commit ids [Certain].

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| `core.hooksPath` unset; delete an INVARIANTS bullet | accepted (no hook runs) |
| `core.hooksPath` set, hooks mode 644 | accepted, with git's hint "hook was ignored because it's not set as executable" |
| Executable, no `.dispatch-scope` | "COMMIT BLOCKED … (fail-closed)" |
| `AGENTS.md` listed in scope | "BLOCKED protected path: AGENTS.md" |
| INVARIANTS bullet deleted, file in scope | "BLOCKED: 1 deletion line(s) in INVARIANTS.md" |
| Additive append to `SLICE_20_FOUNDING.md`, in scope | accepted, no override needed |
| `docs/v2/b.js` with scope `docs/` / with `docs/*` | blocked / accepted |
| Out-of-scope `src/v2/core/k.ts` with `ASTER_PROTECTED_OK=1` | accepted (total bypass) |
| `pre-push` without / with `ASTER_PUSH_OK=1` | "PUSH BLOCKED", exit 1 / exit 0 |

A real clone showed the same before-and-after (Slice 19.5 §9.3, Nova, 2026-10-28): after `npm ci`, a fresh Linux clone at `20dd7ca` rejected a one-line INVARIANTS.md deletion, while "before `0741fee` the same clone ACCEPTED the deletion, because the hook files were mode 100644 and git ignored them."

#### The hooks are off in this checkout

`git config --get core.hooksPath` exits 1 here: the setting is unset, locally and globally [Certain]. This checkout never ran `npm ci`, so `prepare` never ran. Every guard above is inactive in it. That is exactly the caveat in AGENTS.md:100-106: the rules are "mechanically enforced only where those hooks are installed. A fresh clone before npm installation, web editors, and the GitHub UI do not have these local-hook checks." A PR merged on GitHub's website is never checked by these hooks at all.

### B12.8 Tests, the test runner and tests that can fail

#### Tests and the runner

A **test** is code that runs production code and **asserts** an expected result, failing loudly if the result differs. A test is an exam question with a known answer. **`node --test`** is the test runner built into Node.js (built in since Node 18, from memory, verify). A **test file** for Aster's root suite ends `.test.mjs` (a JavaScript module); the MCP package's own tests (MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is how AI agents call Aster's tools; Chapter B10) are TypeScript files, `mcp/test/*.test.ts`. **TypeScript** is JavaScript with type annotations that a compiler checks (Chapter B9).

`tools/run-tests.mjs` is Aster's own wrapper, the "proctor" who must also count every paper handed in. Its header (lines 1-18) explains the shape: one hung file can wedge a single `node --test` run forever, and "a file killed externally VANISHES from node's summary arithmetic … a silent skip is false-green by subtraction".

What it does [Certain: file read]:
- **Discovery** (`walk`, `shouldSkip`, lines 178-197): every `*.test.mjs` under `tests/` and `src/v2/`, recursively, skipping any `node_modules` or `docs` folder.
- **Isolation** (`runOne`, lines 102-148): each file runs in its own child process, `node --test --test-timeout=120000 <file>`.
- **Two timeouts.** A per-*test* limit of 120,000 ms, and a per-*file* wall clock `ASTER_FILE_TIMEOUT`, default 180,000 ms. The second catches module-load hangs, where no test ever starts. A timed-out file's whole process tree is killed (`taskkill /T` on Windows, `kill(-pid)` on POSIX) and recorded as LOAD-TIMEOUT.
- **Accounting** (lines 90-98): the runner checks its own arithmetic with an **accounting identity**, an equation that must hold if no file vanished.

```
files_discovered = files_ok + files_failed + files_load_timeout
   mismatch  ⇒  "ACCOUNTING MISMATCH", exit 1
GREEN  ⇔  failed = 0  ∧  load_timeout = 0
```

AGENTS.md §9.1 rule 1 adds the policy: "A test run is green at N/N or it is not green." Example: 109 discovered, 107 ok, 1 failed, 1 timed out. The identity 109 = 107 + 1 + 1 holds, so the accounting is fine, but the run is red.

One known flaw: `parseCounts` (lines 167-176) takes the *first* `pass N` and `fail N` in a child's mixed output. A log line such as "will pass 2 of 3 probes" printed before the summary makes the headline undercount (reproduced with synthetic output for this guide). STATUS cleanup C15 records a real case: a headline of 302 when the per-file summaries summed to 303. The per-file exit codes and the accounting were right, so the *gate* was right. Quote "109/109 files, 0 failures" as the gate; treat "tests passed: N" as secondary.

#### Worked example 12.3: what the runner sees versus what `npm test` sees

*Inputs:* the discovery rule in `tools/run-tests.mjs`:25, 178-197; `package.json`:12 `"test": "node --test tests/*.test.mjs"`; the files at `cec19e7`.

Step 1. Re-implement `walk` and `shouldSkip` in Python and run them over both roots (recomputed for this guide; re-run in the fact-check).

Step 2. Under `tests/`: 99 files. Of these, 86 sit at the top level and 13 in subfolders (12 in `tests/v2-lambert/`, 1 in `tests/v2-golden/`).

Step 3. Under `src/v2/`: 10 colocated files (for example `src/v2/porkchop/support-boundary.test.mjs`).

Step 4. Total discovered: 99 + 10 = **109**. `git ls-files` agrees: 109 tracked `*.test.mjs` files under those two roots. (The repository tracks 115 `*.test.mjs` files in all; the other 6 are the Slice 16 harness tests in `tools/slice16-harness/test/`, which the runner never visits.)

Step 5. A **glob** is a filename pattern in which `*` stands for any run of characters. Here the shell (or, on Windows, Node's own `--test` pattern matching; from memory, verify) expands `tests/*.test.mjs`. In a filename glob `*` does not cross `/` (unlike a shell `case` pattern, 12.7), so it does not enter subfolders. `npm test` therefore reaches **86**.

Step 6. Missed: 109 − 86 = **23** files (12 + 1 nested under `tests/`, plus 10 under `src/v2/`), including the golden-numbers test. Coverage 86 / 109 = 0.789 = **78.9%**.

*Result:* the full gate is `npm run verify` (`typecheck:v2` then `test:all`, `package.json`:15), which the run reports that ran tests cite (for example `frontA-REPORT.md`:36-41, `ephemeris-roll/roll-LOG.md`:9). Yet AGENTS.md:32 and AGENTS.md:185 still tell agents to run `node --test tests/*.test.mjs`, and so does QA.md. The 2026-07-31 audit measured the same gap at 55 of 71 files (L4-3). Slice 14's locked DEC-14-5 had already asked to "widen the `npm test` glob to `tests/**/*.test.mjs` so `tests/v2-lambert/` actually runs" (`src/v2/SLICE_14_FOUNDING.md`:142), yet `package.json`:12 still has the narrow glob [Certain]. The gap has persisted for at least three months.

#### Recorded suite sizes

These were not re-run here.

| Date | Files | Tests | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-13 | 74 | 256 | AGENTS.md:335-336 |
| 2026-09-21 | 81 | 304 (1 skipped) | STATUS.md:357 (Test State) |

| 2026-11-03 | 107 | 356 | `roll-REPORT.md`:3 |

#### Tests that can fail

A test that compares production code with a copy of itself always passes, like checking your arithmetic by redoing it with the same mistaken method. A **mutation check** is the cure: deliberately break the production code, confirm a test turns red, then restore. A general measure, the **mutation score** (textbook, not used by the repo):

```
mutation score = killed / (total mutants − equivalent mutants)
  killed      = mutants that made at least one test fail
  equivalent  = mutants that do not change behaviour
```

The sanity audit found several tests that could not fail (Theme 4): an architecture test that did not enforce its wall, a Slice 9 tier assertion that compared the fixture to itself, and an "independent re-implementation" of a boundary that was a transcription. Slice 20 Front A strengthened six test groups (E1-E6; E6 is the eight "source-text" copy guards Slice 19.5 left behind) and recorded a mutation for each (`frontA-REPORT.md`:42-77) [Certain, as recorded]:

| Item | Test | Mutation | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | `tests/v2-architecture.test.mjs` | an alias import outside V2 | rejected with the offender's path |
| E2 | `tests/v2-boundary-slice9.test.mjs` | one catalog record changed to planning tier | failed |
| E3 | `src/v2/porkchop/support-boundary.test.mjs` | production `>=` changed to `>` | failed at line 137 |

### B12.9 Continuous integration, line by line

**Continuous integration** (CI) means a server automatically checks out the code and runs checks on every push or PR. It is a neutral second machine that does not share your laptop's quirks. **GitHub Actions** is GitHub's CI service. It reads **YAML** workflow files (an indentation-based configuration format) from `.github/workflows/`. Aster has one: `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, 93 lines.

| Lines | Content | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `name: CI` | The label in the Actions tab |
| 3-8 | comment | History and intent (stale; see below) |
| 10-14 | `on: push: branches: [main]`, `pull_request:`, `workflow_dispatch:` | Triggers: a push to `main`, every PR, and a manual "run" button |
| 16 | `jobs:` | Four **jobs**. Each runs on its own fresh `ubuntu-latest` virtual machine, in parallel by default (from memory, verify) |
| 17-34 | `typecheck` | `actions/checkout@v4`; `actions/setup-node@v4` with Node `'24'` and an npm cache; `npm ci`; `npx tsc --noEmit` |
| 36-53 | `build` | checkout; Node 24; `npm ci`; `npm run build` |
| 55-72 | `golden-numbers` | checkout; Node 24; **no** `npm ci`; `node --test tests/v2-golden/launch-vehicles.golden.test.mjs` |
| 74-93 | `full-tests` | checkout with `fetch-depth: 0`; Node 24; `npm ci`; `node tools/run-tests.mjs` |

Terms in that table:
- **`npm ci`** installs dependencies exactly as pinned in `package-lock.json` (from memory, verify). On the runner it also triggers `prepare`, which is harmless because CI never commits.
- **`tsc --noEmit`** runs the TypeScript compiler as a type checker only (Chapter B9). Its config, `tsconfig.json`, has `"strict": false` and excludes the legacy V1 folders [Certain].
- **`fetch-depth: 0`** asks for full history; the default is one commit (from memory, verify).
- `golden-numbers` skips `npm ci` because "the test only touches node builtins and the self-contained launch-vehicles module" (ci.yml:67-68). It loads that TypeScript module directly through Node's built-in type-stripping, which needs "Node >= 22.18 / 24" (ci.yml:65-67).

The workflow's verdict is the AND of its jobs; one red job makes the run red (from memory, verify). Wall-clock time is roughly the slowest job plus queue time, because jobs run in parallel.

CI never deploys and never writes to the repo. The `build` job proves the Vite build succeeds (Vite is the bundler that turns the source into the `docs/` files; Chapter B9); its output is thrown away with the virtual machine. It never compares its output with the committed `docs/`, so a green build says nothing about whether `docs/` is current (Chapter B9).

#### Worked example 12.4: the golden-numbers "df3225f catcher"

A **golden-numbers test** pins exact production outputs, so any silent change to them turns CI red. The name of this one comes from a past accident. Commit `df3225f` added a New Glenn data point `{ c3: 5, payloadKg: 6360 }` that re-sloped the payload curve; it was reverted in `bcf1738` as failing INV-022 (sourced vehicle data) (`tests/v2-golden/launch-vehicles.golden.test.mjs`:3-7). Both commits are older than this shallow clone, so the story rests on that comment and on `src/v2/SLICE_14_FOUNDING.md`:98. C3 is the launch energy a rocket must give the payload, in km²/s²; Chapter B7 covers C3 and launch-vehicle curves.

*Inputs:* New Glenn Standard anchors from `src/v2/porkchop/launch-vehicles.ts`:157-160: (C3 0, 7,180 kg), (10, 4,930), (20, 2,365), (30, 120), each "NASA LSP elvperf, as-of 2024-02-29" (LSP is NASA's Launch Services Program; expansion from memory, verify). The golden row `['New Glenn', 'Standard', 5, 6055]` (golden test line 51). Production interpolates linearly between neighbouring anchors (`payloadAtC3`, `launch-vehicles.ts`:229-235).

Step 1. C3 = 5 km²/s² lies between the anchors at 0 and 10. The interpolation fraction is t = (5 − 0) / (10 − 0) = 0.5.

Step 2. Payload = 7,180 + 0.5 × (4,930 − 7,180) = 7,180 + 0.5 × (−2,250) = 7,180 − 1,125 = **6,055 kg**. That is the golden value.

Step 3. Re-add the reverted anchor (5, 6,360). Payload at C3 = 5 becomes 6,360 ≠ 6,055, so the job fails.

Step 4. Neighbours shift too. At C3 = 2 the payload goes from 6,730 to 6,852 kg; at C3 = 8, from 5,380 to 5,502 kg (recomputed for this guide; re-run in the fact-check).

*Result:* one pinned row guards the whole curve segment. The test's header states the rule for a legitimate change: update the golden row "in the SAME commit as the data change — never edit production to make this test pass; the test follows the data."

#### What CI does not cover, and where its record lags

- **Stale header.** Lines 4-7 say "Two gates" and that CI "never builds docs/". The file defines four jobs, including `build` running `npm run build` (inside the throwaway runner). CI began as two gates under DEC-14-5 ("Trigger: push to main", `src/v2/SLICE_14_FOUNDING.md`:139-141). The comment fix (Slice 19.5 C9) was routed to Slice 24 [Certain].
- **A likely vestigial setting.** `fetch-depth: 0` came in with `62ddb17` (2026-10-25) because "about-evidence test reads a pinned commit". The next day `cc41045` made that test "pin evidence links without reading git history". At HEAD only `tests/setup-hooks.test.mjs` runs git, in a temporary folder [Likely: full history is no longer needed].
- **Missing suites.** CI runs neither the MCP package's tests (`mcp/test/*.test.ts`, run only by `npm test` inside `mcp/`) nor the six Slice 16 harness test files (`tools/slice16-harness/test/*.test.mjs`). STATUS.md:366 still lists this as "CI gap, still open (L4-1)".
- **Node versions.** CI pins Node 24. AGENTS.md:333-336 records "the laptop" on v24.18.0 (2026-08-13), but the Slice 20 recon ran on "Hudson's laptop" with "node v26.7.0" (`S20_01-REPORT.md`:9-10). If that is the same machine, local and CI now differ by two major versions [Likely].
- **Run history** (STATUS.md:356, 363, 508-520; Slice 19.5 §9.3) [Certain, as recorded]. Runs #70-72 were red from false test-fixture premises (fixed `88b9133`). Run #78 was green at `5a00907` (2026-08-13). Runs #103-#104 were red at `550c29b` and `cb18cc3` from a test-harness race (fixed `111cffa`), and "Slice 19 was locked before CI was confirmed green — a process miss". CI was green on `main` at `fa821cb`, confirmed by Hudson 2026-11-02. No CI result for `cec19e7` is recorded in the repository; it lives only on the GitHub Actions page, which this chapter did not consult.

AGENTS.md §9.1 rule 2 closes the loop: "Red CI on `main` blocks the next push until investigated. Green Pages does not excuse red CI."

### B12.10 Audits

An **audit** is a systematic, read-only check of claims against evidence, ideally by readers who did not write the work. A **multi-lens** audit gives each reader a different viewpoint, and one lens is told to try to *refute*. It is peer review plus a devil's advocate. Aster has two committed repository audits.

#### REPO_AUDIT_2026-07-31

Marker `ASTER-REPO-AUDIT-2026-07-31-A`, audit date 2026-08-01, seven lanes (`tools/audit/REPO_AUDIT_2026-07-31.md`). It now opens with "SUPERSEDED (2026-10-25). Historical record only; do not act on it." Its four CRITICAL items concerned the Slice 16 study (a grader with false passes and failures, a pre-run state committed 74 seconds before collection, a run that crossed its halt threshold at row 147 but reached 275 rows; Chapter B11) and false or incomplete public trust claims, including an npm package that "hides a dirty publish build". Its HIGH item: CI tested neither the MCP package nor the Slice 16 instrument, "the default test command omits 16 files", and there was no root README.

By the time of the next audit, three of this one's summary claims were false: at `69472a3` there was a root README, all fourteen run ledgers were tracked, and a path it cited did not exist (ASTER_AUDIT_REPORT.md §5). The first two were probably true on 2026-08-01 and fixed afterwards (STATUS.md:538 records the ledgers landing as tracked evidence in `c037448`), so on those points the July audit had gone stale rather than been wrong [Likely]. The lesson is the same either way: an audit is a snapshot, and it ages like any current-state record (Section B12.11).

#### The sanity audit at `69472a3`

AGENTS.md §5 names `tools/audit/sanity-69472a3/` as the current audit. Its facts (ASTER_AUDIT_REPORT.md §1-§2, §13) [Certain, as recorded]:

- **Method:** 20 independent domain readers checking their part of the corpus with commands. Findings then went to two verifiers, one reproducing and one told to "try hard to refute it"; "lower-severity findings got a single combined pass" (§1). In the register, 204 of the 305 MEDIUM and LOW rows show "checked 0", meaning single-source (the same 204 that `SLICE_19_5_FOUNDING.md`:49 counts). The 14 HIGH rows with "checked 0" were still queued for verification when the report was written, so the orchestrator checked their load-bearing claims personally (§10a) [Certain: rows counted from §13].
- **Cost overrun:** one reader "spawned six real cloud sessions … about $71", unplanned. That is the origin of AGENTS.md §2.1 rule 7: no agent spawns sessions unless the dispatch says so.
- **Register:** "326 findings survived; 4 were refuted outright": 21 HIGH + 124 MEDIUM + 181 LOW = 326. Eighty findings went through adversarial verification, of which 4 were refuted and roughly a third corrected or downgraded (§10a, line 435).
- **Verdict:** "The V2 math is sound. The V2 record of it has drifted. And what the public actually lands on is neither — it is the V1 app."

Its control-plane findings bear directly on this chapter:
- STATUS.md was 36 commits behind, and "a session following that rule today stops on a false alarm";
- "Hook-enforced" was false in any clone (Section B12.7);
- several tests could not fail (Section B12.8);
- 14 Slice 18 scripts hardcode one machine's paths, so their numbers cannot be regenerated from a fresh clone;
- the structural suggestion (§12): generate STATUS's git-state block by script, and add a CI job that fails when a cited path, commit or count does not resolve.

The report disagrees with itself on one number: §12 says "these 219 findings" while §13 says 326 survived [Certain]. It does not explain the difference.

Slice 19.5, "Honest Front Door", existed to process that register (`src/v2/SLICE_19_5_FOUNDING.md`). Every finding got exactly one **disposition**, a single label saying what will happen to it, chosen from eleven (§2.3): for example ALREADY-FIXED (cite the fixing commit), REFUTED, FIX-USER, FIX-TEST, FIX-CONTROL, DOC-ANNOTATE (an additive note, never an edit) or BACKLOG. DEC-19.5-2, as locked in §9.1 (lines 436-439), states the stance: "A disposition on a row marked audit only (unverified) is a hypothesis. The fixing dispatch verifies at HEAD first."

What it could not finish was routed forward (§9.2, §9.3): tests that can fail (Front E) to Slice 20; evidence that re-runs (Front D) to Slice 21; planetary axes (Front G) to Slice 22; control-plane items C5-C9, including the ci.yml header (C9) and the INVARIANTS index row (C5), to Slice 24; the STATUS generator and citation check (C12) to Slice 25. Two gaps show in that routing [Certain: §9.2 vs §6]. And three Front E items never reached Slice 20 (Section B12.8). ### B12.11 Records: STATUS, HANDOFF, DEVLOG, UPDATES and QA

A project keeps two kinds of written record. A **historical record** should be append-only, like a ship's logbook. A **current-state record** must be refreshed from commands, like the whiteboard showing the ship's position; an old whiteboard is worse than none.

| File | What it says it is | State at `cec19e7` |
|---|---|---|
| `STATUS.md` (584 lines) | "Updated at the end of each session … agents read this before acting." The one rewritable control file. | Stale (worked example below) |
| `HANDOFF.md` | A 2026-07-10 session handoff | Banner: "SUPERSEDED (2026-10-25). Historical record only; do not act on it." |
| `DEVLOG.md` | "Aster Physics Approximations — DEVLOG" | Newest entry Slice 12 (2026-07-02); no banner. Still says the V1 app's Moon is "accurate to ~1-2°" (line 65), which audit finding A5-F01 found false by about 93°. The correction note (Slice 19.5 C11) was not done in 19.5 and has no recorded destination (Section B12.10) |
| `UPDATES.md` | "Integration Update Log … per the orchestrator agent protocol" | V1 era; newest heading 2026-04-21; no banner |
| `QA.md` | "ASTER Phase 5 QA Report" | V1 era; no banner; tells readers to run `node --test tests/*.test.mjs` |

```
staleness = git rev-list --count <commit STATUS pins>..HEAD
house rule: "STATUS commits LAST in any sequence" (STATUS.md:39)
```

#### Worked example 12.5: how far behind main is STATUS.md?

*Inputs:* STATUS.md:36 pins `origin/main` at `fa821cb`; STATUS.md:42 lists the deploy bundles; AGENTS.md:57 says "confirm HEAD matches STATUS.md — if not, STOP and report"; actual `origin/main` = `cec19e7`.

Step 1. `git rev-list --count fa821cb..cec19e7` = **39** commits.

Step 2. `git rev-list --no-merges --count fa821cb..cec19e7` = 33. So 39 − 33 = **6** are merge commits: PRs #5 through #10. `--first-parent` also gives 6.

Step 3. Apply AGENTS.md:57. HEAD `cec19e7` ≠ `fa821cb`, so a session obeying the rule stops on session start.

Step 4. Bundle names. A **bundle** is a built JavaScript file whose name carries a content hash (Chapter B9). STATUS lists `compareV2-CGn7MKlJ.js`, `porkchopV2-4fKCXVgU.js` and `solarSystemV2-GybKye0-.js`. Those are the names in `docs/` at `33461b1` and `5ad9a9b`. At `adda2ab` and `cec19e7` the files are `compareV2-DpGmp5zP.js`, `porkchopV2-BuZQKmsX.js` and `solarSystemV2-C6dR6zLr.js` (also in `frontA-LOG.md`). Three of the four entry bundles differ; only `aboutV2-ca_cBGJA.js` matches.

Step 5. Cause: Front A refreshed STATUS's bundle line at 01:04 (`5ad9a9b`, W1-5) and rebuilt `docs/` at 09:56 (`adda2ab`, W5), in the same PR. The rebuild renamed the bundles after STATUS recorded them.

*Result:* STATUS is 39 commits (6 PR merges) behind main, and its deploy line names three files main no longer ships. This is the third measured instance of the same failure: 38 behind in the 2026-07-31 audit (L3-1), 36 behind at `69472a3` (A1-F01), 39 behind now. The file was not abandoned: four of those 39 commits edit it (`357fb3e`, `9c2c65e`, `ce4dece`, `5ad9a9b`), but the last two patched single lines and left the Git State pin alone [Certain: `git log fa821cb..cec19e7 -- STATUS.md`]. Partial refreshes are how a current-state record drifts.

STATUS has other stale lines [Certain]:
- line 40 calls `s19-5-record` "local-only and NOT merged", though it merged as PR #5;
- line 55 says coverage "ends 2026-10-16 TDB", while line 43 gives the rolled window 2026-11-01..2027-03-31;
- it has no Slice 20 row, although AGENTS.md:48 says "Active-slice founding doc is named in STATUS.md";
- line 582 lists the two `.githooks` mode changes (100644→100755) as a known-dirty local change that is "never staged", yet `0741fee` committed them; it also calls `.dispatch-scope` "never staged", although the file is tracked with Slice 18 content, so it was staged at least once.

AGENTS.md carries one stale fact of the same kind. Its repo map (line 34) calls `_rescued-agent-defs/` "local-only, untracked", yet `git ls-files` lists 6 tracked files there. STATUS.md:584 already notes this and explains it was left alone because AGENTS.md is protected [Certain].

The practical lesson: **before trusting STATUS.md, run `git log --oneline -1` and compare.** The audit's proposed cure, a STATUS block generated by script plus a citation check in CI, is scheduled for Slice 25.

### B12.12 Agent roles and the DEC-20-13 amendment

AGENTS.md:9-16 and §3-§7 define four roles.

| Role | Who | Does | Does not |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Codex** | code-executing agent | executes dispatches; builds, tests, commits by name; reports SHAs and gate results | push; `git add -A`; skip a gate; change a DEC without an "amends DEC-X" record |
| **Claude Code** | documentation and recon agent | reads STATUS and founding docs; writes docs; read-only recon | (before DEC-20-13) write TypeScript or run build/test |
| **Nova** | chat Claude | advises; writes dispatches; proposes amendments | execute commands; touch the repo; declare a DEC locked "without a measurement or oracle reference"; override a STOP gate |
| **Hudson** | owner | reviews; browser checks; pushes; rules DECs; may waive a STOP gate — "not delegable" | — |

This is **separation of duties**: whoever writes an instruction is not the one who executes it, and neither can publish. Architect, builder and inspector, with the owner holding the only key.

#### The amendment

Practice had drifted from the rule. The Slice 18 close-out run had §3 "overridden by Hudson's dispatch for this run only" (STATUS.md:328), and the S20_00 ephemeris roll was run by "Claude Code on Hudson's laptop" (`roll-REPORT.md`:9). DEC-20-13 records that S20_00 "was dispatched to Claude Code against §3 (Nova's error, caught by the executor)" and makes the rule match practice.

The Front A run wrote the paragraph but left AGENTS.md unstaged for Hudson ("PROTECTED PENDING: AGENTS.md", `frontA-REPORT.md`:5, 131). It was then committed as `9b792bb` (2026-11-04 10:09:58 −0500; numstat `2 0 AGENTS.md`), 8 min 24 s before the PR #10 merge at 10:18:22. Hudson presumably made that commit, as the protocol requires; git's author field cannot prove it (Section B12.2) [Likely]. It sits at AGENTS.md:175, directly before §4:

> §3 amendment (2026-11-04, Slice 20 DEC-20-13): Claude Code is the execution agent whenever Codex is unavailable. When it executes a dispatch it may build, run tests and edit TypeScript, under exactly the same rules as Codex (§2, §2.1, §4): the dispatch's write scope, explicit staging, no push, no merge, no overrides, no sessions. Any sentence above that says otherwise is superseded by this paragraph.

The old §3 sentences still stand above it, because the edit was additive. A reader must read to the end of §3. (This chapter's own writer is a Claude Code session acting in the documentation role, which is why no test or build was run.)

Four loose ends in the role model [Certain]:
- AGENTS.md:281 makes Hudson "the sole person who pushes to origin", yet AGENTS.md:165 says Claude Code may "Commit and push documentation changes when Hudson explicitly instructs it to". Front A's report lists that push sentence among those the DEC-20-13 paragraph supersedes (`frontA-REPORT.md`:121-125), but the paragraph itself speaks only of Claude Code "when it executes a dispatch", so the documentation-push case is left unclear.
- AGENTS.md:205 says Nova "does not execute code or touch the repo directly", but Slice 19.5 §9.3 records "Hook proof (Nova, 2026-10-28, Linux, fresh clone …)".
- **Clome** gates visual checks ("[V] visual (Hudson + Clome)") and may open primary sources under the two-run rule, but AGENTS.md never mentions it. STATUS.md describes "Clome runs" on the live site whose "automation tab runs `document.hidden = true`" (STATUS.md:105, 129), so it appears to be a browser-automation agent [Likely].
- Git cannot show which agent did what. All non-merge commits carry author Hudson Clavin (the merges are authored `hudsonclavin-cloud` and committed by GitHub), and none of PR #10's 19 commits has a co-author trailer, so whether Front A was run by Codex or Claude Code is not recorded in git or in the run report.

#### Worked example 12.6: recomputing the symmetric-return error range

Sample-return mode charges the return departure burn as equal to the outbound arrival v∞ (the "symmetric" assumption). Front A's W1-4 disclosure states how wrong that is, using a committed data file rather than a number typed into app code.

*Inputs:* the six rows of `src/v2/data/symmetric-return-error.json` (status "exploratory, unvalidated"). Each gives the assumed v∞ and the computed asteroid-departure v∞ for M = 0 and M = 1, in km/s. The display rule in `tools/slice20-research/derive-symmetric-error.mjs`: two decimals below 1 km/s, one decimal at or above.

Step 1. For each of the 12 (row, M) pairs, error = assumed − computed:

| Body, window | M = 0 | M = 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 433, min-C3 | 6.905 − 3.034 = +3.871 | 6.905 − 1.795 = +5.110 |
| 433, best stack | 1.146 − 2.254 = −1.108 | 1.146 − 1.223 = −0.077 |
| 99942, min-C3 | 5.841 − 1.092 = +4.749 | 5.841 − 1.102 = +4.739 |
| 99942, best stack | 0.103 − 1.972 = −1.869 | 0.103 − 1.565 = −1.462 |
| 2000 SG344, min-C3 | 1.389 − 0.148 = +1.241 | 1.389 − 0.131 = +1.258 |
| 2000 SG344, best stack | 0.0640 − 0.2244 = −0.1604 | 0.0640 − 0.3084 = −0.2444 |

Step 2. Smallest |error| = 0.077 (433, best stack, M = 1). Largest |error| = 5.110 (433, min-C3, M = 1).

Step 3. Round by the display rule: 0.077 < 1, so two decimals: **0.08**. 5.110 ≥ 1, so one decimal: **5.1**.

Step 4. Signs: all six min-C3 errors are positive (the assumption overcharges) and all six best-stack errors are negative (it undercharges).

*Result:* 0.08-5.1 km/s, sign-changing, identical to the file's committed `derived` block `{minAbsErrorKmS: 0.08, maxAbsErrorKmS: 5.1}` [Certain: recomputed for this guide]. `tests/v2-symmetric-return.test.mjs` re-runs the derivation script and also fails if "0.08-5.1", "0.08 km/s" or "5.1 km/s" appears in any `.ts` file under `src/v2/app/` (regex at line 24). So a hand-typed copy of the range in those usual spellings turns the test red. Other spellings would slip past the pattern: an en dash with no unit after it ("0.08–5.1"), no space before the unit ("5.1km/s"), or an extra digit ("5.10 km/s") [Certain: the regex tested on those strings with Node]. A guard of this kind narrows the risk; it does not remove it.

#### Worked example 12.7: checking the slice's own size estimate

*Inputs:* Slice 20 §8, lines 326-334: "about 40–48 h" [Speculative, ±30%], with Front A ~12-14 h, B ~12-16, C ~3-4, D ~5-6, E ~3-4, F ~5, and "At 8 h/week that is 5–6 weeks".

Step 1. Lower bound: 12 + 12 + 3 + 5 + 3 + 5 = **40 h**. Upper bound: 14 + 16 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 5 = **49 h**, not 48.

Step 2. At 8 h/week: 40 / 8 = 5.0 weeks; 49 / 8 = 6.125 weeks. The ±30% band on 40-49 h is 28.0-63.7 h, or 3.5-8.0 weeks.

Step 3. The non-cuttable Fronts A-D alone: lower 12 + 12 + 3 + 5 = 32 h, upper 14 + 16 + 4 + 6 = 40 h, so 32 / 8 = 4 to 40 / 8 = 5 weeks. (Front D's 5-6 h includes its cuttable polish, so this slightly overstates the true floor.)

*Result:* the fronts sum to 40-49 h, a 1-hour slip in the locked text, which can now only be annotated. "5–6 weeks" still holds to the nearest week (6.125 rounds to 6). For scale only [Speculative]: Front A's commits span 9 h 00 min (`b4d1bce` 00:55:56 to `adda2ab` 09:56:12) against its 12-14 h estimate, but a commit span is not effort.

### B12.14 The Aster family and the Lens strategy (overview)

`strategy/ASTER_FAMILY_MASTER_PLAN.md` opens with "STRATEGY DOCUMENT (leads-grade; nothing here locks a DEC)". Treat everything in it as a plan, not a fact about the product.

The idea is one shared **substrate** (the common core every product is built on) with several products, each called a **Lens** because it answers one operational question. One camera body, many interchangeable lenses. The four substrate parts (§2):
- **S1 Evidence Core:** evidence envelopes and the badge design system (Chapter B10);
- **S2 Data Spine:** the 41,906-body catalog and the ephemeris core (Chapters B2-B4);
- **S3 Agent Interface:** the MCP server (Chapter B10);
- **S4 Validation identity:** audits, dual oracles, golden-numbers CI, pre-registered evaluations. "This process IS the brand."

So the governance machinery in this chapter is meant to be the selling point. The family map (§3) uses maturity states:

| State | Lenses |
|---|---|
| SHIPPED | L1 Aster Transit, "this is Aster today" |
| SHIPPED-IN-CORE | L2 Prospect (productization chartered) |

The master plan says "Every non-shipped lens has an entry gate and kill criteria in `ASTER_FAMILY_CHARTERS.md`" (§3). That file has only four entries (Ledger, Survey, Traffic and an "Aster Bench" extension), and every one still reads "CHARTER PENDING" [Certain]. A lens earns its own repository at FOUNDED only "if and only if it has its own deploy target and does not import `src/v2/core` directly" (master plan, line 87). The plan guesses that three or more credible products by mid-2027 have probability about 0.5-0.6 if built in gated waves, against about 0.05 in parallel; these are guesses, not measurements [Speculative]. ### Key takeaways

- A git commit id is a fingerprint of content. Every Aster number that cites a commit inherits git's guarantees, and git's blind spots: it does not know which agent typed a change.
- Since 2026-10-28 every change reaches `main` through a GitHub PR, and because Pages serves `docs/` from `main`, a merge is a deploy.
- A slice runs recon → verification → DRAFT → Hudson's lock → fronts → audit → deploy. Founding docs are additive-only, so the dated lines at the bottom govern.
- DEC, OQ, INV and AMD numbers are permanent addresses. Changes are appended as amendments, never edited in.
- Verify-before-lock, tripwires and STOP gates decide in advance what counts as proof and when to stop. Front A's first attempt shows a correct stop.
- The pre-commit hook enforces a per-dispatch scope, protected paths and additive-only founding docs by counting deletions with `--numstat`. It works only where `core.hooksPath` is set and the files are executable, which is not the case in this checkout.
- `npm run verify` is the real test gate (109 files); `npm test` reaches 86. CI runs four jobs on Node 24, never deploys, and does not cover MCP or Slice 16.
- The audits found sound V2 math and a drifting record. STATUS.md is drifting again (39 commits behind), so always compare it with `git log` first.
- DEC-20-13 lets Claude Code execute dispatches when Codex is unavailable, under Codex's rules. Slice 20 has finished Front A and all of Phase 0 except merging PR #1; Front B (the K1 return-leg math) is next.
